articles.title: Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH 32-inch 4K OLED gaming monitor review: Color, performance and style
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH is one of the best HDR OLEDs I’ve reviewed. It delivers a stunning image with no need for calibration and addictive gaming that will keep you playing for hours.
Reasons to buy
- + Bright and colorful image
- + Exceptional HDR quality
- + Dynamic tone mapping for HDR10 content
- + Matte anti-glare screen is very effective
- + Accurate out of the box
- + Excellent game performance
- + Plenty of inputs and USB ports
- + Unique yet understated styling
- + Solid build quality
- + Good value
Reasons to avoid
- - No internal speakers
- - No variable brightness for SDR
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
If you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck. But 4K at 240 Hz is creeping downward in price and only represents a small upcharge. It also means that you can go to 32 inches and maintain good pixel density. If you have enough video card horsepower to push frame rates over 180fps, the quality is unmatched.
Samsung slides into the neither-expensive-nor-inexpensive position with its Odyssey G8 G80SH. This 32-inch Quantum Dot OLED runs 240 Hz at 4K resolution with Adaptive-Sync, HDR10, HDR10+, wide gamut color, factory calibration, and high brightness for HDR content. Let’s take a look.
Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH Specs
| Panel Type / Backlight | Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode | 
| Screen Size / Aspect Ratio | 32 inches / 16:9 | 
| Max Resolution and Refresh Rate | 3840x2160 @ 240 Hz | 
| Row 3 - Cell 0 | FreeSync and G-Sync Compatible | 
| Native Color Depth and Gamut | 10-bit / DCI-P3+ | 
| Row 5 - Cell 0 | HDR10, HDR10+ | 
| Row 6 - Cell 0 | VESA DisplayHDR True Black 500 | 
| Response Time (GTG) | 0.03ms | 
| Brightness (mfr) | 300 nits full field | 
| Row 9 - Cell 0 | 1,000 nits 3% window | 
| Contrast | Unmeasurable | 
| Speakers | None | 
| Video Inputs | 1x DisplayPort 2.1 | 
| Row 13 - Cell 0 | 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x USB-C | 
| Audio | 3.5mm headphone output | 
| USB 3.2 | 2x down | 
| Power Consumption | 48.8w, brightness @ 200 nits | 
| Panel Dimensions WxHxD w/base | 28.3 x 18.5-23.2 x 10.4 inches (719 x 470-589 x 264mm) | 
| Panel Thickness | 1.9 inches (48mm) | 
| Bezel Width | Top/sides: 0.3 inch (7mm) | 
| Row 20 - Cell 0 | Sides: 0.4 inch (11mm) | 
| Row 21 - Cell 0 | Bottom: 0.6 inch (15mm) | 
| Weight | 17.2 pounds (7.8kg) | 
| Warranty | 3 years | 
First, I want to clear up any potential confusion with another recently reviewed Samsung display, the G80HS. That is a 6K resolution dual-refresh mode model that currently costs around $1,600. The G80SH I’m covering here is a 4K screen with a single 240 Hz mode, and it’s currently selling for $900.
The G80SH delivers the best of everything in the premium OLED category. It’s 4K with a Quantum Dot layer that delivers a measured 106% coverage of DCI-P3. That’s about average among the QD-OLEDs I’ve tested, which range from 104 to 108%. The visual difference there is extremely small, not enough to affect a purchase decision. The G80SH also offers excellent out-of-the-box accuracy courtesy of a factory calibration. Though my sample didn’t need any tweaking, it benefited from a few adjustments. And that capability extends to HDR content, where you have full control of color temp, brightness, and luminance tracking.
Speaking of HDR, you get the requisite HDR10 support that all monitors have, plus Samsung’s answer to Dolby Vision, HDR10+. This extension of HDR10 includes dynamic tone mapping where the content matches its luminance curve to whatever display it’s shown on. Since HDR is mastered to a specific peak luminance, usually 1,000 nits but sometimes as high as 10,000, it’s beneficial when the screen can adapt to the incoming metadata to accommodate a lower or higher limit. You’ll see the same fine detail and nuance that the content creator did.
Gaming benefits from the aforementioned 240 Hz refresh rate plus a flawless implementation of Adaptive-Sync. The G80SH works with equal precision on G-Sync and FreeSync platforms, as well as the VRR output from gaming consoles. To help with your aim, there are reticles available in different colors and shapes, with a dynamic mode that keeps them in contrast with the background.
Like every Samsung monitor I’ve experienced, the G80SH delivers high style and solid build quality. The main color is silver, which you can see everywhere except the front, keeping the screen and surrounding bezel all black. There’s a matte anti-glare coating too, effectively eliminating all ambient light reflections. If you have a sunny room, this monitor can handle it without a degradation in image quality. You also get the latest video interfaces, four in total, plus USB and a headphone jack. LED lighting is featured on the back and can be controlled from the OSD.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
So, just to recap before we jump into the tests, this is the Odyssey G8 G80SH, a 4K 240 Hz OLED that sells for $900. If you’re interested in learning more about the 6K model, my review from a few months ago is here.
Assembly and Accessories
Samsung still uses crumbly foam to ship its monitors, and my G80SH sample arrived safe and sound. The base, upright, and stand assemble with a captive bolt and a snap-on to create a solid package. To keep the panel thin, the power supply is external. It’s quite large, so consider that when fitting it into your space. The accessory bundle includes right-angle power cables plus one each of DisplayPort, HDMI, and USB-C.
Product 360
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The G80SH’s silver trim is visible from the front in the base and a thin border around the screen that wraps around from the back. The actual bezel is very narrow and flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off. A small protrusion in the bottom center says Samsung in tiny letters and houses an equally tiny power LED that can’t be seen from the front. Samsung is one of the few manufacturers to offer matte-screened OLEDs, and this implementation is excellent. Even a bright flashlight can’t throw a reflection onto the screen. Sunny office dwellers, this is your monitor.
In the back, it’s all silver all the time with a smooth finish and minimalist styling. There’s a thin ventilation grill on top, a small logo on one side, and hooray, inputs that face backward. You get two HDMI 2.1, a DisplayPort 2.1, USB-C with 98 watts, and two USB-A downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack. On one side of the I/O panel is a joystick, the G80SH’s sole control key. Around the stand’s attachment point is an LED ring with colors and effects available in the OSD. If you remove the stand, a 100mm VESA mount is revealed should you prefer an aftermarket solution. Fasteners are not included.
That large external power supply keeps the panel thin at just under two inches. The stand is solid and wobble-free and offers 2/25 degrees tilt, 30 degrees swivel, a 90-degree portrait mode and a 4.7-inch height range. Movements are firm and smooth, in keeping with the G80SH’s premium status.
OSD Features
The G80SH’s OSD keeps Samsung’s traditional gaming monitor styling with its control panel appearance. Up top are portholes that deliver information about game-related settings. No refresh rate info, though. It would be nice to have that.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
In the Game menu, you get an Adaptive-Sync toggle, aiming points, a black equalizer to enhance shadow detail, and the LED lighting control. The reticles come in two shapes and three colors. Or you can use AI Mode, which changes the color to maintain contrast with the background. You can also position the aiming point somewhere other than the center of the screen. The lighting has multiple effects or can remain a single static color. One miss here is a frame counter. There’s no way to monitor the refresh rate.
In the Picture menu are all the G80SH’s calibration controls. You get five color temps, all adjustable, and seven gamma presets. The Contrast Enhancer is a field dimming control. True variable brightness is only active in HDR mode. You can choose between static and active tone mapping for HDR, which is handy for HDR10 content because it helps bring out highlights without clipping fine shadow detail.
You won’t find an sRGB mode among the color space choices, but if you pick Auto, the G80SH will render sRGB for SDR content. This is an approach that I like, and almost no other manufacturers do it that way. If you’d rather see the full gamut for all content, just leave it on Native. Peak Brightness does just what it says for HDR content; it raises the peak output. In my HDR tests, I saw 530 nits from a 25% window pattern.
Remaining menu items include port version control, an off timer, DSC toggle, and USB-C control. You also get two panel care options: logo brightness (dimming, actually) and pixel refresh. You can pause the incoming video signal while this is running if you wish.
Samsung Odyssey G8 G80SH Calibration Settings
The G80SH includes a factory calibration with a report saved in the monitor’s firmware. I found visually perfect color and grayscale tracking, but gamma was a little light. Two clicks of the gamma slider made that much better. I noted that though the default picture mode is called Eco, it is just as bright as the other presets, so that you can use it for all content. In HDR mode, you get Display HDR, which has excellent tone mapping and color accuracy. Suppose you want sRGB; just set Color Space to Auto. Then the G80SH will automatically render sRGB for SDR and the full gamut for HDR, which covers 106% of DCI-P3. If you want full color for SDR, set it to Native. My recommended settings are below.
| Picture Mode | Eco | 
| Brightness 200 nits | 27 | 
| Brightness 120 nits | 9 | 
| Brightness 100 nits | 5 | 
| Brightness 80 nits | 1 (min. 78 nits) | 
| Contrast | 50 | 
| Color Space | Auto | 
| Gamma | -2 | 
| Color Temp Warm 1 | Red -4, Green -3, Blue 2 | 
Gaming and Hands-on
The G80SH’s color quality and accuracy make it well suited for duty as a post-production monitor or perhaps an on-site display for location shoots. Only a slight gamma anomaly separates it from perfection. It nails grayscale and gamut tracking, which you can read about on pages four and five. And it’s bright enough for any indoor space. I noted that there was no variable brightness option for SDR, but you can turn on a dynamic contrast option, which equates to field dimming. In HDR mode, dimming occurs at the pixel level, and you can choose between Active and Static tone mapping. The former delivers more punch to HDR10 content.
I also noted the G80SH’s excellent color balance. SDR lets you choose between Native and Auto. Native shows the full gamut, which covers 106% of DCI-P3 and is very colorful. It will be the likely choice for most users. If you prefer sRGB for SDR, set the color space to Auto. Then, it will switch automatically. This is something very few monitors offer. I also noted that the HDR mode allows calibration of grayscale and gamma, another thing I rarely see.
With the image dialed in, I turned to a few afternoons of gaming where the G80SH provided the addictive quality that all premium OLEDs have. It doesn’t have a frame counter, so I had to use FRAPS to monitor the refresh rate, which stayed around 200fps at the max detail settings in Doom Eternal. This was fast enough to provide blur-free motion and input lag low enough to keep up with my most frenetic movements. You’ll see on the next page that it offers response typical of other 4K 240 Hz OLEDs. That means you’ll be able to aim and shoot with speed and precision. I got extra credit in hoard mode for jump shots where I was able to land grenades on target while flying through the air. Turn and shoot became second nature as I mowed through my opponents.
Detail in close encounters made me stop and admire the picture more than a few times. Tiny highlights like sweat and other bodily fluids popped right out, making the characters look three-dimensional. Other textures like stone and metal looked better thanks to strong reflections. These highlights moved smoothly over objects like the player’s weapon, which further enhanced realism. The G80SH has some of the best-looking HDR I’ve seen of late.
It makes a great workday monitor too, with understated styling that stands out but doesn’t scream for attention. The LED lighting is just a ring in the back with smoothly playing effects or static colors available, or you can shut it off. The stand is rock solid with comfortable and usable ergonomics. The joystick navigates the OSD intuitively and efficiently. I really appreciated the rear-facing ports, which were easy to see and access. You get two USB-A downstream ports, which can accommodate peripherals once you make a connection to the USB-C input, which doubles as a charger with 98 watts of power. There are no internal speakers, but headphones plug into the 3.5mm jack.
Takeaway: If Samsung keeps the G80SH’s price below $1,000, it will sell a lot of them. It’s a super versatile display for any form of productivity or entertainment. It’s addictive for gaming, with smooth operation and quick response. The image looks stunning in every respect, whether moving or static. Color accuracy is good enough that calibration isn’t required. It has unique but understated styling and excellent ergonomics with a solid stand and rear-facing ports. Aside from a lack of internal speakers, there is nothing missing here.

Christian Eberle is a Contributing Editor for Tom's Hardware US. He's a veteran reviewer of A/V equipment, specializing in monitors. Christian began his obsession with tech when he built his first PC in 1991, a 286 running DOS 3.0 at a blazing 12MHz. In 2006, he undertook training from the Imaging Science Foundation in video calibration and testing and thus started a passion for precise imaging that persists to this day. He is also a professional musician with a degree from the New England Conservatory as a classical bassoonist which he used to good effect as a performer with the West Point Army Band from 1987 to 2013. He enjoys watching movies and listening to high-end audio in his custom-built home theater and can be seen riding trails near his home on a race-ready ICE VTX recumbent trike. Christian enjoys the endless summer in Florida where he lives with his wife and Chihuahua and plays with orchestras around the state.

I’m going to let you in on a secret: despite having access to some amazing gaming laptops, I rarely use them when I want to play a game.
At heart, I’m a desktop PC guy. I love building my own PC, and the customization options and upgradability make them my favorite way to play. Not to mention, desktop components can be much more powerful than mobile variants.
Gaming laptops always felt to me like a cut-down compromise, as you sacrificed all of that for a device that’s more portable, but because you’ll still need to play your games with the laptop plugged in (graphically demanding games will deplete your battery quickly), and most likely on a desk so you can use a gaming mouse.
Of course, gaming laptops do have their uses, and I can completely understand why someone would rather have one of those instead of a gaming desktop PC. They’re more convenient and easier to set up, can be taken with you when travelling, and don’t occupy as much space as a traditional gaming rig.
But as a desktop-first gamer, I’ve been increasingly drawn to handheld gaming PCs, starting with the Steam Deck and my beloved ROG Ally X, and I’ve been increasingly enamored with the latest generation of handhelds such as the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ and the Acer Predator Atlas 8, which I’m currently reviewing.
“Matt! You hypocrite!” I can sense some of you thinking. Those gaming handhelds suffer from all the compromises I just reeled off when attacking gaming laptops. You can’t upgrade them, they aren’t as customizable, and less powerful than desktops. But with gaming handhelds, those compromises simply don’t matter as much to me, and it’s for one very simple reason: the form factor.
With traditional gaming laptops, I still play on them as I would with a desktop PC, which doesn’t just highlight the shortcomings of a gaming laptop compared to my powerful gaming PC, but it also limits where and when I play on it.
Handheld gaming PCs, however, have completely different designs. As their name suggests, they are designed to be held in your hand, with built-in gamepad controls and relatively small touchscreens.
This instantly makes them more convenient for playing while travelling, as they are smaller and lighter than gaming laptops, and you don’t need a surface to place them on. The smaller screens also mean some of the graphical settings you need to turn down aren’t as noticeable.
Handhelds also force me to play different games due to the built-in controller. For genres where mouse and keyboard are best, such as management sims, real-time strategy, and first-person shooters, I leave that to my gaming PC.
On a handheld, I stick to indie games, platformers, third-person RPGs, arcade games, and other genres I’ve often neglected. It lets me do some deep dives into my Steam, GOG, and Epic Games Store backlogs and mix up my playstyle.
Of course, if you have no interest in those latter genres, a gaming laptop will be a better buy.
What about performance?
If you care about pure performance, as many PC gamers understandably do, then a gaming laptop with a dedicated graphics card is going to easily outperform a handheld, as its smaller size forces it to rely on less powerful integrated graphics.
However, mobile components have come a long way these past few years, and recent handhelds powered by the Intel Arc G3 Extreme are seriously impressive, allowing handhelds to run graphically intensive games such as Cyberpunk 2077 at 60fps and over, with a bit of tweaking.
While you do need to lower some settings to keep frame rates playable, as I mentioned earlier, the smaller screens of handhelds are more forgiving if you drop certain settings and even resolutions to help smooth out performance.
Sticking to older games, or less graphically demanding indie titles, is another good way to get the most out of a gaming handheld. For example, I’m trying to take my mind off the fact that it seems everyone else in the world is enjoying GTA 6 by playing GTA Vice City The Definitive Edition on the Acer Predator Atlas 8, and while I know deep down it’s not going to compete with the latest game from Rockstar, it’s still a bit of a thrill playing an open-world game I first explored on the PlayStation 2 on a device I’m holding in my hands.
What’s the cost?
This is where things get a bit tricky, and why Black Friday deals could really help. Back when the Steam Deck, arguably the first of this modern breed of handheld gaming PCs, launched in 2022 beginning at $399 / £349 (it launched later in Australia), it was a no-brainer for a lot of people.
You simply couldn’t get a gaming laptop for around that price (unless it was very old or underpowered), and even to people with a bit more cash to spend, I was suggesting they consider the Steam Deck over slightly more expensive gaming laptops.
The current situation in 2026 is very different, sadly. The global memory shortage, sometimes called the ‘RAMpocalypse’ has seen prices for all kinds of devices, including both handhelds and gaming laptops, rise steeply.
Back in May, Valve raised the price of its Steam Deck OLED handheld by 50%, so it now starts at $789 / £649 / AU$1,199. Considering that apart from a nicer screen and more storage space to start, this handheld is still running on the same hardware as four years ago, I simply can’t recommend it anymore.
More recent handhelds have launched at wince-inducingly high prices, such as the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, which began at $1,799.99 / £1,399.99 / AU$2,849.
When handhelds start costing as much as upper-midrange gaming laptops, they become a lot harder to justify. Unfortunately for us gamers, gaming laptops have also gone up in price as well.
Still, for around that same price, you could get something like the Acer Nitro V16 from Amazon, which comes with 32GB RAM, an AMD Ryzen 7 processor, and an Nvidia RTX 5070 GPU. This will absolutely destroy the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ when it comes to performance, so it then boils down to the form factor, as you’re paying a premium for the smaller, more portable build of the Claw 8 EX AI+ compared to the Nitro V16, which, as a 16-inch gaming laptop that weighs 4.85lbs (2.2kg), won’t be the most comfortable device to lug around with you.
This is why this year’s Black Friday sales (many of which have already started) could be a real game changer. Not only am I expecting plenty of tempting gaming laptop Black Friday deals, but there should be some great handheld gaming PC deals as well.
Just this weekend, the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ dropped by £300 in the UK for a limited time, and while that deal has ended, I expect similar deals to crop up this week in the run-up to Black Friday itself on Friday 27. That £300 discount suddenly made the Claw 8 much better value, especially when compared to gaming laptops around that same price.
That’s given me hope that Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals this year could make PC gaming great again, by giving us at least a small break in the price rise misery.

articles.title: Jordanian fintech invoiceQ raises $5 million in oversubscribed Series A
articles.text:
Jordanian fintech invoiceQ raises $5 million in oversubscribed Series A
- Jordan-based e-invoicing and tax compliance startup invoiceQ has raised $5 million in an oversubscribed Series A round, led by Manara Ventures and Next Ventures, with participation from Orange Ventures, the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund (ISSF), and the Jordan Small and Medium Enterprises Fund (SME Fund Jo).
- Founded in 2020 by Mohannad Tobal, Mohammad Bassit, Fadi Al Jabali and Amer Ayyad, invoiceQ provides a SaaS platform that enables businesses to automate, manage, exchange and archive tax-compliant electronic invoices, integrating with existing ERP, POS, accounting, e-commerce, banking and payment systems.
- Headquartered in Amman, Jordan, invoiceQ serves more than 1,400 businesses and operates across Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, Qatar, Egypt, Bahrain and Morocco, in addition to its home market. The company holds regulatory qualifications and accreditations in several markets, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Oman.
- The funding will support invoiceQ's next phase of growth as it expands its regional presence and develops its e-invoicing and tax compliance services. The investment also marks SME Fund Jo's second investment in the company.
Press release:
invoiceQ, Inc., a regional e-invoicing and tax compliance technology company, has closed a Series A round that raised $5 million, exceeding the target. The round was led by Manara Ventures and Next Ventures, with participation from Orange Ventures, the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund (ISSF), and the Jordan Small and Medium Enterprises Fund (SME Fund Jo).
Founded by Mohannad Tobal, Mohammad Bassit, Fadi Al Jabali, and Amer Ayyad, invoiceQ provides a SaaS-based e-invoicing and compliance platform that enables businesses to automate, manage, exchange, and archive tax-compliant invoices through a centralized solution.
From its Jordanian base, invoiceQ has expanded across the region, with operations spanning Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, Qatar, Egypt, Bahrain, and Morocco. Today, invoiceQ helps businesses navigate evolving e-invoicing regulations and maintain compliance across multiple markets. Through seamless integration with ERP, POS, accounting, e-commerce, banking, and payment systems, the platform enables organizations to streamline their invoicing operations and meet regulatory requirements without disrupting or replacing their existing infrastructure.
Commenting on this investment, Mohammad Al-Muhtaseb, CEO of the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund (ISSF), said: "invoiceQ's successful closing of its Series A funding round is not only an achievement for the company itself, but also a milestone that reflects the maturity and excellence of Jordan's entrepreneurial ecosystem, and a new success story added to the track record of the business environment in the Kingdom.
This achievement underscores the growing confidence in the ability of Jordanian startups to attract quality capital and lead digital transformation. It also proves that funding and venture capital are available to support ambitious companies that possess successful business models and innovative solutions scalable regionally and globally.At the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund, we are proud to support invoiceQ's journey, which strengthens Jordan's standing as a regional hub for innovation and technology and opens broader horizons for Jordanian entrepreneurs to turn their ideas into regional and global success stories.
Al-Muhtaseb also noted that invoiceQ's early-stage journey was supported by funds within the ISSF portfolio, such as Oasis500, Flat6Labs, and Propeller, in addition to Ahli Fintech. This highlights the pivotal role of the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund and the importance of its strategic work in providing venture capital across various stages within Jordan's investment environment, empowering startups to grow and access markets."
Commenting on the investment, Manara Ventures said: “E-invoicing mandates are transforming how businesses operate across the region, and what stood out to us about invoiceQ is that the company is not simply responding to this shift but actively helping shape it. Seeing a Jordanian team at the forefront of building the region’s compliance infrastructure is a testament to the depth of talent and innovation coming out of Jordan. We are proud to lead this round and support invoiceQ in its next phase of growth.”
Next Ventures added: “Next Ventures invests in founders who position ahead of regulatory change. invoiceQ identified the e-invoicing opportunity early, secured the key regulatory approvals and built a strong customer base. With an exceptional management team and a scalable platform, invoiceQ is well placed to become the regional standard in e-invoicing SaaS, and we are excited to be part of what they achieve next.”
Orange Ventures commented, "invoiceQ addresses a tangible business need through its e-invoicing and compliance solutions. We are pleased to support its development and regional expansion.”
SME Fund Jo added, "The presence of promising Jordanian companies like invoiceQ, with clear visions, successful business models, and innovative, scalable solutions, reflects the strength of Jordan’s entrepreneurial ecosystem and reinforces investor confidence in the ability of local companies to compete regionally and globally.
invoiceQ’s consistent growth, expansion into new markets, and continuous innovation demonstrate the potential of Jordanian businesses to attract investment and achieve sustainable success.
These achievements motivated us to invest in invoiceQ for the second time, reaffirming our confidence in its vision and future potential. We believe that supporting successful Jordanian companies encourages continued investment and strengthens Jordan’s position as a regional hub for innovation and technology.”
invoiceQ currently serves more than 1,400 businesses across the region and has established a strong regulatory and technical footprint. The company is qualified by Saudi Arabia’s Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA), compliant with Jordan’s Income and Sales Tax Department (ISTD) regulations, accredited as an Approved Service Provider (ASP) by the UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) and Oman Tax Authority (OTA), and is a Peppol-certified Access Point (AP) and Service Metadata Publisher (SMP) provider.
The successful close of this Series A round marks a significant milestone in invoiceQ’s growth trajectory and further positions the company within the region’s expanding digital compliance and financial technology ecosystem.
invoiceQ would like to thank its partners and supporters, including Kassim Legal, which acted as legal counsel to invoiceQ.

articles.title: Une arnaque vise les stations-service et les distributeurs de billets en France : comment éviter de se faire piéger ?
articles.text:
Nous avons ici affaire à une arnaque sophistiquée qui cible plus particulièrement les stations-service et les distributeurs de billets. Plusieurs victimes ont été recensées en France ces derniers jours, avec des montants dérobés allant de 500 à plus de 1 000 euros. Il faut dire que cette arnaque est difficilement repérable. Une victime peut effectuer un paiement ou retirer de l’argent en saisissant son code PIN, sans rien remarquer. Cependant, un point précis peut alerter sur la situation.
Une minuscule caméra et un lecteur de carte piégé pour vider vos comptes bancaires
Une nouvelle arnaque, particulièrement élaborée, a été repérée à plusieurs reprises ces derniers jours en France. Cette arnaque vise plus particulièrement les stations-service et les distributeurs de billets. En d’autres termes, tous les dispositifs qui demandent d’insérer une carte bancaire et de saisir un code PIN. Le mode de fonctionnement de cette arnaque est, il faut le dire, sophistiqué. Comme l’explique BFMTV, les arnaqueurs parviennent à intégrer un dispositif dans le lecteur de carte d’un système de paiement. Ce dispositif est ensuite capable d’intercepter les données échangées avec la puce de la carte bancaire. Il est ici plus précisément question de skimming, une technique qui consiste à insérer un boîtier très fin dans le lecteur afin de récupérer les données de la carte.
En parallèle, les arnaqueurs placent une minuscule caméra juste au-dessus du pavé numérique destiné à saisir le code bancaire. Ainsi, les escrocs disposent finalement des données de la carte bancaire, mais aussi du code confidentiel de leur victime. Selon les témoignages publiés en ligne par certaines victimes, les montants dérobés vont de 500 à plus de 1 000 euros.
Comment ne pas tomber dans le piège de cette arnaque
Autant dire que ce type d’arnaque bancaire n’est pas facilement repérable. Cependant, un point précis peut alerter sur la situation. En effet, le dispositif utilisé par les arnaqueurs demande à la victime de recomposer son code PIN. Par conséquent, si un système de paiement vous demande de composer une seconde fois votre code bancaire, il est vivement conseillé de changer de borne ou de faire preuve de la plus grande prudence, en mettant un terme à la transaction et en appelant par exemple un membre du personnel.
Veillez également à masquer le pavé numérique avec votre autre main lorsque vous saisissez votre code PIN. Pour rappel, les escrocs peuvent dissimuler une minuscule caméra juste au-dessus de celui-ci afin de filmer la saisie de votre code confidentiel. Faites également attention au terminal de paiement. Les arnaqueurs ayant placé d’autres appareils pour enregistrer les données bancaires des victimes, des anomalies peuvent être présentes (éléments inhabituels ou mal fixés).
Enfin, privilégiez le paiement sans contact et surveillez de près vos comptes bancaires. En cas de transaction anormale, contactez votre banque sans attendre.

articles.title: AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates
articles.text:
AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates
Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.
Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a new family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.
AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.
After introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.
More decisive agents
With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.
The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.
So far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the company’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.
They also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS said, the new decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.
The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.
Security without sacrifice
Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.
In a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”
Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.
AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s update, it’s getting a new Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.
The idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something important.
Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.
The agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.
AWS said developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.
Like the new decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being launched today. It’s a big step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

articles.title: iPhone 18e também pode ser lançado antes da versão base
articles.text:
iPhone 18e também pode ser lançado antes da versão base
Apple pode separar modelos mais acessíveis e ter três lançamentos de smartphones no ano.
Neste ano vimos, pela primeira vez, a Apple separar o lançamento dos iPhones base das versões Pro, em evento marcado também pela estreia do iPhone Duo. Agora, rumores apontam que até mesmo o iPhone 18e deve chegar às lojas antes dos demais modelos da linha.
A empresa estaria planejando o anúncio de produtos mais “acessíveis” no começo do ano que vem, numa janela entre fevereiro e março, enquanto o iPhone 18 chegaria em uma segunda leva, ainda que também no primeiro semestre.
A previsão, compartilhada pelo jornalista Mark Gurman, da Bloomberg, encontra eco em vazamentos recentes que indicam que o novo CEO da companhia, John Ternus, pretende quebrar a tradição de um evento gigante em setembro para todos os principais modelos da marca.
Caso o calendário se confirme, o iPhone 18 será o último da linha a estrear: os iPhone 18 Pro e 18 Pro Max, além do primeiro iPhone dobrável da Apple, foram apresentados ainda em setembro de 2026.
Segundo o rumor, a ideia é concentrar os primeiros meses do ano em produtos mais acessíveis. Entre fevereiro e março, a principal novidade seria o iPhone 18e, além de um novo iPad de entrada e a segunda versão do MacBook Neo.
O iPhone 18 tradicional deve aparecer pouco depois, provavelmente em um evento separado. Na mesma janela, deve chegar o MacBook Air, o iPhone Air 2, iPad Air com tela OLED, novos iPad Pro e novo MacBook Air.
O iPhone 18e pode aparecer com o chip A20 e 9 GB de RAM, contra os 8 GB da geração anterior, e trazer melhorias na câmera. As especificações de hardware esperadas para o iPhone 18 são semelhantes, assim como um possível aumento de US$ 100 a US$ 200 no preço nos Estados Unidos.
No iPad a atualização deve ser mais significativa. O modelo atual ainda usa o chip A16 e é o último dispositivo da Apple sem suporte ao Apple Intelligence. A próxima geração deve migrar para o A19, acompanhado por 8 GB de RAM e outras melhorias em conectividade, como suporte ao Wi-Fi 7.
A Apple também prepara dois Macs para o período: um novo MacBook Neo com chip A19 Pro, da geração do iPhone 17 Pro, e um MacBook Air com o chip M7, segundo o GSMArena. O notebook deve estrear a nova geração de processadores da companhia, esperada para o ano que vem, após um lançamento limitado no M6.
Entre os tablets, o primeiro semestre ainda deve trazer um iPad Air com tela OLED e novos iPad Pro. Estes últimos são esperados com o chip M6, sucedendo os modelos com M5 lançados em 2025.
Outro aparelho previsto para algum desses lançamento é o ultrafino iPhone Air 2, que tem a dura missão de corrigir, frente ao público, a péssima bateria do primeiro. O dispositivo também pode receber uma câmera extra ultrawide para complementar o conjunto, que conta com uma principal de 48 MP.
Depois da sequência de atualizações, o foco da Apple deve mudar para a nova geração de iPhones, encabeçado pelo suposto iPhone 20. A geração, que marca também os 20 anos de iPhone, deve trazer uma reformulação mais significativa em design, além de uma tela frontal com as quatro bordas curvas.
Os aparelhos também são esperados com chips produzidos em um processo de 2 nanômetros de segunda geração e uma nova versão do modem desenvolvido pela própria Apple.
Segundo Gurman, a Apple também prepara para o período novos Apple Watch, óculos inteligentes e AirPods equipados com câmeras.

articles.title: ASUS Predicts Return to 8 GB of RAM as Budget PC Standard Soon
articles.text:
Monday, November 23rd 2026
ASUS Predicts Return to 8 GB of RAM as Budget PC Standard Soon
It's long been known that the RAM and general PC component crisis, and its related price increases, would continue for some time, but it appears as though things are getting dire, even for bigger PC OEMs, like ASUS. According to ASUS co-CEO, S.Y. Hsu, in the ASUS Q3 2026 earnings call (via StockAnalysis), ASUS may soon have to return to shipping entry-level computers with as little as 8 GB of RAM. The CEO says that ASUS had shifted to 16 GB as the standard to ensure a good user-experience, but rising hardware prices may mean dropping the baseline to 8 GB, which has long since been insufficient for a good Windows experience.
S.Y. Hsu, Co-CEO, ASUSIt used to be that a mid to low tier machine will still ship with 16 GB of memory, but now they may move to 8 GB due to the memory cost increases. We have worked with Microsoft on this one. The old 16 GB spec was really about ensuring user experience. On the new operating system, Microsoft has made adjustments such that even 8 GB is able to yield an acceptable experience.
Back in May 2026, Microsoft updated its website to include a recommendation of a minimum of 32 GB of RAM to ensure a good experience on Windows, although it has since removed references to that recommendation. The good news about ASUS's announcement is that Microsoft may yet continue to optimize Windows for less and less powerful computers, which would be a benefit to all involved. 
Microsoft had also previously set the RAM floor for Copilot and AI features to 16 GB before shoehorning Copilot AI-powered features into every nook and cranny in Windows. It has since pulled back on its "AI everywhere" aspirations, removing or scaling back Copilot integrations from several of the built-in Windows apps, like File Explorer.
Source:

articles.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
articles.text:
President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.
The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).
Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.
Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.
Lead azide risk
Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO following unanimous vote by company board — 11-day exit from company saw stock prices fall by 24% after affair scandal
articles.text:
Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO following unanimous vote by company board — 11-day exit from company saw stock prices fall by 24% after affair scandal
He's back.
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang by a unanimous vote from its board of directors, the company announced Monday.
"Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board," a statement reads. "The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."
Shares of the company surged more than 30% ahead of the Nasdaq's open, erasing all of the losses incurred during Huang's leave of absence. In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump said Nvidia "has made the correct and proper decision" in reinstating Huang, stating the USA needs his leadership and Nvidia to ensure "the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy." He further stated that the U.S. Attorney General has no evidence Huang engaged "in any unlawful conduct."
The board said that it is confident that Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk, and part of this reassurance seems to have come from a senior level of the United States government.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board, stated. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer."
Huang said he was "honored" to return to Nvidia, but took the responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
Huang remains under investigation following reports he was entangled in an extramarital affair with a Chinese intelligence asset, with the board stating the investigation will proceed to conclusion. Reports emerged some weeks ago that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a company under criminal investigation for the export of illicit AI GPUs into China. Meanwhile, a second affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell was brought to light, prompting Huang's resignation.

articles.title: Russia readying nuclear-armed satellite that could destroy every low-Earth-orbit satellite, report claims — Kremlin blasts Sputnik-S claims as ‘unfounded allegations’ and propaganda
articles.text:
Russia readying nuclear-armed satellite that could destroy every low-Earth-orbit satellite, report claims — Kremlin blasts Sputnik-S claims as ‘unfounded allegations’ and propaganda
Western intelligence agencies believe that a launch of Sputnik-S could take place before the end of the year.
Western intelligence agencies believe that Russia could be readying the launch of a nuclear-armed satellite before the end of the year. The satellite, called Sputnik-S, is believed to have been in development for the last several years, with the United States first warning of Russia's plans in February 2023. Now, a German news report believes that the country's armed forces are already "raising the alarm" about the potential impact such a satellite could have. According to one expert, such a weapon could knock out a third of low Earth orbit satellites instantly, eventually disabling all of them with a devastating impact on the planet as a whole. With satellites playing such a vital role for civilian life as well as both military and intelligence operations, it's easy to see why Russia may want such satellite-crippling capabilities.
The report notes that information about Sputnik-S has been exchanged between several NATO member countries, with intelligence agencies having already warned that a launch could happen within 60 days. That report was made in early November, suggesting that Sputnik-S could be in orbit and operational in early December. The Russian embassy in Germany rejected the "unfounded allegations," saying that they are nothing more than "part of a propaganda campaign" against the country.
Perhaps worryingly, the United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) published its own report in which it warned that "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon." Such a move would be a violation of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. The treaty prohibits any country from launching anything carrying nuclear weapons or, indeed, any weapon of mass destruction into Earth orbit. While there has been no suggestion that Russia could turn the nuclear weapons towards the planet, Sputnik-S would still clearly be in breach of the longstanding treaty. One expert cited by the report says that a nuclear explosion in space would knock out one-third of low Earth orbit satellites instantly, with the remaining satellites gradually failing in the following months. The EMP generated could even cause widespread technical carnage on Earth.
As for which satellites could be a potential target for Sputnik-S, there is no shortage of options. SpaceX Starlink satellites are relied upon around the globe for their ability to provide fast, reliable networking to parts of the world not served by traditional connectivity options. Notably, Starlink has been used by Ukraine as it defends itself amid Russian aggression. But amid SpaceX's limiting of performance, Ukrainian officials have chosen to use their own "flying modems" to avoid relying on Elon Musk's company. Russia has been trying to launch its own Starlink rival, with limited success. September saw it lose a batch of 16 satellites during launch.

articles.title: La Poste signe son premier accord sur l'IA, et l'algorithme ne pourra pas décider à la place des postiers
articles.text:
La Poste a signé avec la CFDT, la CGT, FO et la CFE-CGC son premier accord encadrant l'usage de l'intelligence artificielle par les postiers. Le texte porte notamment sur les décisions RH, la formation et le droit à la déconnexion.
L'intelligence artificielle a désormais son mode d'emploi à La Poste, négocié avec les syndicats. Conclu le 19 novembre avec la CFDT, la CGT, FO et la CFE-CGC et officialisé ce lundi 23 novembre 2026, ce premier accord sur l'IA encadre jusqu'à fin mars 2029 la façon dont les postiers se servent de La Poste GPT, de Copilot ou du Chat de Mistral. On y découvre par exemple qu'aucun algorithme ne pourra trancher seul une promotion ou une sanction, et que les signataires avouent ne pas savoir chiffrer le temps gagné.
Chez La Poste, l'IA n'aura pas le dernier mot sur les promotions et les sanctions
Dans un groupe comme La Poste qui emploie plus de 170 000 personnes en France, la règle de base autour de l'intelligence artificielle méritait et devait être écrite. Le principe est que l'IA éclaire, et l'humain décide. L'accord dont on a pris connaissance aujourd'hui, qui couvre tous les personnels de La Poste SA, qu'il s'agisse des fonctionnaires ou des salariés, interdit qu'un système d'IA serve de base unique à une décision sur la carrière d'un postier. Que l'on discute de recrutement, d'évaluation, de mobilité, de rémunération ou de sanction, l'accord précise noir sur blanc que rien de tout cela ne sera confié à la seule machine. Si l'outil suggère une option, le manager peut en choisir une autre, et il en reste pleinement responsable.
Certains usages déjà interdits par l'AI Act, le règlement européen appliqué par étapes depuis août 2024, sont purement et simplement bannis, exclus, y compris dans les outils achetés à des fournisseurs. On peut notamment citer la notation sociale, la manipulation des comportements, et la détection des émotions au travail. Un postier qui échange avec un chatbot, ou suit une formation conçue avec l'IA, devra en être clairement averti. Et s'il tombe sur un résultat aberrant, il pourra le signaler à son manager ou au délégué à la protection des données, avec un retour sur les suites données.
Au nom du droit à la déconnexion, les notifications des outils d'IA pourront être coupées hors du temps de travail. La direction et les syndicats décrivent aussi sans se cacher les effets pervers possibles, par exemple une cadence qui s'emballe quand certaines tâches jugées simples disparaissent, une autonomie qui s'étiole, ou des équipes fragilisées. Pour les projets importants soumis au CSE, l'étude d'impact devra scruter le rythme, la charge et le sens du travail. Quant aux gains de temps, tous reconnaissent qu'il est pour l'heure impossible de les mesurer de façon fiable.
La Poste GPT, Copilot, Le Chat : une IA à apprivoiser
Les postiers ne découvrent pas l'intelligence artificielle avec cet accord. Outre La Poste GPT, l'assistant d'IA générative maison, le texte mentionne des licences Copilot de Microsoft et Le Chat du français Mistral AI, rebaptisé Vibe depuis la fin mai. De manière un peu plus discrète pour le grand public, des algorithmes déchiffrent déjà les adresses dans les plateformes de tri, épaulent le service client et les commerciaux, traitent des factures ou rapprochent les compétences des salariés des postes à pourvoir. La Poste dit compter plus de 500 experts de la data et de l'IA aujourd'hui, notamment dans ses filiales Probayes et Openvalue.
Le gros du chantier, sans trop de surprise, reste la formation. Près de 93 000 postiers sont déjà passés par le programme « Objectif IA », et l'accord prévoit des parcours adaptés à chacun, qui concernent des métiers les plus éloignés du numérique jusqu'aux experts techniques. Au programme, on y retrouve de l'aide pour la rédaction de prompts, la sécurité des données, l'éthique, et même deux modules sur l'AI Act (quinze minutes pour tous, 45 pour les plus concernés). Des badges jalonneront la progression, un label certifiant est en préparation et un réseau d'« ambassadeurs IA » pourra épauler les collègues. Le temps dégagé par l'IA est d'ailleurs censé servir en priorité à apprendre.
Pour veiller au grain, l'accord, qui entre en vigueur le 1er décembre, crée un « Comité IA & dialogue social ». Autour de la table, on retrouve des représentants des syndicats signataires, la direction des ressources humaines et les responsables chargés de vérifier que l'IA respecte la loi et que les données sont bien gérées. Leur mission consiste à anticiper les effets de l'IA sur les métiers, à passer en revue les projets les plus importants et à suivre quelques indicateurs, comme la formation ou la prévention des risques. Le rythme reste plutôt modeste, avec trois réunions la première année puis deux en 2028, et la DRH s'engage à répondre sous un mois aux questions écrites de ses membres. Ce comité ne remplace pas pour autant les CSE, les instances élues qui représentent le personnel, qui peuvent toujours être consultées lorsqu'un nouvel outil d'IA change sensiblement le travail des postiers. Une case reste néanmoins vide au bas du document, celle de SUD, qui n'a pas signé.
Sur le papier, La Poste a donc posé ses règles du jeu. C'est maintenant dans les centres de tri, les bureaux et les services clients que l'on saura si l'IA tient sa promesse, à savoir aider les postiers, sans jamais les déposséder de leur métier.

articles.title: Das Ramageddon ist real: So sehr sind Preise für PCs, Konsolen und Speicher gestiegen
articles.text:
Chipkrise: So stark sind Preise für PCs, Konsolen und Speicher gestiegen
Laptops, Spielekonsolen und andere Elektronikartikel haben sich mit dem Boom um Künstliche Intelligenz deutlich verteuert. Wie das Statistische Bundesamt mitteilte, waren Laptops im Oktober fast 15 Prozent teurer als ein Jahr zuvor und Desktop-PCs gut 13 Prozent. „Ein Grund dafür ist der gestiegene Bedarf an Speicherkapazität für KI-Rechenzentren, der sich auch in der Entwicklung der Verbraucherpreise für Speichermedien widerspiegelt“, heißt es in der Mitteilung.
So verteuerten sich Festplatten im Oktober zum Vorjahresmonat um 40,8 Prozent, Speicherkarten, USB-Sticks und Ähnliches waren gut ein Fünftel (22,1 Prozent) teurer. Auch bei anderen digitalen Geräten gebe es Preiserhöhungen: Spielekonsolen verteuerten sich um 13 Prozent, Mobiltelefone ohne Vertrag um gut zwölf Prozent, Smartwatches, Fitnesstracker oder Ähnliches um rund sechs Prozent. Die Preise für E-Book-Reader blieben dagegen fast unverändert. Zum Vergleich: Die Verbraucherpreise insgesamt stiegen im Oktober zum Vorjahresmonat um 2,8 Prozent.
Preise für Computer mittelfristig gefallen
Den jüngsten Preisanstiegen für Laptops und Co gingen allerdings teils deutliche Preisnachlässe in den Vorjahren voraus. 2025 waren Desktop-PCs gut 16 Prozent und Laptops rund 9 Prozent günstiger als 2020, so die Statistiker. Mobiltelefone ohne Vertrag wurden in dem Zeitraum 11,7 Prozent günstiger, Spielekonsolen 4,2 Prozent und Smartwatches, Fitnesstracker und Co 3,3 Prozent. „Diese Preissenkungen resultierten vor allem aus dem Abbau von Überproduktionen, die während der Covid-19-Pandemie entstanden waren“, hieß es.
Unterhaltselektronik und Haushaltsgeräte billiger
Während Computer zuletzt deutlich teurer waren als vor einem Jahr, verbilligte sich Unterhaltungselektronik. So mussten Verbraucher für Fernsehgeräte im Oktober 9,2 Prozent weniger zahlen und für Kameras 2,5 Prozent weniger.
Auch Haushaltselektrogeräte verbilligten sich: Die Preise für Geschirrspülmaschinen lagen im Oktober sieben Prozent niedriger als ein Jahr zuvor. Kaffeevollautomaten oder Espressomaschinen verbilligten sich um 5,4 Prozent, Waschmaschinen um gut vier Prozent, Toaster oder Grillgeräte um 1,5 Prozent.

articles.title: Lo volvería a comprar una y otra vez para estudiar o trabajar: así es el ratón vertical con muchísima autonomía

El ratón es muy cómodo y no cuesta prácticamente nada acostumbrarse a su formato. À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Dyson V12 Detect Slim Absolute descend à 399,00 € chez Dyson, soit environ 0 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours. Cela représente une économie de 0,00 €.
Une aspiration efficace sur tous les sols et une filtration sans faille

Sur sol dur en mode normal, il a ainsi récolté 100 % des matières en seulement 30 secondes, ce qui garantit un nettoyage rapide sans repasser plusieurs fois au même endroit. Comme nous l'avons souligné dans notre test complet, le système multicyclonique combiné au filtre HEPA assure un air rejeté totalement propre, le laboratoire ayant mesuré 0 g d'encrassement du filtre après l'aspiration d'une grande quantité de poussière.

Points forts

Points faibles

Une utilisation simple malgré une autonomie limitée
Le V12 Detect Slim Absolute se distingue par un entretien simplissime et un écran qui affiche une estimation de l'autonomie restante à la minute près. O Galaxy S26 FE conta com uma câmera tripla traseira com um sensor principal de 50 MP, clicando fotos com Estabilização Óptica de Imagem (OIS) e gravando vídeos em até 8K. Sua câmera frontal de 12 MP registra selfies no Modo Retrato e vídeo em 4K.
A ampla tela AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,7 polegadas entrega imagens detalhadas em resolução Full HD e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz. Além disso, o painel atua com brilho máximo de 1.900 nits, idêntico ao antecessor Galaxy S25 FE.

O Galaxy S26 FE (R$ 3.198,60 no Pix) tem estrutura em Armor Aluminum, acabamento traseiro em vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+ e pesa 193 gramas. Seu certificado IP68 de resistência à poeira e à água permite que o aparelho fique submerso por até 1,5 metros em água doce por até 30 minutos.

Monday, November 23rd 2026
Revopoint Launches MIRACO 2 on Kickstarter: Scan in One, Create with Agents
An all-in-one 3D scanner combining high-precision capture, powerful onboard computing, and AI-driven workflows—with Super Early Bird pricing starting at $1,425.
The Offer is available from today, November 18 on Kickstarter. Grab the Super Early Bird Offer, with up to 38% off, starting at $1,425. 
Back MIRACO 2 on KickstarterTruly Standalone Design with Powerful Onboard ComputingWeighing just 960 g, MIRACO 2 integrates depth computation, 3D scanning, point cloud processing, and basic editing into one portable device.
Powered by an 8-core CPU and 6-core NPU, it supports three operating modes:
- Standalone Mode: Scan, preview, process, and make adjustments directly on its 6-inch 2K AMOLED touchscreen.
- Wireless PC Mode: Connect to a computer via Wi-Fi 6 for a flexible scanning workflow.
- Wired PC Mode: Connect via USB-C 3.0 for a stable, high-performance workflow.
When connected to a GPU-powered PC, Multi-Line Laser scanning can reach speeds of up to 120 FPS.
High Precision Meets Versatile Scanning Capabilities
MIRACO 2 delivers single-frame accuracy of up to 0.02 mm in Multi-Line Laser Mode and offers six scanning modes to handle a wide range of objects and applications:
- 34-Line Blue Cross Laser
- 15-Line Parallel Laser
- Single-Line Deep-Hole Laser
- Full-Field HD
- VCSEL Rapid
- Hybrid HD
With a maximum capture rate of 10 million points per second in Hybrid HD mode, MIRACO 2 can handle challenging surfaces and geometries, including reflective metals, black objects, intricate structures, and human bodies.
Additional capabilities include:
- Markerless tracking for textured objects in laser-line modes (PC mode).
- A recommended minimum scan volume of 10 × 10 × 10 mm.
- A maximum scanning volume of 5 × 5 × 5 m when paired with the optional Photogrammetric Metrology Kit.
- VCSEL working distance ranging from 300 mm to 1,000 mm.
Revo Agents: An AI-Native Ecosystem for 3D Workflows
Capturing an object is only the beginning. Turning scan data into CAD models or inspection results often means navigating complex software and hours of manual processing.
Revo Agents is designed to change that.Introduced by Revopoint as the world's first agent-powered 3D reality ecosystem, Revo Agents acts as an AI-native engineering co-pilot, allowing users to direct complex 3D operations through simple natural language commands.
Its autonomous, prompt-driven pipeline spans:
- Real-time point cloud fusion
- Automated Scan-to-CAD conversion
- Scan-to-Inspection tolerance analysis
Rather than manually navigating each processing step, users can describe the task they want to accomplish and let Revo Agents help carry the workflow forward.
Paired with MIRACO 2, Revo Agents bridges high-precision reality capture and production-ready engineering output—reducing repetitive post-processing while keeping creators focused on design, analysis, and decisions.
You define the task. Revo Agents helps execute it.
Full-Color Capture and Physically Scaled 3DGS
MIRACO 2's dual RGB camera system combines a 2 MP near-field camera and a 50 MP far-field camera for detailed, full-color 3D capture.
In PC mode, it also supports physically scaled 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), allowing users to export 1:1-scale.splat models for XR applications and digital visualization.
AI-powered cleanup tools further simplify model preparation:
- AI Segmentation: Automatically identifies and removes unwanted environmental point clouds.
- AI Cropping: Streamlines model cleanup and editing.
Together with Revopoint's software ecosystem, these capabilities support an integrated Scan-to-CAD workflow, helping users move from physical objects to usable digital models.
Built for Indoor and Outdoor Work
Designed for both indoor and outdoor applications, it supports ambient lighting conditions of up to 100,000 lux. Its 10,000 mAh battery provides approximately three hours of runtime, with 65 W fast charging.
Two configurations are available:
- 16 GB RAM + 256 GB storage
- 32 GB RAM + 512 GB storage
Now Live on Kickstarter
Limited Super Early Bird pricing offers up to 38% off for early backers starting at $1,425.

articles.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
articles.text:
On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.
Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.
“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”
Millions allegedly harmed
Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.
“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.
States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.
Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”
“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.
SpaceX responds
Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.
“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”
However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.
Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.
Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”
In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”
“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”
Grok CSAM, NCII may trigger steep fines
It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”
As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.
“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.
Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.
“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.
Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.
“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data
articles.text:
Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data
Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.
A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.
The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.
The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.
“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”
The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.
“Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”
Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the company’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.
The company is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.
On the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching issues faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.
“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

articles.title: Samsung's $200 32-inch 4K monitor is my top pick for professionals
articles.text:
Samsung's 32-inch ViewFinity S7 4K monitor is just $200 at Amazon for Black Friday, and that's a lot of screen for work
A 32-inch 4K IPS panel with HDR10 for productivity, photo editing, and streaming
I reckon this is the monitor deal to beat in the run-up to Black Friday, with Samsung's 32-inch 4K display dropping to $200. For remote and hybrid professionals, that price makes it an easy recommendation.
Yes, seriously. The Samsung 32-inch ViewFinity S7 4K monitor is $200 (was $290) at Amazon. If you want a big, sharp monitor for your desk without spending much, this one gets my vote.
● Best for: Home office workers and students who want more screen space and sharper text
● Why we like it: A 32-inch 4K IPS panel with HDR10, 99% sRGB color, and HDMI and DisplayPort inputs for under $200
A 32-inch IPS panel at 3840 x 2160 and 60Hz with HDR10, support for over 1 billion colors, and 99% sRGB coverage. It has HDMI and DisplayPort inputs, Samsung's Eye Saver Mode and flicker-free tech, and a stand that tilts.
Why we recommend it
A 32-inch 4K screen is one of the easiest productivity upgrades you can make. You get room for two full-size windows side by side, and text looks crisp at normal scaling. IPS also means wide viewing angles and good color for photo editing. Amazon buyers rate it 4.5 out of 5. Keep in mind it's a 60Hz office monitor, not a gaming screen, and the stand only tilts.
Price Context & Historical Value
Amazon and other retailers list the S71H at $289.99, so $199.99 is $90 off. We don't have much price history on this newer model, but under $200 is a very good price for a 32-inch 4K IPS monitor from a major brand.
Should You Buy It?
✅ Buy the Samsung ViewFinity S7 if...
You want more screen space for spreadsheets, documents, and multitasking, you edit photos and want 4K detail, or you want a big 4K screen for under $200.
❌ Skip the Samsung ViewFinity S7 if...
You play fast games and want a high refresh rate, you need USB-C with laptop charging, or you want a stand that adjusts for height.
