articles.title: South African township delivery startup Gobuddy gets $121k working capital facility
articles.text:
South African logistics startup Gobuddy has secured a ZAR2 million (US$121,000) working capital facility from Anglo American’s Impact Finance Network (IFN) to scale its township delivery model.
Founded by Leon Strumpher during the COVID-19 pandemic, Gobuddy tackles the last-mile e-commerce gap in South Africa’s townships. Traditional couriers often avoid them because of safety risks, long distances and high costs.
The startup first matched parcels with people’s existing commutes, but its data showed that women made up 60 per cent of registered transporters and were less likely than men to own a vehicle, which limited how much they could earn. Gobuddy responded by building a network of community micro-hubs. Couriers drop parcels at local collection points, and vetted residents then deliver them on foot within their own neighbourhoods.
“You don’t need a vehicle. You can walk,” Strumpher said.
Gobuddy now runs 50 micro-hubs in areas such as Soweto, Thembisa, Umlazi, Chatsworth and Motherwell, which together have an estimated 12 million residents. Transporters are recruited and verified through the SA Youth platform, and deliveries are monitored with a tracking system the company spent three years building. Each drop pays around ZAR50 (US$3).
Gobuddy joined IFN in 2024 and received business coaching and investor-readiness support. The new revolving facility will cover the gap between the startup’s weekly payments to transporters and the weeks or months its delivery partners take to pay.
“This facility gives us the working capital to meet our commitments to transporters on time, while allowing us to take on more delivery contracts and grow the business,” said Strumpher.
Gobuddy plans to bring more courier and retail partners onto its platform. It aims to create delivery jobs for 5,000 women over the next three years.

articles.title: Rückkehr zu Nvidia: Jensen Huang kann offenbar machen, was er will
articles.text:
Rückkehr zu Nvidia: Jensen Huang kann offenbar machen, was er will
Jensen Huang hat seine Posten bei Nvidia zurück. Nach der Interimslösung Colette Kress steht jetzt sein dauerhafter Nachfolger fest. Es ist: Jensen Huang. Möglich macht es offenbar der Verwaltungsrat, der einstimmig für die Rückkehr gestimmt hat. Es ist das vorläufige Ende einer Posse, die mittlerweile an Lächerlichkeit nicht mehr zu überbieten ist. Denn wer sagt hier eigentlich noch die Wahrheit?
Wer einmal lügt, dem glaubt man immer
Rückblick: Am 8. November 2026 gibt Huang zu, eine Affäre mit Alice Huang gehabt zu haben, die wiederum im Verdacht steht, für China gearbeitet zu haben. Einem Bericht von Wired zufolge, der sich auf interne Quellen stützt, hatte der Nvidia-CEO dem Verwaltungsrat zunächst bestritten, dass es sich um eine unangemessene Beziehung zu Huang handelte. Stimmen die Angaben, so hat Jensen Huang den Verwaltungsrat wissentlich belogen. Die Geschichte um die vermeintliche Spionageaffäre beiseite gelassen, hätte schon das in vielen anderen Unternehmen gereicht, um den Posten zu verlieren.
Nicht so bei Huang. Zwar wurde eine interne Untersuchung angekündigt, aber erst als Berichte über eine zweite Affäre aufkamen, trat Huang von seinen Posten als CEO, Board-Mitglied und President bei Nvidia zurück. Geräuschlos blieb es daraufhin nicht. Huang brachte sich selbst als neuen alten CEO ins Spiel, so es der Verwaltungsrat denn wolle. Dieser erklärte im Rahmen der Bekanntgabe der Quartalszahlen jedoch: “Der Nvidia-Verwaltungsrat hat seinen Rücktritt einstimmig angenommen und beabsichtigt nicht, Jensen wieder als CEO einzusetzen.” Mit anderen Worten: Die Tür war zu.
Doch auch das ist im Nachhinein gar nicht wahr, wie mittlerweile auf Nvidias Seite zu lesen ist. In mehreren Gesprächen und Sitzungen habe sich der Verwaltungsrat demnach von Huangs “Aufrichtigkeit und seiner Fähigkeit, Nvidia zu führen, überzeugt.” Die Aufrichtigkeit des Mannes also, der noch zwei Wochen zuvor mutmaßlich gelogen, durch sein Fehlverhalten mindestens aber das eigene Unternehmen ins schlechte Licht gerückt und, nicht minder schlimm, die eigene Ehefrau öffentlich lächerlich gemacht hatte.
Hier zieht niemand die richtigen Konsequenzen
Die Gründe liegen für mich auf der Hand. Ich vermute: Geld auf der einen, Macht auf der anderen Seite. Weil Jensen Huang Nvidia in den vergangenen Jahren praktisch allein an der Spitze aufgebaut hat, ohne einen Protegé und potenziellen Nachfolger an der Seite, dürfte beim Board die Sorge groß gewesen sein, ohne diesen einen Mann mit Durchblick die Führungsrolle im KI‑Bereich zu verlieren. Huang wiederum kann es meiner Meinung nach nur noch um Macht, vielleicht noch ums Vermächtnis gehen. An der Spitze eines der größten Unternehmen zu stehen, koste es, was es wolle. Notfalls eben die eigene Glaubwürdigkeit.
Den richtigen Schluss zieht hier keiner. Denn Fehler einzugestehen, sich zu entschuldigen und dann mit ein wenig Restanstand abzutreten oder aber eine Haltung zu verkünden und dann auch den Mut zu haben, dabei zu bleiben, das wären die richtigen Entscheidungen gewesen. Was jetzt passiert, hat allerdings nichts mehr mit Anstand zu tun. Wie soll man Huang bei der nächsten Kontroverse noch glauben? Wie sollen Anleger darauf hoffen, dass der Verwaltungsrat schon das Richtige tun wird? Diese Rückholaktion hat kein Geschmäckle, wie man sonst so schön sagt. Sie zeigt einfach, dass die da oben mittlerweile wirklich einfach machen können, was sie wollen.

articles.title: Frankfurt-based CommerzVentures closes €50 million Fund IV, betting on early-stage FinTech and AI
articles.text:
CommerzVentures, a Frankfurt-based specialist venture capital firm focused on financial services, has closed its fourth fund at €50 million.
The fourth fund — CommerzVentures IV (Fund IV) — is anchored by Commerzbank and is deliberately smaller than its predecessors; the firm managed over €550 million across three prior funds, including €300 million in Fund III.
“Fund IV is deliberately smaller because we want to invest earlier. We aim to combine early conviction with the experience, industry connections and hands-on support founders need to build their businesses,” said Judith Vogel, Partner, CommerzVentures.
Founded in 2014, CommerzVentures is a specialist financial services investor having backed more than 40 companies across its three previous funds. Its notable portfolio companies include eToro, iwoca, Mambu, and Marqeta, several of which have gone on to achieve significant scale or public listings.
The CommerzVentures IV is jointly led by general partners Heiko Schwender and Vogel, supported by venture partners and senior advisers. The pair have backed companies including Deblock, eToro, Marqeta, and Unique, supporting these startups through major growth phases, and in some cases, through to public listing.
With Fund IV, CommerzVentures is making a strategic shift from its past funds to focus on earlier-stage investing. It argues this shift also reflects a maturing FinTech ecosystem, with the strongest companies reaching revenue faster, scaling more quickly, and moving through funding rounds at a pace that rewards investors who come in earliest.
“In financial services, a strong AI product is only the starting point. Founders also need to earn trust, navigate regulation, and connect to complex infrastructure. That is where our experience and network can make a difference,” said Schwender, Partner, CommerzVentures.
The firm says the new fund will back founders building at the intersection of AI and financial services, though it will also selectively back adjacent sectors such as supply chain and cybersecurity, where its financial services expertise and network can add tangible value.
CommerzVentures says its co-founders, Patrick Meisberger and Stefan Tirtey, will continue overseeing CommerzVentures’ existing funds. “We are proud of what CommerzVentures has built together with our founders, our team and Commerzbank as anchor investor. We are delighted to see Heiko and Judith lead Fund IV into its next chapter,” said Meisberger.
The Fund IV will deploy capital at Seed and early Series A stages, primarily across the EU, the UK and Switzerland. CommerzVentures plans to build a portfolio of around 25 companies with Fund IV and ,with its new investment thesis, the firm is positioning itself to catch the next wave of FinTech and AI innovation at its earliest stages.

articles.title: Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs
articles.text:
AI can accelerate derivative designs, but physical constraints and incomplete data limit how much can be automated.
Key Takeaways:
- AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective.
- AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies.
- End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification.
Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges.
Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them:
- The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers;
- Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required.
- Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes.
“There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.”
Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.”
Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications.
But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap.
Software reuse easier than hardware reuse
Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers.
“We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.”
Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.”
Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?”
The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets.
“Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.”
Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand. We need innovation in AI for SoC design.”
Capturing IP data and design knowledge
Before AI can effectively help engineers adapt existing designs to new requirements, it needs access to accurate, organized information about the IP already available, including its configurations, constraints, dependencies, and previous implementations. Capturing and managing that information, along with the engineering knowledge and methodologies used to develop it, is essential to making AI-assisted derivative design scalable.
To help solve these challenges, established EDA vendors and startups are releasing physics-based, assistive AI co-pilot technology to speed up design exploration, PPA optimization, RTL generation, and verification.
However, before deploying an AI tool to create a brand-new design or a derivative design from existing IP, engineering teams must first collect the knowledge already inside the organization. After that, IP lifecycle management software is needed to connect engineering data, automate workflows, improve traceability, and make valuable IP easier to find and reuse.
“How do you pull different IPs, and where is information about that IP?” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You could have information that says this IP works great for certain power levels. If you are developing an earbud, the available power may be much lower, so you know which IP will not be suitable. You have to look for a different source of IP from the finished product. You can create a software bill of materials (SBOM) or hardware bill of materials (HBOM) that lists all the IP you used, and you can confirm whether that was the latest and greatest version of the IP. Were there other variants of the IP? There are all kinds of different ways to do IP management.”
Teams also need a way to share the AI prompts, skills, and workflows they develop so that everyone can benefit from communal wisdom. “We invested in a platform and innovation store that allows our people to share prompts, plugins, check-ins, and solutions across teams,” said Ram Narayan, senior director of engineering at Arm. [2] “That was done primarily with the vision that teams can share skills and upskill themselves through that exchange. They can use the platform to upskill teams across the company, as well. This is an opportunity to bring people together around common ways of working and common learnings, which may have been lost over the years because we have acquisitions of groups, and groups going off and doing things differently. This is a real opportunity to enable these practices.”
An organization’s specific workflows need to be captured to get the best results from agentic AI-based design exploration tools.
“A company’s methodology is as important as the design, and the methodology they have used for the last 20 years to be able to tape out their chip has brought a lot of learning,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “For example, ‘Use this cell/ don’t use this cell. Optimize for PPA that way. Don’t do this. Don’t do that. Or, do this.’ When you are in the ECO stage, and you have crosstalk, you can talk to the customer, and they say, ‘Oh, for crosstalk at this modem company, I have a very specific way of solving it. I have done the same thing for the last 10 years, and I am able to solve the crosstalk.’ That’s what we call the ontology.”
This is a very promising use case for agentic AI. A common approach from EDA tool providers today is to have an agentic collaboration platform sit with the customer, allowing sharing between users while also feeding data, methodology information, and design information back into agentic workflows so they can do the best possible job and deliver the best possible outcome. In ChipAgent’s approach, all proprietary customer data stays on-prem. “This belongs to the customer,” Rahim noted. “It is not something that comes back to us.”
Automating interconnect design
While organizations wrestle with how to apply AI, they also are leveraging improvements in algorithmic optimization, software-driven simulation, and deterministic EDA. This is especially important when it comes to data movement, which is one of the key performance bottlenecks, along with moving data in and out of memories and processors. A tiled, algorithmic fabric is easier to scale up or down for derivatives than crossbars.
“For our switch customers who have been working with crossbars in the past, and have had deep, lived experience over decades, it is still a very hands-on experience with hand-coding RTL to build huge custom networks, and almost hand-wiring things,” said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at Baya Systems. “They say, ‘When this wire comes in, it’s going to come in here, then this other data is going to come from there, and we’re going to make it like an arbiter. This is a painstaking process where the whole design just gets bigger and more difficult by an n-squared factor. This is super painful for engineers, companies, and project managers, as well. It’s an incredible source of risk for them, because it’s iterative. It’s manual. They don’t know if they’re going to find surprises later.”
Massive parallelism and other techniques have transformed what previously looked like a complex engineering project into a very manageable math problem. “Suddenly, this becomes an algorithmic construct that says mathematically we will give you the exact performance properties you need,” Gayen explained. “This will create, literally, a grid of identical tiles. Top-down, you get that guarantee that it meets the performance needs ahead of time. Then in terms of implementation, when it’s the physical design, you actually build it and harden those designs, then figure out how to put it within a chip.”
In today’s landscape, a software-first approach is needed to build hardware, adapt it to new use cases and better products, and reduce customer cost, pain, engineering effort, and time to tape out. “It’s all built step by step,” Gayen observed. “For example, when I came in, we already had a really good software-defined flow, which is new for hardware. People don’t like writing software. They like getting their hands dirty and writing RTL. Having that software perspective of coming in and generating RTL is something that unlocks a different type of thinking and allows breakthroughs like this to happen. Companies are happy, and the engineers are happy because they don’t have to do the painstaking manual work anymore.”
Multi-physics optimization limits
However, for design exploration or reusing IP, no tool yet optimizes timing, IR, and thermal together at the RTL or architecture level.
“Today, we don’t have anything that helps the RTL designer all the way,” said Vinay Patwardhan, senior director, product management at Cadence. [3] “We have something that can help customers from the netlist stage. We have a vision for going all the way to architectural, but right now it’s either timing-based improvement, IR-based improvement, or thermal-based improvement — not all three together as a multi-physics problem. If you want improvement at the RTL stage, you have to incorporate all of them into the source code, which isn’t available because thermal analysis works on layout layers. IR needs the locations of the power sources. At the RTL stage, there is no physical awareness of any of this, so it is a difficult problem. However, if we can find correct ways to model and abstract all those effects at that early stage, then it will be possible. There is some work going on in that phase, but to answer clearly, we don’t have anything in the RTL today. We can optimize the netlist continuously with feedback.”
Tool providers are addressing the challenge from many angles. For example, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench to evaluate AI agents from workload spec and RTL generation through synthesis, physical implementation, and layout verification.
Fig. 3: Key steps from workload specification to GDS. Dashed arrows show problems found downstream that send the agent back to revise an earlier step. Source: ChipAgents
While these advances show AI’s potential to automate increasingly complex design workflows, generating a design is only part of the challenge. Each stage of implementation introduces physical constraints and interdependencies that can affect decisions made earlier in the process. Changes intended to improve one aspect of a design may create problems elsewhere, requiring tools to account for the interactions among electrical, thermal, mechanical, and other physical effects.
The need for agentic tools to be grounded in fundamental physics is one reason why end-to-end solutions are still under development.
“The limiting problems are no longer inside the chip,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO of Vinci. “They’re physical problems that live at the boundaries — heat moving from die to package to board to enclosure, thermo-mechanical stress across heterogeneous material stacks, power density interacting with cooling strategy at the system level. The physical world doesn’t respect the organizational boundaries the industry has drawn around it, and neither do the failures.”
Others agree. “EDA tools must expand beyond single-die optimization to system-level design, including multi-die integration, packaging, and software-hardware co-design, evolving toward intent-centric platforms rather than collections of disconnected point tools,” said Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “One major gap is verification, where rising design complexity continues to outpace engineering productivity despite significant AI advances.”
These challenges become even more complex as designs move beyond the chip and package to the board level, where reused IP and previously verified components must operate within new electrical and physical environments. While reusing proven designs can reduce engineering effort, changes in placement, connectivity, and surrounding circuitry can introduce interactions that were not present in the original implementation. This makes verification a critical part of derivative design, even when the underlying components have already been validated.
Verification at the board level
As with SoC IP data management, a robust data management foundation enables teams to reuse known good blocks on the board.
“They verified them in the past, and they could say, ‘This block doesn’t need to be verified,'” said David Wiens, product marketing manager at Siemens EDA. “If they use that block more than once, they only need to verify it once. But in reality, blocks of data and blocks of designs can and will behave differently depending on what’s around them. It’s a step toward simpler verification, but you still have to be careful. You have this one circuit, and you place it on the top layer of the design, but whatever’s running underneath it that’s native to that, that’s custom to that design and may in fact interact with it. You could put a shield around it if you wanted to really trust it and really make sure that it’s not impacted. But particularly with signal integrity, that’s a bit of a scary proposition to say, ‘I’m just going to trust that it’s more than likely to pass by itself.’ It’s a question of what it interacts with on the board.”
Fig. 4: Data management is a key component of using AI tools to speed up any part of the design flow. Source: Siemens EDA
Agentic AI tools can now shrink verification time. Siemens reported that its HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit reduced the design analysis for 112 high-speed channels from several weeks to a couple hours. “In a manual process, engineers would first need to figure out the signaling protocol,” Wiens explained. “What SerDes protocol is it using? I’ve got to dig up the manual, which can be hundreds of pages long. I’ve got to find the rules within that, and the conditions to set up my simulator. Then I’ve got to push the button and wait for it, and then when I get it back, I’ve got to visualize. I’ve got to look at the results one waveform at a time. Did it pass? Did it fail? And if not, I’ve got to figure out why, and I’ve got to iterate.”
With new agentic solutions, the AI can inspect the database itself. “It can identify potential issues off the bat before it even simulates,” he said. “Then it automates the workflow. That’s a big thing because it’s part of what democratizes the tool. Specialists understand both the workflow and the results. Democratizing that automation, simplifying it, means anybody can push the button. With visualization, when you’ve got a ton of data, you don’t want to look at it one at a time. We can use AI to take that data and visualize it to produce different types of results that aren’t just simple waveforms. The AI can diagnose where the problem is. ‘This eye [diagram] is failing. Here’s where I think the problem is, and here’s what we recommend you do next.’ It takes the engineers through that entire path.”
The speedup doesn’t come only from AI and software capabilities. “It’s about leveraging hardware horsepower, GPU horsepower, CPU cluster horsepower,” said Wiens. “That’s what gets us the speed. But there are also areas of AI that help us explore the design space faster without brute-force simulation. Agentic AI accelerates the steps, mostly through smarter execution, and then delivers trusted outcomes because it’s physics-based. It’s leveraging known good simulation engines, and IP can be managed in a safe way on-prem.”
Leveraging GPUs and CPUs comes with computational costs, a concern raised by Qualcomm’s Achour. Moreover, engineers still must manually implement many of the changes recommended by agentic AI tools.
“What engineers do next is go back to the design, the actual layout or schematic, and make the changes that were recommended,” said Wiens. “Today, that’s still largely a manual process. Watch this space. Automating the actual place and route and things like that is a lot harder than automating workflow.”
What AI still can’t automate
AI-based design tools are advancing rapidly, with vendors introducing new capabilities for RTL generation, design exploration, physical optimization, and verification. These advances are reducing engineering effort in individual stages of the design process, but efficiently adapting existing hardware IP to new applications remains a much broader challenge.
Making derivative chip design more scalable will require more than increasingly capable AI models. Design teams need organized, accessible IP data; reusable engineering methodologies; tools that can evaluate architectural and physical trade-offs; and verification workflows that account for changes in configuration, implementation, and operating environment. Agentic AI may help connect and automate these processes, but the underlying tools must still produce results grounded in physical reality.
At the most fundamental level, many AI tools are text-based LLMs. “They are really, really good at predicting the next word, the next phrase, the next line, then the next paragraph, and that means AI can be used to write text-based chip design specs or chip design documents like RTL design,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “AI can be used to write verification scripts that will test RTL and prove it’s good RTL or not, or find flaws in it. AI can read a long series of debug logs that could be gigabytes long, and humans will take forever to go through that. AI can quickly say, ‘Hey, did you go to line 79? That’s where I see a major issue.’ Largely, that’s what AI is helping with. There are so many other aspects of chip design that are not text-based, not suitable for words, and they still need humans actively.”
For chip architects and design teams, the opportunity is not simply to generate new designs faster, but to reduce the engineering effort required to turn proven IP into new products. Achieving that goal will depend on how effectively AI-driven automation can work with established EDA tools, engineering knowledge, and physics-based verification to identify what can be reused, determine what must change, and validate the resulting design. The real measure of AI’s success in derivative chip design will not be how quickly it generates new RTL, but how reliably it can help engineers transform existing IP into verified, physically viable designs with less manual effort.
References to DAC presentations

articles.title: Piratage de frigos de supermarchés : une opération secrète a évité une catastrophe au Royaume-Uni
articles.text:
Pendant environ trois semaines, une opération de cybersécurité menée dans le plus grand secret a permis de sécuriser des dizaines de milliers de frigos et de congélateurs au Royaume-Uni, révèle la BBC. Seuls les frigos de supermarchés, d’entrepôts, de restaurants, ou de stations-service, sont concernés.
L’opération, qui vient d’être révélée par la presse britannique, devait permettre d’éviter une vague de cyberattaques similaire à celle enregistrée dans plusieurs pays européens le mois dernier. Début octobre, près de 700 supermarchés ont été visés par des pirates. En pleine nuit, ils ont déréglé les frigos, poussant les enseignes à jeter des montagnes de nourriture. Dans certains cas, les frigos en surchauffe ont même provoqué des incendies.
La France a attribué l’attaque aux Gardiens de la révolution iraniens, une unité secrète de l’armée iranienne. Quelques semaines plus tard, une deuxième vague a touché des supermarchés de sept pays européens, dont la Belgique et le Luxembourg. Le même jour, des congélateurs de banques de sang situés en France ont été visés par des cybercriminels, mais le pire a été évité.
« Un problème de mot de passe faible »
Jusqu’ici, le Royaume-Uni semblait épargné. Les magasins britanniques s’appuient en effet sur des équipements différents de ceux du reste de l’Europe. Fin du mois dernier, un employé du cabinet Omega Solutions, spécialisé dans la réfrigération, a voulu savoir si des pirates pouvaient également s’en prendre aux supermarchés britanniques. Il a donc examiné les boîtiers de contrôle de frigos les plus répandus au Royaume-Uni. Ceux-ci sont fabriqués par Resource Data Management (RDM), une société britannique.
 The UK may have narrowly avoided the refrigeration cyberattacks seen across Europe, but its systems weren’t without vulnerabilities.
We were approached by Neil McCourt at Omega Solutions about a significant vulnerability in RDM refrigeration controllers widely used across the UK. @cybergibbons and the rest of our hardware security team subsequently validated the findings and discovered several additional vulnerabilities similar to those affecting Danfoss controllers, but not identical.
What followed was a coordinated effort involving Pen Test Partners, Omega Solutions, RDM, NCSC, and organisations across the food supply chain to identify exposed systems and reduce the risk.
Much of this work took place quietly to avoid alerting potential attackers while remediation was underway.
We’re publishing now to help reach smaller operators further down the supply chain who may still be exposed. We’ve deliberately withheld technical exploitation details while remediation continues.
Organisations should ensure their refrigeration controllers aren’t directly accessible from the public internet and apply RDM’s latest security updates.
Our @TheKenMunroShow and Andrew Tierney explain how it unfolded, how the industry responded, and why there’s still some work to do.
📌 https://t.co/PpQH3ZnfVF
#CyberSecurity #OTSecurity #UKFridges #VulnerabilityDisclosure #FridgeHacks #BBC
— Pen Test Partners (@PenTestPartners) November 20, 2026
Dans les boîtiers, il a rapidement découvert une faille de sécurité. La vulnérabilité a été rapidement confirmée par les hackers éthiques de Pen Test Partners, une entreprise britannique spécialisée dans la cybersécurité. Interrogé par la BBC, Ken Munro, de Pen Test Partners, assure que « ces contrôleurs très répandus avaient un problème de mot de passe faible similaire à celui des appareils Danfoss et des autres contrôleurs attaqués avec succès ». L’expert fait référence aux contrôleurs de la société Danfoss, qui sont à l’origine de l’attaque contre les supermarchés français des 11 et 12 octobre. Une grande partie des installations compromises étaient protégées par des mots de passe faibles et faciles à deviner.
Selon le chercheur, il ne fallait probablement « plus que quelques jours avant que des criminels ou des pirates d’État » ne découvrent la faille, et cherchent à l’exploiter pour lancer des cyberattaques, similaires à celles enregistrées en France. Pour Garry Turner-Smith, d’Omega Solutions, un cabinet de conseil britannique spécialisé dans la réfrigération, des pirates « auraient pu prendre le contrôle total » des boîtiers vulnérables et « perturber les systèmes de réfrigération sur plusieurs sites », rapporte le Guardian. Il ajoute que « cet incident devrait servir de signal d’alarme pour toute l’industrie de la réfrigération ».
À lire aussi : Cyberattaques en cours dans le « monde entier » – le FBI alerte sur une vague d’intrusions menées par ARTEX, une redoutable IA
« Une course contre la montre »
Peu après la découverte de ce problème de mots de passe, le NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre), l’agence britannique de cybersécurité, a été alerté. C’est aussi le cas des ministères de l’Agriculture et de la Sécurité alimentaire du Royaume-Uni. L’alerte a été émise dans le plus grand secret pour éviter que des pirates ne soient mis au courant avant que le problème soit corrigé.
« Nous devions travailler discrètement pour ne pas alerter des hackers moins éthiques et des États comme l’Iran, qui sont actifs dans ce domaine », raconte Ken Munro.
Des milliers de boîtiers ont été déconnectés d’Internet de toute urgence, que ce soit à distance par le biais de panneaux de contrôle, ou à la main. Des employés ont en effet dû débrancher les câbles réseau et surveiller les températures manuellement le temps de colmater les vulnérabilités. Au sein d’une grande enseigne britannique, l’équipe informatique a mis hors ligne des centaines d’appareils chaque jour pendant une semaine.
« On avait l’impression d’une course contre la montre, car nous nous attendions à une nouvelle vague d’attaques », confie un employé à la BBC.
De son côté, Resource Data Management, la société à l’origine des contrôleurs vulnérables, conteste la gravité de la faille. Selon la firme, il faut se procurer un équipement bien précis pour prendre le contrôle des dispositifs mal protégés. C’est pourquoi Resource Data Management estime qu’une attaque était peu probable. À l’inverse de la société, les chercheurs assurent que les hackers pouvaient facilement profiter de la situation. Selon eux, le matériel nécessaire à une cyberattaque s’achète facilement sur eBay. Quoi qu’il en soit, Ged Evans, le patron de Resource Data Management, assure que son entreprise a agi « rapidement pour régler ce problème » et que des « premiers correctifs » ont été colmatés.
« Des efforts considérables ont été déployés en très peu de temps, ce qui a obligé les équipes des enseignes à travailler le soir et le week-end », explique Pen Test Partners.
Des milliers de frigos toujours en danger
En dépit des efforts des chercheurs et de Resource Data Management, la menace n’est pas totalement écartée. Ken Munro estime que « des milliers de petits magasins sont toujours exposés ». Il faut encore du temps pour couper ces boîtiers d’Internet et installer la mise à jour. En attendant que tous les frigos soient à l’abri des pirates, les chercheurs ont soigneusement gardé le secret sur les détails des failles, et sur les méthodes d’exploitation.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

articles.title: Investigadores espiaron conversaciones y siguieron por GPS a un Volkswagen ID.4 mediante Bluetooth
articles.text:
Investigadores de la empresa húngara de ciberseguridad PCA Cyber Security demostraron que un Volkswagen ID.4 puede ser intervenido por Bluetooth para escuchar a sus ocupantes y seguir su ubicación por GPS. Ante esta situación, Volkswagen afirmó que ya distribuye una actualización y que no habrá retiro de vehículos.
La demostración se realizó en Budapest, capital de Hungría, ante periodistas del diario británico The Times. Desde una computadora fuera del auto, los expertos activaron el micrófono del sistema de manos libres, rastrearon el auto y accionaron la calefacción, los limpiaparabrisas y el techo corredizo.
Los investigadores leyeron mensajes de texto y contactos del celular conectado, grabaron una charla entre conductor y acompañante con el micrófono pensado para llamadas a emergencias, y mostraron en la pantalla un mensaje que decía “hackeado por PCA”.
Una cadena de cuatro fallas conocida desde 2025
El ataque usado durante la investigación usa cuatro vulnerabilidades, bautizadas PerfektBlue, en BlueSDK, un programa de Bluetooth de la empresa OpenSynergy que varios fabricantes integran en el sistema de información y entretenimiento de sus autos. PCA publicó el aviso técnico el 7 de julio de 2025. Según ese documento, encadenadas permiten ejecutar código ajeno con un solo clic del usuario.
El aviso detalla que PCA comprobó el ataque en el sistema de un ID.4 y en el de un Skoda Superb, sumado a un banco de pruebas de Mercedes-Benz. También detectó parte de las fallas en varios BMW, aunque no completó un ataque en esos autos.
PCA afirma que OpenSynergy confirmó los errores y distribuyó parches en septiembre de 2024, pero que no todos los fabricantes los recibieron hasta junio de 2025.
Según el mismo documento, PCA comunicó al grupo de respuesta a incidentes de Volkswagen el 19 de junio de 2024, el día en que confirmó las fallas en el ID.4.
Qué dice Volkswagen y qué debe hacer el dueño de cada vehículo
Un vocero de Volkswagen dijo a heise online que la empresa investigó las vulnerabilidades y que el problema afecta a una generación anterior del sistema, que aparentemente ya no se instala en modelos eléctricos actuales como el ID. Polo. Aseguró que los atacantes no pueden acceder dirección, frenos ni acelerador: “En ningún momento hubo ni hay peligro” para clientes o vehículos.
La empresa explicó que corrigió la falla rápido en los modelos ID. con software posterior a la versión 5.0. En las versiones anteriores tardó más porque debió modificar un sistema de gestión ya planificado y completar nuevos procesos de seguridad.
La actualización 3.9.1 llega desde hace unas tres semanas a autos con software anterior a la versión 4.0 y se instala de forma inalámbrica, por red de datos o WiFi, con el auto estacionado. Los autos con versiones posteriores a la 4.0 deben pasar por un taller. Según Volkswagen, los que tienen la versión 5.6 o una más reciente no están afectados.
El ataque exige condiciones concretas: el conductor debe aceptar una solicitud de emparejamiento Bluetooth. Volkswagen aconseja no aceptar nunca solicitudes desconocidas ni conectar dispositivos USB ajenos. PCA advierte que, según cómo cada fabricante configure el sistema, en algunos dispositivos las fallas podrían alcanzarse antes del emparejamiento.
Cuál información queda expuesta cuando falla el sistema Bluetooth
El riesgo principal de una intrusión en el sistema de información y entretenimiento no se limita a funciones del vehículo. Estos sistemas suelen concentrar la libreta de contactos, registros de llamadas, mensajes, ubicaciones recientes y datos de los teléfonos que se conectaron al auto. Esa información puede revelar rutinas, vínculos personales y trayectos frecuentes de los ocupantes.
Asimismo, la separación entre los sistemas de confort y conectividad, por un lado, y los controles de conducción, por otro, reduce la posibilidad de que una falla afecte el manejo del vehículo. Sin embargo, no elimina el impacto sobre la privacidad. Por eso, las actualizaciones de software y una gestión cuidadosa de los dispositivos vinculados son parte de la seguridad cotidiana de un auto conectado.

articles.title: First Circle Capital’s $26 million pre-seed playbook
articles.text:
Fintech remains the biggest recipient of venture capital in Africa’s tech ecosystem, but it is not immune to the sector-wide funding slowdown. In the first half of 2026, African fintech startups raised $488 million across 45 deals, according to TechCabal Insights’ State of Tech in Africa report, a 23.7% drop from the $639 million raised in the same period in 2025.
First Circle Capital, a female-led venture capital firm focused on African fintechs, is positioning itself for the sector’s next phase with what it calls Fintech 2.0, which is a generation of businesses that build on the financial infrastructure established over the past decade, using technology to improve how financial institutions operate and serve customers.
“Ten years ago most fintechs in Africa were payments businesses, focused on building bridge-to-cash distribution networks, aggregating remittance flows or enabling online and in-store payments,” Selma Ribica, co-founder and managing partner at First Circle Capital, told TechCabal in an email on Friday. “The next wave of fintech winners will not simply be existing financial businesses with AI features added on top, but companies built from day one around automation, intelligent decision-making, software-led operations, and radically lower-cost distribution.”
Fifteen years ago, Ribica worked at M-Pesa, which helped bring mobile payments to the mass market and build crucial payment infrastructure on the continent. She co-founded First Circle Capital in 2021 with Agnes Aistleitner and Robert Smith. Now, the firm operates across Kampala, Nairobi, Casablanca, and Cape Town, with a pan-African investment mandate covering markets including Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Uganda, Ghana, and Francophone Africa.
In 2025, First Circle Capital began building its Africa Fund I with a $6 million commitment from the International Finance Corporation (IFC). It announced the fund’s close at $26 million on Wednesday, with subsequent commitments from Bpifrance and Stellar Foundation. Ribica explained that First Circle Capital’s strategy focuses on six sub-segments within fintech, which include insurtech, alternative lending models, interoperability and infrastructure, climate fintech, fintech software-as-a-service (SaaS), and regulatory technology (RegTech). It is also looking for companies that build with artificial intelligence (AI) from the outset, rather than adding AI features to existing financial products.
In this conversation, Ribica explains how First Circle Capital’s Fintech 2.0 thesis differs from the payments era, why First Circle Capital is betting on AI-native businesses, what it looks for in founders, and the deals the firm walks away from. She also discusses the firm’s approach to follow-on investments and who it expects to buy its portfolio companies.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You started with $6 million from IFC about a year ago and closed at $26 million. Your hard cap was $30 million. Why stop at $26 million?
First Circle Fund I team is here for carry, not management fees. I started investing my personal money in African fintechs in 2017 and had great returns from companies like Expensya, THNDR and more. The goal is to optimise performance, not AUM. At the time our most recent LPs committed, BPIFrance and Stellar Foundation, we already had built a well-performing portfolio, and $26 million is to execute our strategy for optimal returns.
You call this “FinTech 2.0.” How is a company you’ll back today different from the payments companies of the last ten years? Why did you select six core areas?
At the time we launched First Circle, the opportunities shifted to building solutions on top of those rails, leveraging technology to deepen financial inclusion for businesses and consumers, and helping African financial institutions leverage lower costs of operations and manage risk, bridging the gap across the industry with new technologies and accelerating digitisation.
First Circle I is a thesis-led fund focusing on six key sub-segments within fintech: Insurtech, Alternative Lending Models, Interoperability & Infrastructure, Climate Fintech, Fintech SaaS, and RegTech. While we believe these areas still represent substantial opportunities for economic and impact returns in Africa, it is important to note that in markets where financial innovation came later, like Morocco, we still back Fintech 1.0 opportunities, as those will be the most lucrative opportunities at the given stage of fintech innovation maturity.
In African markets, where legacy financial infrastructure is often incomplete or inefficient, AI-native fintech companies have the opportunity to leapfrog traditional models and build more scalable, accessible financial services from the ground up.
Describe the founder you’d write a cheque to.
We spend a lot of time understanding founders’ quality of motivation, as well as certain personal characteristics that we believe are highly correlated with success. Founders we back are ambitious yet humble, have a growth mindset and strong ability to self-reflect; they display a track record as top operators, networkers and thinkers who plan for the long-term.
What makes you walk away from a deal even when the numbers look good? Tell me about one deal you passed on and why.
The greatest number of deals we walked away from had one thing in common: founders who want to get rich quick. Building a successful company takes a decade or more, and we never back teams who prepare themselves for less.
You say you want companies that use AI from day one. What does that look like for a pre-seed fintech?
One example is Orca Fraud, a South African AI-native SaaS platform that we backed in 2023. We were the company’s first investors, supporting the founding team at the MVP stage as they developed an AI-powered solution for real-time transaction monitoring and fraud detection.
Apart from money, what do you do for a founder in their first year?
As mentioned previously, we began investing at the onset of the venture capital downturn, which made us particularly conscious of the importance of deploying our capital efficiently and maximising the value we could create for our portfolio companies beyond financial investment alone.
From the outset, we asked ourselves two fundamental questions: what truly moves the needle for fintech businesses at the pre-seed and seed stages, and which unique assets, capabilities and relationships could the First Circle Capital team leverage to make a transformational difference to our portfolio?
Today, we track progress we have made across three key areas: catalysing additional investment, unlocking commercial opportunities and strengthening the operational foundations of our portfolio companies.
We have helped our portfolio companies attract follow-on investment equivalent to 2.2 times the amount of capital we originally invested. On average, our involvement has helped catalyse 50% of each subsequent funding round, rising to 56% when First Circle Capital’s own participation is included.
To date, we have supported 13 portfolio companies in their fundraising efforts, introducing 23 unique investors and helping them secure the additional capital needed to scale their businesses.
Beyond fundraising, we have focused heavily on helping our portfolio companies establish commercial relationships with enterprise customers and high-growth businesses across Africa and internationally. We have facilitated 80 business development introductions, generating 33 active commercial conversations and nine contracts that are already producing revenue.
Collectively, these efforts have created a potential commercial pipeline worth $18.8 million, comprising $1.3 million in contracted revenue, $2.4 million in contracts undergoing final negotiations and a further $15.1 million in advanced discussions. These figures represent cumulative potential contract values over the 2026–2029 period.
Finally, we support our portfolio companies in recruiting senior executives and accessing experienced operators and advisers. Our network includes professionals with experience at organisations such as RedMart, Lazada, Alibaba and Expensya, alongside alumni communities from leading international business schools, including INSEAD, London Business School, Harvard Business School and Wharton.
How much do you put into a first cheque? With 18 companies already backed and about 24 planned, how much of the $26 million is left for new deals, and how much is set aside for follow-on rounds?
We aim for 10% at entry at the pre-seed and seed stages, so our ticket varies from $250,000 to $1.2m. We hold a 40% follow-on reserve.
Most of your money comes from development finance institutions. How do their goals affect which deals you do?
DFI mandates are aligned with our goals: returns and impact come simultaneously and not at the expense of one another. Therefore our investors do not dictate our investment strategy nor deals we chose to do. The decision to invest is based on the company’s ability to transform financial services for the better and generate top decile returns for our investors.
Who do you expect to buy your companies: banks, telcos or bigger fintechs?
We plan for exits from day 1, and work on improving exit chances for our portfolio continuously. We expect the bulk of exits will come from secondary and strategic acquisitions in the financial services industry, while there is also a possibility of a few IPOs.

articles.title: Homelabber's $3,500 build straps four 32GB Nvidia V100s to a Lenovo mini PC for 128GB of VRAM — coreboot, OCuLink docks, and a solder bridge unlock 285 tokens/sec in Qwen3.8-27B
articles.text:
Homelabber's $3,500 build straps four 32GB Nvidia V100s to a Lenovo mini PC for 128GB of VRAM — coreboot, OCuLink docks, and a solder bridge unlock 285 tokens/sec in Qwen3.8-27B
The stock BIOS only had room for two 32GB cards, and custom fan ducts handle the heat.
A homelabber has built a local AI system out of four used 32GB Nvidia V100s and a refurbished Lenovo M720q Tiny mini PC. Ok_Kaleidoscope9103’s construction, detailed on Reddit, relies on the GPUs going over four OCuLink cables from a PCIe switch card, with a solder bridge on the riser and coreboot getting past a BIOS that only booted two cards. The quiet-running build has the full 128GB of VRAM and can hit about 285 tokens per second in total running Qwen3.8-27B across its four cards.
The user, who gives his name as Michael, details his “home AI box” in a YouTube video billed as a “full build guide.” The Australian builder describes the setup as “four docks, four datacentre cards, one little PC” in a “noise optimised build.”
The hardware for this particular build is based on a Lenovo M720q Tiny desktop, which has an i5-9400T CPU with 64GB of DDR4. With a matching Lenovo 01AJ940 riser and a CEACENT CNOL4PE08 PCIe switch card — this has a 24-lane PEX8724 switch on board for an x8 link in and four x4 OCuLink ports out — each GPU card can run at PCIe Gen3 x4. OCuLink is an external PCIe cable connector often used with external GPUs (eGPU).
On the software and firmware end, the Tiny had some roadblocks that had to be overcome. It “only powers its riser slot when the card pulls the presence pin,” which the switch card doesn’t, so a solder bridge was needed on the back of the riser. Then, “Lenovo’s BIOS only leaves a 128 GB window for 64-bit devices,” and each 32GB V100 needs 64GB, which limits the stock firmware to just two cards; a third “hangs at POST.”
His workaround used coreboot 26.09 built for the board with an EDK2 payload and a config setting that allows above-4G allocation. This expands the window to about 486GB and, with three patches, more features were enabled: the riser slot is always on, there is a Wake-on-LAN override, and merged memory type range registers (MTRRs). Flashing it needed a CH341A programmer and SOIC8 clip for the BIOS chip.
He then added four AOOSTAR AG01 eGPU docks, each with a built-in 800 W PSU, and assigned one V100 to each dock. Each dock’s PSU feeds its V100 through a dual PCIe 8-pin to CPU/EPS 8-pin adapter, because the card takes a CPU 8-pin. The Tesla V100s are otherwise passively cooled and rely on chassis or other external airflow.
Then there’s the matter of cooling without ear-bleeding. The V100s each get a 3D-printed 140 mm funnel — designed with the help of AI — with a Noctua NF-A14 iPPC-3000 fan, with all four driven on an ARCTIC 10-port USB fan controller. A separate ARCTIC P12 Silent is mounted in a Dremel-drilled hole in the Tiny’s lid to cool the switch card, as that does run hot. He measured the end result at about 62 dB at a distance of one meter.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
A script tracks the hottest card, stopping work at 83°C and powering the system off at 87°C. To keep temperatures in check, each card is also power-capped to 200 W, or 800 W total. A recent, separate dual-GPU build we detailed needs dual 12W fans to keep the Optane and system memory cool.
With this 4-card setup, 44.7 TFLOPS is doable with FP32 with a 71°C peak; this compares to Nvidia’s rating of 14 TFLOPS for each 250 W card. A single RTX 5090 is rated at 104.8 TFLOPS at 575 W, nearly double the 56 TFLOPS of four V100s. Qwen3.8-27B Q6 can chat at about 40 tokens per second with one card and about 285 per second with all four, each card running its own copy and handling four requests at once. A larger model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B-A6B IQ4_XS, does about 43 tokens per second on chat over all four, or about 116 with eight requests.
The builder says that this cost him “~A$6.5k all-in,” a figure that includes local taxes; he puts it closer to $3,500 in U.S. dollars. Check the table for the cost breakdown. As noted in our coverage of other V100 builds, the cost of some of this hardware — SXM2 V100s, in particular — has climbed significantly this year; he says his PCIe cards “jumped in price” in recent months.
| What he paid in Australia (fans, adapters and printed parts not priced) |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Part | A$ | US$ | 
|---|---|---|
| 4x V100 PCIe 32GB (used) | ~1,070 each | ~699 each | 
| 4x AOOSTAR AG01 dock | ~180–240 each | ~120–155 each | 
| 2x 32GB DDR4 SODIMM | ~275 each | ~180 each | 
| Lenovo M720q Tiny (refurb) | ~259 | ~170 | 
| CEACENT switch card | ~103 | ~67 | 
| Lenovo riser | ~38 | ~25 | 
| CH341A + clip | ~40 | ~26 | 
| ARCTIC fan controller | ~29 | ~19 | 
| Tapo smart plug | ~21 | ~14 | 
Although he calls using the full 128GB a “party trick,” he actually does use the build with Qwen3.8-27B, running separately on each card, to mine stock-announcement data dating back to the early 1990s for his business, which needs to read “millions of documents.” The build has been stable, running “pretty much 24/7 for a few weeks,” and with this setup he expects the system to pay itself back in about three months.
Some commenters wonder why he didn’t take the route of a fellow Redditor, a lawyer, who experimented with 32GB V100s as SXM2 modules on NVLink boards. His answer: noise, and that “the PCIe cards at the time were cheaper.” He also compares his four V100s to an RTX 5090, and says they have 4x the VRAM and about 2x the total memory bandwidth at “about half the price” of a 5090 in Australia. Next up is benchmarking SFNX and Infer-V100 to see how it compares to his llama.cpp setup.cpp setup, and possibly adding a second set of four V100s.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Bell reports some customer information accessed in data breach
articles.text:
Bell and its subsidiary Virgin Plus suffered a data breach earlier this month that exposed some customers’ personal information.
According to a notice published by Bell on its website, an “unknown party gained unauthorized access to an internal Bell system” on Nov. 17, 2026. Bell says it started informing impacted customers as soon as it confirmed that their data had been impacted.
The unknown party may have accessed personal information, including names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and account details like account numbers, product information, business names, and the date and amount of customers’ last payment.
“We have confirmed that no highly sensitive personal information such as credit card number or bank account information was impacted,” Bell said.
The telecom said that it “immediately removed the threat actor and initiated emergency protocols.” It also continues to monitor all systems closely and has engaged the RCMP’s cybercrime unit to help investigate.
Bell also shared some best practices for impacted customers. That includes being wary of any unsolicited requests from people posing as Bell, especially if they’re asking for personal information. Bell says it will never contact customers asking for bank account information, passwords, or PINs.
The company also warned against clicking on links or downloading attachments delivered from suspicious emails or text messages. Customers should also review accounts for suspicious activity.
Notably, Bell is the latest telecom to suffer a breach this year. Telus also suffered a breach between Feb. 2025 and June 2026. Cogeco’s Oxio suffered a data breach as well, as did Rogers and Fido. And Freedom Mobile suffered a breach in January.
And security issues extend beyond carriers, with Loblaw and Canada Computers also reporting breaches this year.
Source: Bell, Virgin Plus

articles.title: À peine sortis, les Xiaomi Clip sont déjà en promotion grâce au Black Friday
articles.text:
Depuis le 17 novembre, les Xiaomi Clip sont disponibles en France, après un lancement en Chine en mai. Ce sont les premiers écouteurs ouverts à clip de la marque, un format qui séduit de plus en plus notamment grâce à la légèreté des oreillettes. Ce ne sont pas les seules qualités de ces Xiaomi Clip puisqu’ils promettent jusqu’à neuf heures d’autonomie sans le boîtier. Pour fêter le lancement de ces nouveaux écouteurs, Amazon profite du Black Friday pour baisser leur prix de 23 euros.
Que retenir des Xiaomi Clip ?
- Un format clip léger (5,5 grammes par écouteur)
- Jusqu’à 38 heures d’autonomie avec le boîtier
- La compatibilité avec l’application Localiser d’Apple
Les Xiaomi Clip ont été lancés pour 149,99 euros, mais Amazon les propose actuellement pour 126,99 euros.
Des écouteurs adaptés à toutes les situations
Les Xiaomi Clip se déclinent en quatre coloris, du Noir, très sobre, à l’Or, plus flashy, en passant par le Blanc et le Violet.
Comme leur nom l’indique, les Xiaomi Clip sont des écouteurs au format clip, c’est-à-dire qu’ils se pincent sur le bord de l’oreille. Chaque écouteur tient grâce à un arceau en fil de titane à mémoire de forme, prévu pour s’adapter à différentes formes d’oreille. Les sportifs apprécieront aussi la certification IP57, qui protège les écouteurs de la poussière, de la pluie et de la transpiration (le boîtier n’est pas concerné).
Le nouveau produit de Xiaomi est aussi pensé pour les sorties longues, que ce soit une course ou un voyage long-courrier en avion. Xiaomi annonce jusqu’à neuf heures d’écoute par charge et jusqu’à 38 heures avec le boîtier, mesurées en Bluetooth AAC à 50 % du volume. Avec le codec haute résolution LHDC 5.0, on tombe à six heures par charge et 25 heures au total. En cas d’urgence, dix minutes de charge redonnent jusqu’à 3,5 heures d’écoute.
Une fiche technique complète
Puisqu’il s’agit d’écouteurs ouverts, les Xiaomi Clip ne possèdent logiquement pas de réduction de bruit active. Côté son, Xiaomi mise sur un haut-parleur dynamique de 11 millimètres et sur le codec LHDC 5.0, réservé pour l’instant aux smartphones Android 17 compatibles. Nous ne les avons pas encore eus entre les mains, et la taille du haut-parleur ne suffit pas à juger du son.
Pour contenir les fuites sonores, Xiaomi a orienté la sortie audio vers le conduit auditif. Le haut-parleur émet aussi des ondes en opposition de phase pour limiter ce que les personnes autour de vous entendent de votre musique ou de vos appels. Xiaomi promet des fuites réduites et conseille lui-même de baisser le volume dans les endroits calmes. Les Xiaomi Clip possèdent un système de quatre microphones (trois classiques et un capteur à conduction osseuse) pour que votre voix soit entendue par votre interlocuteur même dans un environnement bruyant.
Si vous perdez vos écouteurs, vous pourrez retrouver le boîtier grâce à l’application « Localiser » d’Apple, à condition d’avoir un iPhone sous iOS 18 ou plus récent. Un écouteur égaré seul ne remontera pas dans l’application. Le boîtier émettra un bruit afin que vous puissiez le retrouver.

articles.title: Le Black Friday coupe le cordon : la souris gaming sans fil Logitech G502 X PLUS passe à 79,99€ chez Amazon
articles.text:
La Logitech G502 X PLUS est une souris gaming sans fil qui donne accès à 13 commandes personnalisables. Pour le Black Friday, Amazon la propose à 79,99 €, soit 47 % de réduction sur son prix conseillé de 149,99 €.
Si vous travaillez sur le même PC que vous utilisez pour jouer, l’idéal est de disposer d’une souris gaming qui soit polyvalente et confortable à utiliser pendant de longues heures. Avec ses commandes programmables et sa molette débrayable, la Logitech G502 X PLUS répond à ces exigences. Cette souris sans fil est actuellement disponible pour 79,99 € au lieu de 149,99 € sur Amazon dans le cadre du Black Friday. Cette version sans fil intègre également un éclairage RGB personnalisable, si vous aimez avoir un setup lumineux.
La Logitech G502 X PLUS est à 79,99 € au lieu de 149,99 € chez Amazon pour le Black Friday.
Pourquoi choisir la Logitech G502 X PLUS ?
- Pour ses commandes personnalisables : 13 commandes programmables permettent d’attribuer des actions à vos jeux et logiciels.
- Pour sa connexion sans fil : la liaison LIGHTSPEED fonctionne avec un récepteur USB fourni.
- Pour sa molette débrayable : passez du défilement cranté au défilement libre pour parcourir rapidement de longues pages lorsque vous travaillez.
Des réglages utiles pour jouer comme pour travailler
Comme d’autres souris gaming de Logitech, la Logitech G502 X PLUS prend en charge le logiciel Logitech G HUB. Celui-ci permet de personnaliser les commandes du périphérique, par exemple pour déclencher une action en jeu ou retrouver un raccourci souvent utilisé dans un logiciel. La molette propose également un défilement horizontal, ce qui est très pratique pour naviguer dans de grands tableaux. Les clics principaux utilisent des interrupteurs hybrides optiques et mécaniques LIGHTFORCE.
Si son fonctionnement sans fil vous intimide, sachez que Logitech annonce une autonomie qui peut atteindre les 130 heures sans éclairage, contre 37 heures lorsque le RGB reste allumé. La recharge s’effectue à l’aide d’un câble USB-C qui permet de continuer à utiliser la souris.
Une souris polyvalente qui conserve un certain poids
La G502 X PLUS privilégie les nombreuses commandes et une forme avec repose-pouce, ce qui la cantonne à une utilisation de la main droite. Elle pèse 106 grammes, ce qui peut surprendre si vous êtes habitué à des souris très légères, notamment pour les mouvements rapides et répétés dans les jeux compétitifs.
✅ Les points forts
- 13 commandes programmables dans Logitech G HUB.
- Molette débrayable avec défilement horizontal.
- Connexion sans fil et recharge USB-C.
❌ Les limites
- Forme conçue pour les droitiers.
- Poids de 106 g, loin des modèles ultralégers.
À 79,99 € pendant le Black Friday, la Logitech G502 X PLUS permet de passer au sans-fil tout en profitant d’une personnalisation poussée.
Si vous désirez vous équiper d’une souris sans fil confortable et à l’usage polyvalent, la Logitech G G502 X PLUS est un choix adapté, en particulier avec la remise de 47 % actuellement appliquée par Amazon.
En revanche, si vous utilisez votre souris actuelle de la main gauche ou que vous n’êtes pas particulièrement adepte des macros et autres raccourcis en cours de partie, vous pouvez probablement opter pour un modèle plus simple et, éventuellement, ambidextre.
