articles.title: Cómo elegir una lavadora, refrigerador o electrodoméstico antes del precio
articles.text:
Con la llegada del Black Friday, que se realizará la última semana de noviembre, los electrodomésticos vuelven a ocupar un lugar destacado entre las compras de los consumidores. Según Fenalco (Federación Nacional de Comerciantes Empresarios, en Colombia), esta categoría concentró el 24% de las preferencias de compra durante la jornada de 2025.
Sin embargo, elegir una nevera o una lavadora no debería depender solo del descuento disponible en la etiqueta. El tamaño del hogar, la frecuencia de uso y la durabilidad del equipo son factores que inciden tanto como el precio final.
Conocer el hogar antes de mirar el precio
Electrolux identifica cuatro perfiles de consumidores según sus hábitos cotidianos. Para quienes viven solos, una nevera de entre 150 y 250 litros y una lavadora de entre 9,5 y 12 kilogramos suelen ser suficientes.
En hogares de dos integrantes, la recomendación sube a neveras de 200 a 280 litros y lavadoras de alrededor de 12 kilogramos, mientras que para familias de tres o cuatro personas conviene pensar en neveras de 300 a 400 litros y lavadoras de 14 a 18 kilogramos.
Quienes trabajan desde casa deberían priorizar equipos con tecnología Inverter, que reduce el nivel de ruido y mejora la eficiencia energética. Para espacios reducidos o mudanzas frecuentes, una lavadora-secadora de 11 kilogramos integra ambas funciones en un solo equipo y conviene revisar que exista servicio técnico en la ciudad de residencia.
El tipo de carga también importa: la frontal ahorra más agua, maltrata menos la ropa y centrifuga mejor, aunque resulta más costosa. La carga superior, en cambio, es más económica y permite añadir prendas a mitad del ciclo.
En ambos casos conviene priorizar motores Inverter, sin escobillas, que reducen el consumo eléctrico y suelen incluir garantías de entre 10 y 20 años en esa pieza.
Para las neveras, el primer paso es medir el espacio disponible en la cocina y dejar al menos 5 centímetros libres a los lados y atrás para que el motor disipe el calor. La tecnología No Frost evita la formación de escarcha y mantiene una temperatura más uniforme sin necesidad de descongelar manualmente.
Si el uso del refrigerador supera al del congelador, los modelos con congelador inferior resultan más cómodos. En todos los casos, revisar la etiqueta de eficiencia energética y buscar clasificación A o superior ayuda a reducir el gasto eléctrico a largo plazo.
El precio suele ser lo primero que capta la atención al comprar un electrodoméstico, pero una encuesta global de Samsung Electronics muestra que la durabilidad ocupa el segundo lugar entre las prioridades de los consumidores. El 48% la identificó como una consideración central, y el 36% afirmó que su importancia aumentó frente a hace tres años.
Cómo aprovechar ofertas reales durante Black Friday
Para distinguir un descuento genuino de una rebaja inflada, conviene anotar el modelo exacto y su precio normal entre tres y cuatro semanas antes del evento. Esa comparación previa es la forma más confiable de verificar si el precio de Black Friday representa un ahorro real.
También, es útil considerar otras fechas clave, como el Cyber Monday, los días sin IVA o los aniversarios de grandes cadenas, además de los períodos entre enero y marzo, cuando las marcas renuevan catálogo y los modelos del año anterior bajan de precio sin perder funciones.
Revisar alianzas bancarias puede sumar descuentos adicionales de entre el 10% y el 20%, o cuotas sin interés. Por último, conviene calcular el costo total sumando el flete y la instalación, ya que un precio algo mayor que incluya entrega gratuita puede representar un ahorro neto frente a una oferta aparentemente más barata.

articles.title: How Toronto is making it easier for actors and indies to collaborate on games
articles.text:
Canadian film and TV productions are having a bit of a moment. Crave’s Heated Rivalry and Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie. CBC’s North of North. Netflix’s Below. Over the past year, all of these titles, among others, have been glowingly received around the world, not just here at home.
But something that historically hasn’t gotten nearly as much attention is Canada’s video game industry. Despite being one of the largest game development hubs in the world thanks to over 800 studios bringing in $5.1 billion to our GDP, there isn’t all that much awareness about, well, any of it.
ACTRA Toronto, the trade union representing more than 15,000 of the city’s performers, is hoping to help with that. Over the past few years, the organization has been making a concerted effort to bring together its members and our many local developers to make games. Most prominently, this includes a recently ratified three-year agreement with publishing giant Ubisoft, which records many of its AAA titles in Toronto. But of course, that’s only one part of the equation, given that so many other games are made here, especially on the indie front.
To address that, ACTRA Toronto has recently come forth with a new low-budget video game agreement aimed at making it easier for smaller teams to work with union talent.
“This all came about through a very passionate conversation at a union picnic a couple of summers ago, where I literally was like, ‘I was a lead in a video game. Why am I not auditioning for things?'” says Elana Dunkelman, ACTRA Toronto councillor and vice president who was also nominated for a Canadian Game Award for playing the titular lead role in Ubisoft Quebec’s Immortals Fenyx Rising. She says some peers she knows were going years without work, which is a particular problem since, contrary to popular belief, the majority of actors are far from millionaires.
On the video game front, specifically, conversations with those in the industry led the union to realize that there wasn’t much information readily available for developers interested in working with actors.
“Let’s say you’re a developer and it’s 3 a.m. and you’re like, ‘Hey, you know what? I actually want to do voice,’ and you Google ‘voice actors Toronto,’ and ACTRA Toronto pops up. And then you go to the website, and there’s no rate chart. You’re just going to automatically assume that it’s way too expensive and way too difficult, and you’re going to close the browser and pick a different route,” says Dunkelman. “So we made the recommendation that ACTRA Toronto build our own low-budget indie video game agreement to make rates transparent and accessible to developers, and then […] it was developed and brought forward to members for input.”
As ACTRA Toronto director of contracts and production Gail Haupert explains, the previous lack of such an agreement created a “lot of hurdles” for developers and performers alike.
“So our performers do have to be under a contract; they have to work on an ACTRA contract of some kind,” she says. “We’re generally able to work out some terms with producers, but without having a specific agreement to point to say, ‘These are the rates, this is how our performers can work,’ there wasn’t anything for our performers to turn to if they were approached by a video game company saying, ‘We want to work with you.’ And we wanted to be able to change that. We’re all about creating opportunities both for the indie producers as well as our performers.”
With this new agreement, developers can clearly see different rates for actors depending on the budget of their game, which Haupert says will provide flexibility.
“In all honesty, we heard from a bunch of producers. We had letters of understanding in place with some smaller video games before we had a bigger agreement in place to encompass it all, so some of the feedback we heard is their budgets were too low for a specific rate, or budgets that were offered, say, to a AAA game company, the performer rates they couldn’t afford because they don’t make the kind of revenue that a AAA game does to put into their video games,” she says. “So we decided to tier our rate system. We have tiers one through six. So based on the budget you’re working with, you have a different rate of what you would pay the performer.”
View this post on Instagram
This includes options for developers who may not necessarily have the budget to fully buy out an actor (an “in perpetuity” deal). Dunkelman says this structure will help developers go into a project with a clearer sense of budget.
“I think having the rate charts ahead of time, and getting a rough estimate of how much money you’re going to need to be able to hire actors and incorporating that into your funding application, is going to be a game-changer,” she says.
That sentiment is shared by Lindsey Gardner, a veteran Toronto-based freelance casting director, voice director and voice performer. When it comes to video games, she’s voice directed on such big titles as Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed Shadows and Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora, alongside extensive work in animation, audiobooks, commercials and more.
For Gardner, ACTRA Toronto’s new agreement allows developers to tap into a vast talent pool that might otherwise have been overlooked.
“A lower budget does not mean lower quality in the performances. You still want the best. You might not be able to get high level A-listers, but the talent pool, especially with the new actor agreement, is phenomenal,” she says. “So you’re not compromising on the talent that you’re accessing. You’re just sort of accessing them in a different way — in a possibly more secure way as well, knowing that they have a resume as a performer.”
In particular, she notes that many of the actors in Toronto are trained in theatre, allowing them to bring a level of gravitas to gaming projects.
“Performers that have spent the volume of their time studying those types of performance are in the union for the most part. Those are our theatre actors. Those are our performers that are on film and television,” she says. “And so, by having this agreement, you’re getting access to the people that know not just how to use their voice, but know how to use their voice to create a character, to create depth, to create realism […] When you give direction to try something different, they have the range to try something completely different, even with that same line.”
And, of course, a lot of actors are themselves gamers, and that passion can naturally be funnelled into a game to great results. Look no further than ACTRA member Jon McLaren, whose lead role as Star-Lord in Eidos Montreal’s Marvel’s Guardians of Galaxy landed him a coveted BAFTA nomination. Notably, the Ottawa native is a lifelong gamer and regular streamer in between acting gigs, and because of that, he’s long wanted to work on more games. The previous lack of a uniform indie agreement, however, has made that difficult.
“With this new agreement, that’s hopefully going to allow us to participate more and have these conversations with indie developers. Because there’s nothing more exciting than meeting someone at a level of passion that you have, and I’m sure it goes both ways with the developers,” says McLaren. “It’s about that passion that is in some of us who just love video games and want to contribute and want to be a part of them more than anything.”
For him, the goal is to be more involved in video games, regardless of their size.
“I just want every single opportunity that I can get to be in the next video game. And it doesn’t matter if you’re a AAA developer or you’re an indie developer. I just want to work with really great people who are telling awesome stories,” he says. To demonstrate this openness, he even asked to share his personal email here for developers: hello@jonmclaren.com.
“We’re in constant conversation about how we can formulate a plan to raise awareness with indie developers, this article included. I hope we can get this out to as many people and hit developers to help educate them to know that there are options out there. Because I’ve been to a few things around Toronto, like Toronto Game Expo and stuff like that. We’ve talked to people, and they’re like, ‘Oh, I didn’t know you could do that!'” he says.
“If people have been hesitant or think that it’s not possible — anything is possible! And certainly, from my perspective, especially with these new agreements, I’m happy to help do some of the groundwork if it means we get to bring your idea and your game to life. I’m so excited to be a part of it.”
Blessing of Resthaven
So far, the first indie game to incorporate ACTRA Toronto’s new low-budget agreement is Curse of Resthaven, a recently released narrative roguelite about a governor who has to manage a cursed island while searching for his missing niece. It was developed by Toronto-based Hilltop Studios, the team behind 2024’s acclaimed Lil’ Guardsman that also has deep ties to Canada’s arts scene.
That’s because the studio’s founder, Scott Christian, is a veteran musical director, composer, arranger and pianist who’s performed across Canada, a prolific artistic background that he wanted to leverage on his burgeoning game development journey.
“We make relatively low-budget indie games, and I’m always thinking about how to bring a level of polish and production value that lifts us above the pack. With both Lil’ Guardsman and Curse of Resthaven, we had wonderful artists, but very small teams and no dedicated animators. So the creative math became: let’s go all-in on full voice acting to compensate a little,” says Christian.
“And that gamble really paid off. I know firsthand that people’s memories of our games often suggest there’s more animation than there actually is! I think a lot of that is the power of voice acting. Great performances give characters a sense of life and personality that can literally trick your brain as you lose yourself in the experience.”
Given that Christian’s network of friends now consists of many folks in both the game development and acting scenes, he says he was inspired to help come up with a way to better combine those two fields. This led him to work closely with ACTRA Toronto to develop the new low-budget agreement and incorporate it into Curse of Resthaven, his sophomore game.
“He was just so supportive and just a huge champion for this agreement, and he provided his input. And then when he was ready, he actually piloted it, and he’s been very vocal online about the amazing actors that he has cast in his game, and the fact that he had piloted the agreement,” says Dunkelman. “I think having such a strong voice in the indie space like Scott is so important because a lot of what I’m learning as [someone who is] not a developer is that word of mouth is just so important. Because people talk to each other and learn from each other, and it’s such a strong community. And having Scott champion it has been so, so amazing.”
“I think one of the real benefits of the new agreement is that it’s something that’s been developed with input from ACTRA membership, so actors can take it to their agents and it feels very solid and legit,” explains Christian. “That’s a lot easier than presenting an agent with a Frankenstein’d, one-off contract that’s been cobbled together for the individual project. In our case, the voice cast were all people who were excited about working on the game, and having the agreement in place made it a really smooth process to make that happen.”
Certainly, Curse of Resthaven speaks for itself with its impressive assortment of seasoned Canadians actors from across the film, TV and, yes, gaming spaces. This includes Wade Bogert-O’Brien (Beacon 23), Raoul Bhaneja (Star Trek: Starfleet Academy), Jan Alexandra Smith (Mass Effect), and Alana Bridgewater (Cuphead).
For Bogert-O’Brien, a longtime friend of Christian, Curse of Resthaven presented the special opportunity to lead the sort of narrative adventure game he adored as a kid while doing something uncommon in the space.
“So many indie games don’t have voice acting at all. Even narrative-heavy visual novel-style games often don’t have full voice acting. My guess is that this largely comes down to cost, but I think voice acting really adds a lot to the experience and immersion of a game,” he says. “It’s been really cool to see how excited so many players are that Curse of Resthaven is fully voiced. Without this agreement I probably wouldn’t have been able to be involved at all. Either Hilltop wouldn’t have been able to afford to do voice acting or they would have hired non-union performers.”
He adds that it’s a good deal for both performers and developers, especially in the long-term. “The structure of this agreement seems to allow the studios to engage ACTRA performers under an affordable day rate, but ensures those actors will be compensated additionally if the game becomes a big hit,” he explains. “This seems like a fair compromise for the studios to be able to afford to engage union performers, while ensuring performers will get a fair share of the proceeds from their work.”
Curse of Resthaven is out now on Steam!
Congratulations to @playhilltop.bsky.social on launching Curse of Resthaven, the first game made under the ACTRA Toronto Low Budget Video Game Agreement.
— ACTRA Toronto (@actratoronto.bsky.social) October 29, 2026 at 1:24 PM
Bhaneja, who plays General Oliver Bolingbroke in Curse of Resthaven, says he enjoys the transformative nature of gaming work and was “thrilled” to channel that in an independent Canadian project with longtime theatre collaborator Christian.
“I need to work on union projects. I am a member for 30 years and many decades with SAG-AFTRA as well, so it’s important to me,” he says. “A new agreement that supports independent Canadian developers and with roles I am interested in playing makes it a no-brainer. These guys wrote some intelligent story and dialogue so it wasn’t just grunts, yells and other efforts!”
He says union talent is a “great boon” for indie developers, and Curse of Resthaven is the perfect example of that.
“The quality of some of the performers is very high, as they recruited some of the best theatre actors in Toronto and around to contribute, particularly for a period/fantasy game. It’s nice to have that weight behind it,” he says. “I hope this allows for more collabs in the future between union actors and creators. As long as we are compensated for our work and have a slice of future profits, it’s fair to me.”
And best of all, Hilltop’s success proves that indies don’t need extravagant equipment to produce results. By Christian’s own admission, voice recordings for both of his games were done with actors in his basement studio under the direction of him and co-writer Matt Bernard.
“There are options at pretty much every scale and budget. If you have the money, you can bring in an external team, rent a beautiful recording studio, and get some absolutely stunning results. But if you have someone on your team who handles sound or audio, a half-decent microphone and a reasonably quiet space can get you surprisingly far,” says Christian.
“We’ve won awards for the voice work in our games, and I can tell you that our recording setup is much, much closer to the latter than the former! You don’t need a AAA production pipeline to get wonderful performances. You need good actors, someone who can give them direction, and a little bit of care and attention to the process. Start with what you have and don’t let the lack of a fancy setup scare you off.”
Next steps
Of course, the low-budget agreement is just one part of ACTRA Toronto’s wider gaming push.
For Dunkelman, a key focus is spreading the word about working in games in general. Those efforts are clearly on display, as she’s frequently been with fellow ACTRA Toronto member Myles Dobson (The Next Step), Samy Osman (Rainbow Six Siege) and other colleagues at events like the XP Game Summit and Toronto Game Expo throughout their outreach efforts. Dunkelman says she’s heartened to see the community start to recognize actors at these shows and ask for more information about the union, and she has hopes to take that even further.
“My dream is that we get into schools to start not only providing information about the union and the agreement, but also skills sharing where we can share tips and tricks on working with actors, so that they feel more confident about actually incorporating voice into their games. Because I think sometimes developers don’t even consider that, and that’s okay. Obviously, some games don’t have voice, and that’s totally fine,” she says.
“But if there are any barriers in terms of someone maybe being nervous about working with an actor or unsure, I want them to feel so confident and have the skills to be able to direct actors, to put out a casting call that they know that they’re going to get the the right voice for that character because they know how to create a breakdown. I want it to be so second nature by the time that they get into the workplace that they’re excited to work with actors. They are already thinking about voice as opposed to adding it on at the end or not even considering it.”
So far, Haupert says she’s optimistic based on ACTRA’s conversations with studios.
“In all honesty, we’ve seen a lot of games come forward. We had one game from around 2020 that came forward. We told them the rates. They said, ‘Sorry, we can’t afford it,’ tried to go off and do it non-union, came back to us and said, ‘We couldn’t find the voices to do it non-union,” she says. “[They] turned the whole thing into an ACTRA production, got the voices banged out in one session, and the game — I don’t think I can name the game right now — went on to be pretty successful after that. And then this company wanted to keep working with us because of the caliber of the voices that they were able to get.”
Christian wholeheartedly agrees.
“I hope that five years from now, we can look back and say this agreement helped encourage more indie teams to embrace voice acting in their games, and gave more professional actors opportunities to get into the medium. So many of them are hungry to!” he says. “It was really cool to have a handful of recognizable names in the cast of Curse of Resthaven, but there’s also an enormous wealth of underexposed and under-utilized talent here in Toronto. We have so many phenomenal performers who haven’t become household names, but are absolutely attainable at an indie budget level.”
While this might all seem like “inside baseball,” Dunkelman brings it all back to the average gamer with a relatable anecdote of recently playing through the Mass Effect trilogy, which stars Canadian actors Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale. In the wake of the closure of Edmonton-based Mass Effect developer BioWare, we’ve seen Meer and Hale back hundreds of thousands of fans who have passionately called for the return of the beloved sci-fi series.
“You spend more time with a video game character than you do for any character for a TV show or movie — hundreds of hours. No wonder people get extremely attached to characters!” she says. “And I think that’s something I’m really trying to reiterate to performers and tout why it’s important to have experienced actors and what we bring to a game.”
More information on ACTRA Toronto can be found on the union’s website.
The organization is also hosting a free panel on Monday, Nov. 23 at George Brown Polytechnic Waterfront to discuss bringing voiceover to games and share more about the new low-budget agreement.
Curse of Resthaven is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2 and PC.

articles.title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
articles.text:
Frontier models are improving design automation, but layouts, waveforms, and other semiconductor-specific data presents challenges that general-purpose AI has yet to fully overcome.
Key Takeaways:
- Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure.
- Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical.
- Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures.
Experts at the Table: Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence; Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at Siemens EDA; Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at Synopsys; and Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.
L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako.
SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management?
Drako: The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data.
Alpert: There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing, even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them.
Balasubramanian: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do.
Narayanaswamy: In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’
Drako: An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used.
Narayanaswamy: If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve.
Rance: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to help with real IP reuse, but it comes back to those foundational pillars that our customers are seeing in that challenge — quality, trust, and how we cover and trace it.
SE: Scaling was mentioned right off the bat. What does this mean for EDA data management today?
Drako: An engineering project to design a chip may be 10 engineers, 100 engineers, or 1,000 engineers. But what we want, to overcome the productivity issues that everyone’s bringing up, is to use agents to augment those engineers. So maybe have those engineers, instead of operating in 10 workspaces in one workspace each, have 10 or 20 agents that each of them is directing. They get parallelism with all these agents doing work, and they’re more like the director of the orchestra, and so their productivity goes up. To do that, those agents need workspaces. They’re checking stuff out of the version control system or out of the design management system, they’re doing work on it, and then they’re checking it back in, and so you’ve just 10× or 20×’d the load on your design management system, your network file system (NFS), and you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy from Cadence or Siemens or Synopsys or Keysight, or whoever, because you know that that much more is going on. So there’s a scaling issue. We focused on scaling the design management piece, which we’ve always been very strong at. But if you go and say, I’ve got 1,000 engineers, which used to have 1,000 workspaces that you’re managing and updating on an hourly basis, now I’ve got 25,000. The scaling problem is quite large, so that’s one aspect. Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component. NFS is a great solution, but everything has to go over the network. It’s very inefficient. It’s a very chatty protocol, so it’s slow. That means all our customers are constantly fighting speed issues with the file system and the servers. When you want to launch a regression run, and it’s going to launch at 10 p.m. when everybody’s out, but it’s going to launch on 5,000 servers, you’ve got to get all 5,000 servers to have the same data so that you can run all those regression tests. That’s a huge load on the file systems. We had one customer who would launch the regressions every night, and the elevator would stop running because they’d somehow hooked the elevator into the local network, so nobody could leave. So we introduced what is essentially an NFS booster to help with that problem. And then you’ve also got scaling of CAD. If you think about it, there’s a small organization of CAD and IT guys supporting 100 or 1000 engineers. Now they’ve got to support 100,000 engineers plus 10,000 agents, who are also trying to use that same infrastructure to get work done.
Narayanaswamy: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity. We were running some experiments, and somebody said, “Look, we run these 20 epochs, but it’s actually over 20 nightly runs. Suddenly, those 20 epochs are happening in 8 hours. So you grab the LSF queue, and your agent is hanging on to it. So the bursty workload is one thing. Predictability is another.
Drako: One of the things customers are very concerned about, and is a big focus, is security. Inside of [our technology], there are a lot of security components to limit access, often for government contracts, often for locations in other countries where they don’t want them to have full access to everything in the design. There are lots of very practical reasons that aren’t really obvious when you just think about it, and so all of those security components, security restrictions, or security controls are going to be critical in the AI execution as well because the AI can get a little rambunctious and actually kind of start creating things like you mentioned and try to get to things. We’ve seen a bunch of stories in the press about AI going rogue and digging into places it shouldn’t. With those security issues, oftentimes there’s security by obscurity, or mediocre security constraints, or people haven’t thought through the security a whole lot. There’s going to be a lot more in the data management world around security with AI in the game, because AI doesn’t necessarily have the same conscience that an employee might, and it isn’t bound by the same laws.
Narayanaswamy: That’s why we’re going around doing secure sandboxes. The more conscious customer is really saying, ‘There’s an LLM call. I need to know what access that sub-agent is going to have.’ It needs to be bounded. Most customers have gotten smarter. They used to do the air gap themselves.
Balasubramanian: One customer said, ‘Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away. If I’m trying to say, ‘Do this in a way that does this,’ that’s the way I’m actually designing or doing something. I’m actually giving advice, so we really are planning to go for air-gapped on-prem.’ I would say everyone is thinking about it right now.
Alpert: That trend’s reversing now. A year and a half ago, all customers were saying, ‘Oh yeah, only air-gapped on-prem. We need to use open-source models.’ But frontier models like Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini have gotten so good that people don’t want to sacrifice quality. They’re figuring out how they can use these and connect with them. I’d say more customers are on that side of the fence now, but maybe they’re also making special deals where they can host it themselves.
Drako: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new, there’s a big strategy question: ‘Do I go and invest in my own AI models and train them on my designs?’ These are all LLMs, and they do very well when it’s language. If I’m looking at Verilog, they’ll do well. If I’m looking at a waveform file, they don’t understand it, so they convert it to text. If I’m looking at layout, they don’t understand it. They’ve never been trained on it. They’ve never seen it, and it’s not words. There’s a big question of who’s going to create AI models that are trained on it and understand it. Is that going to be the EDA companies, or the Nvidias and AMDs who are going to go do that? They don’t know right now. Everybody’s trying to figure it out.
Rance: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that, where we’re training our own models, but then we’re creating the infrastructure to provide to them. So they can add and create their own models in conjunction with that, and get a lot more value when they combine our EDA tools with the models and the data. Then they’re using the environment to train and create their surrogate models, put that into the workflow, and build trust between the two. ‘This is what it’s doing. It’s contained to that, secured. We don’t have to worry about it going rogue.’ They’re doing it in small phases and rolling it out, but they’re creating agentic workflows that are very tightly constrained right now to prevent leakage.
Narayanaswamy: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point. When you need reasoning, if you don’t use a frontier model, you may be applying the wrong tool. But for the more domain-specific stuff, there’s this hybrid where you could have sub-domain models, even some very specialized things. Models seem terrible at things like assertions, which are very specialized temporal assertions that reason over time. And you could say, ‘Let’s have a model that is quite good at assertions — but for reasoning.’ That is the tension. Maybe folks like Anthropic need to come to the table and provide a level of trust. It’s a ‘trust me’ business with all of them. Something has to change there.
Alpert: When it comes to training models, the problem with that is like, ‘Okay, let me pick a model to train. It’s probably open-source, which means it’s probably already behind the frontier models. Now I’m going to work on that for three to four months and deploy it to the customer. But now it’s probably a year behind because some new model will come out. That means the training we’ve done has to be good enough to pass. That’s a tough, tough game, and it’s a cat-and-mouse game. It’s like, ‘I train on this model, but now I have to retrain on some new model.’ The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained. That’s happened before. Will it continue to happen? I don’t know. Maybe they’re stuck in a place. Then three months from now, it’s like, ‘Oh, there’s a model that’s pretty good at that and understands it.’
Balasubramanian: The frontier models are getting better, but one thing they still lack is enterprise data. They just don’t have access to it. On the front-end side, they can probably get away with it, but not on the RTL generation side.
Drako: They don’t need it. There’s enough RTL code out there publicly that they can get. They can do it, but there are not a whole lot of layouts in the public world.
Alpert: Here’s where I’ll disagree. We can now do skills. We can now give expertise to LLMs, so you could say a lot of people who do place-and-route actually never look at it. They’re just command-line junkies, and they get reports and the like.
Drako: That’s if you’re using the tool. But that’s the command-line interface, the log files, the human interface. The LLM can plug in and do what the human did on the tool. But if you actually want to get AI in the tool, and the results aren’t a log file, you want to look at the layout and say, ‘Oh, that’s not the layout I want.’
Alpert: It’s one thing to say we’re trying to make humans more productive, so we can now automate the job they did with the stuff with the command line. What you’re saying is that you think we could reach a higher level of PPA.
Drako: You’ve just got to differentiate those two piles.
Alpert: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap, that’s not needed. You don’t need trained models. But if you want to reach that next level, then now it’s time for some real creativity. What’s going to be really interesting is how we as an industry, for example, write a new place-and-route tool that’s truly agentic, image-based, and all that.
Drako: It will eventually happen. It’s inevitable.
Alpert: But quantum computing is a matter of time, and I’ve been hearing about it for 30 years. I’ll be retired by the time it comes out.
SE: Quantum is 5 to 10 years out.
Alpert: Quantum might be available today, but when is more than 1% of semiconductor revenue going to go to quantum? That’s my bar. Like, is that 5 years, 10 years, 20 years? I don’t know.

articles.title: 12 startups named winners at 2026 South African Startup Awards
articles.text:
Twelve startups, including Community Wolf, WaFunda and VezoPay, have been named winners at the 2026 South African Startup Awards.
Run by Startup Club ZA and now in its fourth year, the South African Startup Awards held its awards ceremony at the Homecoming Centre in Cape Town’s District Six last week, attended by around 250 founders, investors and ecosystem players and livestreamed nationally.
This year’s awards drew 179 entries this year, with 51 finalists across 12 categories. Winners were chosen through a combination of 9,000 public votes cast over five days and scoring by a 24-strong judging panel that included the founders of iKhokha, Retail Capital, OrderIn and Payfast.
Community Wolf, which builds safety products that turn ground-level observations into usable intelligence, won the AI & Big Data category, while smart metering and energy trading startup Switch Energy took Climate & Sustainability. VezoPay, which makes battery-free payment wearables, won Consumertech, and AI-native energy management platform Tavas won Deeptech.
WhatsApp-based back-to-school concierge Zumii won Digital Commerce, learning resources provider Edufern took Edtech, and WaFunda – which helps graduates unlock qualifications withheld over unpaid fees through income share agreements – won Fintech.
Skills simulation platform LEVRA won Future of Work, clinical platform GreenNotes took Healthtech, and AskMandla, a WhatsApp service that helps households employ domestic workers legally, won the Informal Market category. CitiPods, which operates rest hubs for delivery riders and outdoor workers, won Mobility & Logistics, while mobile 3D mammography provider Radhiant Diagnostic Imaging was named People’s Choice.
“This year we saw a massive uptake in public participation, with public votes more than doubling, alongside a strong field of entries and real buy-in from key stakeholders across the country’s startup and venture capital ecosystem,” said Mathew Marsden, founder of Startup Club ZA.
The awards were presented in partnership with FNB, RMB, E Squared Investments, Canva Africa and the Western Cape Government, among others.

articles.title: Forget Sonos, this stunning Dolby Atmos soundbar from a home theater newcomer is easily my favorite model I’ve tested — I'd even chose it over Bose, JBL, Sony, and more
articles.text:
Marshall’s awesome Dolby Atmos soundbar is the stunning centerpiece of my living room, and easily my favorite Sonos Arc Ultra alternative — here's why I prefer it over options from Bose, JBL and Sony
The most beautiful soundbar ever made, now at a record-low price
A Dolby Atmos soundbar can take movie nights to a whole new level — expansive, multi-dimensional audio, crystal-clear dialogue, and powerful bass can make it feel as if you’re down at the local multiplex, rather than sitting in the comfort of your own home. articles.title: Ladybird, le navigateur qui veut affranchir le web de Google, est enfin là. Et son créateur veut qu’on le pirate
articles.text:
Il a été construit de zéro, sans une ligne de code venue de Chrome, Safari ou Firefox. Le navigateur Ladybird est téléchargeable depuis le 23 novembre 2026 sur macOS et Linux. C’est déjà un petit événement en soi, car presque tous les navigateurs actuels reposent sur l’un des trois moteurs existants, Blink chez Google, WebKit chez Apple ou Gecko chez Mozilla.
Le profil de son créateur, Andreas Kling, nourrit aussi l’engouement autour du projet. Cet ancien ingénieur d’Apple, où il a travaillé sur Safari, et de Nokia, sur le moteur WebKit, connaît bien l’un des moteurs qu’il veut aujourd’hui concurrencer. C’est d’ailleurs lui qui signe l’annonce de la mise en ligne, accompagnée d’une demande peu commune, celle de parvenir à pirater son navigateur.
Ses développeurs demandent aux hackers de l’attaquer
« J’attendais depuis longtemps de pouvoir écrire ce billet. » Si la joie de Kling est palpable dans son annonce, il admet aussi qu’il reste « une montagne de travail ». Le billet a le mérite d’être transparent et rappelle qu’il s’agit d’une version alpha, encore loin de pouvoir remplacer le navigateur habituel des utilisateurs.
Kling reconnaît ainsi que certains sites ne fonctionneront pas et que le navigateur plantera parfois. Il assume aussi de ne rien promettre en matière de sécurité. « Nous voulons que les passionnés de sécurité le piratent ! Un nouveau navigateur se fait pirater, encore et encore, et cela fait partie du processus », écrit-il, avant de demander à ceux qui y parviendront d’expliquer comment ils s’y sont pris, « pour que nous puissions renforcer Ladybird ».
Pour aider l’équipe, les utilisateurs peuvent signaler un site défaillant directement depuis le navigateur, et lire chaque rapport de plantage avant de décider de l’envoyer. Les développeurs promettent aussi des mises à jour automatiques et régulières, qui permettront de suivre les progrès du projet sans avoir à compiler soi-même le logiciel, comme c’était le cas jusqu’ici.
Ladybird veut prouver qu’un navigateur peut se passer de l’argent de Google
L’équipe compte donc sur les premiers utilisateurs pour repérer les bugs et les failles du navigateur.
Ladybird est d’abord né au sein de SerenityOS, un système d’exploitation que Kling écrivait lui aussi de zéro. Le projet s’est depuis émancipé et il est porté, depuis juillet 2024, par la Ladybird Browser Initiative, une association à but non lucratif que Kling a cofondée avec Chris Wanstrath, cofondateur de GitHub, qui y a versé un million de dollars. Wanstrath estimait alors que tous les grands moteurs sont « financés par l’empire publicitaire de Google », Safari compris, puisque Google verse des milliards à Apple pour être le moteur de recherche par défaut de Safari.
De son côté, Ladybird ne vit que de dons et de sponsors et dit refuser tout accord de moteur de recherche par défaut. Sur son site, le projet se présente comme un navigateur « exempt de conflits d’intérêts », sans monétisation ni cryptomonnaie, qui ne cherche à être rien d’autre qu’un navigateur.
L’équipe s’était fixé une feuille de route précise, avec une alpha en 2026, une bêta en 2027 et une version stable en 2028.

articles.title: Überraschendes Comeback: Jensen Huang wird wieder Nvidia-Chef
articles.text:
Der US‑Chiphersteller Nvidia hat in einer überraschenden Kehrtwende seinen Mitbegründer Jensen Huang an die Spitze des Unternehmens zurückgeholt. Mit sofortiger Wirkung solle er wieder die Aufgaben als Präsident und Firmenchef übernehmen, teilte das Unternehmen mit. Auch solle Huang wieder in den Verwaltungsrat einziehen. Das Gremium habe nach mehreren Gesprächen und Treffen mit Huang einstimmig für die Wiedereinsetzung gestimmt und sei von dessen Führungsqualifikationen überzeugt. Die Nvidia-Aktie legte auf die Neuigkeiten hin im vorbörslichen US-Handel um fast ein Viertel zu.
US-Präsident Donald Trump zeigte sich hocherfreut über die Rückkehr des Nvidia-Chefs: Der Verwaltungsrat habe die „richtige und angemessene Entscheidung getroffen“, schrieb er auf seiner Plattform Truth Social. Seit Huangs Rücktritt hatte sich Trump immer wieder für dessen Rückkehr ausgesprochen und ihn in Schutz genommen.
Rückkehr zu Nvidia: Jensen Huang kann offenbar machen, was er will
Rücktritt als Nvidia-Chef nach Affären
Huang war vor rund zehn Tagen als Nvidia-Chef zurückgetreten. Zuvor wurden mindestens zwei außereheliche Affären bekannt. Eine der Frauen war Managerin des Nvidia-Kunden Megaspeed und wird laut Medienberichten von US-Sicherheitskreisen verdächtigt, vom chinesischen Geheimdienst angeworben worden zu sein. Bei der anderen handelte es sich Berichten zufolge um eine Huang unterstellte Top-Managerin von Nvidia.
Danach gab es auch mehr Fragen dazu, was Nvidia wann über widerrechtliche Lieferungen von KI-Chips nach China wusste. Megaspeed wurde zur Zeit von Huangs Affäre mit der Managerin von Behörden verdächtigt, in Umgehung von US-Verboten Nvidia-Technik nach China weitergeleitet zu haben.
Die Wendung kommt überraschend: Erst vergangene Woche hatten Interimschefin Colette Kress und Verwaltungsratschef Harvey Jones noch gesagt, Huang werde nicht zurückkehren.
Einige Brancheninsider und Verbündete hatten in den vergangenen Tagen für Huangs Rückkehr plädiert, vor allem mit dem Argument, er sei unersetzlich für Nvidia – und Nvidia sei unverzichtbar für die Tech-Industrie und die KI-Zukunft. Huang war bis zum Rücktritt das Gesicht von Nvidia.

articles.title: German startup Playbook secures €8 million to help pharma companies deploy AI safely
articles.text:
Munich’s Playbook, a startup developing neurological AI to ensure rule-based compliance in pharmaceutical industries, has raised €8 million to turn documents into data AI can read, but not change.
Heal Capital leads the round, together with Bayern Kapital and existing investor Capnamic. The company raised €2.5 million in 2025.
“Our ambition is to help Pharma use AI to develop, manufacture and deliver medicines faster and more safely, while keeping it aligned with the protocols that govern the work,” said Dr. Nikolai Wessendorf, CEO and co-founder of Playbook, in a public statement.
Playbook’s funding follows several 2026 European investments in enterprise AI infrastructure and software designed to structure operational knowledge and support controlled AI deployment.
In Germany, Munich-based Interloom raised €14.2 million for AI-agent knowledge infrastructure, Berlin-based Cognee secured €7.5 million for AI memory technology, and Stuttgart-based Blockbrain attracted €17.5 million for secure enterprise AI agents.
Elsewhere, London-based Pharosyn raised €2.5 million for pharmaceutical intelligence software, while Barcelona’s Mafer AI secured €2 million for AI-enabled R&D and regulatory workflows, and Barcelona and San Francisco-based Modern Relay raised €2.5 million for enterprise AI infrastructure.
Together, these rounds represent approximately €46.2 million in 2026 funding, rising to €54.2 million including Playbook’s new investment.
EU-Startups previously covered lead investor Heal Capital’s participation in Swiss startup CGC Genomics’ €1.7 million round, supporting regulated AI applications in oncology.
“In the pharmaceutical industry, errors can cost millions and, in the worst case, put patients at risk. The potential for AI is enormous, but unlocking it requires more than powerful models. Playbook has developed technology that helps companies ensure quality and safety when using AI. The company already counts major pharmaceutical companies among its customers. We believe this approach can define a new category of enterprise software,” adds Christian Lautner, Partner at Heal Capital.
Founded in Munich in 2022, Playbook develops Operating Memory, a data model that helps AI agents follow approved procedures in regulated industries such as pharma. The technology translates work instructions into a controlled and auditable data model that people, software systems and AI agents can query for precise guidance.
Work instructions in pharmaceutical companies define who may perform which step under which conditions, and what evidence is required. They govern processes from drug development and manufacturing to quality control, storage and distribution. Together, they hold the combined knowledge of how companies ensure quality for safe medicine.
Operating Memory makes these instructions available as structured data that people, software systems, and AI can access whenever they need them and from any system.
Playbook extracts data from files stored in document, quality and learning management systems and organises it in a graph database that is controlled, audited, and updated by humans. In this data model, a single link connects several elements together at once, such as a process step, the responsible role, the applicable conditions and the required evidence.
If a temperature sensor fails in a pharmaceutical storage facility, for example, warehouse operators can see which actions must be taken, who is responsible and what needs to be documented.
“Our vision is that every company will eventually have an Operating Memory that guides both people and AI. In the future, companies will no longer need to rely on documents that are too often not found, read, and understood correctly,” says Dr. Wessendorf.
The company reportedly has more than 50 customers, including two of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies.
The new funding will support research and development, with a particular focus on making Operating Memory available to a wide range of autonomous AI systems. It will also be used to expand enterprise sales across Europe, the UK and the US.

articles.title: India AI funding nearly doubles to $1.6B in Jan-Sept 2026: Tracxn
articles.text:
India AI funding nearly doubles to $1.6B in Jan-Sept 2026: Tracxn
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double the level in the year-ago period, according to a report by Tracxn Technologies.
This, in fact, is the highest funding grosser across the nine-month periods covered since 2019.
"India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in nine months 2026, up 96% from $822 million in nine months 2025 and 162% from $616 million in nine months 2024, marking the highest funding total across the nine-month periods covered since 2019," the report by data intelligence platform Tracxn Technologies' said.
According to the 'India AI - 9M 2026' report, the funding was raised across 87 rounds, compared to 149 rounds during the year-ago period. This indicates that the increase was driven by a relatively small number of large deals.
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
The ten largest rounds in 2026 raised $1.5 billion, 90% of the $1.6 billion total.
Neysa, a Mumbai-based AI cloud provider, raised the largest chunk, a $600 million Series B in February, equivalent to 37% of all funding. Sarvam, the Bengaluru-based generative AI developer, raised $255 million in a Series B in June and a further $90.4 million in August. Yotta raised $150 million in July.
"Series A and later rounds fell 33% to 24 from 36, and first-time funded companies fell 60% to 24 from 60," the report said.
Globally, AI companies raised $383.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026; India's $1.6 billion was 0.4% of that, ninth among countries.
Early-stage funding rose 191% to $1.3 billion between January and September, up from $434 million in the year-ago period. Early-stage rounds fell 38% to 21. The average early-stage round was $60.2 million against $12.8 million in the year-ago period.
According to the report, 111 investors backed India AI companies in the first nine months of 2026, down from 169 in the year-ago period. First-time investors fell to 43, and international investors fell to 29.
Peak XV Partners led early-stage investors with three investments, followed by Prosus and Khosla Ventures with two each. Antler, IvyCap Ventures and Finvolve made two seed investments each, while SoftBank Vision Fund and Creaegis backed one late-stage round each.

articles.title: Que signifie la petite clé qui apparait en haut à droite de votre smartphone Android ?
articles.text:
L’icône en forme de petite clé qui s’affiche dans la barre d’état de votre smartphone Android signale simplement que votre trafic web passe par un VPN. Android l’active dès qu’un réseau privé virtuel chiffre les données Wi-Fi ou mobiles de votre appareil.
À quoi sert un VPN sur Android ?
Installé sur un téléphone ou une tablette, un VPN (réseau privé virtuel) sert d’abord à créer une liaison chiffrée entre votre appareil et internet. En masquant votre adresse IP réelle (pour la remplacer par une autre), il empêche votre fournisseur d’accès ou l’administrateur d’un Wi-Fi public de voir vos activités en ligne. Vos données circulent à l’abri des regards indiscrets, ce qui est un bon moyen pour sécuriser votre navigation.
L’autre usage très répandu d’un VPN est le contournement des restrictions géographiques qui permet de simuler une connexion depuis un autre pays. Cela permet notamment d’accéder à des catalogues de streaming vidéo ou des contenus bloqués dans le pays où l’on se trouve. Pour autant, un VPN ne garantit pas totalement votre anonymat. En effet, si vous restez connecté à vos comptes Google ou Facebook par exemple, les sites peuvent toujours suivre votre profil utilisateur.
Une petite clé dans la barre d’état sur Android
Ce pictogramme confirme donc qu’un VPN est activé sur votre appareil. Si la clé disparaît, cela signifie que le chiffrement ne fonctionne plus. C’est donc un moyen très utile de voir en un coup d’oeil que votre connexion est sécurisée. La plupart des smartphones interdisent donc de masquer cette icône qui donne une information importante, mais les propriétaires d’appareils Samsung Galaxy peuvent le cacher en passant par l’application de personnalisation Good Lock (via le module QuickStar pour les connaisseurs).
Comment activer ou désactiver un VPN sur Android ?
© 01net
Chaque smartphone Android fonctionne différemment, mais beaucoup de constructeurs proposent aujourd’hui un VPN intégré à l’appareil. C’est notamment le cas de Google sur ses téléphones Pixel où l’option se trouve dans : Paramètres > Réseau et Internet > VPN > VPN de Google > Utiliser le VPN. Par défaut, il n’y a que le VPN de Google, mais vous pouvez en ajouter d’autres si vous le souhaitez.
© 01net
Pour désactiver le VPN sur Android, vous avez simplement à appuyer de nouveau sur le bouton « Utiliser le VPN ». Vous pouvez également afficher un bloc dans le panneau des réglages rapides pour l’activer ou le désactiver en un clic.
Quelques contraintes à connaître
Lorsque vous naviguez sur internet avec un VPN, certains sites peuvent identifier les adresses IP qui vous sont attribuées comme suspectes, ce qui peut déclencher des vérifications CAPTCHA assez pénibles. Certains services en ligne vont même jusqu’à bloquer totalement l’accès aux pages tant que le service reste actif. Utiliser un VPN pour chiffrer votre connexion peut aussi avoir un impact sur la vitesse à laquelle vous naviguez sur internet.
À lire : Que signifie le point vert qui apparait en haut à droite de votre smartphone Android ?
On vous conseille donc d’ajuster les réglages selon vos besoins réels plutôt que de l’activer en permanence. Les raccourcis ainsi que l’affichage du petit symbole en forme de clé devraient vous aider à mieux garder la main sur les paramètres de votre VPN Android.

articles.title: Cronología del lío de Nvidia: las fechas clave desde el contrato con Megaspeed hasta la vuelta de Jensen Huang como CEO
articles.text:
Jensen Huang vuelve para liderar Nvidia. La junta ha votado por unanimidad este lunes para reincorporarlo como presidente, director ejecutivo y consejero, con efecto inmediato. En el comunicado, la compañía aclaraba que había recibido información de “altos cargos del gobierno de Estados Unidos” y que confían en que su regreso no supone ningún riesgo para la seguridad nacional.
Como estas últimas semanas han estado muy agitadas en las oficinas de Nvidia, hemos pensado que igual tener una cronología de toda esta montaña rusa de sucesos nos puede ayudar a comprender un poco el panorama. El tema viene de bastante antes, así que bajo estas líneas te lo resumimos.
La cronología
Octubre-Diciembre 2023: Nuevo cliente
- Cuatro días después de cambiar de propietarios, la empresa de centros de datos de Singapur Megaspeed se convertía en socio de Nvidia Cloud. Hasta entonces, Alice Huang (que por si acaso quedaba alguna duda, no tiene relación ni parentesco con Jensen Huang) la había dirigido durante ocho meses.
- The Straits Times informaba de que ambos fueron vistos en un restaurante de Singapur ya en diciembre de 2023. The Wall Street Journal contaba que Kang Wei, un empresario al que Jensen conocía desde hacía años, los presentó. Y precisamente el medio también señalaba que Kang era el marido de Alice Huang.
- Precio de las acciones de Nvidia en ese momento: aproximadamente 41-49 dólares (ajustadas por división de acciones, aproximado).
2024-mediados de 2025: Washington empieza a hacer preguntas
- Funcionarios del Departamento de Comercio abrieron una investigación sobre Megaspeed en 2024. En septiembre de 2024, un oficial del departamento encontró supuestamente equipos de Nvidia aún en sus cajas en su centro de datos de Malasia, según comparte el NYT.
- Una declaración conjunta de Comercio y Justicia indica que Nvidia incluyó a Megaspeed en su lista de “no vender” en junio de 2025. Singapur había abierto su propia investigación en febrero de 2025.
9 de octubre de 2025: suenan las alarmas contra Megaspeed
- El NYT informó de que Comercio estaba examinando si Megaspeed estaba ayudando a empresas chinas a eludir las normas de exportación. Añadía que Megaspeed estaba a punto de comprar alrededor de 2.000 millones de dólares en tecnología de Nvidia y que uno de sus ejecutivos había socializado con Huang.
- Acciones: alrededor de 192 dólares, un máximo histórico en aquel momento.
Primavera de 2026: advertencias dentro del Gobierno
- Desde el Times señalaban que el secretario de Estado Marco Rubio escribió un comunicado interno clasificado sobre la relación de Huang, con fecha del 30 de marzo. CNN informa que Trump recibió una sesión informativa en mayo, antes de un viaje a China al que se sumó Huang.
- Según explican los medios, a Huang no se le dio ninguna información al respecto.
6 de octubre de 2026: Nvidia toca techo
29 de octubre de 2026: la exclusiva del NYT
- El medio alega en un artículo que funcionarios estadounidenses veían a Huang como el objetivo de una operación de inteligencia china. Sospechaban que Alice Huang era un activo de inteligencia, y ella había estado bajo vigilancia.
- Huang dijo a Bloomberg que los tratos con Megaspeed eran “completamente normales y nada inusuales”. China calificaba el informe de infundado.
- Acciones: 213,66 dólares, luego 204,64 dólares al día siguiente.
6-7 de noviembre: más malas noticias
- El mismo NYT compartía un comunicado interno donde se explicaba que el Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado de China había reclutado a Alice Huang. El Financial Times añadía que Washington creía que la relación era romántica.
- Acciones: 186,64 dólares (cierre del 6 de noviembre).
8 de noviembre: la confesión
- Huang lanzó un comunicado disculpándose ante el personal de Nvidia y su familia por infidelidad, tal y como contaban desde el WSJ. No mencionó el nombre de la otra persona. La junta anunció una investigación, pero dijo que no tenía motivos para creer que la seguridad nacional o los secretos de la empresa se hubieran visto comprometidos.
- Acciones: 178,67 dólares (cierre del 9 de noviembre).
11-12 de noviembre: una segunda relación y la dimisión
- El mismo NYT señalaba, citando a empleados de Nvidia, otra relación de Jensen Huang con Kimberly Powell, vicepresidenta del departamento de Salud en Nvidia. En ese momento el WSJ dijo que la junta se estaba preparando para destituirlo.
- La junta aceptó su dimisión el 11 de noviembre y la anunció el 12, al día siguiente. La directora financiera Colette Kress se convirtió en directora ejecutiva interina y Harvey Jones fue nombrado presidente.
- Acciones: 173,73 dólares (11 de noviembre), 166,19 dólares (12 de noviembre).
13-16 de noviembre: repercusiones y rumores de un regreso
- Reuters compartía en otro artículo una relación de Huang con una segunda empleada. Por otro lado, el Financial Times informaba de que Huang estaba sopesando regresar, pero varios medios señalaban que la junta no lo estaba considerando.
- Acciones: 162,85 dólares (13 de nov), 156,14 dólares (16 de nov).
17 de noviembre: “Honrado”, pero la junta dice que no
- Huang dijo en X que había cometido “graves errores” y que se sentiría honrado de regresar si la junta lo consideraba oportuno. Ese día, Jones dijo en la conferencia sobre resultados que la junta no tenía intención de reincorporarlo.
- Acciones: 155,46 dólares.
19-20 de noviembre: la peor semana
- Reuters y el NYT informaron de una investigación de la SEC sobre la contabilidad de Nvidia. Las acciones cayeron casi un 14 % el 20 de noviembre, y alrededor de 2,7 billones de dólares en valor de mercado se habían esfumado desde el máximo de octubre. Trump dijo que quería que Huang tuviera una segunda oportunidad.
- Acciones: 145,98 dólares (19 de noviembre), 125,53 dólares (20 de noviembre).
23 de noviembre: Huang está de vuelta
- La junta votó por unanimidad reincorporarlo tras reuniones que la dejaron satisfecha con su “franqueza y capacidad de liderazgo”. Kress vuelve a dedicación plena a su puesto de directora financiera. Las acciones subieron más de un 30 % antes de la apertura, borrando las pérdidas de sus 11 días de ausencia.
- Acciones: alrededor de 166 dólares en las primeras operaciones (cierre del viernes: 125,53 dólares).
Lo que aún está sin resolver
- La cuestión del espía. El fiscal general de Estados Unidos, Todd Blanche, dijo que el Departamento de Justicia no había llegado a ninguna conclusión sobre si Alice Huang era una espía. El NYT informaba de que funcionarios estadounidenses confiaban en sus contactos con la inteligencia china, y el país niega cualquier implicación. Singapur dijo que no la investigó por espionaje.
- Las investigaciones. La investigación independiente de la junta “continuará hasta su conclusión”, según la publicación de la SEC. Este organismo, junto al Departamento de Justicia y el fiscal general de California también están investigando a Nvidia y a Megaspeed.
- El Congreso. Huang ha aceptado acudir a una entrevista en la Cámara de Representantes el 1 de dic. El Comité Bancario del Senado también le ha pedido que comparezca.

articles.title: South Korea’s power giant KEPCO confirms data breach impacting 1.5 million
articles.text:
A threat actor breached the internal network of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) and accessed two systems containing customer, employee, and contractor data.
The attack exposed details of more than 1.5 million individuals before the company blocked access from external IP addresses and suspended the affected services.
KEPCO is South Korea’s main electric power company and a state-controlled, major operator of the country’s critical infrastructure.
The organization detected the attack on November 20, when it confirmed unauthorized access to its KEPCO ON electricity billing platform and its electronic procurement system (SRM).
“On Friday, November 20, Korea Electric Power Corporation (hereafter KEPCO), led by President Kim Dong-cheol, confirmed that some customer information held in its IT systems had been exposed,” the power company states.
“The company is making every effort to prevent harm.”
ON is an integrated customer platform that allows customers to view and pay electricity bills. SRM is the company’s procurement system for contracting services.
According to the announcement, published on Sunday, the following was exposed:
- for 650,487 KEPCO ON customers: names, ID information, phone numbers, addresses, bank names, bank account numbers, account holder names, card issuers, card numbers, cardholder names, and electricity charge and billing information.
- for 426,827 company representatives: names, ID information, email addresses, and company addresses.
- for 442,934 KEPCO employees: names, affiliation, employee ID number, mobile phone number, email address, company phone number.
The company says the data breach resulted from “advanced technologies such as AI,” but it shared no specific details about the initial access method or the attack chain.
KEPCO is notifying exposed individuals directly, has filed a report with the data protection authorities, and is coordinating with government and financial authorities to block abuse such as unauthorized transactions.
Potentially exposed individuals are warned that the exposed information could be used for targeted phishing and impersonation. They are advised to report any attempts to the police or Korea’s Internet and Security Agency.
It is also recommended to avoid installing unknown apps, entering information into suspicious forms, and sharing sensitive data or verification codes over calls or texts.
A threat actor using the “Noiem” alias has claimed the attack and advertised the breach on a hacker forum on November 19, saying that they had KEPCO user data, supplier records, and bidding and contract documents.
South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission separately confirmed that KEPCO received an email from a hacker claiming data theft on November 19.
While these claims match the available evidence, attribution to Noiem remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Associations of Physical Activity and Sedentary Time From Childhood to Adolescence With Cognition in Adolescence: The PANIC Study. Pediatric Exercise Science, 2026; 38 (3): 268 DOI: 10.1123/pes.2025-0083
