Banking
Kenya’s big banks want more time
Kenyan banks and the central bank are already arguing over one capital deadline. Now, the country’s biggest lenders want to push it back further.
Top Kenyan banks have asked the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) to delay new capital requirements by at least 12 months, arguing that implementing them during the 2027 election year could slow lending to businesses and households.
The rules are scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Explain like I’m new here: The CBK wants stricter rules for banks considered too important to fail. These are large, highly connected lenders whose collapse could disrupt the wider economy.
Under the proposed rules, these banks would have to hold additional capital buffers of 0.5% to 2.5% of their loan books. Banks falling below a specified capital ratio of 8.625% would also face restrictions on paying dividends to shareholders.
The idea is to ensure Kenya’s biggest lenders can absorb losses without risking the financial system.
Why the pushback? Kenya’s banks are worried about losing momentum. Private-sector credit growth recovered from a 2.9% contraction in January to 10.6% growth in September 2026.
The Kenya Bankers Association (KBA) argued that requiring banks to hold more capital could limit lending, particularly to small businesses and farmers, just as credit demand is recovering.
Another disagreement already exists: The CBK and Kenya’s Treasury are at odds over when all commercial banks must meet a KES 10 billion ($77 million) minimum capital requirement.
The CBK is sticking to December 2029, while Treasury wants to extend the deadline to 2032. The industry’s request for a one-year pause concerns different rules aimed specifically at the biggest banks.
Zoom out: Kenya’s smaller banks are fighting for more time to raise their minimum capital. Now, the largest lenders want more time to build additional buffers. The CBK wants a banking system strong enough to withstand a crisis. Banks want enough room to keep lending through an election year.
Venture Capital
South Africa returns from Silicon Valley with a $5.7 million AI plan
South Africa went to Silicon Valley with 300 delegates and big AI ambitions. It returned with a R100 million ($5.7 million) startup fund proposal, and the man who put the first money on the table wasn’t a Silicon Valley billionaire.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced plans for a venture capital fund to support South African AI and technology startups, with the government promising to match contributions from private investors.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa wants to build a stronger AI industry, but developing AI products can be expensive. Startups need access to powerful computers, particularly graphics processing units (GPUs), to train and run AI models.
Between November 14–21, Ramaphosa led a week-long delegation of ministers, entrepreneurs, researchers, and students to California, the United States, to attract investment and learn from the world’s biggest AI companies. The delegation met executives from Google, Microsoft, and Cisco, although critics questioned the absence of some of Silicon Valley’s most prominent CEOs.
State of play: During the visit, Andile Ngcaba, founder of investment firm Convergence Partners, proposed the fund and offered to contribute R25 million ($1.4 million), provided other investors joined him.
Ramaphosa backed the proposal and said the government would match private-sector contributions. However, the government hasn’t specified its contribution, and no foreign investors have been confirmed as funders.
Between the lines: South Africa went looking for international AI investment, but the fund’s first named backer is a local entrepreneur. Ngcaba’s offer is also conditional; the R100 million ($5.7 million) remains a fundraising target.
Zoom out: AI startups need more than investment capital. They need expensive computing power, skilled workers, and customers willing to pay for their products. The proposed fund could help with some of those costs, but its immediate challenge is getting investors to commit the remaining money.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
  November 14, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: OPINION: Europe's rearmament risks creating empty factories
articles.text:
Weapons factories are springing up all over Europe as proof, many say, that the continent is taking its rearmament seriously. It seems so simple. Build factories, manufacture arms and kit, and Europe, faced with aggression on its eastern flank and the changing realities of a complex, multipolar world, will be able to take care of itself and its interests after decades of low defence investment.
Of course, it is not so simple. Because supply chains, the networks of production and distribution on which all manufacturing relies, are not all in Europe, and do not scale in proportion to manufacturing.
To think that they do is to believe, wrongly, that a company may get funding, massively improve its production capacity, and never have to worry that a chip, or some unusual component, might stop it from manufacturing anything.
Factories do not exist in isolation: they rest on broad industrial foundations, the absence of which means they cannot deliver. Hence Europe cannot both rebuild its defence industry and let its wider industrial base atrophy. To ramp up military manufacturing is also to ramp up manufacturing as such.
The industrial policy question
The question, then, relates not to whether Europe has enough factories. Indeed, weapons factories are expanding at three times the rate they did in peacetime, covering some 7 million square metres of new industrial development, but whether Europe is pursuing the right industrial policy.
For decades, parts of Europe have gone in precisely the wrong direction: France through de-industrialisation, and Germany through policies that suggested defence manufacturing, direct or indirect, was something to be avoided.
Whether such a policy is right depends on the kind of technology involved. For instance, there are emerging forms of technology, such as those developed by SpaceX, which in effect shape and scale the whole market. The companies making these kinds of products may need components at a volume that has never been needed, limiting vendors and capacity.
On the other hand, there are technologies that have a mature market, developed by companies that are just a tiny proportion of that market; the supply chains can thus absorb additional demand without trouble.
Between these two poles are the kinds of technologies whose market is developing. Here, supply can grow along with the manufacturers, but there needs to be some shared certainty about the future of that market and coordination, usually from the government, as well as long-term buying commitment that justify the investment from suppliers.
When markets cannot meet demand
In the eyes of some European governments, all technology belongs to this second class. In other words, it’s as if suppliers and manufacturers will expand together so long as there is demand.
But in my own world of optical communications and in similarly advanced fields, such as quantum, this just isn’t the case. There is no real market to speak of; suppliers may lack both confidence and capital; and, in short, governments have to step in to ensure that there is the supply, the talent and the sourcing to support the manufacturer as they increase capacity.
In practice, they may need to invest in shared facilities or make long-term buying commitments.
Supply chains are ecosystems, not chains
In many ways, the term supply chain is an unhelpful metaphor. It isn’t really a chain, with various links along the way. It’s more of a network, or an ecosystem.
Components are not homogeneous; some are sourced from mature markets, others from small ones, others from highly specialist ones. An advanced system is made up of a wide range of parts all at different phases of industrial maturity. All require a different approach to sourcing. All come with their own challenges.
You can replace a standard part because there is plenty of supply. That isn’t true for a highly specialist one. Indeed, some may not be replaceable.
Here, governments must think hard about what is easy to buy, what requires coordination from its suppliers, and what must have an industrial base built around it.
Rearmament means reindustrialisation
If there is one point that I wish to get across in this piece, it is this: rearmament is not a simple matter of building factories.
A factory can only produce what a factory produces if all the parts that make up the final product are there in sufficient quantities. Today, that means optics, machinery, advanced materials, and chips, as well as those individuals with the skill and experience to work with them, must be available.
And until they are, a factory can only do so much. It certainly cannot drive European rearmament.
The hard but necessary question that European policymakers need to ask themselves is whether the network of suppliers on which factories rely are in place, and sufficiently sophisticated to support the mass-production of arms and equipment for the long term.
If the answer to that question is no, then defence-industrial growth is at an impasse. More defence factories means, or ought to mean, stronger, broader industrial ecosystems in which defence is just one major area of output among many.
Effective European rearmament is European reindustrialisation.
Perhaps the real risk here is mistaking what looks like rearmament for rearmament proper, and growing complacent when, to state the obvious, constant vigilance and effort are what’s required.
We in Europe must rebuild the industrial base that makes defence factories possible.

articles.title: El Tamagotchi que nació en 1996 cumple 30 años y hoy es un accesorio retro
articles.text:
El Tamagotchi cumple 30 años desde que Bandai lo lanzó en Japón el 23 de noviembre de 1996. La mascota digital de tres botones revive como icono retro, impulsada por adultos que crecieron con ella, jóvenes atraídos por la estética de los 2000 y niños que descubren ahora su sistema de cuidados.
El aniversario confirma que el pequeño dispositivo con forma de huevo no quedó limitado a una generación. La compañía japonesa busca convertirlo en un objeto de colección, un accesorio de moda y una puerta de entrada al juego para nuevos usuarios. Las celebraciones incluirán lanzamientos especiales, colaboraciones y una aparición en las pantallas de Times Square, en Nueva York.
El Tamagotchi nació de una idea ligada al cuidado
Taro Tsuji, director ejecutivo de Bandai y responsable de Tamagotchi, explicó que el origen del juguete estuvo en una imagen cotidiana de Japón: un niño que atrapa un insecto, lo guarda en un recipiente y lo cuida.
Esa costumbre se trasladó al mundo digital mediante un aparato pequeño, portátil y con una mascota virtual que exigía atención. El usuario debía alimentarla, limpiarla, jugar con ella y vigilar su estado. Si descuidaba esas tareas, el personaje podía enfermar o desaparecer.
Bandai desarrolló el producto en una etapa de dificultades financieras, cuando la compañía buscaba lanzar algo distinto. La mezcla entre un objeto de bolsillo, una pantalla de cristal líquido y una rutina de cuidado convirtió al Tamagotchi en un fenómeno durante los últimos años del siglo pasado.
Tres generaciones sostienen el regreso de la mascota virtual
Tsuji divide a los compradores actuales en tres grupos. El primero está formado por personas de alrededor de 30 años que recibieron un Tamagotchi durante el lanzamiento original. Para ellos, el juguete funciona como un vínculo con la infancia.
El segundo grupo reúne a jóvenes de 20 años que conocieron la franquicia por la serie animada de 2008 y por el regreso de la moda ‘dosmilera’. El tercero corresponde a niños que se acercan al dispositivo como una experiencia distinta a los teléfonos y las consolas actuales.
La nostalgia retro ayudó a expandir la marca desde 2025. Tsuji vinculó ese impulso con el llamado “boom de las niñas de Heisei”, una tendencia japonesa que recupera la estética, los accesorios y la cultura popular de las décadas recientes.
“Sin este auge de nostalgia retro, no habríamos podido crear una ola tan grande como la actual”, señaló el ejecutivo. Según su explicación, Bandai llevaba tiempo preparando productos y estrategias para conectar con ese interés.
Los adultos compran juguetes para recuperar recuerdos
El aniversario coincide con una tendencia entre adultos que adquieren juguetes vinculados con su infancia. Valerie, una compradora austriaca entrevistada por EFE en Harajuku, contó que su madre nunca le compró un Tamagotchi y decidió obtener uno al ver los productos del 30 aniversario.
Para ella, el objeto comparte una lógica con Furby, Polly Pocket, Playmobil y otros juguetes populares durante los años noventa. Comprar uno en la adultez permite volver, aunque sea por un momento, a una etapa asociada con menos responsabilidades laborales.
Sayran, una seguidora australiana de la franquicia, mantiene varios dispositivos en su bolso y los cuida durante todo el día. Recibió su primer Tamagotchi mientras estudiaba desde casa y lo sintió como “su primer amigo”.
El dispositivo ocupa una posición particular frente al teléfono móvil. No busca reunir todas las funciones digitales, sino concentrarse en una tarea sencilla: cuidar a un personaje virtual. Esa limitación también explica su vigencia como accesorio y objeto de colección.
Bandai busca convertirlo en accesorio de moda
La empresa ampliará esa estrategia con los Tamagotchi Ring, anillos jugables que llegarán a partir de febrero como parte de las celebraciones. La propuesta intenta integrar la mascota virtual en el estilo personal de quienes cuelgan los dispositivos de bolsos, mochilas o llaveros.
Tsuji considera que el pequeño huevo ofrece una alternativa a la frialdad tecnológica del celular. Su formato permite llevarlo visible, tocar sus botones y establecer una rutina breve de interacción con el personaje.
Bandai también busca acercarse a los niños mediante colaboraciones. Una de ellas fue desarrollada con Roblox, plataforma donde los jugadores pueden trasladar avatares y participar en experiencias vinculadas con Tamagotchi.
El modelo original utilizaba una pantalla sencilla de cristal líquido. Durante tres décadas, la franquicia incorporó infrarrojos, pantallas a color, conexión Wi-Fi y nuevas funciones de interacción. Tsuji atribuye parte de esa continuidad a la escucha activa de los seguidores en internet.

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
articles.text:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.
Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.
Every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.
He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.
On failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.
For team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.
Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

articles.title: Amazon starts putting $5 delivery price hike warnings on packages in fight against NYC labor bill
articles.text:
Facepalm: Amazon isn't backing down in its fight against a New York City labor bill that would force certain delivery operators to directly employ drivers. After it recently used its website and app to warn customers about potential price rises of up to $5 per order, the company is now placing the same warnings on stickers being applied to packages. Unsurprisingly, a lot of people aren't too pleased about this, with some customers questioning how honest Amazon is being about the claim.
A photo posted to Reddit's Amazon Prime community shows what New Yorkers are now finding on their doorsteps. The sticker warns that the City Council could add up to $5 to an order and includes a QR code shoppers can scan to contact their council member. As reported last week, Amazon's online warning appeared alongside its Black Friday deals, complete with an "Act now" button that brought up a prewritten objection to the bill.
"Probably missing some key information on that sticker," wrote one Redditor. Quite a bit, as it happens. The Delivery Protection Act, also known as Intro 518, contains no per-order fee, and Amazon's message to customers doesn't explain how it arrived at $5.
Something about this just feels off to me
by u/Playful_Bowler_5805 in amazonprime
What the bill would change is who pays the person bringing your orders to your door. Despite driving Amazon-branded vans and wearing Amazon-branded clothing, many drivers are employed by small businesses called Delivery Service Partners rather than Amazon itself. To keep operating its delivery stations in the five boroughs, Amazon would need a city license and would have to hire the drivers who spend more than eight hours in any 30-day period making deliveries from those sites. Workers who sort packages there would also be covered.
Amazon says the proposal threatens more than 40 of its delivery partners in the city and the livelihoods of their 5,000-plus employees. There is a provision for those drivers, though. If a partner lays them off because Amazon ends its contract to comply with the law, Amazon would have to offer them their jobs on terms at least as good as before.
Amazon says it could move its delivery stations outside the city, leaving New Yorkers waiting longer and paying more. Mayor Zohran Mamdani backs the bill, while Council Speaker Julie Menin has called the campaign "deceptive."
"If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong," Menin said.

articles.title: Black Magalu: Edge 70 Fusion Plus (512 GB) tem o menor preço que já vimos
articles.text:
Black Magalu: Edge 70 Fusion Plus (512 GB) tem o menor preço que já vimos
Celular da Motorola com tela AMOLED de 144 Hz e câmera Sony de 50 MP recebe desconto de 43% no Pix com cupom na semana da Black Friday 2026
O Edge 70 Fusion Plus de 512 GB está em oferta por R$ 2.399 no Pix com cupom LU300 no Magazine Luiza. O celular da Motorola, com tela AMOLED de 144 Hz e câmera Sony de 50 MP, atinge o menor preço visto pelo Achados, com desconto de 43% sobre o original de R$ 4.199, a dias da Black Friday 2026.
A tela Extreme AMOLED de 6,8″ do Edge 70 Fusion Plus é pouco maior que a de 6,78″ presente no Edge 70 Fusion. Com taxa de 144 Hz e brilho de até 5.200 nits, ela reproduz cores excelentes com fluidez acima da média, além de ter visibilidade garantida. O vidro Gorilla Glass 7i protege-a em acidentes diversos.
Seu chip Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 e os 12 GB de RAM física dão conta de apps em multitarefa e funções do Moto AI. Os 512 GB de espaço interno dão e sobram para guardar muitos vídeos e fotos.
O kit de câmeras inclui wide com sensor principal Sony LYTIA 710 de 50 MP e OIS, ultrawide de 13 MP para cenas ao ar livre e telefoto de 10 MP com zoom óptico de 3x para aproximações, ausente no Edge 70 Fusion. A frontal de 50 MP, mais nítida que a de 32 GB de seu “irmão”, tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
O corpo do Edge 70 Fusion Plus possui certificações IP68/IP69 e MIL-STD810H, que conferem proteção contra poeira intensa, mergulhos acidentais e altas temperaturas.
Sua bateria de 5.200 mAh resiste a até 39 horas, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao carregamento TurboPower de 68 W permite receber uma carga completa em apenas 10 minutos.
O Motorola Edge 70 Fusion Plus de 512 GB (R$ 2.399 no Pix com cupom LU300) começou a ser atualizado para o Android 17 e por isso, só conta com mais dois updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Motorola possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0 e NFC.
A Magalu e outras lojas estão se preparando para a Black Friday 2026 nesta sexta-feira (27), oferecendo cupons de promoções em eletrônicos com descontos e condições especiais desde o início até o fim do mês.
Acompanhe o Achados no Telegram ou WhatsApp e aproveite todas as ofertas.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Peninsula Energy Halts Trading After Cyber Incident Hits US Uranium Mine
articles.text:
Australian uranium company Peninsula Energy (ASX: PEN; OTCQB: PENMF) has requested a trading halt after a cybersecurity incident hit its uranium mine in the United States.
The incident, the company told the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX), occurred on Friday night and impacted the Lance Project in Wyoming, US.
“The company is undertaking a preliminary investigation of the incident and an assessment of the timing and impact, which will temporarily affect its operations,” Peninsula Energy said in a Monday filing.
According to the filing, the incident resulted in a breach of its “operating system”, while administrative systems in the US and Australia were not affected. It did not specify which technical systems were compromised or whether uranium production had been interrupted.
“Peninsula wishes the trading halt to remain in place until the earlier of the commencement of normal trading on 25 November 2026 or when the company releases the announcement regarding the cybersecurity incident,” the company said.
The wholly owned Lance Project, located in Crook County, relies on in situ recovery to extract uranium, which is then processed into yellowcake, which can be turned into nuclear fuel.
In 2025, the US added uranium to the federal list of critical minerals, and the Lance Project, which is expected to become a key supplier, has likely become an attractive target for hacking groups.
In fact, threat actors have also used influence campaigns against rare-earth mining companies in the US and Australia, although those campaigns involved disinformation rather than confirmed intrusions into mining systems.
SecurityWeek has emailed Peninsula for additional information on the incident and will update this article if the company responds.
The attack on Peninsula was disclosed roughly three weeks after global mining company AngloGold Ashanti disclosed in an SEC filing that it detected unauthorized activity on certain systems on October 16, but said the incident was contained and its mining operations were not affected.
Between July and September 2026, cybersecurity firm Dragos observed 19 ransomware attacks targeting mining organizations. Overall, industrial ransomware activity went up during the timeframe, with North America and Europe being the most affected regions, the company says.

articles.title: Amazon snaps up Decart's AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
articles.text:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video-generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post.
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

articles.title: Hope Is Not A Strategy: What First-Silicon Success Really Takes
articles.text:
Most re-spins are caused by logic and functional flaws, not hard-to-predict physical effects.
Only about one chip in twenty now works the first time it comes back from the fab. For an industry that invests years and millions in every tape-out, that is a disconcerting thought.
It was also the starting point for a recent episode of ‘Wearing Flip Flops’, where host Ronen sat down with Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari. The conversation traveled from AI silicon and power bugs to the place of formal engineers in a verification team. But one idea ran through all of it: Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.
Here is what that idea means in practice and why we believe it matters more today than ever.
The latest Wilson Research Group functional verification study puts first-silicon success at around 5%, down from 14% in 2024. At Axiomise, that number doesn’t surprise us.
Look at who is building chips. Two years ago, the survey was shaped by a wave of new RISC-V teams, where design was moving faster than verification could follow. Today it is the turn of custom AI silicon, built not only for hyperscalers but for phones and cars too. For verification, this is an unknown territory.
Formal is in more projects than ever, perhaps 30 to 40% of them. But “using formal” can mean very different things. It might be a lint or connectivity app, assertions that only ever run in simulation, or formal trusted to sign off functional verification. Only the last really improves the chances of success at tape-out.
By our estimate, fewer than a dozen of the world’s 200-plus silicon houses use formal as a sign-off criterion today. The appetite is growing fast: at DVCon US this year, NVIDIA’s VP of graphics predicted that formal will eventually replace simulation. Yet the journey has barely begun.
That 5% is the latest point in a long slide. For years, roughly three projects in ten got silicon right first time. The figure fell to 24% in 2022 and to 14% in 2024, which Harry Foster of Siemens EDA called the lowest point in more than twenty years of tracking. In 2026 it reached 5%, while around three in four projects are still missing their original schedules.
Every one of those failures means a re-spin: fixing the design and manufacturing the chip again. At 3nm, a mask set alone costs tens of millions of dollars, and a single re-spin at an advanced node can wipe out an entire product cycle. Half of all projects need more than one re-spin, and some large chipmakers now plan for as many as four.
The data also shows where the trouble starts. Logic and functional flaws remain the most common reason chips fail and around 70% of re-spins trace back to design errors caused by changing specifications. In other words, most re-spins are not caused by hard-to-predict physical effects. They are functional bugs that verification should have caught and that exhaustive methods such as formal are designed to find.
Back in the days of the 386 and the Pentium, life was simpler. A processor was built to run a known version of Windows, and everyone understood the scope of the job. Today, an AI chip must run models from OpenAI, Anthropic and many others, and those models change far faster than any hardware schedule.
The hardware has changed too. Many AI chips grew out of GPUs, which were originally designed for graphics, so older graphics hardware now sits alongside new AI-specific units. To squeeze out more speed, designers add layer upon layer of coherency, the mechanisms that keep every part of the chip working with the same up-to-date data: one coherent NoC, then another, then coherency across whole clusters. Every layer creates interactions that never existed before, and many are never reached in simulation.
Power adds its own surprises. One story from the episode stays with us: a GPU on a test chip that refused to start. The failure showed up at system, FPGA and OS level, but the root cause was an X value read from an uninitialized FIFO, left behind by a low-power optimization. A tiny functional bug had brought down the whole chip.
Clock gating tells a similar tale. On paper, proving that a gated design behaves exactly like its ungated twin is a well-defined problem, and one that formal sequential equivalence checking is built to solve. In practice, the constraints come from firmware and software, and on large designs they are hard to capture. So, clock-gating checks tend to land at the very end of sign-off, just when there is least time to deal with what they find. The answer is not a different tool, but bringing formal in earlier, with the firmware and software teams at the table.
The people behind the study are reaching a similar conclusion. Harry Foster argues that verification has succeeded for decades by splitting the problem into specialist domains and that the next challenge is interaction complexity: parts that work perfectly alone but fail together across hardware, firmware, power, safety and security.
At Axiomise, this is the problem we work on every day. Simulation samples behavior: it checks the scenarios someone thought to write. Interaction bugs live in the scenarios nobody thought of, such as an interrupt, a power transition and a coherency request arriving in just the wrong order. Formal starts from every possible input sequence and asks whether any of them can break the design. That is why we built our apps around the places where interactions hide: nocProve for networks-on-chip, formalISA for processors, floatrix for floating-point units and footprint for redundant logic.
None of this replaces simulation. It means using each method where it is strongest. Formal excels at concurrent, control-heavy logic such as NoCs, coherency, arbiters and FIFOs. Simulation and emulation remain essential for software, performance and end-to-end system behavior. Our role is to help teams combine them in the right measures, at the right time, for the right reason and to prove, with mutation and scenario coverage, that the formal part has truly done its job.
Formal has a measurement problem. With equivalence checking, the answer is clear: the proof converged, synthesis broke nothing, job done. Functional formal is less tidy. Some proofs are bounded rather than exhaustive, and any VP of silicon will reasonably ask: “If you haven’t got the proofs, what have you got?”
At Axiomise, we answer that question by measuring formal in six dimensions. Alongside the familiar counts of assertions written, passed and failed, and the coverage figures EDA tools already provide, two measures do the heavy lifting.
Mutation means planting bugs on purpose and showing that the checkers and constraints catch each one. If they don’t, you have found a gap before the silicon does.
Scenario coverage means proving that each scenario in the verification plan can happen and always happens. Instead of claiming “every RISC-V instruction works”, a team can show that debug was checked against interrupts, that loads and stores complete under every dependency, and that each result traces back to a requirement. We built this approach into formalISA, our RISC-V app, and it gives designers, verification engineers and managers something rare: a shared language.
Tying results to requirements matters more than ever. If around 70% of re-spins begin with a changing specification, verification that isn’t linked to requirements can quietly end up checking the wrong thing. With scenario coverage, a changed requirement points straight to the scenarios and proofs that need revisiting.
That matters, because today’s leaders receive formal numbers and simulation numbers that cannot easily be compared. Without a way to bring them together, the tape-out decision becomes “let’s try it and see.” And that is how you arrive at a 5% success rate.
The big three EDA vendors build excellent tools for linting, X-propagation, CDC and connectivity checking. These apps tend to sit at either end of a project. Axiomise works in the space between, using formal for full functional verification, safety and security.
Our apps run on the axiomiser platform and work together: nocProve for complete NoC grids, floatrix for floating-point units, formalISA for RISC-V processors and footprint for redundancy and power. Their strongest results come from designs that were already considered verified, where they still find bugs others missed.
A security core, and a fix that broke something else. cheriot-ibex, Microsoft’s CHERI-extended RISC-V core, had already been verified with both simulation and formal. Within days of integrating it with formalISA in 2024, a standard RTYPE check failed in JasperGold in 20 seconds. An illegal CHERI load was never squashed: it went out to memory and the data it brought back corrupted the AND instruction behind it, putting stores, and therefore memory, at risk too. The designers pointed us to a fix. On re-running, the load bug was gone, but bit-manipulation proofs that had previously passed now failed. A fix in one corner had opened a hole in another, exactly the kind of interaction that formal is built to catch.
A vector FPU in ninety minutes. On the Tenstorrent Ocelot core, floatrix was surfacing bugs within an hour and a half of cloning the repository, on a design that had already been extensively tested.
Late, but not too late. For Akeana, our team ran footprint before tape-out, covering unexpected scenarios. Redundancy is the bug nobody looks for. In one AI design, a control bug meant that each 512-deep FIFO in a chain only ever used a single location. Reachability analysis reported 99.998%, every flop toggled, and standard coverage saw nothing wrong. Yet the chip was burning area and power on storage it never touched. It is like renting an entire hotel for a single guest.
LLMs can now produce SystemVerilog assertions, constraints and even whole testbenches. That is a genuine productivity boost, and we use AI agents in-house at Axiomise. But walk the floor at DAC this year and one question came up again and again among experienced designers: how do we know we can trust it?
AI-generated checks still need auditing. Even when they produce proofs, someone has to confirm that every corner case was actually expressed. In inexperienced hands, AI can even slow a team down, because every line needs a human review.
This is where determinism earns its place. On every engagement, we build a full mutation coverage plan. Customers can plant bugs themselves without telling us, or hand us a plan to script into the environment, while we inject our own mutations independently to avoid shared blind spots. When every planted bug is caught, you have evidence rather than hope. Our rule is simple: if we can’t show that every bug that could be planted is caught, we won’t put our name to the result.
In many companies, “DV” still quietly means simulation, and formal engineers are called in late, as rescuers rather than partners. We would like to see a different picture: formal and simulation engineers sitting at the same table as architects, designers, and firmware and software teams, from the moment the specification is written.
For teams planning their next tape-out, that starts with a few practical shifts:
- Bring formal in at the planning stage, not only at the end.
- Agree what “formal” means on your project, from apps to full functional sign-off.
- Measure the quality of formal with mutation and scenario coverage, not proofs alone.
- Tie every result back to requirements, so formal and simulation can live in one plan.
- Treat AI-generated verification as a first draft and prove that it really catches bugs.
One chip in twenty is not a law of nature. It is the result of choices, and better ones are available. Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.
Listen to the full conversation between Ashish and Ronen on ‘Wearing Flip Flops’.

articles.title: Samsung por fin arregla uno de los problemas más molestos de la Galería en One UI 9.5
articles.text:
Samsung arreglará por fin uno de los problemas más molestos de la aplicación Galería. La nueva actualización de One UI 9.5 permitirá unir varias imágenes sin recortarlas ni recurrir a aplicaciones de terceros. Conocida como Photo Stitching, la herramienta ya apareció como función nativa en la primera beta del sistema operativo en el Galaxy S26 Ultra.
De acuerdo con AndroidHeadlines, Photo Stitching (o unión de fotos) se integra en Samsung Gallery, la aplicación de galería que viene preinstalada en todos los móviles Galaxy. Haciendo honor a su nombre, la herramienta evita que tengamos que depender de la función de collage tradicional. Si bien esta última combina varias fotos en una sola, el sistema las adapta a diseños predeterminados, lo que deriva en fotos recortadas en zonas aleatorias.
One UI 9.5 deja atrás eso y une las imágenes conservando sus dimensiones originales. Esto permite colocarlas de forma vertical u horizontal sin perder información en el camino. Los usuarios podrán elegir el arreglo que deseen en función del tipo de contenido que quieran compartir. Por ejemplo, si necesitan combinar varios recibos en una sola imagen, o registrar toda una conversación, podrán apilar las capturas de pantalla sin temor a que se recorte por temas de formato.
Los usuarios que ya tienen acceso a la beta de One UI 9.5 en su Galaxy S26 Ultra pueden probar la función seleccionando varias imágenes en la galería y pulsando el botón Crear. Una vez hecho eso, solo hay que elegir Collage y luego seleccionar Photo Stitching. El sistema ofrecerá diseños específicos para que las fotografías se unan automáticamente y ampliar la vista previa para comprobar que están alineadas antes de guardar el resultado final.
¿Qué otras funciones llegan en One UI 9.5 para tu Samsung?
Además de Photo Stitching, One UI 9.5 incluye un cúmulo de novedades para todos los móviles compatibles. La actualización se ejecuta bajo Android 17 e incluye mejoras en el diseño y la interfaz de usuario, con retoques en algunos elementos. Samsung mantendrá el lenguaje de diseño que vimos en One UI 9, aunque con un estilo más moderno y diseño similar al Liquid Glass del iPhone.
Entre las funciones destacadas se encuentra un nuevo modo Pro para fotografías y vídeos, el cual ofrece un control más granular sobre los ajustes de la cámara. Dado que la beta de One UI 9.5 está disponible primero en el Galaxy S26 Ultra, el modo Pro es una de las mejores funciones para sacarle provecho a sus cámaras. Aquí podremos cambiar la apertura, velocidad de disparo, ISO, autoenfoque, balance de blancos y compensar la exposición de la toma.
También se incluye un bloqueo de apps con un PIN o datos biométricos de forma nativa. Si necesitas blindar el acceso a ciertas aplicaciones para que nadie acceda a ellas, podrás hacerla a través de tu huella o un código. El apartado de accesibilidad añadirá funciones para acceder a los controles para auriculares desde el panel de las notificaciones, mientras que los nuevos atajos flotantes brindarán acceso con un toque a los controles esenciales.
Móviles compatibles con la actualización One UI 9.5
One UI 9.5 ya está disponible para los dueños de un Galaxy S26 Ultra que vivan en Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Polonia, Alemania, India y Corea del Sur. La actualización también llegará a los siguientes modelos, aunque todavía se desconoce la fecha oficial.

articles.title: Francophone Africa-focused VC Saviu closes 2nd fund at $44m
articles.text:
Paris and Abidjan-based VC firm Saviu has reached the final close of its second fund, Saviu II, at around EUR40 million (US$44 million), and will use it to back around 20 tech startups and tech-enabled SMEs across Francophone Africa.
Founded in 2018, Saviu invested in 12 startups through its first fund between 2018 and 2023, mostly in Ivory Coast and Senegal, and was an early backer of the likes of Lapaire Glasses, Julaya and Paps.
The firm has already notched up several exits, including the sale of ICT4Dev to Push in 2023, Lapaire Glasses to Creadev in 2024, and Rubyx to Cofina last year.
The second fund is four times the size of Saviu’s debut fund, which closed at EUR10 million (US$11 million), with the final close seeing the African Development Bank (AfDB), including via a tranche invested on behalf of the European Commission, and French public investment bank Bpifrance, through its Averroès Africa funds-of-funds, come on board as LPs, along with several corporates and private investors.
They join an existing investor base that includes development finance institutions (DFIs) Proparco and the Dutch Good Growth Fund (DGGF), pan-African group Axian, and more than 60 private investors.
Saviu II will write initial tickets of between EUR0.5 million (US$550,000) and EUR3 million (US$3.3 million), with Saviu leading all its deals as either a reference minority or majority shareholder. The fund is sector-agnostic, but will target digital and tech-enabled business models in sectors such as fintech, healthtech, edtech and climate tech.
Its geographic focus is Francophone Africa, including Ivory Coast, Senegal, Cameroon, Gabon and Morocco, though it will also invest in selected English-speaking markets such as Kenya and South Africa.
The fund has already made 11 investments and recorded one exit. Portfolio companies include Cameroonian telemedicine startup Waspito, Senegal’s Soram, which recycles and leases corporate printers, Gabonese fleet management software provider Pozi, Moroccan tech-enabled real estate agency AgenZ, and South African robotics and coding platform Resolute.
“We are very happy to welcome new institutional and strategic investors within Saviu II,” said Benoit Delestre, managing partner at Saviu. “Their involvement not only validates our investment approach in Francophone Africa but also strengthens our ability to deliver greater value to our portfolio, by fostering impactful connections with corporate partners and international organisations.”
Saviu II follows the firm’s “Seed and Build” model, under which it concentrates on a small portfolio of high-potential businesses rather than spreading capital widely, and works hands-on with founders on business development, recruitment, international expansion and follow-on fundraising.
“The support of long-standing institutional investors such as the African Development Bank and Bpifrance will be a key asset to our renewed investment strategy, providing even greater support to our current and future portfolio companies,” said Samuel Touboul, managing partner at Saviu. “This milestone marks an exciting new chapter in our mission to support talented African founders, building innovative and sustainable companies across the continent.”

articles.title: Microsoft Azure flaw exploited to steal customers' API credentials
articles.text:
Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies.
Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data.
In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day.
"Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory.
Microsoft told BleepingComputer that the vulnerability impacted the Developer, Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers of Azure API Management (APIM) Classic, but that the Consumption tier of APIM Classic and all APIM v2 tiers were not affected.
According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices.
This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service.
Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed:
- Secrets stored in Named Values
- Client secrets associated with identity providers
- Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers
- Subscription keys
- Tokens used to call direct management APIs
These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions.
Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate.
However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed.
"This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned.
"However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed."
The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted.
Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access.
In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token.
"Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed.
The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances.
According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix.
BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations.
The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.
In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management.
The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected.
Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered.
Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised.
While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update.
The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update.
In a statement to BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that its November 19 remediation was fully deployed to Microsoft-hosted API Management instances and required no customer action.
However, Microsoft did not clarify why Norway's NSM continued advising customers to check their APIM runtime versions and warning that instances below certain versions remained vulnerable.
Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances.
This Azure API Management incident comes just days after Microsoft confirmed another security breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, where attackers exploited a vulnerability to steal tenant configuration information and administrator email addresses.
Update 11/23/26: Added further information from Microsoft about what APIM tiers were impacted.

articles.title: Ces coins de la carte de GTA VI cachent l’arrivée du futur GTA Online
articles.text:
Des casinos fermés, un zoo fermé, un cimetière et même une petite ville… Plusieurs zones de l’immense carte de GTA VI sont toujours inutilisées dans l’histoire et les missions du jeu. Ce qui laisse à penser que Rockstar Games y prépare son futur GTA Online, voire des extensions narratives.
Pourquoi ces zones de la map de GTA VI restent inutilisées ?
C’est le journaliste de Kotaku Zack Zwiezen qui raconte son aventure sur GTA VI et qui a commencé à émettre des théories, après avoir publié son test comme le reste de la presse. Il explique que plusieurs zones majeures de Leonida ne sont ni visitées par Jason et Lucia, ni exploitées par les missions principales ou secondaires. Zack Zwiezen a pourtant vu deux grands casinos fermés, un zoo particulièrement détaillé (surtout que ce nouvel opus a particulièrement développé la faune), un vaste cimetière et même une petite ville située dans le nord de la carte.
Il a alors interrogé Stephen Donkin, vice-président du design chez Rockstar Games, qui a confirmé que la carte de Leonida avait été pensée « pour le long terme ». Stephen Donkin ajoute que « La carte a été conçue dans une perspective à long terme et en tenant compte de nombreux facteurs. Ainsi, certaines zones de la carte nous offrent des possibilités pour l’avenir, si nous en avons besoin pour le gameplay ou la narration ».
GTA Online, nouvelle histoire… que cachent ces zones de GTA VI ?
Il y a deux lectures possibles face à cette phrase de Rockstar Games. La première : GTA VI pourrait profiter d’une extension narrative dans une future mise à jour. DLC ou mise à jour gratuite ? Impossible de le savoir, mais si cette extension était payante, force est de croire que les joueurs seraient révoltés.
Seconde lecture : ces lieux préparent l’arrivée de GTA Online sur GTA VI. Stephen Donkin a confirmé auprès de Kotaku que les casinos ne feront pas partie de l’expérience avec Jason et Lucia, les deux personnages principaux qu’on peut incarner dans le jeu. D’autant plus que cela pourrait permettre à Jason et à Lucia de gagner facilement de grosses sommes, ce qui déséquilibrerait la progression dans le jeu. Ce qui signifie peut-être qu’avec son propre personnage dans GTA Online, on pourrait jouer au casino. Attention, il ne s’agit que d’une hypothèse, mais une hypothèse plausible.
Avec la taille de Leonida, Rockstar Games a tout l’espace pour développer des activités (notamment économiques), des missions ou même faire évoluer certaines zones, sans devoir retravailler toute la carte. La carte de GTA VI étant environ deux fois plus grande que celle de GTA V, on devrait pouvoir s’y occuper très longtemps et c’est sans doute ce qui est prévu pour GTA Online sur le jeu. cela fait 13 ans que GTA Online est sorti sur GTA V. Lorsqu’il arrivera sur GTA VI, il pourrait occuper les joueurs encore plus longtemps avec encore plus de contenu, surtout avec une carte aussi vaste.

articles.title: Nuevo golpe de EEUU a China: también perseguirá los chips más básicos utilizados en televisores o teléfonos móviles
articles.text:
El Departamento de Comercio de EEUU acaba de asestar un golpe más a China. Su nueva regulación endurece los mecanismos de control sobre los circuitos integrados de 16 y 14 nm, así como sobre algunos nodos avanzados. Estas tecnologías de integración son relativamente antiguas, pero continúan siendo muy utilizadas en la fabricación de chips para electrodomésticos, teléfonos móviles y coches. Y son muy importantes para la industria china de los semiconductores.
Las nuevas normas no condicionan solo a las compañías estadounidenses; también afectan a cualquier empresa de semiconductores que utilice tecnologías y patentes desarrolladas en EEUU. Y TSMC, el mayor fabricante de circuitos integrados del planeta, lo hace, lo que lo ha llevado a paralizar una parte de sus envíos de chips a China para cerciorarse de que sus entregas satisfacen los últimos requisitos impuestos por la Administración estadounidense.
Hasta ahora la regulación de EEUU perseguía principalmente limitar la llegada a China de semiconductores avanzados, pero su estrategia a partir de ahora restringe también la venta de chips maduros. Y lo hace porque el Gobierno de EEUU sabe que estos circuitos integrados son muy importantes para China. Tanto, de hecho, que muchos fabricantes chinos de electrodomésticos, televisores, dispositivos electrónicos y coches los usan en sus productos.
No obstante, la dependencia de las empresas chinas de TSMC en este escenario es parcial. SMIC, Hua Hong Semiconductor y otros fabricantes chinos de semiconductores tienen la capacidad de producir circuitos integrados maduros, por lo que no está en juego su desaparición del mercado chino. Lo que todavía no está claro es si los fabricantes chinos de chips serán capaces de responder a toda la demanda de semiconductores maduros que reciben de sus clientes.
Los chips maduros son esenciales para la industria china. Y EEUU lo sabe
Durante los dos primeros meses de 2026 China exportó circuitos integrados por un valor de 43.300 millones de dólares, lo que representa un incremento del 72,6% frente al mismo periodo de 2025. Esta información procede directamente de los registros de las aduanas de China, por lo que presumiblemente es fiable. No obstante, lo más asombroso es que el conjunto de las exportaciones de este país creció un 21,8% durante enero y febrero, por lo que es evidente que la industria de los semiconductores fue estimulada con mucha más intensidad que otros sectores.
Durante los dos primeros meses de 2026 China exportó circuitos integrados por un valor de 43.300 millones de dólares
La demanda interna ha sostenido durante los últimos años el crecimiento de la industria china de los chips, pero las cifras que he recogido en el párrafo anterior demuestran que la demanda externa también es muy fuerte. En ese contexto es razonable que nos preguntemos de qué tipo son los circuitos integrados que están produciendo de forma masiva los fabricantes chinos.
La respuesta es muy reveladora: se trata de chips derivados de tecnologías de integración maduras, habitualmente de 28 nm o menos avanzadas. Buena parte de los fabricantes chinos de chips, como Hua Hong Semiconductor, China Resources Microelectronics o Guangzhou ZenSemi, está fabricando circuitos integrados de 28 nm o con tecnologías aún más antiguas. Y la empresa Beijing Yandong Microelectronics (YDME) va a construir una planta de 4.600 millones de dólares expresamente para producir semiconductores de 28 nm en obleas de 300 mm.
Es evidente que estas compañías no se volcarían de esta forma en la fabricación de chips maduros si no fuese una estrategia rentable, y, sobre todo, necesaria para sostener la industria china de los circuitos integrados en un momento tan crítico como el actual. EEUU es consciente de que esta capacidad de producción es uno de los pilares de la estrategia china para alcanzar la autonomía tecnológica. Este es el motivo por el que ha decidido ampliar sus restricciones a unos semiconductores que, aunque están lejos de la vanguardia tecnológica, son imprescindibles para sostener buena parte de su industria.

articles.title: Ionic Wealth secures Rs 177 Cr from Angel One, others
articles.text:
Ionic Wealth secures Rs 177 Cr from Angel One, others
The wealthtech platform will use the funds to expand its portfolio of services, technology, and footprint in India and beyond.
Ionic Wealth, a wealthtech platform and a subsidiary of Angel One, has raised Rs 177 crore in strategic funding to accelerate its growth trajectory. The funding was led by Angel One and marquee families.
This takes the company's cumulative funding to Rs 466 crore. According to a statement, all investors from the previous round also participated in the latest round, comprising business families, Bollywood personalities, fintech entrepreneurs, global CXOs, board advisors and media houses.
As part of its growth plans, Ionic Wealth will strengthen portfolio-led proposition, global capabilities, and AI integration in the wealth-tech experience. It will also scale the UHNI business and expand its footprint in India and beyond.
The fresh capital will be used to double down on the company's early bets, leverage technology, advance GIFT City-led global investing, and develop a differentiated UHNI proposition for India's leading families.
Ionic Wealth was founded in 2024 by Srikanth Subramanian, Shobhit Mathur, and Dharmendra Jain. It today has an AUM (assets under management) of over Rs 16,000 crore and more than 2,900 HNI and UHNI clients across 12+ cities.
“As investor needs evolve, our focus is to move beyond traditional product-led offerings towards a more comprehensive platform approach to wealth creation, informed by our institutional-grade investment intelligence across global markets and asset classes,” said Srikanth Subramanian, Co-founder and CEO, Ionic Wealth.
Ionic Wealth attributes its growth to rising HNI numbers, appreciation in asset value, and growing income and savings.
Dinesh Thakkar, Founder, Chairman and Managing Director, Angel One, said, “India’s wealth management industry is at an important inflection point, driven by the growing aspirations of affluent investors and the increasing sophistication of their financial needs.
"Ionic is being built to serve this opportunity by bringing together investment expertise, technology and a client-first approach. We have strong conviction in the founding team and the institution they are building."
Edited by Swetha Kannan
