articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
  November 13, 2026
- Source:
  Princeton University
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: WhatsApp permitirá enviar mensajes de texto que desaparecen al leerse una vez
articles.text:
WhatsApp prepara una función que permitirá enviar mensajes de texto que solo podrán leerse una vez. La herramienta llegará primero a algunos usuarios de las versiones beta de Android y iPhone, y añadirá protecciones contra capturas de pantalla, copias, reenvíos y grabaciones mientras el destinatario consulta el contenido.
La novedad amplía la privacidad más allá de las fotos y los videos de visualización única. Con este sistema, el remitente podrá enviar información puntual que no permanecerá disponible en el historial del chat después de que la otra persona cierre la ventana de lectura.
El mensaje se enviará desde el botón habitual
Para usar la opción, el usuario deberá abrir una conversación, escribir el texto en la barra del chat y mantener pulsado el botón de enviar. WhatsApp mostrará entonces un menú con dos alternativas: programar el mensaje o enviarlo con visualización única. Al elegir esta última opción, la aplicación enviará el contenido de inmediato, sin que sea necesario activar un ajuste permanente en la conversación.
Cuando la característica esté disponible, WhatsApp también mostrará una indicación encima del campo de escritura para explicar el gesto. La empresa busca que el acceso no quede oculto dentro de los menús, aunque su distribución gradual significa que muchos usuarios todavía no verán la opción.
Cómo funcionará la visualización única del mensaje
El receptor tendrá que tocar la burbuja correspondiente para abrir el mensaje. El texto aparecerá en una pantalla independiente, donde podrá leerse antes de desaparecer. WhatsApp explicará allí las restricciones aplicadas al contenido y mostrará que se trata de un mensaje de visualización única. Cuando esa interfaz se cierre, el contenido dejará de estar disponible para ambas partes.
En el chat quedará un indicador de “abierto”. El remitente podrá saber que la otra persona consultó el mensaje, pero ninguno de los dos podrá volver a leer el texto. La medida diferencia este formato de una conversación común, donde las palabras permanecen visibles hasta que alguien las elimine manualmente.
Capturas, copias y reenvíos quedarán bloqueados
Las protecciones anunciadas impedirán hacer capturas o grabaciones de pantalla mientras el receptor lea el mensaje en un iPhone. Tampoco podrá copiar el texto, reenviarlo a otro contacto ni guardarlo mediante las acciones habituales del chat. Mantener pulsado el mensaje no abrirá un menú de opciones, de modo que la única acción disponible será leer el contenido antes de cerrar la interfaz.
Estas barreras se aplican dentro de la aplicación y buscan limitar el almacenamiento directo desde el dispositivo que abrió el texto. Sin embargo, ningún sistema puede impedir por completo que otra persona reproduzca el contenido por otros medios, como fotografiar la pantalla con un segundo teléfono.
La visualización única no funciona igual que los mensajes temporales
Los mensajes temporales desaparecen después de un plazo establecido, sin importar si el destinatario los abrió o no. La nueva opción funciona de otra manera: el mensaje desaparece una vez que se lee y se cierra su pantalla específica. Además, WhatsApp bloquea las acciones que permitirían conservar o compartir el texto desde esa interfaz.
La diferencia puede ser útil para compartir contraseñas temporales, instrucciones puntuales o información privada que no deba permanecer en una conversación. Aun así, la función no sustituye otras prácticas de seguridad, como confirmar el destinatario y evitar enviar datos sensibles cuando no sean necesarios.
WhatsApp detectó la herramienta en la beta 2.26.45.6 para Android y en la beta 26.45.10.73 para iOS, distribuida mediante TestFlight. Por ahora, solo algunos probadores reciben el acceso. La empresa activa las funciones por etapas, por lo que instalar una versión compatible no garantiza que el botón aparezca de inmediato.
La visualización única ofrece una capa adicional de control sobre textos sensibles, pero no elimina los riesgos humanos. Verificar destinatarios, limitar datos compartidos y mantener prudencia seguirá siendo indispensable, porque la privacidad depende de las herramientas como del uso responsable.

articles.title: Why Canada invested in Cohere
articles.text:
Today we have another edition of what is becoming a quarterly accountability check-in with Canada’s AI Minister, Evan Solomon.
“Simply put, Canada is not gonna wait for others to build the AI—maybe people we don’t know or don’t trust. We’re gonna build it now.”
The last time the minister was on the podcast, it was shortly following the release of Canada’s AI strategy. This time, we’re checking in right after Budget 2026, and we talk through some of the budget components the minister is most passionate about in their support of entrepreneurs. We also cover how some of those steps are designed to help prevent more AI companies like Taalas and Tenstorrent from being acquired or fleeing south—for his part, Minister Solomon said it’s his job to give those companies reasons not to leave.
But we also talk about the big news that dropped right before the budget: the federal government’s investment in AI champion Cohere. If you’ve seen the minister on The BetaKit Podcast before, or are familiar with BetaKit’s coverage generally, this news should not surprise you.
But public investments in private companies are relatively novel in Canada, and now that every Canadian has skin in the game, they’re coming armed with a lot of questions. As Build Canada’s Lucy Hargreaves put it, “Ottawa is becoming the owner, the funder, the customer and the regulator of the same companies.” How is that going to work?

articles.title: Jensen Huang retorna ao comando da Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang retorna ao comando da Nvidia
Executivo assume os cargos de presidente e CEO.
Só durou 11 dias: a Nvidia reconduziu Jensen Huang ao cargo de presidente e CEO nesta segunda-feira (23/11). O conselho diretor aprovou a volta por unanimidade e disse ter ouvido altos escalões do governo dos Estados Unidos. Também disse estar confiante de que o retorno não representa risco à segurança nacional.
A investigação interna sobre alegações de que Huang foi alvo de uma ação de inteligência estrangeira continuará até o fim, e ele afirma que vai cooperar. A empresa também criou um comitê de segurança nacional e controle de exportações e vai contratar um diretor de compliance (Chief Compliance Officer).
Huang também volta a assumir uma cadeira no conselho diretor da Nvidia.
Na semana passada, a companhia chegou a descartar o retorno do executivo. Durante a sua ausência, a diretora financeira Colette Kress assumiu como CEO interina, enquanto a Nvidia passou a buscar uma nova liderança.
Jensen Huang nasceu em 17 de fevereiro de 1963, em Taiwan, e passou a infância na Tailândia antes de emigrar para os Estados Unidos. Formou-se em engenharia elétrica na Universidade Estadual do Oregon em 1984, tendo entrado no curso aos 16 anos, e concluiu o mestrado em Stanford em 1992. Antes disso, trabalhou como garçom e lavador de pratos na rede de restaurantes Denny’s, e depois projetou microprocessadores na AMD e chegou ao cargo de diretor na LSI Logic.
Em 1993, fundou a Nvidia com os engenheiros Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem, e assumiu a função de CEO desde o início. Sob sua gestão, a empresa deixou de ser uma fabricante de placas de vídeo e passou a fornecer os processadores gráficos usados para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, o que a levou ao clube do trilhão. Com cerca de 4% das ações da companhia, Huang tem fortuna estimada em US$ 190 bilhões pela Forbes, cerca de R$ 1,1 trilhão, o que o coloca entre as dez pessoas mais ricas do mundo.

articles.title: Jensen Huang isn't out of the woods yet
articles.text:
It’s safe to say no one expected this.
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.
Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the U.S. government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.
Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, The New York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.
With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating U.S. export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself.
Then there are the questions raised by Trump’s intervention. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.
All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.
If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.
I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market, and, ultimately, direct intervention from the president of the United States.
But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

articles.title: Físico cria buraco negro em chip e descobre que ele pode “vazar”
articles.text:
Buracos negros são conhecidos por sua capacidade de atrair matéria e impedir que qualquer coisa escape de seu horizonte de eventos. Mas um experimento realizado pelo físico Antonino Flachi, da Universidade Keio, no Japão, apresentou um comportamento diferente. Ele construiu uma versão digital de um buraco negro em um circuito eletrônico e descobriu que pequenas perturbações poderiam atravessar parcialmente sua fronteira.
O experimento não reproduz um buraco negro real, mas cria uma simulação capaz de imitar algumas de suas propriedades físicas. Ao alterar um único bit de informação dentro do horizonte de eventos digital, Flachi provocou uma perturbação que, em parte, conseguiu escapar. O resultado oferece uma nova ferramenta para investigar quais características desses objetos são universais e quais dependem das regras físicas de cada sistema, segundo informações do portal Science Alert.
Para quem tem pressa
- Físico da Universidade Keio, no Japão, criou um buraco negro digital em um circuito eletrônico;
- O sistema reuniu cerca de 604 milhões de bits organizados em uma grade que simula o fluxo de um fluido;
- O horizonte digital permaneceu estável por três horas e reproduziu fenômenos como ringdown e superradiância;
- Ao alterar um bit dentro do horizonte, o pesquisador provocou uma perturbação que conseguiu escapar parcialmente;
- O resultado não indica vazamentos em buracos negros reais, mas ajuda a investigar propriedades desses objetos.
Como funciona um buraco negro digital?
Buracos negros são difíceis de estudar diretamente porque não permitem que a luz escape de seu horizonte de eventos. Por isso, cientistas desenvolvem experimentos que reproduzem algumas de suas propriedades em laboratório. Uma das abordagens tradicionais utiliza ondas sonoras em fluidos em movimento.
Quando um fluido se desloca para dentro de uma região mais rápido do que o som consegue se propagar na direção contrária, as ondas ficam presas. Esse limite funciona como um horizonte de eventos, formando o que os físicos chamam de buraco negro acústico.
Flachi substituiu os fluidos e equipamentos físicos por um circuito digital composto por células que armazenam informações em bits, unidades representadas por zeros e uns. A estrutura reuniu aproximadamente 604 milhões de bits, organizados em uma grade. A cada ciclo de relógio, portas lógicas atualizam os dados seguindo regras inspiradas na dinâmica dos fluidos.
Essas regras simulam um fluxo que se desloca para dentro de uma região, enquanto também determinam como as perturbações se propagam pelo sistema. Quando o fluxo simulado alcança a mesma velocidade de propagação das perturbações, surge um horizonte acústico digital.
O que aconteceu quando o físico alterou o sistema?
Para testar o modelo, Flachi analisou cinco propriedades: a estabilidade do horizonte de eventos, sua estrutura, a propagação de perturbações, o chamado ringdown e a superradiância. Esse último fenômeno ocorre quando ondas podem ganhar energia ao interagir com um buraco negro em rotação.
O horizonte permaneceu estável durante três horas, e o circuito reproduziu os comportamentos previstos para o ringdown e a superradiância. Como o sistema funciona com regras digitais precisas, também permite repetir os experimentos em condições idênticas, controlando cada bit de informação.
O resultado mais inesperado surgiu quando o pesquisador alterou um único bit localizado dentro do horizonte de eventos. A mudança provocou uma perturbação que permaneceu quase totalmente confinada, mas uma pequena parte conseguiu escapar por meio de ondas de comprimento curto, capazes de se propagar mais rápido do que a velocidade efetiva do som no circuito.
O que a descoberta revela sobre os buracos negros?
O vazamento diminuiu exponencialmente conforme a alteração ocorria mais longe da fronteira do horizonte. Isso significa que a capacidade de impedir a saída de perturbações dependia do comprimento de onda e da distância em relação ao limite.
Leia mais:
- O que é um buraco negro?
- O que é um buraco negro, e por que a 1ª imagem comprova teoria de Einstein
- Buracos negros supermassivos: como se formam os maiores monstros do Universo?
O resultado não indica que buracos negros reais permitam a saída de informações ou matéria de dentro de seus horizontes de eventos. Ele mostra que as propriedades de um buraco negro analógico podem depender das regras físicas usadas para construí-lo. Assim, diferentes sistemas podem reproduzir alguns comportamentos desses objetos sem apresentar todas as mesmas características.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

The R20 did a decent job on mid-pile carpet, too, clearing large and small particles well, but required a few passes to get everything completely clean. The slightly lower score on hard floor was due to the floorhead causing debris to pool up when the vacuum was pulled backwards over the spillage.
The R20 is lightweight for a stick vacuum, which means it's relatively comfortable to use, despite a lack of any padding or shaping on the handle. In handheld mode I appreciated that the main body was compact in shape, making it easier to wield, although I did find the finger rest could dig in.
The combination of trigger-operation and a lock button for continual running makes it great for both quick cleanups and longer sessions (surprisingly, it was the only vacuum in my test to offer this user-friendly setup). Although the floorhead pivots extremely well, the connections on my test model were incredibly stiff, making changing attachments a major challenge.
The Dreame R20 uses a flashy-looking screen to convey information, including battery status (shown as a percentage) and any error messages. The modes aren't the most intuitive to understand, but after some use I ascertained that a green fan meant 'regular mode with auto-adjustment based on dirt detected' and a white fan meant 'boost mode'. You get a separate soft head for delicate hard floors, but oddly Dreame hasn't included headlamps here – instead, they're on the general floorhead, and they're not that bright in any case.
Dreame promises a maximum of 90 minutes of cleaning per charge, which is the longest runtime I've heard quoted on the market. However, you'll only achieve this on a relatively clean, hard floor – there's no 'Eco' mode, so the lowest suction option is the auto-adjusting Standard mode. I timed seven minutes of cleaning in Boost mode, which is good but not great.
The best cordless vacuum for pet hair

Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
If pet hair is your biggest vacuuming headache, the Shark PowerDetect Cordless is a particularly strong contender. It was the only model in our comparative tests to score 5/5 across every pet-hair challenge. This is a more positive result than our original review, which tested the Pet Multi Tool on human hair on upholstery rather than pet hair across multiple surfaces, might suggest.
Aside from pet hair, it also delivers strong suction across hard floors and carpets. Its redesigned floorhead helps it pick up debris when pulled backwards as well as pushed forwards, and the automatic suction adjustment takes some of the guesswork out of cleaning different surfaces.
The bendable wand is another useful addition, making it easier to reach under furniture without having to crouch down. However, all this comes in a fairly bulky package. At 3.7kg, it's one of the heaviest cordless vacuums we've tested, and isn't as nimble as lighter alternatives.
The Shark PowerDetect came top in every single cleaning test, scoring a perfect 5/5 in every pet hair test and every medium-pile carpet test. In our comparative pet-hair testing, it cleared almost all of the hair from the test surfaces in a single pass. Its excellent performance is down partly to outright power, and partly to a clever floorhead design.
Shark has added a flap that lifts to enable the vacuum to suck up particles when it's pulled backwards over them, rather than causing them to pool up, as is the case with every other vacuum I tested here. This feature is especially useful on hard floors.
Now for the bad news. The Shark PowerDetect is the heaviest vacuum in my group test, and feels noticeably chunkier and less nimble than the rest of the bunch. The weight is more evenly distributed than it is on the Gen5detect – which is heavy and also top-heavy – making it a little easier to use in both handheld and floor-standing modes than that model.
To its credit, Shark has also made a big effort to improve comfort, by shaping the handle ergonomically and adding a rubberized grip and padding. Nothing digs in or sits awkwardly as you clean, which is more than can be said for a number of other models I tried here.
Shark has excelled at the special features, but dropped the ball when it comes to basic usability. The vacuum switches on with a one-press button (good for long sessions but annoying for quick cleanups, because the button isn't reachable from the handle, so you'll need to use your other hand) and it takes a second or so to kick into gear each time, rather than responding immediately, as all the other vacuums did.
When switched on, the screen cycles though various icons representing the suction modes – a leaf for Eco, a boost icon, a target representing the Auto mode, and a water droplet to represent... actually, I have no idea what this is for. I've scoured the product manual for clues, but it's not mentioned anywhere (it's notably absent under "Instructions for use" and "Error codes").
Initially, I couldn't find any way to manually switch between the modes, so I ended up stuck in Auto, which fortunately is the most useful mode. Eventually, I discovered there's a button for mode-switching where the trigger would usually sit – a setup that took some getting used to, and felt especially counter-intuitive as I was moving between the PowerDetect and other vacuums that are trigger-operated. There's a colored ring to indicate how much dirt has been detected, but it's not immediately clear which color means what.
Usability niggles aside, this vacuum has one of the most comprehensive feature lists of any vacuum I reviewed. It can auto-adjust suction based on floor type and dirt levels, but also boost suction on the relevant side of the floorhead when the vacuum approaches the edge of a room, and brighten the headlamps in particularly dark areas. There's also an optional auto-empty dock, complete with odor-neutralizing puck.
My battery-life tests were scuppered somewhat by the fact that I couldn't find any way to manually change to suction mode for this vacuum. However, Shark promises a maximum of 70 minutes cleaning per charge, which is a very solid runtime. The caveat, of course, is that that figure is for relatively clean, hard floors, and runtimes will decrease for anything more challenging.
The best premium cordless vacuum

View Original
View Original
View Original
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Gen5detect is the best premium option. It has the best design of all the vacuums I tested, offering advanced features paired with outstanding usability. It managed the joint-longest runtimes, and was a runner-up in all the cleaning tests. However, it's the priciest vacuum of the bunch, and also one of the heaviest.
The Gen5detect was a close second behind the Shark PowerDetect in all my cleaning tests. It suffered from being slightly too powerful in Auto mode on deep-pile carpet, but the suction was strong enough in Eco mode that it cleared spillages very effectively while being much easier to push.
Usefully, Dyson has added an air intake slider to the floorhead to help release some pressure as required (this was missing the Dyson V11 that I also tested, to its detriment). It also proved excellent at handling pet hair, both with its main floorhead and its mini motorized tool.
The Gen5detect is the second-heaviest vacuum I tested, with the heaviest top section. The fact that the weight is concentrated in the top section, which is really rather long, makes it unwieldy to use, with or without the wand attached.
Dyson has added some welcome padding above the handle, but I still found the battery casing could dig into my wrist when I used the vacuum as a handheld. This model switches on and off with a one-press button, which is great for long cleaning sessions but annoying for quick cleanups as it requires both hands to be free (as with the Shark PowerDetect, the button can't be reached from the handle).
The Gen5detect is packed with special features, but unlike with the Shark PowerDetect, Dyson hasn't neglected basic usability factors. A screen near the handle conveys information in an unambiguous way – it'll spell out exactly how long you have left on the battery in your current cleaning mode, as well as flagging any issues and telling you how to fix them. This screen will also tell you, in words, which mode you're using, which after trying to decipher various icons and color-coding systems on other machines, I truly appreciated.
Like a number of vacuums in my group test, the Gen5detect can auto-adjust suction depending on how much dirt it detects on the floor, but this model goes a step further and will report the size and number of particles being sucked up as you clean via a colorful, animated on-screen bar graph. You'll also get a soft floorhead for delicate hard flooring, and it's equipped with a nice, bright laser to illuminate dirt.
You'll get a maximum of 60 minutes of cleaning time in Eco mode, which is not as long as some competitors, but still very decent. (Also factor in that the Eco mode here is powerful enough to still be very useful.) I managed 15 minutes of cleaning in the ultra-powerful Boost mode, which is excellent.
The best budget cordless vacuum
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Hoover HF3 DynamicClean is proof you don't need to spend Dyson money to get a capable cordless vacuum. It cleans well, weighs very little, and its Anti-Twist brushbar lives up to the hype by preventing hair from wrapping around the roller. The compromises are exactly where you'd expect for the price: battery life, build quality and a little extra noise, but none are deal-breakers if you're shopping on a budget.
The HF3 punches well above its price tag when it comes to cleaning. During testing it picked up everyday dust, crumbs and pet hair with confidence across both carpets and hard floors, only occasionally needing an extra pass on thicker rugs or larger debris. Hoover's Anti-Twist brushbar also deserves a mention, preventing hair from wrapping around the roller and removing one of the more tedious maintenance jobs altogether.
Weighing just 2.54kg, the HF3 is one of the lightest cordless vacuums we've tested, and you notice it straight away. It's easy to carry upstairs, comfortable to push around the house, and the self-standing design is surprisingly handy when you need to stop and move furniture. It isn't quite as nimble around chair legs and awkward corners as pricier Shark or Dyson models, but for everyday cleaning it's an easy vacuum to live with.
Hoover has focused its budget where it matters. You get practical extras including HEPA filtration, LED headlights, a battery display and Anti-Twist technology, rather than flashy features you'll rarely use. The trade-off is that some of the plastics and attachments feel a little flimsy, while the narrow dustbin can be awkward to empty completely, but those feel like reasonable compromises at this price.
The quoted 60-minute runtime comes with a fairly hefty asterisk: it's only achievable in Eco mode. In day-to-day cleaning you'll spend most of your time in Standard mode, where battery life is closer to half that figure, while Turbo empties the battery in around 15 minutes. That's plenty for flats and smaller homes, but larger houses will probably need a mid-clean recharge.

The Detect Pro is perfectly capable of dealing with day-to-day cleaning, but outright suction isn't its biggest strength. It performed particularly well on hard floors, where the automatic Detect mode quietly adjusted power as we moved between surfaces and dirtier patches. The main drawback is the floorhead, which has a habit of pushing debris into small piles when pulled backwards – something Shark later addressed on the PowerDetect.
This is where the Detect Pro earns its place in the lineup. It's the lightest vacuum in our testing, making it effortless to carry upstairs, steer around furniture and convert into a handheld. While the wand can be a little fiddly to remove, it's an exceptionally easy vacuum to live with, particularly if you clean little and often.
Shark packs in plenty of useful technology without overcomplicating things. Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and dirt levels, while edge detection boosts power where dust tends to collect. The optional auto-empty dock is another welcome addition. The small dustbin and limited selection of included tools prevent it from matching the Dyson Gen5detect for overall usability.
Battery life is respectable rather than exceptional. While Shark quotes up to 60 minutes in Eco mode (40 minutes in the US), using Detect mode or Boost cuts that figure down considerably. It'll comfortably cope with most small and medium-sized homes, but larger properties may need a recharge before you've finished.

The Dyson V11 Advanced may no longer be the newest Dyson in the lineup, but it's still one of the best cordless vacuums we've tested when it comes to outright cleaning performance. It excelled on carpets and pet hair during testing, while its clear LCD screen and excellent battery life make it easy to live with. The main drawback is that it lacks some of the smarter features now found on newer Dyson models, making it harder to justify at full price.
The V11 impressed throughout our cleaning tests, particularly on medium-pile carpet where it cleared both fine dust and larger debris with ease. It was also one of the strongest performers for pet hair, and delivered solid results on hard floors. The only real compromise came on deep-pile carpet, where the lack of an air intake slider made it harder to push despite its powerful suction.
Despite its top-heavy design, the V11 is easy to steer around furniture and lies almost flat for cleaning under sofas and cabinets. It feels noticeably less balanced in handheld mode, however, while the trigger-operated design can become tiring during longer cleaning sessions because there's no lock for continuous running.
The V11's LCD display remains one of the clearest and most intuitive we've used, displaying remaining runtime, cleaning mode and maintenance alerts at a glance. However, newer Dyson models have moved the game on with features like automatic suction adjustment and laser floorheads, leaving the V11 feeling a little dated despite its premium build quality.
Battery life is one of the V11's biggest strengths. It exceeded Dyson's claimed 60-minute Eco runtime during testing, while Medium mode delivered a healthy 33 minutes and Boost lasted around 15 minutes. The removable battery adds some welcome longevity, and the live runtime countdown on the LCD screen takes much of the guesswork out of longer cleaning sessions.
Also tested
Hoover HF3 DynamicClean
The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder remains a strong budget cordless vacuum, particularly for US shoppers who can't yet buy the Hoover HF3 DynamicClean. It offers reliable cleaning performance, a brilliant mini motorized pet tool and excellent value, although its small bin and short battery life make it better suited to smaller homes.
Read our full Hoover HF3 DynamicClean review
Dyson V8 Cyclone
This model is a strong all-rounder, but was just pipped to the post when it came to my top five. The design is basic, and there are no special features to speak of, but this vacuum's cleaning scores were strong, with a 4 or higher on carpet (medium- and deep-pile) and pet hair. At the time of writing, it's not available in the US.
Read my full Dyson V8 Cyclone review
Roborock H60 Hub Ultra
This vacuum earned middling scores in most categories. The cleaning performance was mixed, with a high score for medium-pile carpet, but low scores on deep carpet and hard flooring. 
Read my full Roborock H60 Hub Ultra review
Dyson V16 Piston Animal
The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson's newest vacuum, and big disappointment for me. While the battery life is excellent and I was impressed with many design elements and special features, the cleaning performance was weak across the board, which is inexcusable given the sky-high price. 
Read my full Dyson V16 Piston Animal review
Comparison charts
Testing methodology
Finding the best cordless vacuum isn't all about testing suction power – there are multiple factors that play into how well a vacuum performs. Here's a rundown of the key areas vacuum expert Ruth Hamilton focused on in her group test, why they're important, how TechRadar tests the vacuums, and which models came out on top in each area.
The following was written by Ruth Hamilton.
Carpet cleaning performance
Carpet cleaning ability is of course a key factor in a cordless vacuum cleaner's performance. To efficiently clean carpet, a vacuum needs a good amount of suction, but there's more to it than that. If the suction is too strong a vacuum will be difficult to push, so an air intake slider on the floorhead can help here by reducing the suction pressure. A well-designed beater bar (the roller in the floorhead), with bristles to agitate the carpet fibers and release ground-in dirt, is also a must for efficient carpet cleaning.
How I tested
For the carpet cleaning test, I used dry tea to represent fine particles, and a dry rice and lentil mix to represent chunky particles. I sprinkled a set amount of each on the carpeted floor, then ran over it once with each vacuum on its 'medium' setting, or dropping to its low setting if that proved too difficult to push. I then assessed how much of the spillage had been picked up, and continued cleaning until the spillage was clear. I ran these tests on medium-pile carpet and deep-pile carpet.
I made notes on each vacuum's performance in each test, and gave it a score out of five for its fine particle clearing ability and for its chunky-particle clearing ability. The average score for each floor type is the two scores divided by two.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runner up: Dyson Gen5detect
Hard floor cleaning performance
Cleaning a hard floor requires less suction than tackling carpet, because all the dust and debris is sat on top of the surface. Great hard floor head cleaning performance relies on a floorhead that doesn't cause particles to ping about or pool up. It may also be kitted out with headlamps that illuminate debris that might get missed, and/or a separate soft floorhead designed specifically to buff and clean hard floors without risking scratches.
How I tested
For the hard floor cleaning tests, I used fine particles (dry tea) and chunky particles (a mix of dry rice and lentils). I sprinkled a pile of each on my vinyl floor floor, then approached it forwards with each vacuum in its 'medium' setting to see how efficiently it cleared the mess and if there was any pinging or pooling. I also reversed the vacuum backwards over each spillage to see if it cleared it or simply pushed the particles about. I checked my findings on the studio's own wood laminate flooring.
I made notes on each vacuum's performance and awarded each a score out of 5 for each particle type. The overall score for hard floor cleaning is the two scores divided by two.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runner up: Dyson Gen5detect
Pet hair cleaning performance
Pet hair can be one of the trickiest substances to clean from carpet and upholstery. Great pet hair cleaning relies on strong suction and a floorhead that can effectively lift the hair from carpet fibers so it can be vacuumed up. I also look for a mini motorized tool that can effectively tackle pet hair on furniture.
How I tested
I took bags of dog clippings from a friendly local groomer, and rubbed the hairs into my deep-pile and medium-pile carpet samples. I then passed over it once with each vacuum on its 'medium' mode to see how much hair was removed. I adjusted the setting if required, and continued cleaning until the carpet was clear.
I made notes on performance, and I awarded each vacuum a score out of five for medium-pile carpet and for deep-pile carpet. The overall pet-hair score is an average of these two scores.
To test furniture-cleaning performance, I rubbed hair into a velvet cushion, and used each vacuum's mini motorized tool (if included) to clear it. I made notes on how efficiently it removed the hair, and I've used this information to influence my recommendations. However, I didn't score this element or include it in the overall average for pet hair because not every model I test came with a mini tool included, but most have a compatible tool that's included with some bundles.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runners-up: Dyson Gen5detect and V11 Advanced (tied)
Design and features
In this category I look at the basic design of the vacuum, plus any special features that have been added. I want a vacuum that boasts useful advanced features, but is still user-friendly and doesn't neglect the basics.
For usability, I'm looking at how the machine relays information like remaining battery life and charge level, blockages, which mode is in use, and (if relevant) how much dirt has been detected. I'll also consider the process for emptying the bin and switching attachments.
In terms of special features, I'll look for things like automatic adjustment capabilities (to account for factors like dirt levels, floor type, proximity to room edges, or light levels), a second soft floorhead for delicate hard flooring, a compatible auto-empty dock, and lasers or LED headlamps to light the way or illuminate dust.
How I tested
I scored each vacuum out of five for its interface design, with the highest scores going to machines that present plenty of information nice and clearly, and the lowest going to machines that show minimal information or are confusing in their presentation.
I then scored each vacuum based out of five based on how many special features it offers, and how well those features are executed. The total 'Design and features' score is an average of these two marks.
Highest scorer: Dyson Gen5detect
Runners-up: Dyson V16 Piston Animal, Shark Detect Pro, Shark PowerDetect (tied)
Comfort and maneuverability
One of the big benefits of going for a cordless stick vacuum over a bulky upright is that it's easy to maneuver. That benefit is undermined if the vacuum is too heavy, uncomfortable to hold, or won't maneuver smoothly.
Things that play into this section are the weight of the vacuum and how that weight is distributed, whether the handle is shaped or padded, how ergonomic the design of the handheld section is, and how easily the floorhead pivots. I'll also look at how the machine switches on and off, and if that's conducive to both quick cleanups and longer sessions.
How I tested
I weighed the handheld section of each vacuum (with no wand and no attachments) and then added the wand and primary floorhead to assess the weight in general upright use. I scored each model out of five based directly on these weights, with lower scores going to the heaviest models and higher scores going to lighter ones.
I then gave each vacuum a subjective score out of five for comfort and maneuverability. To gauge this I used each vacuum in floorstanding and handheld mode. The total score for this section is an average of those two marks.
Highest scorer: Shark Detect Pro Cordless
Runner up: Dreame R20
Battery life
The joy of going cable-free can quickly turn sour if your cordless vacuum doesn't have enough battery power for a whole-home clean without you having to stop to recharge. Battery life is a more complicated metric than you might first imagine, though. Many of the models I test these days have an Auto mode, where suction (and thus battery use) increases or decreases based on dirt levels or floor type, making it impossible to give a runtime for this mode.
It's important to consider how much power is tied to that runtime – an Eco mode might last 90 minutes, but if the suction is too weak to pick anything up, that's not useful to anyone. If you're dealing with really ground-in dirt, an ultra-powerful Boost mode that drains the battery quickly is arguably better than one that lasts longer but isn't powerful enough to pull the dirt up.
You'll also want to factor in that a vacuum's runtimes will likely deplete as time goes by. I'd prioritize a removable and swappable battery when choosing a cordless vacuum, as the battery is often the first thing to go – all the vacuums in this group test have a removable battery.
How I tested
I recorded the maximum runtime for each battery (i.e., in its lowest-powered mode). I also recorded how long each model lasted in its highest suction mode. I scored each vacuum out of five in each of those tests based on a set scale – so in Max mode, 3 for 10 mins or less, 4 for 11-15 mins, and 5 for 16+ mins. The overall Battery score is an average of the two scores.
Highest scorers: Dyson Gen5detect, Dyson V16 Piston Animal, Dyson V11 Advanced (tied)
Runners up: Dreame R20, Shark PowerDetect, Roborock H60 Ultra (tied)

articles.title: Jensen Huang vuelve como CEO de NVIDIA tras el escándalo por una espía china
articles.text:
Jensen Huang ha vuelto como CEO de NVIDIA. En un movimiento que recuerda al despido de Sam Altman en OpenAI, la junta directiva de NVIDIA anunció la restitución inmediata de Huang como presidente, director ejecutivo y miembro del consejo de administración. La decisión llega a 11 días de que el ejecutivo fuera despedido por mantener una relación amorosa con una supuesta espía china.
"La junta directiva votó por unanimidad la reincorporación del Sr. Huang tras una serie de discusiones y reuniones con el Sr. Huang, tras las cuales el Consejo se mostró satisfecho con respecto a la franqueza del Sr. Huang y su capacidad para liderar NVIDIA", menciona el comunicado de prensa. Según la publicación, la junta recibió "aportaciones de alto nivel" del gobierno de Estados Unidos, por lo que decidió restituirlo con confianza de que no habrá riesgos de seguridad nacional.
La reincorporación de Jensen Huang como CEO de NVIDIA pone fin a un culebrón que comenzó a finales de octubre, cuando surgieron los rumores sobre su relación con una espía china. Según los primeros reportes, Alice Huang se acercó a Jensen con el objetivo de desviar miles de millones de dólares en chips de IA hacia China. La amante aprovechó su estatus de socio preferente de la compañía para mover hilos y evadir el bloqueo de Estados Unidos hacia China.
Un reporte de The Information afirmó que Alice Huang tuvo acceso a más de 240.000 placas H100, H200 y A100, las cuales desvió hacia China. Alice, también conocida como Huang Le, habría sido reclutada por un agente del Ministerio de Seguridad del gobierno para obtener información sobre los chips de IA. Alice montó una red de empresas en China y Singapur junto con su esposo y hermana, una de las cuales era socio de NVIDIA.
Donald Trump presionó a NVIDIA para restituir a Jensen Huang como CEO
Si bien el comunicado solo menciona "aportaciones de altos niveles del Gobierno", una filtración confirmó que fue el mismo Donald Trump quien intervino en la restitución de Huang. De acuerdo con Semafor, el presidente de Estados Unidos llamó a la junta directiva de NVIDIA para argumentar a favor de su regreso. Trump ha sido uno de los que más ha apoyado a Jensen desde que surgieron los primeros rumores sobre su "affair" con la espía china.
"La Junta Directiva de NVIDIA ha tomado la decisión correcta y adecuada de devolver a Jensen Huang al puesto de CEO. El país necesita el liderazgo de Jensen en NVIDIA para garantizar el éxito y la prosperidad no solo de la empresa, sino de la economía estadounidense", dijo Trump en una publicación de su red social. Por su parte, el director de comunicaciones de la Casa Blanca confirmó que el mandatario estuvo involucrado en el regreso de Huang, ya que el país tiene que proteger a sus genios.
Donald Trump también publicó un meme en su cuenta de Truth Social para conmemorar la decisión:
El reporte de Semafor añade que, además de la presión del gobierno de Estados Unidos, otro incidente ayudó a impulsar esta decisión. Una facción que se oponía a Huang no consiguió fichar a Rene Haas, CEO de ARM, puesto que este último firmó un contrato que lo amarra hasta 2033. Sin un candidato del nivel de Jensen para dirigir a la empresa, la junta directiva se quedó sin opciones.
El anuncio del regreso de Jensen Huang como CEO también tuvo efecto en las acciones de NVIDIA, que revirtieron la racha negativa que comenzó en octubre.

articles.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
articles.text:
A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
Anthropic warned investors that AI might be conscious—but acting accordingly could hurt its business. So what’s the plan?
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.
Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.
This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).
But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.
Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.
You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.
The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.
But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.
Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”
It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.
Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.
Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.
But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

articles.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
articles.text:
Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.
Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.
Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.
When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.
Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.
The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.
The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.
The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.
The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.
Clive Robinson • November 23, 2026 8:10 AM
@ Bruce,
You not the US Big Tech are trying to avoid legal liability for anything they do.
But you did not mention the,
“Who and the How”
Of it starting.
Some of us are old enough to remember Bill Gates throwing the toys out the pram over people copying BASIC.
It was not long after that that he and others at Microsoft decided to hide behind “leasing” to avoid legal responsibility for the products Microsoft produced.
Thus arguably with leasing human rights were stripped away and the Software industry could push any legal nonsense they liked in the “EULA “inside the box”, where opening the box tied you into the EULA and at sone point you had to consent to “arbitration” that the software companies controlled like glove puppets.

articles.title: The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released
articles.text:
Arion Kurtaj, who pleaded guilty last week to hacking Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games and other companies, including Uber and Revolut, was sentenced to seven years in prison but released on license, the BBC reports. After hacking Rockstar, Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI in 2022, years before the game’s public release last week.
The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released
Arion Kurtaj, who hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 videos of the game, was released after pleading guilty.
Prior to his sentencing, Kurtaj had already spent time in a hospital because of his autism and in prison.
“You are obviously a very talented young man,” the judge in the case said, according to Sky News. “Don’t waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison.” Kurtaj cannot use platforms Telegram and Discord as part of a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order, the BBC says.
Rockstar launched GTA VI last week to positive reviews. The studio said the game made $3.79 billion in its first day of sales.

articles.title: CRA, AI Robotics, Motor Control, Digital Energy at electronica 2026
articles.text:
The Singapore-based MCU and security-IC supplier showed 35 applications and solutions in Munich and argued that European buying decisions now turn on three things: evidence a chip can survive a Cyber Resilience Act audit, real-time response in AI robotics, and efficient power conversion for digital energy.
NSING Technologies, the Singapore-based fabless semiconductor arm of NSING Group (300077.SZ; 02701.HK), has concluded its participation in electronica 2026, which closed on 13 November at Messe München, after displaying 35 applications and reference designs on its Hall C2 stand (Booth 741), grouped around the questions European OEMs brought to the show: how to prove a product is cyber-secure before the EU Cyber Resilience Act becomes fully binding in December 2027, how to make a robot joint respond in real time, and how to convert power efficiently in digital-energy systems.
The show’s official themes — artificial intelligence, network resilience and energy efficiency — ran through the booth. What tied them together, according to the company, was a shift in where the difficulty now sits: less in any single chip’s peak specification, more in the compliance file, at the joint and in the power stage.
CRA: reporting obligations are already live; the deadline is next December
A sizeable share of the booth went to the EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), which is less about features than about evidence. The regulation entered into force on 10 December 2024. Reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents took effect on 11 September 2026. The main obligations — conformity assessment and CE marking — apply from 11 December 2027.
For procurement teams, that sequence mattered more than the headline date. The reporting duty is already enforceable, and the design changes plus documentation needed to pass assessment have roughly a year to land. “Future compliance” is no longer an accurate description of the situation.
NSING maps its portfolio onto the regulation’s classes. N32S security ICs and TPM devices at CC EAL4+ support third-party assessment for Critical-class products. Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M7 MCUs, including the N32H and N32G4 families, are positioned for Class 2, with chip-level SESIP certification in progress. Cortex-M0 parts such as the N32G0 and N32WB fit the Class 1 self-declaration route.
Beyond the silicon, the company packages what an OEM has to put in the file: an ECR (essential cybersecurity requirements) mapping table, a software bill of materials, a compliance support pack and introductions to notified bodies. These are organised around a five-step route — classification and threat modelling, secure development practice, validation and bill-of-materials control, system documentation with a vulnerability reporting channel, and assessment plus CE archiving.
Post-quantum migration sits on the same axis. NSING’s MCUs integrate ML-KEM (512/768/1024) and ML-DSA (44/65/87), starting with the N32H4xx and N32H7xx and extending across its Cortex-M4-and-above N32 line, covering key establishment, device identity, firmware update and secure boot, and data integrity checks. The implementations coexist with RSA, ECC, SHA, and ship with drivers, a crypto abstraction layer, example code and a porting guide — the building blocks for an assessment, hybrid-verify, migrate and evolve sequence.
Digital energy: power conversion and battery management
On the power-conversion side, the pitch is topology coverage rather than a single headline number. The N32DP474 runs PFC, LLC resonant conversion and multiphase interleaved topologies from one device; NSING characterises peak efficiency at up to 99% under rated load, and says a reference design built on it is already in volume production with server-power customers. For energy storage, the NB1802 analog front end monitors 18 series-connected cells, covering 1500 V container systems and residential packs.
Humanoid robots: a three-tier architecture from joint to machine
The bottleneck in humanoid robots is not the model. It is the joint — torque, speed and position loops that have to close deterministically while the rest of the machine stays synchronised — and the coordination above it.
NSING splits that work across cores. The N32H785EC pairs a Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz, dedicated to field-oriented control across torque, speed and position loops plus dual absolute-encoder decoding, with a Cortex-M4F at 300 MHz handling CAN FD and EtherCAT. A 100 ps high-resolution timer and hardware CORDIC/FMAC units support multi-axis synchronisation on high-load joints. Secondary joints at the wrist, ankle and torso use the N32MD473, which integrates a three-phase gate driver. Dexterous hands move to a distributed arrangement of a main controller plus per-channel drivers, so wiring and heat dissipation stop setting the size of a finger.
Around the joints, the company supplies NB1802 battery management ICs, N32WB BLE SoCs and NS350 TPM rated CC EAL4+. NSING says these designs are shipping in volume as part of complete humanoid, quadruped, collaborative-arm and dexterous-hand platforms.
The same control IP appeared elsewhere on the stand: the VIGX π6 exoskeleton uses the N32H49x for high-precision position control; 3D printers run real-time motion planning and stepper drive on the N32G45x with the N32G003 handling housekeeping; collaborative arms implement multi-axis interpolation on the N32H78x.
Industrial, automotive and motor control: the revenue base underneath
Underneath the headline demonstrations sat the business NSING earns today. The N32H7 family serves servo drives, PLCs, inverters and integrated motion controllers. The N32H785EC includes a Beckhoff-licensed EtherCAT slave controller and holds multi-axis synchronisation jitter to the microsecond range; the N32H47x and N32H48x carry IEC 61508 SIL 2 and SIL 3 functional-safety certification. The stand also showed a servo drive controller built on the N32ZH785EC, an industrial I/O module based on the N32H760, and an industrial gateway that pairs an N32S032 security IC with the main controller.
On the automotive side, the N32A455, N32A052 and N32A003 are AEC-Q100 qualified and specified from −40 °C to 125 °C. NSING says they are in volume production with body-radar designs at major Chinese EV makers, and that applications are moving outward from body control into on-board chargers, T-Boxes and smart-cockpit functions. A body control module, a reversing-radar design on the N32A455 and a headlight design on the N32G435 were on display.
Motor control is where the portfolio’s integration showed most clearly. The company’s matrix spans Cortex-M7, M4 and M0 cores and can drive one, two, four or six motors from a single MCU, cutting bill-of-materials cost for appliance and power-tool designs. Three parts carried the demonstration: the N32M016, which integrates a 150 V three-phase 6N gate driver, LDO and differential PGA in a 5×5 mm package to deliver 800 W at 90,000 rpm for drills and handheld vacuums, with back-EMF sensing and three-level overcurrent protection; the N32M012, with a 3P3N driver covering 6–40 V and sensorless sinusoidal FOC for ceiling and pedestal fans that runs stably from 200 rpm; and the N32G033K8Q7-1, a 64 MHz M0 part with three op-amps and a 25 µs current loop that supports 120,000 rpm hair dryers and adaptive-start refrigerator compressors.
One silicon platform across four kinds of building device
The building-automation demonstration was organized around a single data chain rather than individual products. Smart locks and access control pair the N32WB Bluetooth SoC with a security IC, so identification and unlock authorisation happen on the endpoint. The N32G45x drives elevator-car human-machine interfaces. Occupancy and daylight sensing dimming built on the N32G45x, N32G03x and N32WB connects lighting control to energy monitoring. The N32L43x smart breaker folds circuit-level metering, protection and remote control into the same link. For an OEM, the reusable part is that one silicon platform, one provisioning method and one back-end data format can cover all four device classes in an office building.
Why Europe, and what comes next
During the show the NSING team met global end customers, distributors and trade press, and continued talks on distributor coverage and joint reference designs. The company framed electronica 2026 as a live test of its global strategy: compliance, functional safety, long-term supply and local support — the four things European customers ask about first — are the areas it has been investing in for several years.
NSING said it will keep investing in global product development and ecosystem partnerships, with AI computing infrastructure, embodied intelligence and edge AI as its stated priorities, alongside security, SoC, RF and power management as established strengths.
About NSING Technologies
NSING Technologies, an NSING Group member founded in Singapore in 2018, delivers high-performance semiconductor solutions for the global industry. Its expertise spans general MCU, secure IC (TPM), BLE and BMS, with advanced capabilities in Arm/GPU multi-core architectures, low-power design and secure-zone IP. Its solutions power a wide range of applications, including AI, robotics, industrial automation, consumer electronics, smart home, automotive electronics, IoT devices, medical equipment, energy storage systems and wearable technology, enabling customers to innovate with confidence. NSING was established in 2000, listed on ChiNext in 2010 and on HKEX in 2026 (300077.SZ, 02701.HK). Together, we create a secure, smart and sustainable future.
