articles.title: Designing A Microarchitecture From Formal Proof To Full-System
articles.text:
Combining architectural proof, software-driven verification, simulation, emulation, and cloud-based compute infrastructure.
Data center and high-performance computing workloads are pushing CPU designers to deliver higher per-watt throughput and support complex multicore systems. Meeting these goals requires specialized compute cores. This reality is forcing engineers to rethink not only how cores are built, but also which instruction set architecture (ISA) can scale efficiently, support software validation, and still create product differentiation. To meet these challenges, a lean R&D team from a startup company in Austin, Texas, chose the RISC-V ISA as the foundation for its first CPU IP microarchitecture.
Designing the microarchitecture involved balancing software-visible architectural behavior, RTL implementation details, and internal performance and power tradeoffs, which together introduced verification requirements that extended well beyond isolated hardware blocks. When these interactions are not addressed early in development, system-level issues can emerge later, making them more difficult to resolve. These decisions also expanded the scope of verification. The core had to be validated with actual software under full-system scale, including interactions that extend beyond individual hardware blocks.
To manage the complexity, the engineers adopted a formal-first verification strategy. By applying formal analysis during the design cycle, key architectural properties were proven before transitioning to large-scale simulation and system bring-up. Formal verification handled block-level functionality and end-to-end checks of functional intent. Simulation and emulation addressed long-running behavior in the full-core environment. Some failures may not emerge until the design has run for tens of millions of cycles under full operating system (OS) stress.
The design and verification group used a tightly integrated Cadence tool flow spanning architectural proof, software-driven verification, simulation, emulation, and cloud-based compute infrastructure. Figure 1 below illustrates a type of multicore CPU architecture that the Cadence verification methodology is designed to validate.
Fig. 1: A representative multicore CPU subsystem showing the processors, cache hierarchy, and system interfaces that engineers verify as the RTL design evolves. (Source: Cadence)
The Jasper Formal Verification Platform supported the implementation of a formal-first methodology to validate architectural intent early in the design. Formal Property Verification was applied across the fetch, decode, execution, and instruction-flow paths to ensure that key correctness properties were maintained throughout the pipeline. Jasper Superlint identified structural and coding issues early, preventing common RTL problems from propagating into later verification stages. Jasper XPROP addressed X-propagation risks associated with initialization and reset behavior, reducing simulation uncertainty and increasing confidence in system-level results. These results were then used to focus long-running simulation and emulation workloads on architecturally sensitive areas rather than simply increasing regression volume.
While formal verification established early architectural correctness, validating full OS behavior required executing long instruction streams, which challenged the practical limits of traditional simulation. To address this requirement, a snippet-based simulation flow was developed using the Xcelium Logic Simulator. This allowed long-running software execution to be divided into manageable segments while maintaining architectural state and full debug visibility across boundaries.
To exercise the design under realistic system conditions, the team ran Linux as the primary software workload on a QEMU-based virtual platform. The workload advanced in one-million-cycle increments, with the complete architectural state captured at each checkpoint to create a reusable snippet representing a defined window. Each snippet was then loaded into Xcelium with full signal visibility, allowing engineers to debug a specific region without rerunning the entire OS boot sequence.
Across the full verification flow, approximately 120 snippets were generated, enabling analysis of instruction streams spanning more than 35 million cycles. Extended instruction-stream execution also tested interrupt handling and exercised pipeline behavior. This approach reduced the turnaround time for long software workloads from days to hours and enabled detailed root-cause analysis of complex interactions. Xcelium achieved a simulation rate of approximately 100,000 cycles per second while preserving full debug visibility.
Debugging was done using Verisium Debug, which provided traceability across long instruction sequences and preserved context across simulation runs. This capability enabled efficient analysis of failures observed under software stress without sacrificing visibility.
Combining formal proof with logic simulation enabled a consistent way to connect the results and measure progress across verification stages. Within the platform, Verisium Manager provided a central dashboard for test planning and coverage tracking against defined targets. This unified view showed which coverage targets had been met, where gaps remained, and where to focus next. Verisium Debug complemented these capabilities by maintaining traceability across extended runs and linking simulation and emulation results.
The company transitioned to the Cadence Palladium Enterprise Emulation Platform for Linux bring-up and multicore software workloads. The platform provided the speed and hardware/software visibility needed to execute complete operating-system boot sequences. The team booted Linux on a single-core system in 50 minutes and on a dual-core system in 90 minutes. This confirmed system functionality and architectural scalability. Additionally, the engineers verified coherency and interrupt handling while identifying performance hotspots in concurrent workloads.
Cadence OnCloud platform provided the scalable compute capacity needed to maintain that visibility as verification workloads grew more complex. This emulation stage exposed system-level behavior, supported validation of operation and scalability, and made full-system bring-up practical within the engineering schedule.
By leveraging Cadence OnCloud, compute resources could be scaled to match verification demand during peak periods without requiring a fixed infrastructure commitment at the start of the project. At the same time, built-in security aligned with industry standards such as ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017 helped ensure that sensitive IP remained protected throughout the process. The project validated both the approach and the platform.
The company uncovered complex interactions between cores and subsystems to achieve first-silicon success. For a small team, the biggest constraint was not methodology or tooling. It was the amount of work that could realistically be pushed through the system at any given time. Using a Cadence verification tool flow removed that barrier by providing additional capacity when verification demand peaked and turnaround time directly affected development momentum. The team could prioritize critical work instead of scaling back verification to fit the available infrastructure.
First-silicon success provided evidence that the cloud environment could meet the verification demands of a complex CPU design. Future processor development can move more system-level validation into the pre-silicon phase. At-speed prototypes provide a way to evaluate multicore operation and hardware-software interactions before silicon. On-demand access to emulation and prototyping capacity can expand with changing design needs, allowing system-level integration work to begin earlier without requiring an in-house lab.

articles.title: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.text:
Rebook the Sharks’ stadium, boot up Toy Jensen, and get those leather jackets out of the yard sale pile—Jensen Huang is back.
In a move that has shocked industry-watchers and laymen alike, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. Huang will also rejoin Nvidia’s board, though Harvey Jones will remain chair.
As said previously, this turn of events would be too far-fetched for an episode of the HBO series Silicon Valley. In a soap opera, having a billionaire CEO return after admitting to an affair with a Chinese spy amid reports of a second affair with a direct report would be dismissed as unbelievable. In fact, a tech CEO hasn’t had a dramatic comeback like this since OpenAI fired and rehired Sam Altman that time.
Nvidia’s board has said that it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
The board is confident. Confident? Then why not wait until the independent investigation it commissioned a week ago had run its course and found him not guilty? The answer is most likely Nvidia’s stock price, which had taken a nosedive since Huang resigned. President Trump himself had reportedly dialed in to Nvidia’s board meeting to personally plead the case for reinstatement.
Trump shared on Truth Social that bringing Jensen back was “the correct and proper decision.” “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote.
So, Huang is back, with immediate effect, complete with character reference from President Trump.
How Huang and the Nvidia board are going to enforce legal and ethical business practices both within Nvidia and more broadly with customers following this affair appears to be on their minds.
Nvidia’s board wrote in its statement that it is searching for an executive to fill a newly created position, chief compliance officer. Now that Huang is untouchable, what kind of executive would take a position that requires you to enforce export control rules Huang has lobbied against, while having him yell at you that he’d like to rip off your arms and beat you to death with them?
Pity, too, the board member tasked with telling Huang that Nvidia really needs a proper succession plan going forward. As we considered potential candidates for Nvidia CEO this week, it became clear that no single person could meet all three facets of Huang: Huang the technical leader, Huang the dealmaker, and Huang the rockstar. Even assuming no more scandals emerge to threaten Huang’s tenure, Nvidia’s board should expect the unexpected. And it is time to reassure investors that there is indeed someone on the planet capable of running Nvidia should the worst happen.
Going forward, Nvidia’s brand and Huang’s personal brand are so closely linked that it’s difficult to tell how the perception of either will change. Are Huang’s personal indiscretions detrimental to his rockstar image, or do they bolster it? Is that good or bad for Nvidia? Is bringing back Huang, the founder and visionary, a genius move or an inexcusable mistake from the board? Is Huang personally now more, or less, in thrall to the U.S. government, the Chinese, or both?
Nvidia will go back to business as usual, at least on the surface, but this affair has set a precedent across U.S. public companies: Affairs with foreign spies and even employees no longer count, provided you are making money. Billionaire bad behavior is only going to get worse.

articles.title: Apple plant die nächste Produktrunde: Diese iPhones, iPads und Macs kommen im Frühjahr
articles.text:
Apple plant die nächste Produktrunde: Diese iPhones, iPads und Macs kommen im Frühjahr
Apple plant laut einem Bericht von Bloomberg für Februar oder März die nächste große Produktrunde: Dann sollen neue iPhones, iPads und Macs erscheinen. Im Mittelpunkt stehen demnach vor allem günstigere Geräte. Erst in den vergangenen Wochen hatte Apple neue iPhone-Pro-Modelle, faltbare Geräte, OLED-Tablets und mehrere Macs vorgestellt.
Warum das iPhone 18 erst noch kommt
Bei den Smartphones hat Apple in diesem Jahr seine Strategie geändert und die Veröffentlichungen entzerrt. So will der Hersteller sowohl im vierten als auch im ersten Quartal richtig Kasse machen – und nicht nur beim Weihnachtsgeschäft. Im September zeigte Apple das iPhone 18 Pro, das 18 Pro Max und das iPhone Duo, das allerdings erst im Oktober in den Handel kam. Das Standard-iPhone fehlte erstmals. Es soll nun im Frühjahr folgen – parallel zu einem weiteren Einsteigermodell. Laut Bloomberg erscheinen die Geräte zusammen mit iOS 27.4. Das iPhone 18 soll die Standardversion des A20-Chips (aus dem iPhone 18 Pro und Duo) bekommen, dazu eine leicht verbesserte Kamera, mehr Arbeitsspeicher (9 statt 8 GByte), etwas mehr Akkulaufzeit und frische Farben.
Das iPhone 18e, das sich besonders an Firmenkunden wendet, behält demnach die Bauform des 17e aus dem vergangenen März, die auf die noch viel älteren Generationen 13 und 14 zurückgeht. Auch hier rechnet die Gerüchteküche mit dem A20-Chip und längerer Akkulaufzeit. Die Einkerbung am oberen Displayrand, die Notch, soll hier bleiben. Dafür könnte auch das 18e ebenfalls 9 statt 8 GByte RAM erhalten. Denkbar ist zudem eine zweite Variante des besonders flachen iPhone Air. Beobachter erwarten hier einen A20-Pro-Chip, eine verkleinerte Dynamic Island, eine Ultraweitwinkel-Kamera und Apples neuen Modemchip C2.
Was Apple bei iPads und Macs plant
Bei den Tablets stehen zwei oder drei neue Modelle an. Das Einsteiger-iPad soll erstmals Apple Intelligence unterstützen, also Apples KI-Funktionen, und den A19-Chip erhalten. Geplant sind außerdem der Einbau des stromsparenden Mobilfunkchips C1X und Apples N1 mit Wi-Fi 7. Das iPad Air könnte auf den M5-Chip wechseln und erstmals ein OLED-Display bekommen. Damit stünde ein dünneres und leichteres Gehäuse an. Offen bleibt, ob Apple schon neue iPad-Pro-Modelle mit M6 oder M7 zeigt oder damit bis zum Sommer (oder gar Herbst) wartet.
Bei den Macs muss Apple das MacBook Air noch auf den M6-Chip bringen. Bloomberg erwartet das Gerät im Frühjahr. Dazu kommt die zweite Generation des MacBook Neo, dem günstigsten Notebook des Herstellers. Apple rüstet dort vermutlich auf den A19 Pro aus dem iPhone 17 Pro auf. Der Vorteil: Der Arbeitsspeicher wächst auf 12 GByte, ist also endlich weniger knapp. Auch neue Farben sind möglich.

articles.title: GlobeTopper loses $2.5 million after hackers steal $70k in gift cards
articles.text:
A cyberattack disrupted operations at B2B top-up solutions provider GlobeTopper, causing an estimated $2.5 million in lost revenue, while the attacker redeemed digital gift cards worth $70,000.
Parent company iQSTEL said that the intrusion was detected on October 22 and GlobeTopper responded by suspending its platform and starting an investigation.
GlobeTopper is a business-to-business digital gift card distributor. Various retailers, fintech apps, and rewards platforms use its API. According to the platform’s website, it is used by more than 4,000 brands across 65 countries, including IKEA, Adidas, Spotify, Target, and Roblox.
In a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), iQSTEL said that GlobeTopper detected more unauthorized activity the day after it identified the attack. In response, the company "took the platform and all affected servers offline" in the early hours of October 23 to investigate and fix the problem.
The company deployed a completely rebuilt platform on AWS on October 31, while commercial operations were restored in stages, starting November 1.
GlobeTopper says the attacker obtained certain client API credentials and integration keys, which have been revoked and replaced, and it has observed no unauthorized use of them yet.
“During its investigation, the Company determined that the unauthorized party obtained API credentials and integration keys of certain GlobeTopper business customers,” iQSTEL says.
“All affected credentials and integration keys have been revoked and rotated, and affected business customers have been issued new credentials subject to additional access restrictions.”
The company further stated that an investigation is ongoing to determine whether other customer, personal, payment, or provider data was accessed or acquired.
Regarding the digital gift cards the attackers redeemed, the company says it cannot block, recover, or reclaim them, and will incur the losses.
iQSTEL said the incident hurt GlobeTopper’s fourth-quarter transaction volume and operating results, but as of the filing, it has not determined it to be material.
BleepingComputer has emailed iQSTEL with additional questions regarding the incident, but the company declined to share further information.
At the time of writing, no ransomware groups have listed iQSTEL or GlobeTopper as victims on their extortion portals.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Ship lets Claude approve routine pull requests
articles.text:
Anthropic’s Claude Ship lets Claude approve routine pull requests
Anthropic on Monday launched Claude Ship, a set of three agents that can review pull requests (PRs), fix them, and approve them — if the team’s policy allows.
The first of these three agents, Code Review, already became generally available in October. The other two are new and in beta.
PR Steward pushes fixes for failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback, while Claude Approvals reads a policy in the team’s GitHub repository to determine whether a PR still needs a human reviewer.
For a while now, Anthropic has been saying that Claude already writes most of the code for Claude Code. The slow part, the company argues, now comes after a developer opens a PR. By the time the review comes back, that developer may have already moved on to something else. This means even a minor change means putting that work aside to push a fix, wait for the checks to run again, and track down someone to approve it.
Most companies don’t work at the pace of Anthropic, but the bottleneck of code reviews — and the DevOps lifecycle in general — is something that slows down virtually all businesses at this point.
Who has to sign off?
Most companies won’t be willing to completely trust AI to review all code, but as Anthropic notes, maybe it means not every change needs two reviewers to agree, for example.
In practice, this could mean a change to a mission-critical billing service would still need two reviewers besides the author, including someone from the payments team. But for most other code, a clean review from Claude could cut the number of necessary human approvals to just one. And, if the change only touches documentation, that same review lets Claude approve it on its own.
To set all of this up, teams write those rules in .claude/approvals.yml, where they can also define their own classifiers in natural language. Anthropic recommends running the policy in observe-only mode first to see which PRs Claude would approve, before making its sign-off a required check.
PR Steward does its work before a PR gets to that point. It can act on feedback from people and other review tools, but it can’t approve or merge a PR. After each push, it comments on what it changed and how to undo it.
Admins can enable Claude Ship for a whole repository, and developers can also run /ship in Claude Code to push a change, open a PR, and work through feedback and failing checks. The command runs locally for up to seven days, so the session has to stay open and the computer awake.
How GitHub, Cursor, and CodeRabbit handle approvals
Unsurprisingly, other coding tool vendors are tackling the same bottleneck. GitHub, for example, introduced approvals for Copilot code review on Sept. 1 and made them generally available on Oct. 28. Admins can restrict which paths Copilot can approve.
Cursor’s PR Routing & Approval agent applies a team’s risk threshold and reads the APPROVAL_POLICY.md file closest to the changed file. CodeRabbit lets teams set separate limits for merge risk and security risk in .coderabbit.yaml.
GitHub’s Max review level, now in public preview, also uses models from different providers and reconciles their findings. In Claude Ship, all three agents use Claude.
How Anthropic uses Claude Ship
Anthropic says the Claude Code team uses Claude Ship on many of its own PRs. When a customer flagged a misleading passage in the Analytics API docs, for example, a product manager asked Claude
Tag, the company’s Slack agent, about it. Tag opened a PR, Code Review found nothing blocking it, and a docs reviewer signed off. The fix merged that evening.
From June to September, the company says, the team more than doubled the number of PRs it merged while the share it reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
It’s worth noting, though, that Claude Ship covers only part of that overall process. The team’s own engineering post from October, for example, also describes a separate security review that can block a merge.
TELUS Digital and Carvana are among the early customers. In a statement Anthropic provided, Vatsal Bhatt, director of engineering at TELUS Digital, says, “We keep a human in the loop.” He adds that PR Steward has helped contributors fix issues Code Review caught before a person got to the PR.
Carvana’s pilot uses PR Steward to work through review feedback, according to Alex Devkar, its senior vice president of engineering and analytics. Neither customer describes using Claude to approve a PR on its own.
Pricing and availability
Team and Enterprise customers can enable Claude Ship for GitHub repositories unless they use Zero Data Retention, Anthropic’s HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.
Anthropic bills by the token. At Code Review’s launch in March, the company put the average cost at $15 to $25 per review (which isn’t exactly cheap, but cheaper than shipping broken code…).
Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage, and while Claude Approvals has no base charge of its own, classifiers consume billable tokens just like any other model use. Policies that call for Code Review trigger a paid review, even in observe-only mode. 
There is a bit of a trial period, though. Eligible Enterprise customers have until Jan. 15, 2027, to claim “at least” $10,000 in Claude Ship credits, Anthropic says, but they have to use them within 30 days of claiming those credits.

articles.title: Au revoir Gmail et Apple Mail : le client mail français Open Mailbox débarque sur iOS et Android
articles.text:
Dans la galaxie des clients de messagerie sur mobile, il y a généralement trois écoles : ceux qui utilisent l’application Gmail, ceux qui utilisent Outlook, et ceux qui configurent l’appli Apple Mail sur leur iPhone. Des choix qui sont souvent guidés par le fait que les fournisseurs d’e-mails proposent leur propre application, comme c’est le cas pour Gmail et Outlook. Et pour cause, ces applications proposent une intégration parfaite avec les différents outils proposés par les éditeurs. Mais ces clients de messagerie ont tous un point commun : celui d’être développé par des géants de la Tech.
Il existe pourtant pléthore d’alternatives souveraines pour lire vos e-mails sur votre smartphone Android ou votre iPhone. Open Mailbox en fait d’ailleurs partie. Cette application développée en France par l’entreprise toulousaine Soluce Technologies est gratuite, open source, et compatible avec les principaux fournisseurs de messagerie.
Un client de messagerie qui mise sur la confidentialité
Outre son code ouvert et sa gratuité, Open Mailbox met en avant sa philosophie misant sur la confidentialité de vos données. Le client de messagerie, qui ne nécessite aucune inscription ni aucun compte pour être utilisé, communique directement vers les serveurs IMAP et SMTP de vos fournisseurs d’e-mail.
Vos messages ne transitent par aucun serveur intermédiaire et aucune copie de vos messages n’est conservée nulle part. Vos identifiants restent par ailleurs stockés dans l’espace sécurisé propre à votre smartphone.
Par ailleurs, l’application n’embarque aucun traqueur, aucune publicité et aucun outil de télémétrie visant à analyser vos habitudes d’utilisation. Open Mailbox bloque d’ailleurs par défaut toutes les images distantes dans les emails entrants pour éviter le pistage.
Quid du modèle économique ? L’éditeur explique en réponse à un commentaire d’un redditeur que son « modèle économique repose sur le développement de logiciels, leur intégration et la fourniture de services managés aux entreprises, notamment autour de solutions open source comme Nextcloud ».
« Ces activités commerciales financent notre entreprise et nous permettent de développer et de maintenir des applications open source pour la communauté, notamment Open Mailbox. Nous ne dépendons donc ni des dons ni des abonnements à nos applications pour assurer le fonctionnement de notre entreprise. » complète l’entreprise toulousaine Soluce Technologies.
Un client mail complet mais avec quelques limitations
Comme la plupart des clients de messagerie, Open Mailbox propose une boîte de réception unifiée regroupant toutes les messageries que vous configurez. Open Mailbox trie vos messages localement sur votre smartphone en organisant ceux-ci par catégories.
Le client de messagerie privilégie également le fonctionnement hors ligne. Ainsi, tous les emails sont conservés localement sur votre appareil. La recherche textuelle intégrée fonctionne également entièrement hors ligne avec la mise en surbrillance des termes recherchés.
Comme dans la plupart des clients de messagerie, Open Mailbox permet d’annuler une action (comme l’archivage ou la suppression accidentelle d’un message) pendant 5 secondes. L’application vous permettra également de vous désinscrire facilement des listes de diffusion en un clic.
L’application est compatible avec Gmail, iCloud, OVHCloud, IONOS, Yahoo ainsi que tous les serveurs IMAP / SMTP standard. À noter toutefois que la configuration de vos comptes de messagerie se fait manuellement et ne passe pas par une connexion via l’interface de votre fournisseur. Pour les utilisateurs de Gmail, par exemple, il sera indispensable de créer au préalable un « mot de passe d’application » dans votre compte Google pour pouvoir connecter votre messagerie dans l’application.
Par ailleurs, Open Mailbox ne prend pour l’instant pas en charge les messageries de Microsoft (Outlook, hotmail, etc.), celles-ci utilisant le protocole d’authentification Oauth qui n’est pour l’heure pas encore pris en charge par Open Mailbox. L’éditeur précise néanmoins que la prise en charge de ces comptes est prévue et en cours de développement dans l’application.

articles.title: Trump reportedly called into Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang's return
articles.text:
A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.
Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”
According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.
“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC.
Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.
Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Our testing covers the full spectrum, from straightforward filter and pod machines to one-touch bean-to-cup models and hands-on espresso makers.
The result is a curated lineup tailored to different budgets and brewing styles. Whether your ideal morning calls for a quick, no-fuss cup before work or a slow, café-style latte on the weekend, we’ll help you find a machine you’ll genuinely look forward to using.
The Black Friday deals are well underway, with the discounts sure to peak on Black Friday proper on November 27 and Cyber Monday on November 30. The automatic milk frother worked well with our tester's 2% milk, creating creamy microfoam for lattes and cappuccinos. It wasn't so well suited to oat milk though, which we've found tends to be the case with auto milk systems. The Philips Baristina is an excellent little coffee maker, particularly if you're making the switch from capsules to whole beans, and want to keep things as simple as possible. It's compact, smart-looking, and remarkably affordable at $449.99 / £299.99 / AU$599. In fact it's the cheapest bean-to-cup machine I've tested, and Philips hasn't skimped on quality to his that bargain price point.
The Baristina uses what Philips calls a "one-swipe" system. Push the portafilter handle into place, pick your drink (espresso or lungo, with the option to increase the dosage for a stronger brew) and the Baristina will do the rest. Just step back and watch while it measures and grinds a dose of coffee into the filter basket, tamps it down, then propels it over to the brew group and pulls your shot.
At the end, pull out the handle, clean out the basket, rinse the brew group by holding a button for a few seconds, and empty the drip tray. It's a million times easier than cleaning an automatic coffee maker where all the messy parts of coffee-making happen inside the case.
For me, the biggest downside of the Philips Baristina is the inability to adjust the grind size. On one hand, this is one less thing for new users to worry about, but on the other it means that there's nothing you can do to change the extraction rate. If it's too fast or slow, you'll need to try a different coffee until you find something that works with the Baristina as-is. There's no steam wand for preparing milk either, though you can buy the Baristina bundled with a separate Philips milk frother if you're into your lattes.
All in all though, this is a superb little entry-level coffee maker at a bargain price, and one that's easy to recommend.

✅ You want consistent café-style drinks at home: The Aromis 8000 Series delivers reliably excellent espresso and milk drinks, so every cup is as good as the last.
✅ You like variety and easy adjustments: With over 50 drinks and the ability to personalize recipes via the app or touchscreen, you’re never stuck with just one style.
✅ You want cleanup to be quick and simple: Milk carafes and the brewing unit are designed for easy, thorough cleaning, making daily upkeep straightforward.
❌ You want to mix and match hot and iced drinks: The brew group needs to cool down before making cold milk drinks, otherwise your iced latte may come out warmer than expected.
❌ You’d prefer a single, all-in-one milk system: Having two separate milk carafes (for hot and cold drinks) means there’s a bit of extra cleaning to do compared to simpler milk setups.
If you want café-style drinks at home with almost no effort, the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is the most hands-off, premium bean-to-cup machine we’ve tested yet. Its vast menu of over 50 hot and cold drinks and huge, bright touchscreen means new and interesting brews are easy to find, and we consistently enjoyed excellent coffee, shot after shot, throughout our review.
What makes the Aromis so practical is its approach to milk drinks and cleaning. You get two separate milk carafes — one for hot foam, one for cold — and both disassemble into three pieces, making them far easier to clean than any system with fiddly tubes or hidden chambers. The maintenance hatch is also thoughtfully designed: it’s hinged, so you won’t misplace it, and the brew unit lifts out in one go for a proper rinse. These touches make it genuinely low-fuss to keep hygienic, even if you’re making milky drinks every day.
Customization is another strong point. The mobile app (with its Barista Assistant) lets you tweak recipes and save your preferences, so your morning espresso is always just how you like it — whether you want a punchy pick-me-up or something smoother.
There’s one quirk to be aware of: if you rush from a hot espresso straight to an iced milk drink, the brew group needs to cool down first, or you’ll end up with a warm ‘iced’ latte. But for most users, the Aromis’ premium build, straightforward maintenance, and sheer breadth of drinks genuinely justify its price. It’s the ideal choice if you want barista-level drinks at the touch of a button, without the daily cleanup or learning curve.

The Ninja DualBrew Pro is a two-in-one drip coffee maker, able to use either coffee grounds or K-Cups. We found the control panel a little more complicated than most other coffee machines we've tested, but we got the hang of it after the first few brews, and the rest of the DualBrew Pro is no harder to use than any other filter coffee machine.
We appreciated the indicator lights, which let you know how far along the brewing process the machine is, the mess-free design that closes the brew basket once it's done, and the well extracted coffee it produced every time, whether we used grounds or a cup. There's a water line for brewing tea (great if you don't have a kettle handy) and a milk frother, which is very unusual for a drip coffee maker. ✅ You're short on counter space: This is an exceptionally compact coffee maker, with a cable that can be routed to either side so you can push it close to a wall.
✅ You want coffee without the faff: There's just one button and a large, easy-to-use lever, so brewing is quick and straightforward.
❌ You want one-touch milk drinks: There's no built-in milk frother, so you'll need a separate frother for lattes and cappuccinos.
❌ You don't want to monitor the coffee as it brews: The Jolie Evo doesn't have an automatic timer, so you need to press the button again to stop the flow.
❌ You want easy-to-recycle capsules: A Modo Mio pods are mostly plastic and can only be recycled at designated collection points, which aren't available everywhere.
The Lavazza A Modo Mio Jolie Evo is a tiny capsule coffee machine that makes surprisingly good espresso for its size and price. During our tests, it produced some of the best espresso we've tasted from a capsule machine, with Lavazza's A Modo Mio pods offering a good range of blends and roasts without the added flavors found in some rival capsule systems.
It's also exceptionally easy to use. There's just one button and a large lever, which makes loading a capsule straightforward and gives the Jolie Evo a reassuringly tactile feel. It heats up quickly, takes up very little counter space, and the power cable can be routed to either side, making it particularly well suited to small kitchens.
There are a couple of compromises. The Jolie Evo doesn't have a timer, so you'll need to press the button again to stop the coffee flowing, and there's no built-in milk frother. Its plastic A Modo Mio capsules are also harder to recycle than Nespresso's aluminum pods, with recycling dependent on having a suitable collection point nearby.
The Jolie Evo is widely available in the UK, but availability in the US has been limited. If you can't find one where you live, our trusty best Nespresso machine guide is a good place to look for alternative capsule coffee makers. If you're after a small, affordable machine that prioritizes good espresso over bells and whistles, though, the Jolie Evo is a very apt option.

❌ You prefer traditional coffees: If syrup and cold brew aren't your thing, you can get excellent results from a more affordable machine such as the standard Siemens EQ900.
❌ You're a bit clumsy: The wide and shallow drip tray can be prone to spilling if you're not careful, and the J10 won't warn you until it's very full.
Does your usual coffee shop order bring baristas out in a cold sweat? The Jura J10 is the coffee maker for you. Not only does it brew superb espresso, it also creates the most authentic-tasting cold brew we've had from a home coffee machine.
Unlike most other machines capable of brewing cold, the Jura J10 forces pulses of water over your freshly ground coffee at high pressure (as shown in the video below). The result is impressive, and noticeably more flavorsome than cold brew from other machines I've tested - mellow and well-rounded. Toss in a couple of ice cubes and you'd be hard-pressed to tell the difference between the J10's cold brew and coffee made the traditional way overnight.
The Jura J10 also has a particularly good milk-texturizing system, with an option to add a syrup of your choice, which is distributed evenly throughout the foam as it's dispensed. Since the syrup isn't concentrated in the bottom of your cup, you only need a little to achieve plenty of flavor, and the syrup never enters the coffee machine itself so you don't need to worry about it tainting your next drink.
It's all very impressive and beautifully executed, but the price tag is firmly in luxury territory. Think champagne taste, rather than bargain hunting.

The De'Longhi Dedica Duo is my pick for the best small coffee machine around right now, and it's one of the most affordable too, with a list price of just $299.95 / £279.99 (details for Australia are yet to be announced).
It's a successor to the excellent De'Longhi Dedica Style, and retains all the features that made that machine so successful, including a fast-heating boiler, consistent boiler pressure, and a solid build that you might not expect from a coffee machines at such an affordable price.
It measures a mere 12 x 5.9 x 13 inches / 30.4 x 14.9 x 33cm, meaning you can tuck it into even a tiny kitchen (I currently have it between my toaster and the wall), and the Duo has a more modern-looking design with cleaner lines and a wider drip tray to more easily accommodate two espresso cups at once. It also comes in a more contemporary range of colors, including pistachio, rose, and vanilla shades inspired by gelato (according to De'Longhi).

We test new coffee machines every month here at TechRadar. Here are some we've reviewed recently that didn't quite make our shortlist.

The Melitta AromaFresh Therm Pro brings a built-in grinder into the equation, making it a neat alternative to the Sage Luxe Brewer Thermal for anyone wanting an all-in-one filter setup. During testing, however, the grinder’s inconsistency was noticeable and ultimately limited the quality of the brew.
Read our full Melitta AromaFresh Therm Pro review
How to choose the best coffee maker for you
There are so many different options on the market that it can be hard to know which is the best coffee maker for you.
If you enjoy a simple americano and don’t like milk-based drinks, then a drip filter coffee maker will be a great option. Plus, these machines can make as many as 12 cups of coffee in one go.
If you just want small quantities of coffee, though, we’d recommend a single-serve coffee maker from Keurig or Nespresso.
If you like milk-based coffee, then there are quite a few options available. Some models are fully automated and have a built-in frother that will be able to create a variety of milk textures, while others have steam arms which you place into a jug of milk and froth the milk yourself. There’s a third option too - and this includes buying a separate milk frother which is a stand-alone machine. You’ll be able to use these to make everything from lattes to hot chocolates, and they make a great accompaniment to a pod coffee maker.
Coffee drinkers that like plenty of customization options will be best suited to a coffee maker that lets you adjust the strength of your brew and create different sizes of hot drinks. Many premium coffee makers will let you do both of these things, but you can also adjust the strength and the aroma of your coffee with a good drip filter model.
The final thing to consider is how involved you’d like to be in the coffee-making process – and the clean-up afterwards. Some designs are smart-enabled so you can simply switch them on from your phone, however, others will require you to pack down ground coffee and pull your own shot of espresso before frothing the milk yourself. Some of the best coffee machines have self-cleaning systems which purge the steam wand to prevent milk residue drying in the pipes, while others have systems to flush out any build-up in the machine.
If you’re still not sure, you can find a more detailed breakdown in our article covering which type of coffee maker to buy.
Frequently asked coffee maker questions
Can espresso machines make regular coffee?
Yes, technically speaking, as espresso forms the foundation of nearly every café drink, an espresso machine can easily double as a versatile all-rounder. If your machine has a dedicated hot water dispenser (a common feature on many top models), you can top up a shot to make an Americano. For milk-based favorites like lattes, cappuccinos, and flat whites, you’ll just need a model with a built-in steam wand—or you can pair a basic espresso maker with a standalone milk frother.
How do coffee makers work?
With so many different types of coffee makers on offer, it’s no surprise that each type of machine works slightly differently. Here we focus on espresso machines and pod coffee makers but for a more detailed explanation, head to our feature on how coffee makers work.
Espresso machines work by using a pump to push pressurized water through coffee grounds so that it infuses with the water to make a smooth shot of espresso. If an espresso machine has a milk frother, it will use a boiler to push steam out of the machine which is then used to give the milk a velvety texture. Pod coffee makers work by using a compacted capsule of coffee and piercing a hole in the capsule. Hot water is then powered up through the machine and pushed through the capsule to create a coffee. Some more advanced pod machines, such as the Nespresso Vertuo Next, spin the coffee pod around at high speeds so that the contents evenly infuse with water for an even smoother cup of coffee.
How to clean a coffee maker
Keeping your coffee maker clean will not only ensure it looks great, but it’s crucial for maintaining working order and keeping it hygienic. We’ve written a full feature on how to clean a coffee maker and all its parts but the good news is that you’ll be able to clean thoroughly using products you’ve most likely got at home already. To clean your machine’s water tank, you can make a solution with one part water and one part white vinegar and simply leave it to soak inside your water reservoir for a couple of hours. To give the pipes a good flush through, let the vinegar solution run through the machine by switching it on as you would do normally for water.
We're also got a dedicated article on how to clean a Nespresso machine and how to clean a Keurig, for those that have single-serve coffee makers at home.
What is the best coffee maker for home use?
Whether you’re working remotely or cutting back on daily coffee shop visits, the right home coffee maker delivers café-quality drinks for a fraction of the price.
For authentic espresso, a dedicated espresso machine lets you fine-tune flavor and strength by adjusting water volume, brew time, and puck tamping pressure. They take some practice and cleanup, but the results are worth it. Short on space? Try the Breville Bambino or Bambino Plus (branded as Sage in the UK). Have more room and budget? Consider the De’Longhi La Specialista Arte EC9155MB or the Breville/Sage Oracle Touch.
If you prefer convenience over tinkering, a single-serve pod machine offers great espresso with minimal mess. We like the Nespresso Vertuo Next; check out which Nespresso machine is best for more models, or read Nespresso vs Keurig if you're in the US and weighing both brands.
Which type of coffee maker should I choose?
For those that want to perfect their coffee-making skills, consider an espresso machine. This is the best coffee maker for people who prefer to handle every part of the brewing process, from compacting the coffee grounds into a puck or small disc (a process known as tamping) to the brew volume and duration to create the perfect cup of coffee to suit you. If you’re new to this type of coffee maker, discover how to use an espresso machine in-depth in our article.
Alternatively, for the same coffee-shop standard hot drinks but with a hands-off approach, opt for a bean-to-cup coffee machines, which automate the processes described above to rustle up a cup of joe at the touch of a button.
If you’re looking to make a cup of coffee with as minimal amount of fuss as possible, a single-serve coffee maker is the best fit. Also known as pod coffee machines, they use capsules filled with ground coffee to create a hot drink with far less mess than espresso machines.
Nespresso and Keurig are the biggest brands when it comes to single-serve coffee machines and offer a range of machines each. However, pod coffee machines have a poor reputation when it comes to sustainability as many of the capsules end up in landfill. Follow our guide on how to recycle Nespresso pods to help ensure this doesn’t happen.
Finally, the drip coffee maker is a familiar style to most of us and it's the best coffee machine for those that want to brew large quantities of Java at any one time. Discover in-depth how coffee makers work in our article then, find out how to make your favorite coffee at home
How we test the best coffee makers
We take testing the best coffee makers seriously and put all the machines through their paces to see if they really can do everything they promise to. We test each coffee maker for the crema it produces on an espresso, how easy it is to use and set up, and also for consistency from one cup to another.
When we’re testing, we take into account the overall design of each coffee maker - how it looks, how much space it’ll take up on your kitchen counter, whether the water tank is removable for easy refills, and how the machine looks as a whole.
For coffee makers with milk frothers, we test the milk texture to see if it’s silky and smooth and of course, we wouldn’t be doing our jobs if we didn’t drink plenty of coffee along the way to see how each cup measures up for the overall taste.
We test models to see how much control you have over each cup of coffee, and whether it’s a case of simply pressing a button or whether more of a hands-on approach is needed. All the best coffee machines will require regular cleaning so we’re always sure to note what maintenance is involved and how easy these machines are to keep in top condition.

articles.title: Nova espécie! Cientistas brasileiros identificam nova perereca em Minas Gerais
articles.text:
Pesquisadores da Universidade Federal de Viçosa (UFV) identificaram uma nova espécie de perereca de aproximadamente 3 centímetros na Zona da Mata mineira, em Cataguases. Chamado de Ololygon cataguas, o pequeno anfíbio foi encontrado em um riacho no distrito de Glória.
A pesquisa durou 13 anos até que a espécie fosse classificada como um novo achado. Em 2013, os pesquisadores recolheram cerca de dez animais para estudá-los, até identificarem que faziam parte de um novo grupo para a fauna brasileira. Os resultados foram publicados na revista Herpetologica.
Para quem tem pressa:
- Pesquisadores da Universidade Federal de Viçosa (UFV) identificaram uma nova espécie de perereca na Zona da Mata mineira. Batizado de Ololygon cataguas, o anfíbio mede cerca de 3 centímetros e foi encontrado em Cataguases;
- A descoberta levou 13 anos de pesquisa e considerou características físicas, material genético e o canto do animal. Uma das marcas que ajudam a identificar a espécie é uma mancha em formato de “W” entre os olhos;
- O nome científico homenageia a cidade de Cataguases e o povo cataguás, que habitava a região. Novos estudos devem investigar a dieta e as condições necessárias para a sobrevivência da perereca, contribuindo para sua preservação.
Um canto diferente
A identificação da nova espécie passou por algo muito subjetivo: o canto do Ololygon cataguas. O biólogo Clodoaldo Lopes de Assis, morador de Cataguases, ouviu o som do animal e percebeu que ele era diferente do canto de outras pererecas conhecidas da região.
A partir daí, ele coletou os anfíbios e os levou para a UFV, onde cursou o mestrado em Biologia Animal.
Durante as observações, os pesquisadores identificaram um padrão na espécie, uma mancha em “W” entre os dois olhos do animal. Além disso, também foi possível estabelecer uma diferença de tamanho entre machos e fêmeas. As fêmeas medem entre 2,7 cm e 3,4 cm, enquanto os machos ficam entre 2,2 e 2,5 cm.
A pesquisa para identificar a espécie contou com análises do material genético, do canto e das características físicas do animal. Os resultados consolidaram o Ololygon cataguas como um novo grupo de anfíbios.
O nome científico dado à nova espécie homenageia a cidade de Cataguases e o povo cataguás, população indígena que habitava a região.
Leia mais:
- Nova perereca é identificada no Cerrado de Minas Gerais
- Perereca brasileira pode ser primeiro caso de anfíbios polinizando flores
- Venenoso, brilhante e monogâmico: conheça o novo sapo descoberto na Amazônia
Agora, novas pesquisas buscam explorar as particularidades do animal, como sua dieta e as condições necessárias para sua sobrevivência.
Esse aprofundamento se torna muito importante para sua preservação. Como o Ololygon cataguas foi encontrado em uma região de preservação, é possível que suas necessidades de habitat e vida sejam muito específicas. Assim, os resultados podem ajudar no tratamento e continuidade da espécie.
O caso já é a segunda descoberta de novos anfíbios em Minas Gerais somente neste ano. Em fevereiro, pesquisadores da Universidade de Brasília identificaram o Ololygon paracatu, uma nova espécie de perereca no cerrado mineiro.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
articles.text:
The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
Plus: AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.
Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.
Find out where AI progress is running into tougher challenges.
—Grace Huckins
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.
The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.
But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.
Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering.
—James Temple
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem
Anthropic’s Claude was used to prove the Riemann hypothesis. (WSJ $)
+ Two groups have independently verified the proof. (Guardian)
+ It could be the biggest math breakthrough in decades. (New Scientist $)
+ AI may be changing who gets to do math. (MIT Technology Review)
2 The COP31 climate talks have collapsed after a fossil fuels row
The EU rejected a deal it called “greenwashing.” (NBC News)
+ Saudi Arabia, Russia, and India opposed mentioning fossil fuels. (BBC)
+ Calls are growing for “net negative” instead of just net zero. (Nature)
+ Last year’s talks avoided fossil fuels. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The woman at the center of Nvidia's scandal has ties to China's military
Firms in her family's network work with Chinese defense contractors. (NYT $)
+ Her associate allegedly ran the chip smuggling behind the scenes. (WSJ $)
+ US intelligence says she was in touch with a Chinese spy official. (ABC)
+ Republicans are pushing a new AI strategy to counter Beijing. (Reuters $)
4 Hackers have breached the FBI’s criminal information database
It contains information used by law enforcement at all levels. (AP)
+ Hackers also breached an Agriculture Department system. (NBC News)
+ And the Austrian foreign ministry’s website. (Reuters $)
5 Russia, the US, and Israel have stalled global rules on “killer robots”
The UK, Japan, South Korea, and Turkey also resisted binding rules. (Politico)
+ Around 100 nations backed regulations, but arms producers balked. (CNBC)
+ Talks will continue through 2028. (AP)
6 Trump says he’ll ban US companies from building data centers abroad
He threatened them with a “tremendous tax.” (CNBC)
+ Electricity is fuelling the data center backlash. (MIT Technology Review)
7 US lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars
They plan to prohibit sales of Chinese vehicles in the US. (Quartz)
8 Trump’s visa crackdown has pushed tech workers to leave the US
It’s driving engineers and researchers overseas. (Bloomberg $)
9 GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could free up farmland larger than Italy
Their use could transform the global food system. (Conversation)
+ They may also slow biological aging. (MIT Technology Review)
10 BepiColombo has become the second spacecraft to orbit Mercury
Its probes will study the planet’s surface and surroundings. (Nature)
+ Mercury’s ancient ice could hold clues to the origins of life. (New Yorker $)
Quote of the day
“It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.”
—John Kennedy, US senator from Louisiana, tells NBC’s Meet the Press that Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could prove costly for efforts to prevent China from obtaining AI chips.
One more thing
On the ground in Ukraine’s largest Starlink repair shop
Starlink is critical to Ukraine’s fight against Russia, but Donald Trump’s fickle foreign policy and reports of Elon Musk restricting Ukraine’s access to the service have cast the technology’s future in the country into doubt.
For now, Starlink access largely comes down to the unofficial community of users and engineers, including the expert “Dr. Starlink”—famous for his creative ways of customizing the systems—who have kept Ukraine in the fight, both on and off the front line.
He gave MIT Technology Review exclusive access to his unofficial Starlink repair workshop in the city of Lviv. Here’s what we learned.
—Charlie Metcalfe
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: Espectacular tráiler final de ‘Avengers: Doomsday’: la batalla definitiva de Marvel llega a los cines
articles.text:
Marvel acaba de lanzar por fin el esperado tráiler final de Avengers: Doomsday. Cuando tan solo restan cuatro semanas para disfrutar de la nueva película de los Vengadores en cines, la compañía ha decidido liberar su último avance. Y con él han dejado claro que será la entrega más ambiciosa de la historia de la compañía. Porque, efectivamente, no se han guardado nada. Incluido el primer vistazo al regreso de Kate Bishop.
En el tráiler final de Avengers: Doomsday, la cinta se centra nada menos que en Steve Rogers. El antiguo Capitán América vive una vida tranquila junto a Peggy Carter tras haber devuelto las Gemas del Infinito en Avengers: Endgame. Ambos tienen un hijo que, sin embargo, no sabe que su padre fue un héroe. Pero todo cambia cuando alguien llega a su casa para buscarle.
Los 4 Fantásticos aterrizan en el jardín de Steve y Peggy preguntando por él. Por ello, se ve obligado a explicarse a su hijo, ya un adolescente, quién fue realmente el Capitán América. Tras esto, se unirá a los héroes del Edificio Baxter para viajar al presente, donde se reúne con el resto de superhéroes de la franquicia. Por otro lado, el tráiler de Avengers: Doomsday también muestra a los héroes habituales enzarzados en una violenta lucha contra los X-Men antes de unirse en la batalla definitiva contra el Doctor Doom y sus enormes centinelas.
Mira el tráiler final de Avengers: Doomsday
En Avengers: Doomsday, los héroes de tres universos distintos se verán implicados en un enfrentamiento letal y deberán hacer frente a una amenaza como nunca antes habían visto. Todos los equipos de las distintas Tierras tendrán que aprender a entenderse entre sí mientras sus mundos colapsan si quieren evitar el caos total en el multiverso.
"Es lo más trascendental que le ha pasado jamás al UCM. Se percibe como el fin de los tiempos. La AVT se creó precisamente para proteger las líneas temporales del colapso, y ahora se encuentran en medio de un colapso catastrófico", explicaba hace unos meses el director Joe Russo en una entrevista concedida a Empire.
Avengers: Doomsday se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: How Can AI Build Faster And Better Silicon For Physical AI?
articles.text:
Shortening the path from design intent to verified implementation could put custom silicon within reach of more teams.
The age of physical AI is here, and with it comes a significant increase in the demand of custom silicon.
By 2025, five million industrial robots were operating worldwide. As these systems become more capable, their demands on silicon become more distinct. Each must balance computation and memory with the realities of power, latency, reliability, and security.
Fig. 1: Annual installations of industrial robots, 5 largest markets, 2025. Source: International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics 2026. Chart redrawn by ChipAgents.
For humanoid robots in particular, application-specific hardware can provide the agility and speed required to perform specialized tasks in real time. As those requirements diverge, specialized ASICs become more attractive, because they can be optimized for the exact workloads, latency targets, power envelopes, and operating environments of a particular system.
The constraint to this innovation is development speed: AI models and software evolve faster than the conventional silicon tape out cycles, creating a need to accelerate the entire path from design intent and exploration to physical implementation and validation.
For agentic AI to deliver that acceleration, it must meet three requirements.
Agents need a shared, persistent representation of the design and the engineering knowledge behind it. A design ontology provides structure: it connects design flows, RTL design, verification, verification tools, error diagnosis and repair, synthesis, timing, and PPA optimization methodologies. Organization-specific methodologies and prior decisions add the rationale for how the design should evolve. To remain useful across tasks, this context must track provenance, design versions, and dependencies, so agents can distinguish current evidence from assumptions or superseded results.
Consider a 3D-IC, where logic, memory, die-to-die interfaces, packaging, power delivery, and thermal behavior are coupled. An RTL change that preserves functional behavior can alter switching activity, placement, or interconnect demand, affecting timing, power integrity, and temperature after implementation. Persistent context helps agents trace those dependencies across die and system boundaries, identify which analyses and verification results may no longer be valid, and invoke the appropriate tools to reassess them. AI then also converts improvement from specific cases into reusable knowledge, helping reduce recurring mistakes and repeated investigation across similar tasks.
Second, agents must carry design objectives through many dependent steps, measuring progress against verified engineering outcomes: functional correctness, physical feasibility, and target power, performance, and area within schedule and compute budgets.
Novel architectures for physical AI introduce more configurations, interfaces, and corner cases. Accelerating individual tasks delivers limited value if downstream verification or physical implementation cannot converge. Every action must therefore serve the overall objective, with explicit acceptance criteria guiding execution and determining when the work is complete.
This requires co-optimizing models, tools, and compute across the workflow. Complex reasoning may benefit from a larger model, repeatable operations from deterministic procedures, and numerical analysis from specialized engineering tools. CPU and GPU allocation, memory capacity, and parallel execution must be selected according to their contribution to the final result. The relevant measure is total time and cost to a validated outcome.
Third, all systems produced must be held to a critical standard of verifiability and security.
Physical AI applications operate in the real world, often in environments where failures can create direct safety risks. Specialized hardware also introduces hardware-specific security requirements and potential vulnerabilities that must be identified and verified before deployment. Agentic AI can help automate portions of that process by checking implementations against security requirements, surfacing potential vulnerabilities, and generating additional verification scenarios. That being said, to achieve an entirely autonomous workflow, you need traceable decisions, reproducible tool runs, explicit verification assumptions, and engineer review and signoff. Trust in this system is dependent on the evidence supporting each engineering decision.
At ChipAgents, we’re building toward a question: what would it take to make chip development 10× faster? Our approach brings organizational design ontology, physics-aware models, and LLM agents together in IC-STAR, the chip neural engine powering our platform. We study how models and multi-agent orchestration can work together to reach verified outcomes faster, with lower inference cost. Our ambition is to shorten the path from design intent to verified implementation, which could put custom silicon within reach of more teams, opening new possibilities for machines that sense, move, and act. We see a future where more engineering ideas make it beyond the drawing board and into the world.

articles.title: SA's Lumepay is helping African businesses move money across borders
articles.text:
South African startup Lumepay has built a business-to-business (B2B) cross-border payments platform that makes it cheaper and more reliable for African businesses to move money in, out of and across the continent.
Founded in October 2025 and led by CEO Harry Huang, the Cape Town-based Lumepay serves SMEs, corporates and financial institutions. Its rail-agnostic platform combines traditional banking channels with stablecoin rails to deliver fast, cost-effective and transparent B2B transfers within and between African jurisdictions.
“Too often, funds get stuck in local markets, which limits businesses’ ability to invest and grow in Africa. Lumepay is built to solve that: we make moving money in, out of and across Africa possible, seamless, efficient and affordable. That in turn empowers African businesses to take part fully in regional and global trade,” Huang told Disrupt Africa.
A single Lumepay account gives businesses access to multiple currencies to receive, convert and pay, with collections and disbursements offered in local African markets across several payment rails. Clients use the platform to receive international payments into local currency, make bulk local-currency payouts, pay overseas suppliers in currencies such as US dollars and Chinese yuan, manage foreign exchange and move money along intra-African trade corridors. The startup is also preparing to launch private US dollar, euro and British pound accounts held in the customer’s own name.
“African businesses still lose time and money moving funds across borders, and three things cause most of it: fragmentation, inefficient liquidity and execution risk,” said Huang. “Businesses need systems designed for how Africans actually trade, with the liquidity, infrastructure and speed to match.”
Lumepay counts banks, fintechs and both traditional and non-traditional remittance businesses among its competitors, but Huang says none offers its full suite of products in one place. Its main edge is that it is not tied to a single route.
“Each payment can go over the traditional banking channel or a stablecoin rail, whichever suits that corridor best. This lets us move money faster, at a lower cost, and into more markets than a single-rail provider can,” he said.
The startup launched Lumetrade, its digital asset and stablecoin trading venue, in April 2026, before rolling out the Lumepay payments platform in June. Across the two platforms it has since onboarded around 6,000 businesses and individuals, most of them SMEs and corporates paying suppliers in China, Europe and across Africa, businesses receiving foreign payments into local currency, and financial institutions using Lumepay for liquidity.
“What is most encouraging is repeat usage. Once a business moves its supplier payments to us and sees the money arrive the same day at a fair rate, it tends to stay,” said Huang.
Integrated with more than 20 payment providers and banks across Africa, Lumepay is live in eight markets beyond South Africa – Kenya, where it recently launched after receiving clearance from the Central Bank of Kenya, as well as Tanzania, Nigeria, Ghana, Malawi, Mozambique and the West and Central African CFA franc zones. It is awaiting further regulatory approvals to expand its payment capabilities in these markets, and is eyeing Zambia and Angola next.
The startup makes money mainly from a transparent spread on each currency conversion that accompanies a payment, which it says is well below what businesses typically pay through banks or informal channels. It also charges transaction fees and earns from institutional trading and liquidity services. Lumepay does not disclose revenue figures, but says revenue has grown exponentially since launch.
“Our focus is building a business with sound unit economics, not buying growth at any cost,” said Huang.
Disrupt Africa reported earlier this month Lumepay had raised US$6 million in seed funding, alongside US$10 million in capital float. The funding has gone into its payment rails, banking relationships, regulatory approvals, licensed partner network, security and technology platform, and the startup is now laying the groundwork for its next round.
Getting here has not been easy, however. Huang said liquidity is expensive, as capital must be in place before the first client can be served, which is why the float mattered as much as the raise. Every market also has its own payments and foreign exchange rules, so Lumepay goes to market through licensed local partners while it pursues its own approvals, and only goes live where it has clearance.
The startup also had to rethink its technology after an outsourced initial build fell short.
“We failed fast. It cost us, but we learnt from it. We went after the best engineering talent relentlessly, led by our CTO, rebuilt the platform in-house, and delivered something we’re proud of in record time,” said Huang.
Winning the trust of businesses has been another hurdle, as has finding people with the right skills and attitude for a regulated startup.
“Starting any company is difficult, and starting one at this scale especially so. But the hard part is done. Now it’s time to grow,” Huang said.

articles.title: « Welcome to Vice City » : Miami se met aux couleurs de GTA 6, et tout le monde n’apprécie pas
articles.text:
La série de jeux vidéo Grand Theft Auto a pour habitude de se dérouler dans une version parodique et satirique des États-Unis et GTA VI ne fait pas exception. Le dernier opus de Rockstar Games se déroule à Leonida, une Floride à peine déguisée dont la ville principale, Vice City, reprend largement les traits de Miami. Plutôt que de prendre ses distances avec une série connue pour ses braquages et ses fusillades, la métropole a choisi d’en profiter. Comme le rapporte l’Associated Press, le comté de Miami-Dade a conclu avec Rockstar Games un accord de 3,9 millions de dollars, qui comprend notamment un immense panneau « Welcome to Vice City » sur le toit du Kaseya Center, la salle des Miami Heat.
L’enceinte a d’ailleurs accueilli mercredi dernier, à la veille de la sortie du jeu, une soirée « A Night in Vice City ». Les joueurs du Heat ont évolué sur un parquet blanc, rose et bleu orné d’un « I love Vice City », vêtus d’un maillot spécial, tandis que les fast-foods fictifs du jeu, Cluckin’ Bell et Burger Joint, s’invitaient aux buvettes. Les villes de Miami et de Miami Beach ont aussi signé leurs propres accords de promotion, Rockstar a commandé des fresques dans le quartier de Wynwood, et le club E11EVEN s’est rebaptisé NINE1NINE, comme son double virtuel.
 Introducing the Vice City hardwood 🏀
See it for one night only, tomorrow vs Milwaukee. https://t.co/ZBpxND08hO
— Miami HEAT (@MiamiHEAT) November 17, 2026
Un jeu qui récompense le crime ?
Cette lune de miel ne fait toutefois pas l’unanimité. La shérif du comté, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, s’est opposée à l’utilisation de ressources publiques pour promouvoir un jeu qui récompense le crime, y compris la violence contre les forces de l’ordre. Conseiller municipal de Miami Beach, ville qui a dépensé des millions de dollars pour reprendre le contrôle du Spring Break, David Suarez refuse lui aussi d’« associer notre marque à quelque chose dont nous essayons si désespérément de nous éloigner depuis quelques années ». Sa collègue Monica Matteo-Salinas juge au contraire ces craintes exagérées : selon elle, la ville « peut miser sur ce matériel promotionnel, qui ne dure que six semaines, sans pour autant cautionner le jeu vidéo lui-même et les actions qui s’y déroulent ».
« Je ne peux peut-être pas faire ça dans la vraie vie, mais je peux clairement le faire dans GTA. » Un fan de la série à Miami, cité par l’AP
Une Floride reproduite avec soin
Si Miami se reconnaît autant dans Vice City, c’est que Rockstar a fait ses devoirs : ses équipes ont sillonné la ville et les Keys, survolé les Everglades et interrogé des habitants, dont d’anciens policiers et d’anciens membres de gangs. Un travail salué par Julie Fornary, guide pour la Miami Design Preservation League, pour qui aucune concession n’a été faite sur les néons et les façades Art déco d’Ocean Drive. « Nous avons le clinquant, mais aussi le crasseux. […] C’est le Miami que nous connaissons tous, nous qui vivons ici », résume-t-elle.
À lire aussi : GTA 6 : voici la façon la moins chère d’y jouer
L’engouement est tel aux quatre coins du monde qu’il se mesure aussi côté voyage. Selon Expedia, les recherches d’hébergement à Miami ont bondi de 55 % depuis la diffusion de la bande-annonce, le 15 octobre, par rapport à la même période l’an dernier, et celles pour Panama City, la station balnéaire qui a inspiré la ville de Port Gelhorn, de 65 %. Le groupe rattache ce phénomène à l’une des tendances de son rapport Horizons 2027, les séjours placés sous le signe du « retour à l’enfance », où les voyageurs troquent les programmes millimétrés contre des escapades ludiques et sans obligation. « Avec la sortie d’un titre aussi culte, on voit à quel point le besoin de déconnecter du quotidien et de retrouver une forme d’insouciance est fort chez les adultes », explique Xavier Rousselou, porte-parole d’Expedia.
