articles.title: Anatel quer antecipar autenticação de chamadas
articles.text:
Anatel quer antecipar autenticação de chamadas
Proposta em consulta pública prevê antecipar para 2027 as novas regras contra fraudes e chamadas abusivas.
A Anatel pode antecipar para outubro de 2027 a implantação da autenticação de chamadas no Brasil, atualmente prevista para novembro de 2028. A alteração está em consulta pública e depende de uma decisão definitiva da agência.
A antecipação integraria a proposta aprovada em 19 de novembro, que também trata do bloqueio de comunicações irregulares, da identificação de empresas nas ligações e de uma base centralizada de números telefônicos.
A Consulta Pública nº 52 foi publicada nesta segunda-feira (23/11) e busca regulamentar a medida provisória publicada pelo governo em outubro, que estabeleceu novas exigências para enfrentar fraudes e chamadas abusivas.
A autenticação permite verificar se a ligação realmente partiu do número apresentado ao destinatário, dificultando o spoofing, fraude em que criminosos adulteram essa informação para simular chamadas de bancos, empresas ou outras instituições conhecidas.
A Anatel já havia decidido tornar a autenticação obrigatória, com prazo de três anos para adaptação. A proposta atual é encurtar esse calendário. Pelas regras da MP nº 1.396/2026, a operadora de origem deve autenticar a chamada, enquanto as redes intermediárias precisam preservar essa informação. A prestadora que entrega a ligação ao destinatário fica responsável pela verificação antes de completar o contato.
O texto também prevê o bloqueio de chamadas não autenticadas, com exceções a serem definidas, como serviços públicos essenciais. Para ligações de pessoas jurídicas, está prevista a apresentação do nome empresarial e logotipo. A proposta dispensa dessa identificação as empresas que não excederem 100 mil chamadas mensais.
Uma base de numeração integrada às soluções de autenticação e identificação de chamadas reunirá os telefones e titulares. As operadoras deverão fornecer e manter os registros atualizados, sob supervisão da Anatel. O sistema proposto também permitirá consultar qual empresa é titular de um número. O usuário também poderá contestar aqueles que não reconhecer.
Enquanto a proposta segue em discussão, outras medidas contra o uso abusivo da telefonia já estão em vigor. Os responsáveis podem ficar impedidos de fazer ligações por 15 dias. O bloqueio exige realizar, no mesmo dia, mais de mil chamadas por linha ou mais de 10 mil no conjunto de linhas.
Além disso, pelo menos 85% das chamadas precisam ser curtas (ligações não completadas, destinadas à caixa postal ou atendidas com duração de até seis segundos).

articles.title: UK-based Agon raises €63.98 million at €411.3 million valuation to build Europe’s sovereign defence AI infrastructure
articles.text:
Agon, a London-based defence AI startup building sovereign infrastructure for autonomous military systems, has raised a €63.87 million ($70 million) Series A round at a valuation of €411.3 million ($450 million).
The round was led by Northzone with participation from returning investors Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, and Global Founders Capital. The UK Government’s Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) also joined the round, marking their first joint investment. Roelof Botha, the former head of Sequoia Capital, has come on board as a personal investor.
“AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era,” said Kanishka Narayan, UK Minister for AI.
The investment from the UK Government’s Sovereign AI Fund forms part of the government’s broader Sovereign AI agenda. At the Budget, the Chancellor announced an additional £140 million for the Sovereign AI Fund, which will back promising early-stage AI companies with a meaningful UK presence. The funding for Agon marks the fund’s expansion into a new focus area: Physical and Industrial AI, covering robotics, autonomous systems, and advanced manufacturing.
Founded by former British Army officer and Anduril and Applied Intuition alumnus, Tristan Constant, alongside Junaid Hussain, co-founder of Cambridge Aerospace and Iconic, Agon wants to become Europe’s sovereign defence AI lab. Its primary product is a synthetic virtual lab, a virtual training environment where AI models for autonomous defence systems can be tested rapidly and affordably against realistic battlefield simulations.
The company, which has a second office in Berlin, has assembled talent from Anduril, Applied Intuition, Google, Helsing, Palantir, Amazon, and Havok, and is chaired by David Helgason, founder of gaming engine company Unity. The raise brings Agon’s total raised to date to €94.1 million ($100 million), following its emergence from stealth earlier this year with €28 million in Seed capital.
“Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors, and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety. Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend. We founded Agon to build that capability here, giving European defence the infrastructure and models it needs to retain technological advantage,” said Hussain, co-founder of Agon.
The bulk of the fresh capital will go towards recruiting world-class AI researchers and funding the significant compute infrastructure requirement to run a full-scale AI lab.
“Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match,” said Constant, co-founder and CEO of Agon.
Agon wants to become the foundational AI platform for European autonomous defence, developing and training the foundation models that the continent’s military system will rely on. “We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities,” added Constant.

articles.title: WiFi de 2,4 GHz vs 5 GHz vs cable Ethernet: cuál es mejor para ver películas en 4K
articles.text:
La elección entre WiFi de 2,4 GHz, WiFi de 5 GHz y cable Ethernet define si una película en 4K se reproduce de forma continua o si aparecen pausas, pérdida de calidad y demoras en la carga. En una casa con varios dispositivos conectados, la ubicación del televisor y la distancia hasta el router pasan a ser factores decisivos.
Para ver contenido en alta resolución no existe una única respuesta válida para todos los hogares. La banda de 5 GHz suele aportar más velocidad cerca del router, la de 2,4 GHz llega mejor a habitaciones alejadas y el cable Ethernet ofrece una conexión física que evita parte de los problemas habituales de una red inalámbrica.
Cuándo conviene usar WiFi de 5 GHz para ver películas
El WiFi de 5 GHz suele ser la alternativa inalámbrica más adecuada para un televisor cercano al router. Esta banda transmite más datos en menos tiempo y, según la información de O2, tiene menos interferencias que la frecuencia de 2,4 GHz en zonas donde hay muchas redes domésticas alrededor.
Su principal límite aparece con la distancia. La señal de 5 GHz pierde fuerza con mayor rapidez al atravesar paredes, puertas y suelos. Si el router está en el salón o en una habitación próxima al televisor, puede ofrecer una reproducción más estable. Si ambos aparatos están separados por varios ambientes, la mejora de velocidad puede diluirse.
En qué momento es útil el WiFi de 2,4 GHz para reproducir contenido en 4K
El WiFi de 2,4 GHz puede reproducir contenido en 4K, aunque su desempeño depende más de la saturación de la red y de los aparatos conectados. Su ventaja está en el alcance: al operar en una frecuencia más baja, atraviesa paredes y obstáculos con más facilidad que la banda de 5 GHz.
Esa cobertura puede ser útil cuando el televisor se encuentra lejos del router. En una casa grande, una conexión de 2,4 GHz con buena señal puede ser preferible a una red de 5 GHz que llega débil o se desconecta.
El inconveniente es que esta banda comparte espacio con aparatos como microondas, teléfonos inalámbricos y varias redes vecinas. En edificios con muchos departamentos, esas interferencias pueden afectar la transmisión.
Por qué el cable Ethernet suele ser la opción más estable en casa
El cable Ethernet conecta el router y el televisor de forma directa, sin depender de la intensidad de la señal inalámbrica. Esa conexión reduce la exposición a interferencias, a paredes intermedias y a los cambios de rendimiento que puede sufrir el WiFi cuando varios dispositivos se conectan al mismo tiempo.
Para una pantalla fija, como un televisor, suele ser la alternativa más previsible. Si la instalación lo permite, un cable de red evita tener que elegir entre las bandas de 2,4 GHz y 5 GHz. Es útil para quienes utilizan el televisor para videojuegos en línea, donde la estabilidad de la conexión puede ser tan clave como la velocidad.
La desventaja es práctica: hace falta tender un cable entre el router y el aparato, algo que no siempre es posible sin afectar la distribución de la casa. En esos casos, una red de 5 GHz cercana o un sistema que mejore la cobertura pueden ser opciones intermedias.
Qué alternativa conviene según la ubicación del router en casa
Si el TV está cerca del módem y es compatible con ambas bandas, la red de 5 GHz aparece como la primera opción para una película en 4K. Ofrece mayor capacidad de transmisión y suele estar menos congestionada.
Cuando el aparato está lejos, con varias paredes de por medio, la banda de 2,4 GHz puede mantener una señal más consistente. En este escenario, una red aparentemente más lenta puede evitar cortes si llega con mejor intensidad.

articles.title: BDC to manage Canada’s $100-million contribution to NATO Innovation Fund
articles.text:
Two years after earmarking the funds, Canada has finally joined the NATO Innovation Fund, and the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) will manage its stake.
The news: Canada became the 25th Allied nation to back the NATO Innovation Fund this past weekend, making an investment of 64.6 million euros ($100 million CAD). BDC will hold and manage Canada’s investment in the fund through its Defence Platform, working alongside the Department of National Defence and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.
The NATO Innovation Fund, which has now courted more than 1.1 billion euros ($1.7 billion CAD, is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund investing in technologies with defence, security, and resilience applications. By joining the fund, Canada is giving its defence tech companies another avenue for customers and capital.
From the source: “Defence is about much more than financing companies. It’s about connecting them to opportunity,” BDC senior vice-president of defence strategy Peter Dawe said in a statement. “BDC can help bridge the gap between Canadian businesses and the organizations buying, building and investing, whether that opportunity is here at home or across NATO.”
The context: The NATO Innovation Fund launched in 2022 and invests three to 15 million euros in deep tech, dual-use companies from the seed to Series B stages. The United Kingdom, Germany, and Türkiye are among the 24 other participating members, but not the United States. Canada pledged to join the fund in 2024, even earmarking the funds to do so, but it hadn’t actually joined until this week.
By managing Canada’s stake in the fund, BDC takes on even more responsibility in seeing through Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pledge to “rebuild” the Canadian Armed Forces and increase its defence spending commitments under NATO. In March, BDC expanded the investing and financing capacity of its Defence Platform up to $6 billion. This past September, BDC became Canada’s sole entrant in an investor network for NATO’s defence accelerator.
Final thought: The extra responsibility comes as the Crown corporation faces some uncertainty about its future. The 2026 budget revealed that the government is launching a transition process to merge BDC with Export Development Canada (EDC) to create a single federal development bank, with few details and no timeline for the merger to be completed.
Image courtesy Madison McLauchlan for BetaKit.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion
articles.text:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
Zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.
CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.
In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.
The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

How to choose an espresso machine
Espresso machines are some of the best coffee makers. They come in all shapes and sizes, including some of the best bean-to-cup coffee machines, and the best espresso makers help you achieve barista-quality results. They often include their own integrated bean grinder for your convenience but do bear in mind that extra equipment adds bulk and often increases the price as well. If you're looking for something fast, cheap and that doesn't need a lot of counter space you might prefer a single-serve or pod coffee machine.
If espresso is definitely for you, the first decision is to choose whether you want an espresso machine that offers manual control over dispensing water or a device that takes on that work for you; the latter is probably better for those new to playing barista.
Next, consider if you want a machine that you can use with ground coffee, single-serve pods, or a mixture of the two. Coffee pods are less messy than using ground coffee. They can be handy if you occasionally want to make decaf coffee using the machine – but they don’t produce the thick, rich crema you get with freshly ground coffee.
If you regularly make espresso for two or more people, look for a coffee machine with a double spot on the tray that can fill two separate cups simultaneously. And if you like longer coffee drinks with milk, such as cappuccinos and lattes, choose an espresso machine with a built-in steam wand or factor in the cost of a standalone milk frother.
Finally, take note of the size of the espresso maker to see if you have sufficient room for it on your kitchen countertop – or, if you plan to store it away in a cupboard, consider its weight to see that you’ll be able to lift it easily.
If you're on a budget, take a look at our guide to the best cheap coffee maker deals, too.
How we tested these espresso machines
We put every espresso machine through rigorous testing to see if it truly lives up to its promises. First and foremost, we judge the coffee itself; we look for a rich, intense shot free of bitter or burnt notes, topped with a thick, stable crema that holds its own even after sugar is sprinkled on top. We also measure extraction temperatures to ensure cup-to-cup consistency and monitor how loud the machine gets during brewing.
If a machine includes a built-in steam wand, we test its ability to microfoam both dairy and plant-based milks, checking for tiny bubbles that create a velvety, smooth texture; again keeping an ear out for excessive noise.
Finally, we evaluate the day-to-day user experience: how intuitive it is to set up and operate, whether it offers enough manual control for aspiring home baristas, and how easily the water tank removes for refills. We also factor in overall aesthetics and how much counter space it will claim in your kitchen.
Espresso machine FAQs
How do I make an espresso?
Espresso is made by passing water at high pressure through compacted ground coffee.
However, a set ‘recipe’, which usually refers to a ratio and brewing duration, is generally given by the roaster (the brands that roast and blend coffee beans). The most common recipe is 1:2 in 25 to 35 seconds, effectively turning each gram of ground coffee into 2g of liquid espresso in that period.
How compacted the ground coffee is will affect how quickly or slowly the espresso brews. If the coffee is too tightly packed, it will take longer to brew and be too strong; loosely compacted coffee means it will be dispensed too quickly and subsequently weak. Prefer a cappuccino, latte, or a flat white? Find out how to make your favorite coffee in our article.
If you'd like expert advice on making coffee-shop-worthy drinks at home, we have some great tips and tricks for you – and while you're at it, check out our guide to the game-changing coffee maker trick that will ensure you never drink bitter espresso again.
How is an espresso machine different from a coffee machine?
An espresso machine differs from other coffee machines because it uses pressurized hot water passed through a disc of compacted coffee grounds called a puck. It's possible to adjust the volume of water passed through the grounds and how tightly packed the coffee is to change the strength of the hot drink brewed.
Single-serve coffee machines, or pod coffee machines as they're sometimes known, still use pressurized hot water, but the coffee is contained in a capsule or pod. The coffee machine punctures the capsule several times to allow the water to flow through the coffee ground to brew the drink. However, while some single-serve coffee machines let you adjust how much water is used to create different volumes of coffee, it's impossible to tweak how compacted the grounds are.
Finally, drip coffee makers pass hot water through compacted coffee grounds. As a result, it's not at the same pressure as when using an espresso machine, and there's no set volume of water used. Instead, the brewing takes place until the water tank runs dry or the coffee maker is switched off. This creates a more traditional filter coffee rather than espresso.

articles.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
articles.text:
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Spreading alkaline rock on fields to lock away carbon helps farmers at first, but new research shows that those benefits could be strictly limited.
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.
But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.
These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.
“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”
How it works
There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.
The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.
If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.
“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.
ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.
But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).
“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”
“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”
Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.
“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.
Agricultural limits
But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.
A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.
Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.
The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.
“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”
The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.
Rising popularity
Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.
Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.
Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.
He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.
All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.
Tempered expectations
The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.
In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.
CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.
Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”
Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.
Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis. 
A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
Healthy debate
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?
Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.
“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.
Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.
But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

articles.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.text:
Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development.
Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
Looking for a web browser without Google Chrome underneath? You can try this independent web browser now on macOS and Linux.
The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We’ve seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000, Apple’s WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE’s KHTML. A decade later, the Google-backed Chromium project forked WebKit to create Blink, which now powers Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, and more.
Ladybird is backed by a nonprofit organization with the goal of creating “an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web,” according to its website. Though Ladybird development initially began as part of a C++ project, its developers eventually began porting the code to Rust using AI.
In his post announcing the alpha, Kling notes that the browser built around the Ladybird engine “is modest but functional,” adding that “some websites won’t work” during the alpha. A Windows version of Ladybird will arrive during a “later stage” of the project.

articles.title: The Sovereign AI Paradox: Who Controls the Compute?
articles.text:
On Nov. 20, President Trump threatened penalties on American companies building data centers overseas. The announcement came one day after new U.S. export controls took effect, restricting certain shipments of advanced computing equipment to data centers that provide remote processing capacity to entities in restricted jurisdictions.
The measures address different issues, but together they create a difficult question for the semiconductor industry. If Washington wants the world to depend on American AI technology while placing tighter conditions on where and how that technology can be deployed, how will foreign customers respond?
Saudi Arabia is already providing one answer.
The architecture behind sovereign AI
In August, AMD, Cisco, and Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN announced that AI infrastructure built around AMD Instinct MI355X accelerators and Cisco Silicon One networking was operational. For a sovereign computing operator, the choice of suppliers carries implications well beyond processor performance.
Nvidia’s CUDA ecosystem has a substantial advantage in software maturity, optimized libraries, and developer adoption. AMD’s ROCm provides an alternative, although migrating workloads between the two involves testing framework compatibility, adapting specialized kernels, and retuning performance. Those engineering costs matter when governments expect infrastructure investments to remain productive for a decade or longer.
Networking introduces another set of decisions. Nvidia’s NVLink and InfiniBand technologies provide tightly integrated communication capabilities for large accelerator clusters. Ethernet-based architectures offer alternative approaches to scaling, equipment sourcing, and interoperability.
The Ultra Ethernet Consortium’s specification 1.1, released in October, extends the industry’s efforts to improve Ethernet for demanding AI and high-performance computing workloads.
For operators building sovereign infrastructure, the ability to introduce new hardware generations without replacing an entire networking or software environment has financial as well as technical value.
Two different markets for sovereign inference
The distinction between training and inference makes these choices more consequential.
Training frontier models requires large clusters, high memory bandwidth, and fast communication among accelerators. These requirements favor tightly integrated systems capable of handling enormous computational workloads.
Inference is creating two distinct infrastructure requirements. At one end, large language models with long context windows, substantial key-value caches, and demanding throughput requirements still benefit from high-end accelerators with large amounts of high-bandwidth memory.
AMD’s MI355X illustrates this category. With 288GB of HBM3E memory and up to 8TB/s of theoretical memory bandwidth, it is designed for demanding AI training and inference workloads. Its memory capacity can help accommodate large model weights and growing context requirements, while bandwidth remains critical to token-generation performance.
At the other end, governments and enterprises are deploying smaller, specialized, and quantized models for applications such as document processing, industrial monitoring, and customer services.
These workloads can favor smaller accelerators, systems using conventional DRAM or hybrid CPU-GPU configurations, provided they meet the required latency and throughput targets.
The distinction matters because the economics are different. A large sovereign AI cluster may justify expensive HBM-equipped accelerators, while a regional inference deployment must balance model accuracy, utilization, power consumption, memory requirements, and cost per delivered token.
The result is a broader hardware market, spanning high-end AI systems and more economical regional deployments. Each creates different opportunities for processor, memory, networking, and power management suppliers.
Export controls reach the infrastructure design
The U.S. Commerce Department’s Nov. 19 rule adds a further complication.
Under specified circumstances, exports, reexports, or transfers of covered advanced computing items require authorization when data centers provide access to more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5 jurisdictions, or whose ultimate parent companies are headquartered there.
The threshold can apply across linked data centers, including digitally connected facilities. The regulation defines these as facilities connected through networking infrastructure that enables resource sharing, workload balancing, and data replication as a unified system. In practice, data center interconnects, often using high-capacity optical networks, can support such arrangements. The regulatory definition focuses on how the facilities share computing resources, rather than prescribing a particular network technology.
For operators, this makes the allocation and accessibility of computing capacity across multiple facilities relevant to compliance. Customer verification, access controls, and reliable records of resource allocation become part of infrastructure design.
Hardware security technologies can support this effort. Nvidia’s confidential computing capabilities, combined with CPU technologies such as AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX, enable hardware-backed isolation and attestation of supported execution environments.
These mechanisms help protect sensitive workloads and verify aspects of the environment in which they run. Regulatory compliance also depends on customer due diligence, applicable licenses, and operational controls.
Securing a workload and establishing who is legally entitled to access computing capacity are related engineering and governance challenges, but they require different safeguards.
The supply chain remains global
Even locally owned infrastructure depends on an international semiconductor supply chain. Advanced AI accelerators rely heavily on TSMC’s manufacturing capabilities, sophisticated packaging technologies such as CoWoS, and a concentrated ecosystem of HBM suppliers.
Europe’s efforts to develop processor technologies through initiatives involving RISC-V and domestic high-performance computing reflect a growing interest in controlling more of that value chain.
Yet designing an accelerator is only part of the challenge. Manufacturing, packaging, memory integration, system software, and developer tools determine whether it becomes a viable commercial platform.
For many governments, the immediate objective is operational control: owning the infrastructure, governing access to data and workloads, and securing dependable technology supply. Over time, those priorities could influence which processor architectures, software environments, and networking technologies receive investment.
Washington’s unintended incentive
American semiconductor companies have spent years building technology ecosystems that attract customers worldwide. Their competitive advantages extend from accelerator performance to software, networking, and system integration.
Sovereign AI customers bring a different set of purchasing priorities. They want competitive performance, but they also need predictable access, long-term support, and confidence that their infrastructure can adapt to changes in technology or regulation.
Trump’s proposed restrictions on American companies building data centers overseas introduce another consideration.
If U.S. hyperscalers face new barriers to expanding their infrastructure abroad, governments and regional operators may have stronger incentives to develop and own that capacity themselves, potentially purchasing American processors and networking equipment directly.
Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN illustrates how locally controlled infrastructure can be built around American semiconductor technology. This creates a tension for Washington. Restrictions intended to preserve American technological leadership may also encourage overseas customers to invest in alternative architectures, software ecosystems, and domestic engineering capabilities.
That is the sovereign AI paradox. American processors may continue to power much of the world’s advanced computing infrastructure. But the decisions surrounding those processors, from software and interconnects to security and system ownership, could increasingly be made by customers seeking greater independence from their suppliers.
For chipmakers, the next competition may be as much about giving customers control over their computing future as about delivering the fastest processor.

Can the Nvidia Monopoly on AI Chips Be Broken?

Sovereign AI: Ambition or Illusion?

articles.title: Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j
articles.text:
This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.
OpenJDK
Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.
JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.
JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector<Float16> vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.
JDK 28
Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.
Java4Shell
A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:
[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.
Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.
Spring Framework
It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.
The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.
Azul Payara
The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:
- CVE-2026-90908, a vulnerability in the GenericAdminAuthenticator class that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass JMX/RMI administrative access restrictions by spoofing the client host address that may lead to remote code execution.
- CVE-2026-110003, A vulnerability in the administration REST interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass secure-admin remote-access restrictions by supplying an arbitrary value in the X-GlassFish-authToken HTTP header that grants execution of arbitrary administrative commands, equivalent to complete compromise of the server.
Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.
Hibernate
The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.
Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.
More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.
Java Operator SDK
The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
BellSoft
Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.
With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.
Helidon
The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.
LangChain4j
The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.
Micrometer
After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.
Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

articles.title: Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
articles.text:
After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.
It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.
Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback”
Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday.
News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.
Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”
But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.
The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report, as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.
The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.
The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.
Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts. Although Trump had previously cast doubt on multiple reports that Alice Huang was a spy, The New York Times reported on Sunday that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year.” According to the Times, which cited multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, Kang Wei — Alice Huang’s business partner and, by some reports, husband, who reportedly introduced her to the Nvidia CEO — worked with the same Chinese intelligence agency. But on Sunday evening, Trump still argued for Huang’s return and managed to continue flipping Nvidia’s board in his favor after a weekend’s worth of efforts.
“[I]ndefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible”
If the board maintained any hang-ups about bringing Huang back as CEO, Trump’s power over the executive branch — and the pressure he could exert with it — might have offered a compelling counterargument. The Securities and Exchange Commission had previously opened an investigation into whether Nvidia “misled investors,” according to The Wall Street Journal. But in a post on Truth Social Monday, Trump said that the attorney general “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Reached for comment, the DOJ did not provide an on-the-record response in line with The Verge’s editorial policy.
Key Democrats have indicated that both Nvidia and the Trump administration will be under fire when the new Congress is sworn in — and momentum has built behind GPU export controls, which Huang lobbied extensively to loosen. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said in a post on X, adding they’d work “on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.” Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible” and pledged to investigate “business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce.” He called for “traditional Republicans” to join in the effort.
“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, “A real Congress will find out” whether Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had any alternative incentives for their role in Nvidia’s dealings. Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, called Trump’s intervention to bring back Huang “outrageous.” Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-TX), a member of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees, which are interviewing Huang next week, said he wants to know how Trump stands to benefit from “personally champion[ing] Huang’s return.”
“We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO”
At closed-door hearings next week, Democrats say they intend to press Huang and the administration further, and several accused the administration of corruption. “We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC’s access to our most sensitive technology,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement to The Verge. The board’s decision is “outrageous,” said Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), a member of the House Select Committee on China. “We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement, calling for Huang to testify publicly. “Reinstatement is no substitute for accountability,” Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), another China Committee member, said in a statement.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta also intends to continue an investigation into the company. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang does not change the fact that the American people deserve to know what happened here — whether Nvidia misled investors and the public,” California Department of Justice spokesperson Elissa Perez said in a statement.
Last week, before Huang was reinstated, at least two Republican China hawks opposed the idea. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), a rumored potential presidential candidate, told reporters that he would not like to see Huang return to the top post, but would “defer to the board how they want to run their company. If it were me and a guy who just was caught up in a Chinese honeytrap — I think is the technical term for it — I don’t think that I would impose massive security concerns, not just for the company, but for American national security.”
While it was up to the board to decide whether to bring Huang back, Hawley said, “We in Congress ought to be concerned about the American national security implications and I think we should be looking into that.”
Huang “has a serious credibility problem”
House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said on stage last week at the Aspen Cyber Summit in Washington, D.C., that Huang “has a serious credibility problem, and I don’t believe he would be as effective now as he was before.” His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment after Huang’s reinstatement.
Sitting beside Moolenaar on stage last week, Rep. Greg Stanton (D-AZ) gave his advice to the board: “Don’t do it. Don’t bring it back. And at the very least, slow your roll, because there are so many questions that have to be answered. What else is out there that Jensen Huang has done to put US national security at risk?” Stanton warned that Congress is just beginning to probe what happened here. “There are going to be very serious investigations with very serious ramifications if in fact it is as it seems,” he said. “The company needs to know this ain’t going away for a while. This is a very serious issue.” After news of Huang’s return, Stanton doubled down on calls for investigations.
Other Republicans — some of whom are leaving Congress — notably disagreed with Trump’s jubilance for Huang’s return. “It’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) told CNBC. “To me it’s a failure of character.” Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement,” and said he must still testify before Congress. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips,” he wrote. Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton (R-AR) wrote on X that he’s not done investigating. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”
“Congress has much to investigate”
Market analysts have been watching and waiting for a Huang comeback since reports that he had assembled a “war room” of allies to help with his possible reinstatement. Not only did Huang cofound one of the world’s most valuable companies and arguably the most important one in the AI boom, but he has personally helped secure hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure funding from US financial institutions. Demand for Nvidia chips constantly outpaces supply, and Huang has had the president’s ear for months. Despite all that, though, Huang’s clout seemed like it wouldn’t help him up until the past 24 hours.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, wrote in a note that although investors may consider this a “good move given his history of value creation at the company,” questions remain about the best way to provide corporate governance and oversight at such an important company.
Jacob Bourne, an eMarketer analyst specializing in ad tech and consumer technologies, said in a statement to The Verge that it was difficult to gauge “how much protection Trump’s assurances will ultimately provide Nvidia.” And Heather West, head of Eurasia Group’s geo-technology practice, highlighted the fact that Trump recently met with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. The timing offers Democrats and China hawks “a great deal to work with in 2027 as they begin scrutiny into the administration, potential corruption, and large tech companies[‘] actions here,” said West.
Analysts at Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Monday that they consider Nvidia a $300 stock with Huang and a $225 stock without him, due to his hard-to-replace influence in the sector. They said an interim structure “could not replicate” his supply relationships with TSMC and others, as well as his place in AI industry dealmaking.
“This is a board that reversed itself because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia at the start of the Rubin cycle with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders, and it chose to pair the reversal with the governance architecture investors will want to see around him,” the Yorkville Ives analysts wrote.
Even Trump admits, though, that a true comeback story can’t be called in a single day. “I’ve seen some pretty good comebacks but I’ll tell you, what you have to have for a comeback, really, is longevity,” he told CNBC. He described the pep talk he gave Huang the night before. “I said, ‘You’ve got to promise me one thing. You’ve got the brain, you’ve got everything going, you’ve got to work hard. And if you work hard nobody can beat you.’”
According to Trump, Huang told him, “I’m going to work harder than I’ve ever worked.”
