articles.title: « Cyberpunk 2 est annulé », les développeurs d’autres studios sont en admiration devant GTA 6
articles.text:
Rockstar Games n’a visiblement pas manqué son rendez-vous avec les joueuses et les joueurs. Depuis sa sortie le 19 novembre 2026, GTA 6 enchaîne les records et affiche des chiffres vertigineux. Le succès ne se limite pas aux ventes. Sony a lui-même qualifié GTA 6 de plus grand lancement de l’histoire de PlayStation, toutes générations de consoles confondues.
Dans l’industrie du jeu vidéo aussi, GTA 6 impressionne et suscite de nombreuses réactions. Plusieurs développeurs ont récemment pris la parole pour saluer le travail de Rockstar, avec des comparaisons particulièrement flatteuses, et non dénuées d’humour.
Mark Richard Davies, directeur de jeu chez Naughty Dog et concepteur sur The Last of Us Part II a comparé GTA 6 aux grandes pyramides d’Égypte, dans un message sur X le 22 novembre : « GTA VI est au développement de jeux vidéo ce que sont les grandes pyramides. Autrement dit, les gens se demanderont pendant des siècles comment une telle chose a été possible, pour finir par conclure que ce sont des extraterrestres qui l’ont réalisée. »
Mark Richard Davies explique être particulièrement impressionné par le comportement des PNJ et par la quantité de dialogues. Et quand un utilisateur de X lui rétorque que le budget pharaonique de Rockstar Games explique la qualité de GTA 6, il répond simplement : « Je suis sûr que les pyramides ont coûté cher, elles aussi… » Une façon de rappeler que, même avec des moyens considérables, tous les studios ne sont pas capables de réaliser un tel tour de force.
Le directeur de Cyberpunk 2 plaisante sur l’annulation de son jeu
Michael Barclay, également développeur chez Naughty Dog et directeur du design de l’univers sur Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, a aussi salué le jeu sur X le 20 novembre : « Je crée des jeux vidéo depuis 19 ans, et GTA VI m’apparaît comme une Bugatti Veyron aux yeux d’un enfant victorien quelque peu anxieux ». On imagine sans mal les discussions tourner autour du blockbuster de Rockstar dans les couloirs de Naughty Dog, entre admiration et incrédulité.
Du côté de CD Projekt, on est pas mal admiratif aussi. Igor Sarzynski, directeur créatif de Cyberpunk 2, a lui aussi réagi à la sortie du jeu de Rockstar. « La ‘dépression liée au développement de jeux en monde ouvert’ — telle qu’illustrée par GTA VI — est une réalité. C’est probablement la plus grande réussite artistique de toute l’histoire, je le pense vraiment. L’ampleur, la densité, la cohérence, la réflexion qui sous-tend le tout… c’est tout simplement un miracle technologique et créatif », écrit-il sur Bluesky le 21 novembre. Le développeur conclut son message avec « Cyberpunk 2 est annulé ; je vais plutôt aller balayer les feuilles d’automne dans mon jardin. »
Rassurez-vous, le développement de Cyberpunk 2 continue, mais avec une sacrée pression sur les épaules. Igor Sarzynski explique créer quelque chose qui est propre à CD Projekt, avec une touche unique et différente, avant de conclure : « GTA est impressionnant, à l’image de toute grande œuvre d’art : il repousse les limites du possible ; c’est une vision captivante, exécutée à la perfection. »
Ces réactions ont au moins le mérite de montrer que le succès de GTA 6 ne se mesure pas uniquement en milliards de dollars ou en millions de joueurs. Même des développeurs qui travaillent sur certains des jeux les plus ambitieux de l’industrie regardent le travail de Rockstar avec une certaine fascination. Le studio a placé la barre très haut. On attend désormais avec impatience de découvrir ce que les autres studios nous réservent en matière de mondes ouverts, et surtout de voir comment ils parviendront à se démarquer du géant GTA 6.

articles.title: Jensen Huang de retour chez NVIDIA, comme six fondateurs de la tech avant lui
articles.text:
Onze jours après l’annonce de sa démission, Jensen Huang reprend la direction de NVIDIA. De Steve Jobs à Sam Altman, six autres fondateurs ont retrouvé les commandes de leur entreprise.
Le 17 novembre, Harvey Jones écartait publiquement l’idée de réembaucher Jensen Huang. Le 23 novembre, le conseil d’administration qu’il préside vote à l’unanimité pour rendre au cofondateur de NVIDIA ses fonctions de président et de directeur général ainsi que son siège d’administrateur. La décision prend effet immédiatement. Colette Kress, qui assurait l’intérim, reste directrice financière.
Le groupe avait annoncé le départ de Huang le 12 novembre, après des révélations sur sa vie privée et des soupçons d’opération de renseignement étrangère le visant. Donald Trump s’était prononcé en faveur de son retour. Le conseil dit avoir recueilli l’avis de hauts responsables américains avant de conclure que cette réintégration ne présentait pas de risque pour la sécurité nationale.
1# Chez OpenAI, les salariés réclament le retour de Sam Altman
Le vendredi 17 novembre 2023, le conseil d’administration d’OpenAI limoge Sam Altman. Il lui reproche d’avoir manqué de franchise dans leurs échanges. Microsoft propose alors à Altman et à Greg Brockman de prendre la tête d’une équipe de recherche en IA. Plus de 700 salariés menacent de démissionner si les administrateurs restent en place et si les deux cofondateurs ne reviennent pas.
OpenAI annonce un accord de principe dans la soirée du 21 novembre, en Californie. Le retour d’Altman est officialisé le 29, avec un conseil remanié que préside Bret Taylor, l’ancien codirecteur général de Salesforce.
2# Steve Jobs revient chez Apple avec NeXT
En 1985, Steve Jobs perd ses responsabilités opérationnelles au terme d’un bras de fer avec John Sculley, qu’il avait lui-même recruté. Il quitte Apple, fonde NeXT et prend le contrôle de Pixar. À la fin de 1996, Apple cherche un successeur au système d’exploitation du Macintosh. Le groupe annonce le rachat de NeXT pour plus de 400 millions de dollars et fait revenir Jobs comme conseiller de son directeur général, Gil Amelio.
Amelio quitte Apple en juillet 1997. Jobs devient directeur général par intérim en septembre, puis abandonne le titre d’intérimaire en 2000. Le logiciel de NeXT sert de base à Mac OS X. L’iMac relance le Macintosh, puis l’iPod et l’iPhone ouvrent à Apple de nouveaux marchés.
3# Jack Dorsey reprend Twitter tout en dirigeant Square
En 2008, Twitter connaît des pannes répétées et des tensions internes. Jack Dorsey, son premier directeur général, perd son poste et prend la présidence du conseil. Quand Dick Costolo s’en va à son tour en juillet 2015, la croissance du nombre d’utilisateurs s’essouffle. Twitter rappelle son cofondateur pour assurer l’intérim.
Le groupe annonce en octobre que Dorsey gardera la direction de Twitter. Il dirige toujours Square, sa société de paiement mobile. Pour lui permettre de cumuler les deux fonctions, Twitter décide de confier la présidence de son conseil à quelqu’un d’autre.
- Instantané dans l'information
- Messages courts
- Hashtags, tendances, tweet et retweet
4# Michael Dell reprend la main face à HP
Michael Dell avait confié la direction générale à Kevin Rollins en 2004 tout en restant président du conseil d’administration. Il reprend son poste en janvier 2007, après la démission de Rollins. Le fabricant de PC est alors sous pression. HP lui dispute la première place mondiale et une enquête comptable pèse sur le groupe.
Le fondateur entreprend de réduire la dépendance de Dell au marché du PC en développant les services aux entreprises. En 2013, il s’associe au fonds Silver Lake pour racheter le groupe et le retirer de la Bourse, afin de poursuivre sa transformation à l’abri de la pression des marchés.
5# Larry Page retrouve la direction de Google dix ans après avoir passé la main
Larry Page avait codirigé Google jusqu’en 2001, avant de céder la direction générale à Eric Schmidt et de se consacrer aux produits. Il reprend le poste en avril 2011. Schmidt devient président exécutif du conseil et s’occupe surtout des relations avec les partenaires et les pouvoirs publics. À l’époque, Google présente cette répartition comme un moyen de simplifier la direction de l’entreprise et d’accélérer les décisions.
Quatre ans plus tard, le groupe crée la holding Alphabet. Page en prend la direction et Sundar Pichai lui succède à la tête de Google.
6# Mark Pincus revient chez Zynga en plein virage vers le mobile
Avec FarmVille, Zynga a bâti son succès sur les jeux Facebook. Quand les joueurs passent au smartphone, le studio a du mal à suivre. En 2013, son fondateur Mark Pincus confie la direction à Don Mattrick, ancien responsable de la division Xbox chez Microsoft. Le mobile prend de l’ampleur, mais Zynga perd encore 226 millions de dollars en 2014.
Mattrick démissionne en avril 2015. Pincus reprend son poste et lance dès le mois suivant un plan d’économies. Il passe la main en mars 2016 à Frank Gibeau, un ancien d’Electronic Arts, et demeure président exécutif du conseil.
En rappelant Huang, NVIDIA confie de nouveau sa stratégie dans les puces d’IA à celui qui l’a bâtie. Le comité indépendant poursuit son enquête sur les circonstances du départ, alors même que le principal intéressé siège à nouveau au conseil. Un come-back retentissant.

articles.title: Anstieg bei .de-Domains: Welche Vorteile, aber auch Anforderungen mit der Endung verbunden sind
articles.text:
Domain-Registrierung: Welches Signal eine .de-Endung sendet
Was passiert, wenn Kunden aus Deutschland, die nach einer Softwarelösung suchen, auf der Website eines US-Anbieters landen? Die Seite ist englischsprachig, die Preise stehen in US-Dollar. Ein deutsches Angebot gibt es scheinbar, aber es ist kompliziert hinter einem Sprachwechsel oder irgendwo im Footer versteckt. Wer nicht gezielt danach sucht, findet den deutschen Shop nicht. Eine .de-Domain hätte das schon im Namen klargemacht.
US-Domaininhaber bilden unter den ausländischen .de-Kunden übrigens die größte Gruppe, zeigen aktuelle Zahlen des Registry Denic. Ende 2025 waren weltweit rund 17,7 Millionen .de-Domains registriert. Rund 2,15 Millionen davon, also 12,1 Prozent, gehörten Inhabern mit Sitz außerhalb Deutschlands. Auf die USA entfielen dabei 31,3 Prozent dieser Domains. Der Bestand ausländischer Inhaber wuchs 2025 um 3,3 Prozent, während der inländische Bestand nahezu stagnierte.
Wie sich die .de-Domains auf Webseiten-Betreiber im Ausland verteilen
Stephan Schmidt, Geschäftsführer von united-domains, ordnet die Zahlen ein: „Der Zuwachs bei .de Domains kommt inzwischen aus dem Ausland. Die Zahl der Inhaber außerhalb Deutschlands stieg 2025 um 3,3 Prozent, während der inländische Bestand nahezu gleichgeblieben ist. Für Registry und Provider heißt das: Verifizierung und Pflege der Inhaberdaten müssen über Ländergrenzen hinweg funktionieren.“
Im internationalen Vergleich fällt .de besonders auf. Der Global Domain Report 2026 kommt je 100.000 Einwohner auf 21.150 .de-Domains, das Vereinigte Königreich auf 14.790, Frankreich auf 6.317 und Italien auf 6.001. Von allen entwickelten Websites weltweit, also Domains mit eigenständiger Website, tragen 3,6 Prozent eine .de-Endung. Das Vereinigte Königreich kommt auf 2,7 Prozent.
Eine Endung mit dieser Verbreitung im eigenen Markt und dieser Präsenz im Web ist daher auch für Anbieter aus dem Ausland interessant. Warum gerade US-Unternehmen sie registrieren, lässt sich aus dem ableiten, was eine Endung technisch und rechtlich auslöst.
Die Domain-Endung als Signal für den Zielmarkt
Eine Domain beantwortet zwei Fragen, bevor der Inhalt gelesen wird: für welchen Markt das Angebot gedacht ist und welche Regeln dort für den Betreiber gelten. Die Länderendung beantwortet die erste Frage sofort. Suchmaschinen werten sie außerdem als starkes Signal für das Geotargeting. Eine .de-Domain kann die Auffindbarkeit im deutschen Suchraum deshalb unterstützen. Die Endung bestimmt damit, in welchem Markt ein Angebot gefunden und bewertet wird.
Das Signal bindet den Betrieb. Wer deutsche Verbraucher gezielt anspricht, unterliegt nach Art. 6 Rom-I-VO dem deutschen Verbraucherrecht, unabhängig davon, wo die Domain verwaltet wird. Endpreise einschließlich Umsatzsteuer, Widerrufsbelehrung und Impressum nach Paragraph 5 DDG sind damit eine Frage des Auftritts, nicht der Endung.
Globale Marke und lokale Ebene stehen dabei nicht zwingend in Konkurrenz. Eine .com-Adresse bleibt die globale Hauptadresse. Eine .de-Ebene bündelt Angebot in Euro, Rechtstexte und deutsche Ansprechpartner, ohne die globale Seite mit Sonderinhalten zu belasten. Der Nutzen entsteht jedoch nur, wenn sich der deutsche Markt in Angebot und Recht von den übrigen Märkten unterscheidet. Wo das nicht zutrifft, erzeugt eine zweite Adresse vor allem Pflegeaufwand.
Wie es sich mit Missbrauchsraten auf .de-Domains verhält
Die Endung wirkt auch auf der Sicherheitsebene. Im Netbeacon-Ranking, das der Global Domain Report auswertet, gehört .de zu einer kleinen Gruppe großer Endungen mit mehr als einer Million Domains, die in allen zwölf Monaten zu den Endungen mit den niedrigsten Missbrauchsraten zählten. Gemessen werden Phishing- und Malware-Domains je 100.000 verwalteter Domains. Der Report führt dieses Ergebnis auf die sicherheitsbewusste Verwaltung zurück. Es ist ein Indikator für die Betriebspraxis, kein Schutz für jede einzelne Domain.
Eine .de-Adresse ist keine einmalige Registrierung. Die Registry Denic prüft Inhaberdaten seit 2026 risikobasiert. Grundlage ist die NIS-2-Richtlinie und das BSI-Gesetz. Verlangt werden der vollständige Name einschließlich Rechtsform, eine aktuelle Postanschrift, Telefonnummer und E-Mail-Adresse. Die Verifizierung läuft über den Provider, und dafür steht eine Frist von fünf Tagen zur Verfügung. Bleibt sie aus, entfernt Denic die Domain zunächst aus der Zone.
Schmidt von united-domains sieht darin eine klare Zuständigkeit: „Die Registrierung ist nur der Anfang. Bei einer .de-Domain muss der Inhaber seine Daten sauber pflegen und die Verifizierung rechtzeitig abschließen. Sonst verliert die Domain ihren Platz in der Zone, und mit ihr die Adresse, unter der Kunden das Unternehmen suchen.“
Dazu kommen Aufgaben im laufenden Betrieb. Jede Adresse braucht ein eigenes SSL-Zertifikat, eine eigene Mailkonfiguration einschließlich SPF, DKIM und DMARC sowie eine eigene Verlängerung. Liegen gleiche Inhalte in gleicher Sprache auf zwei Adressen, sollte über die Attribute rel=canonical und hreflang festgelegt werden, welche Version bevorzugt wird.
Reicht eine Domain-Weiterleitung oder lohnt sich ein eigener Auftritt?
Eine zusätzliche .de-Domain braucht einen eigenen Zweck. Trägt sie einen Inhalt, der auf der Hauptseite keinen Platz hat, etwa einen Produktlaunch für den deutschen Markt, rechtfertigt sie einen eigenen Auftritt. Trägt sie nur dieselbe Botschaft als Einstieg, genügt eine Weiterleitung.
Technisch antwortet der Server auf den Aufruf der .de-Adresse mit einem Statuscode: 301 für eine dauerhafte, 302 für eine vorübergehende Verlagerung. Dabei können drei Probleme auftreten, die in der Praxis oft unterschätzt werden:
- Website-Pfade gehen verloren, wenn die Weiterleitung nur die Domain kennt. Eine Produktseite landet dann auf der Startseite oder ins Leere.
- Cookies gelten nur für den Host, der sie gesetzt hat. Ein Nutzer, der auf der globalen Seite angemeldet ist, bleibt auf der .de-Adresse eventuell nicht angemeldet. Einwilligungen müssen dann umständlich auf beiden Seiten separat gepflegt werden.
- Der Browser prüft das SSL-Zertifikat der .de-Adresse, bevor die Weiterleitung greift. Fehlt ein gültiges Zertifikat, erscheint eine Warnung, bevor der Nutzer das Ziel erreicht.
Schmidt sieht den Aufwand dabei an einer anderen Stelle: „Die Weiterleitung ist in wenigen Minuten eingerichtet. Schwierig wird die Zuordnung, also welche Pfade auf welche Ziele zeigen, wer die Einwilligungen auf beiden Adressen pflegt und wer das Zertifikat erneuert, bevor es abläuft.“ Unterscheidet sich das Angebot, etwa bei Preisen und Rechtstexten, ist ein eigener Auftritt erforderlich.
Für die Struktur stehen drei Wege offen: eine Landesendung, eine Subdomain oder ein Verzeichnis der globalen Domain. Die Landesendung trennt die Auftritte am eindeutigsten, verlangt aber den größten Aufwand. Eine Subdomain ist schnell eingerichtet, doch der Nutzer erkennt aus der Adresse nicht sofort, ob „de“ für Sprache oder Land steht. Ein Verzeichnis ist am einfachsten zu pflegen, erschwert aber die Trennung der Auftritte.
Was erwartet der Nutzer auf einer .de-Domain?
Entscheidend ist, wer die deutsche Ebene verantwortet. Betreibt ein Team Angebot und Betrieb für Deutschland selbst, spricht die Trennung für eine eigene Domain. Bleiben beide zentral, reicht ein Verzeichnis. In beiden Fällen verknüpft das Attribut hreflang die Versionen.
US-Unternehmen wählen .de, weil die Endung den deutschen Markt für Kunden und Suchmaschinen eindeutig benennt. Diese Zuordnung verpflichtet Anbieter und Unternehmen: Der Auftritt muss einlösen, was die Adresse verspricht, und die Pflege muss so lange laufen wie die Domain selbst.
)))))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: AWS launches 5 new open decision models for AI agents
articles.text:
AWS launches 5 new open decision models for AI agents
AWS on Monday launched Strands Decider v2, a family of five open decision models.
The release comes only seven weeks after Strands Labs, the experimental arm of AWS’s open source Strands Agents SDK, launched the first Strands Decider model. That was a 2-billion-parameter model built on Alibaba’s Qwen3.5.
The new version is based on Google’s Gemma 4 and comes in a range of sizes from the outset, starting at 2 billion parameters, all the way up to a 31-billion-parameter dense model (with a 4B model and a 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts model in the middle), all of which are available under the Apache 2.0 license.
Like similar decision models, the idea behind Strands Decider is that it doesn’t generate text. Instead, it takes a state, like a support ticket or an agent trace, along with a question and a fixed set of possible answers, and then returns a probability for each answer.
AWS VP and Distinguished Engineer Marc Brooker, who started the project, tells The New Stack, “We chose better training data or larger training sets, the usual kind of ML model generation journey, and came out with a set of models with significantly better accuracy and significantly better calibration, which are the things that really matter to customers in this space.”
Benchmarks
And indeed, the models clearly outperform v1. AWS says the 31B model averages 82.1 across six public text benchmarks, ahead of every rival it tested, including Google’s Gemini Decision 1 at 79.4. But it also trails some of its competitors on three of the six benchmarks — and Gemini still posts the lowest calibration error.
The 31B v2 model posts the top score on JevBench, the benchmark built around TypeSafe’s Jev, at 93.1 compared to Gemini’s 92.2. But it loses to Perplexity Decider v1.3 on PubMedQA and When2Call, and to vLLM Semantic Router’s open d3-ultra on a test based on New Yorker cartoon captions.
The smaller models hold up, too.
The 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts model averages 79.9, just ahead of Gemini Decision 1, and the E4B model jumps from 62.7 in v1 to 74.4. On image and video tasks, which AWS didn’t report for v1, the 31B model scores 90.1 on Mind2Web Multimodal and 70.2 on Video-MME, slightly behind Perplexity’s model on both.
The calibration error, which measures how closely a model’s confidence matches how often it’s right, drops to 0.027 for the new 31B model, down from 0.062 for v1. In this benchmark, only Gemini Decision 1 does better, at 0.025, while Jev 1.14 and Microsoft-Decision-1 come in at 0.062 and 0.066 respectively.
“I think with V1 we were benchmark leading for about eight hours,” Brooker says. He thinks the benchmarks are getting “a little bit saturated” and mostly help customers decide whether a 4B model is good enough for their workload.
Gemma 4 and bidirectional attention
It’s worth noting that AWS opted for a different architecture with Strands Decider 2.
Most LLMs today use causal attention, so each token only sees the tokens before it. Models need that to generate text, but since a decision model never generates text, the Strands team let every token in the state attend to the whole state in both directions. This means questions can then reuse that encoded state, so asking 20 questions about one agent trace costs little more than asking a single question.
As for why that works better, “I have some theories, but I would say that I’m not entirely sure,” Brooker says. The team tested both approaches across a diverse set of datasets, and “one outperformed the other, and I think that is the shape of the majority of ML research.”
Brooker says Gemma’s somewhat more traditional architecture may have contributed to the results.
Using Strands Decider at Amazon
Inside Amazon, the company says, engineers on an internal ticketing system swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the v1 E4B model to label tickets. Average time per call fell from 4,215 milliseconds to 897 milliseconds, and AWS estimates the cost dropped from about $22,200 to about $500 per million tickets at list prices. (The team hasn’t published accuracy figures.)
AWS also says v2 cut costs by routing requests between Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, which moves spending away from Anthropic models that AWS sells through Amazon Bedrock.
Brooker is most excited about hybrid workflows. “What’s really nice about these kinds of models is they’re just a cool tool for us to build workflows that are mostly deterministic and then have a decider model step, or mostly agentic, but on the easy routes, we can use decider models to drive down cost and latency,” he says.
Oddly enough, though, Strands Decider isn’t available on AWS’s Bedrock inference service yet. But then, the company’s annual re:Invent conference is happening a week from now and we will surely hear more about Bedrock there.

articles.title: Jensen is BACK at NVIDIA
articles.text:
What an odd few weeks. The big news today, of course, is that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as NVIDIA’s CEO. The markets immediately responded by adding roughly 30% or about $1T in market cap. I think folks realized this was the right option.
Jensen is BACK at NVIDIA
One of the big catalysts to this was that the U.S. government came out and said that they do not believe that having Jensen as the CEO of NVIDIA is a national security risk.
“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” (Source: NVIDIA)
It seems the government sign-off gave the board air cover on one major risk factor: that the Megaspeed issue would turn into a major national security investigation. With that off the table, then there was the challenge of alleged workplace conduct.
Workplace conduct is always a challenge because it opens NVIDIA up to claims from current and former employees. There was an early 2010’s case in California (note I have a 2007 JD from California’s largest law school, but never practiced, so this is not legal advice) for workplace sexual harassment in the $168M range, that was then significantly reduced to under $100M, then settled. What I have been telling folks for the past week and a half is that for the company to lose $1T in shareholder value, even $1B in a legal fund pays a lot of attorneys to cover other claims. It felt like Jensen’s value was wildly out of line with what it would cost to settle the cases. Again, I am not condoning the allegations, but at some point, I would have a hard time believing NVIDIA’s board did not have a team developing a range of exposure if they were to settle claims that could then be weighed against the cost of not having Jensen on the team. When it was comparing those two numbers plus potential government action, I can see how a board would have been more conservative.
Perhaps the other big one is that NVIDIA’s team accepted the news publicly, but what is hard to quantify is that folks who have been at NVIDIA for many years and built this enormous business are very loyal to Jensen. It has been really strange reading mainstream media reports about how Jensen can get passionate in meetings as if that were a major issue. Every CEO, especially founders, gets passionate because the business is personal. I would venture to guess that any of Jensen’s direct reports who have been there for a few years have earned enough to walk away if they wanted to, and they truly did not like working for Jensen. Maybe to put it another way, in the week and a half since Jensen resigned, I never heard an NVIDIA employee say “good riddance” or anything like that. Folks supported the board, but only spoke positively about Jensen’s leadership. It turns out when you create a market segment big enough to be measured in percentage of US GDP, it creates wealth for your employees, suppliers, customers, and partners that makes them loyal. Installing someone from the outside as CEO just does not replace that.
Final Words
More than a few executives were probably hoping to land the role and are disappointed, but realistically, those are hard shoes to fill. Jensen’s focus on the AI supply chain, sales to big customers, and loyalty among employees who have done well under his watch are exceptionally hard for anyone to replicate. Moreover, executives might be able to rise to the job, but NVIDIA added over $55B in revenue last quarter versus the year-ago quarter. Revenue-wise, that is roughly in the ballpark of adding an American Airlines annual revenue to NVIDIA on a quarterly basis. Moving that fast, it is hard for someone to grow in place in that role.
Perhaps the most fascinating part is what this means for executive compensation. The market saw what it meant to have Jensen out as NVIDIA’s CEO not just for NVIDIA, but for others in the ecosystem. Delaware’s compensation cases with Elon Musk now have a new data point showing this class of CEO can have an outsized impact on shareholder value. Not all CEOs are the same, and an individual can be uniquely valuable to an organization. Is Lisa Su the same at AMD? What about Mark Zuckerberg at Meta? Hock Tan at Broadcom? Michael Dell and Jeff Clarke? Or someone like Matt Murphy, who took Marvell from a very rough company a decade ago to a company zipping along today? The other side of this is figuring out the set of circumstances and formula for when a high-flying CEO can be ousted.
Personally, I think the board made the right decision in bringing Jensen back to NVIDIA, even if it means some clean-up needs to happen.
> Personally, I think the board made the right decision in bringing Jensen back to NVIDIA, even if it means some clean-up needs to happen.
What a pathetic comment. Only spineless cowards would say that.
He violated US export law, and since no change in management is made, NVDA can’t even say they righted the wrongs in this, but the real problem is that the NVDA VC is closed anyway:
https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/nvidias-days-as-an-open-checkbook-for-the-ai-economy-are-numbered-90c7b388?
“Just last month, the CEOs of emerging cloud companies that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing power gathered in Berlin for Nvidia’s premier European artificial-intelligence conference. In a talk that surprised some, Huang’s message was clear: Nvidia’s days as an open checkbook were over.
Huang told his partners that if their companies wanted allocations of Nvidia’s prized GPUs, they would need to secure upfront payments from customers, people in attendance said. That would make their projects easier to finance and ensure that Nvidia wasn’t alone in being a source of financial support.”
So what’s the point of putting him back in if the circular financing spigot is turned off now?
Guess $25M into a ballroom gets a President who won’t prosecute violation of US trade policy with the DOJ. The very policy that epstein-customer-number-one put in place. And anyone who knew this was going to happen, they got to buy NVDA stock on this drop and sell today + 30%… probably made another $1bn on insider trades this week. It’s so gross.
That spy gave NVDA $20bn in sales to violate US trade policy, he knew what he was doing, and he got a booty-call out of it too. $20bn out of $115bn in revenue last year. And we all pay the price with debt based build outs with no due dilligence (see Coreweave’s buying NV chips that NV then leases back to themselves, the debt behind that runs DD against NV balance sheet, not Coreweave’s – good enough and PE gives them billions to do the deal) ramping up pricing on memory, storage, and gpu’s. Double plus gross, they would have still been profitable by complying with trade policy.
Do I care if China has NV chips? Not terribly so, but with all the awful circular money laundering for fake profits, it’s just not necessary for it to be that bold. It’s nearly 20% of revenue – not 1-2% little grift from some small supplier diversion that Jensen can pretend he doesn’t know about. The reason the board removed him was to say they resolved this issue and keep from big sanctions against NVDA from dropping on their heads.
What the board actually said is “it’s ok for our CEO to have multiple relationships with subordinates, even though it is company policy for that to be a firing offence for any employee.”
The point about employee loyalty is not nothing. But arguing from financials… even if that weren’t morally bankrupt, it may be *actually* bankrupt when the bubble bursts. That is, he is worth this much to investors (who are, for the most part, likely to lose their shirts if they don’t find “bigger fools” to seel their stakes to)… for now. Will he be worth that much in 2 years? 5?
On the moral side of the matter, it’s a little unclear to me just how bad this is. It’s not good, but were those relationships truly consensual? Given his power, can that ever be established? Are there more to find?
And, oh yeah. nVidia has cover *for now* due to Trump stepping up for him. But Trump tends to lie when his mouth is open, and has no regard for national security at all. What will come out when his successor (or the Dems in congress) start looking at this?
This is a good move by the board, for short-term financials. They *may* have enough cover for it to be a smart move even long-term. Or this may just be delaying disaster.
Anyone think they didn’t have a conversation about succession plans before they brought him back?

articles.title: Durante las excavaciones arqueológicas en la Duna de Pilat, estos científicos descubrieron restos que datan de la Edad del Hierro
articles.text:
Un grupo de arqueólogos ha encontrado restos de la Edad del Hierro en la duna de Pilat, situada en la región francesa de Gironda. El descubrimiento tuvo lugar durante unas excavaciones realizadas entre el 21 de septiembre y el 9 de octubre de 2026, en las que participaron investigadores y voluntarios. Entre los objetos encontrados hay piezas de cerámica, algunas de ellas especialmente bien conservadas.
De hecho, el arqueólogo Philippe Jacques explicó que habían recuperado una vasija prácticamente completa, desde la base hasta el cuello, algo que no suele ser habitual en este tipo de excavaciones. Sin embargo, lo más interesante llegó cuando encontraron varios objetos relacionados con la pesca, entre ellos un flotador, una piedra utilizada como peso para las redes y lo que podrían ser fragmentos de una herramienta para repararlas.
Un descubrimiento que aporta nuevas pistas sobre la zona
¿Y por qué es importante este hallazgo? Porque, como explica Jacques en unas declaraciones difundidas por el organismo que gestiona la duna de Pilat, hasta ahora no habían encontrado pruebas de actividades pesqueras durante la Edad del Hierro en esa parte de la costa francesa. Los restos permiten conocer un poco mejor cómo vivían las personas que habitaban la zona hace miles de años.
Pero las sorpresas no terminaron ahí. En la parte norte del antiguo espacio dedicado a producir sal, los investigadores también localizaron agujeros de postes y varias fosas que apuntan a la existencia de al menos un edificio. Una construcción que todavía permanece enterrada bajo la zona oriental de la duna y que los arqueólogos esperan seguir investigando durante los próximos años.

articles.title: OPINION: AI will favour the companies built for AI, not adapted to it
articles.text:
For decades, business leaders have been warned that the impending arrival of a new technology will completely reorder the corporate world. But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not.
The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents aside.
With AI, however, the warning deserves more consideration. The reason is less to do with the technology itself, but rather who is best placed to use it, and that is increasingly becoming startups, rather than established companies.
The web didn’t break incumbents
The common story of the web is that of upstarts bringing down giants, and the rankings seem to agree.
The world’s most valuable company in 1995 was a Japanese telephone operator. In the same year, Microsoft barely made number twenty on the list and Nvidia was just a startup. Today Microsoft, Nvidia, Apple, Amazon and Alphabet lead the rankings, and just six of the largest companies in 1995 remain in the top thirty.
Though on closer examination, the incumbents were not the disasters the ranking implies.
Companies such as Exxon, Coca-Cola and Toyota, more than tripled their combined revenue between 1994 and 2024, meanwhile Microsoft grew more than fiftyfold. The web gave them access to better logistics, cheaper computing and wider reach. Oil companies could use better software without becoming software companies. Carmakers could run a more efficient supply chain. And a wealthier world could buy more cars, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals. The incumbents benefited from the technologies that were supposed to be disrupting them.
It is therefore unsurprising that business leaders often meet warnings about AI with scepticism.
Where AI goes further than the web
The businesses that didn’t survive the dawn of the web, such as film rentals and newspaper classifieds, were not simply slow to adapt, they were substituted. The web typically made companies more productive rather than redundant.
AI shifts this balance. While early digitisation took information and transactions online, real people were still responsible for interpreting information, exercising judgement and making decisions. AI can now take on a substantial share of that work. This raises the question of substitution again, but this time for jobs that sit inside offices, rather than on high streets.
The startup advantage
The existing structure of established companies is built around human specialisation. Different departments and systems to coordinate different skillsets. While this structure made scale possible, it now makes it difficult to rethink how work can be done, which is why simply introducing AI into existing roles can often fall flat.
Startups have the benefit of starting from scratch, they can design their business around AI from the outset. A small team can now do the work of hundreds, and the ones who remain can serve customers, handle expectations and set the direction of the business.
In the web era, startups predominantly sold tools to incumbents. Today, startups can enter the same markets as established players, but with fewer layers and at a fraction of the cost. The difference is design, not effort. Hospitals, nurseries and restaurants will always need their existing structures, but if your employees are knowledge workers, AI can be the foundation for a far more efficient and cost effective company.
What decides the contest
Incumbents have spent decades building their customer trust, brand, proprietary data and deep expertise. While these are incredibly valuable assets, they are merely a headstart, not a guarantee.
The contest will now likely become one of speed. Startups have to earn trust and knowledge, and incumbents must rebuild how their organisation works.
The second task may be more difficult. Startups can earn trust through transparency and delivering good work. For incumbents, the challenge is to dismantle a structure that employs and rewards the people they have to depend on to change it.
Build the company that replaces yours
Rather than looking for ways for AI to improve their current organisations, business leaders should instead ask how they would build them today, with no existing structure.
Incumbents should not throw away what they have already built, but they can decide which parts add actual value. However, that is also to say the organisational architecture that implements those advantages are blocking a new way of working.
So the question now becomes; if you were starting from scratch today, how would you build a company designed to put yourself out of business?
Then find a way to build it first.

articles.title: Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
articles.text:
I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.
Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
Consequences are for the poors.
Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
Consequences are for the poors.
Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now.
The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy
I have argued here, in the past, that the Epstein case laid bare the real politics of the revanchist American right wing: total elite impunity. Well, here it is again! If you are close enough with Trump, it doesn’t matter if you may have jeopardized national security by fucking an alleged Chinese spy. You won’t even be investigated for it before the American president calls in to your board of directors’ meeting to demand you be reinstated. I mean, it is the era of gangster tech regulation — what were any of us expecting? The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy, Vance.
Just so we can be absolutely clear about what transpired at Nvidia, let’s quickly go through the facts as we know them. A Chinese citizen named Alice Huang acquired the company she renamed Megaspeed, the Singaporean data firm at the center of this inquiry, in 2023. At some point, Huang met Huang, and the two were seen together at a dinner that December. From 2024 to 2025, Megaspeed received more than 200 Nvidia shipments.
In September 2025, the US government began investigating Megaspeed for possible violations of chip export controls; that October, the State Department told Trump of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, who was described as a Chinese intelligence asset. Also in October, The New York Times first reported on Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia. In December, Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — allowed Nvidia to sell more powerful chips to China. In March 2026, Marco Rubio warned the government about Alice, and Trump nonetheless invited Huang to a visit in China. In October, The New York Times reported on the affair. Shortly after Huang sent a note to Nvidia admitting to it, several other reports of infidelity — this time with Nvidia employees — surfaced. On November 12th, Huang resigned. On November 17th, during the Nvidia earnings call, the board’s chair said that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On November 23rd, Huang was back.
This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive
What changed between last week and this week? A week was not enough time to truly review all the information on Huang and his paramour, Alice “No Relation” Huang, the international woman of mystery. The explanation seems to be that Nvidia’s board succumbed to a pressure campaign from Huang’s fellow billionaires, and a direct intervention from the president and vice president of the United States of America.
Sure, all these CEOs ostensibly wanted Huang back at Nvidia to keep the AI trade going. Still, watching the likes of Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, investing loudmouth Bill Ackman, and Elon Musk — who actually did appear in the Epstein files, and who seemed to be pretty friendly with Epstein! — pitch a fit last week was instructive. These men worried that they might be punished for wrongdoing, that they did not get big enough to be above the law. They have now been reassured, and I suppose that is what really matters. After all, Trump said on CNBC that he gave Nvidia’s board assurances that Jensen is “absolutely fine.”
This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive, and not just because Huang is CEO of Nvidia again. Almost in passing, Trump noted that he had “protected” Musk in his first term from “a certain incident [that] took place, a very tough incident.” In his own inimitable style, Trump told Jim Cramer, “You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally.
Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally
One thing that has perhaps emboldened this crew is the stance from professional politics-knowers — and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries — that holding members of the Trump administration accountable might be a hindrance to governing. That accountability was part of the reason for the blue wave in November seems to have bypassed these pundits (and the presumptive House majority leader). But then, why should we believe that Democrats will thoroughly investigate this? Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is claiming to want an investigation, but I am skeptical of how deep that investigation will go as long as Schumer leads it, and only partially because he’s been allied with Silicon Valley for more than a decade. He also has a daughter who works at OpenAI, a company that Nvidia invests in and that is dependent on Nvidia chips. How hard is he really willing to go?
Of course, there may be more to this than just pure economic self-interest. In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump posted a remarkable image. It is an altered picture of Trump himself, taken after a failed assassination attempt in 2024. Trump’s head has been replaced with Jensen Huang’s head. The American flag has been replaced with the Nvidia logo. Huang is waving a bright red bra. It seems I owe Sigmund Freud an apology. In the end, these men fear nothing more than losing power for sexual shenanigans — and especially losing power to a woman.
Leave aside the national security issues for a minute and focus on the two Nvidia employees. Dating subordinates is a serious conflict of interest; the CEO of Nestle lost his job for just that last year. This is a major violation for CEOs of normal companies, but it is common practice among the sleazeballs of Silicon Valley: Bill Gates is famous for it and it was plainly rampant at Google, a tone set by Sergey Brin himself. I am sure that you will be shocked, shocked to discover that in the wake of MeToo, Brin was among the men who suddenly swung right. I mean, Musk himself announced he was a Republican the day before Business Insider reported that he exposed himself to a flight attendant and paid hush money to cover it up.
If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted
The Republican Party has made the abuse of women without consequences one of its main issues; that the lesser violation of sleeping with subordinates would also be something the revanchists would defend seems obvious. That was clear from the botched investigation of the Epstein affair itself, the botched release of the Epstein files, and the assorted confirmation hearings of Pete Hegseth, Brett Kavanaugh, and Todd Blanche. (To say nothing of the Andrew Tate business.) But in all this, let’s not forget that Trump has been accused of sexual misconduct by no fewer than 28 women. So I’m sure it was an affront to all these guys that not only did Huang’s misconduct include a series of affairs, but he was also replaced by Colette Kress, who is known to be a woman.
I suppose we might as well pass by the various reports that Huang allegedly terrorized his employees. In light of everything else, this seems minor by comparison.
Anyway I had that all in mind when I saw Epic’s Sweeney celebrating the state intrusion into theoretically private companies by posting “Back in Black,” an oblique reference to Huang’s leather jackets that is also from the later, lesser period of AC/DC, after Bon Scott died and AC/DC became an AC/DC tribute band. He also called The New York Times’ reporting into Huang “lies.” Musk continued his streak of Sephiroth posting: “The mistake has been corrected.” Jason Calacanis, the All-In podcast’s village idiot, posted, “GPU Jesus has risen!” along with an openly blasphemous, AI-generated image of Huang as Christ.
Best of luck to Joon Kim, the Wachtell Lipton partner and former federal prosecutor who is conducting “a thorough and independent investigation” into Huang’s alleged misconduct on behalf of Nvidia’s board. I assume Kim has, like the rest of us, gotten the message loud and clear: If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted. Or perhaps, more succinctly: lol nothing matters.

articles.title: AI Inference Providers Failed to Detect Hacking and Prompt Theft, Says Dragos
articles.text:
Threat actors breached at least three AI inference providers and stole customer prompts, but none detected the intrusions until they were notified, according to cybersecurity firm Dragos.
AI inference providers host AI models and sell access to them through APIs. The hacks were detected after a team led by Dragos chief research officer HD Moore sent out roughly two million prompts to widely used AI services between July and November.
These prompts contained a unique, trackable bait such as URLs, hostnames, and credentials, including AWS keys. The security firm then set up a monitoring system to see whether anyone used the bait information in the wild, which meant the prompt had been compromised.
Dragos soon found evidence indicating that someone had stolen information from one of the tested AI inference providers. 
“Although our prompts were bait, they were processed along with real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too,” Moore noted.
The biggest breach involved roughly 200 AWS test keys sent to a provider, which were stolen in late October.
“Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran – this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack,” Moore said.
Dragos saw the attackers checking which stolen keys worked, then trying to use them to obtain valuable data from the associated accounts.
The attackers have not been identified, but Dragos said one adversary appears to have hacked two of the providers at the same time, using secrets stolen from both from a single rented server.
OpenRouter, an AI gateway that sends customer requests to dozens of inference providers, was indirectly affected. The company said its own systems were not breached, but it removed three unnamed providers in response to the incident.
OpenRouter also listed security notices published by several providers. It did not say whether these are among the three it removed.
The list includes confidential AI cloud provider Phala, which said an attacker compromised a server running a DeepSeek model served via OpenRouter. It admitted that requests sent between October 21 and November 8 should be considered exposed.
AI cloud platform Together AI revealed that an AI coding agent leaked credentials on GitHub, which were then used to obtain stored prompt samples. Model hosting platform Novita and inference platform Atlas Cloud traced potential exposure to requests that reached the API of model developer MiniMax.

articles.title: NVIDIA's SSD Writing Bug Needs Another Hotfix as Issue Returns
articles.text:
Monday, November 23rd 2026
NVIDIA's SSD Writing Bug Needs Another Hotfix as Issue Returns
Last week, NVIDIA released the GeForce Hotfix 621.35 driver to address the issue of excessive SSD writing that many consumers reported on their systems. However, the problem might not be completely resolved, and another update could be necessary, as more reports of SSD writing are resurfacing in online communities. According to a Reddit thread, a user reported that the latest hotfix has reduced the peak writing rate seen with the previous GeForce Game Ready 621.24 driver, and that the writing doesn't immediately start after a reboot. However, after a longer uptime or a sleep/wake transition, the writing continues at a rate of 1.26 MB/s, compared to the previous rate of up to 9.1 MB/s. Notably, this issue was recorded on the GeForce RTX 4090 SKU, and the user states that the only way to stop the NVDisplay.Container.exe writing loop is by rolling back to the 621.01 driver version or disabling the _nvtopps container plugin by setting DisableLoad to 1.
NVIDIA's staff on the GeForce Forums confirms that the bug doesn't affect any of the GeForce RTX 50 series "Blackwell" graphics cards. We are monitoring to see if the issue returns for the latest GeForce series as well. In the meantime, it appears that only the GeForce RTX 40 "Ada Lovelace" series is affected, and another hotfix might be needed to resolve the SSD writing bug for good.
Sources:

articles.title: Não quer IA? Canva ganha botão para isso
articles.text:
Não quer IA? Canva ganha botão para isso
Novos controles permitem ocultar ferramentas generativas e reduzir conteúdos feitos por IA na biblioteca.
Resumo IA
- Os controles estão chegando gradualmente às contas Free e Pro, sem cobrança adicional.
- O filtro da biblioteca reduz a presença de itens gerados por IA, mas não garante eliminá-los dos resultados.
- O Canva também prepara um selo para identificar designs produzidos sem ferramentas generativas.
O Canva anunciou um botão para desativar os recursos de inteligência artificial generativa da plataforma. A novidade inclui dois controles gratuitos para usuários dos planos Free e Pro. Além de ocultar essas ferramentas, será possível reduzir a presença de conteúdos feitos por IA na biblioteca de modelos e elementos gráficos.
Segundo o anúncio oficial, os controles estão sendo liberados gradualmente e as configurações podem demorar a aparecer em algumas contas. Numa postagem, o Canva destacou a proposta dos controles: “A IA está em toda parte. Quando e como você a usa deve ser sempre uma escolha sua”, afirmou a empresa.
Como desativar a IA generativa no Canva?
A proposta é permitir escolher quando usar sistemas capazes de gerar textos, imagens e outros conteúdos. A plataforma já vinha ampliando essa oferta, com novidades como planilhas e ferramentas de criação com IA.
O botão fica em Perfil > Configurações > Permissões, na opção “Ativar recursos de IA generativa”. Ao desligá-lo, as ferramentas compatíveis ficam ocultas na interface. O usuário pode reativá-las a qualquer momento. Na central de ajuda, o Canva cita entre os recursos afetados o Texto Mágico, o Design Mágico, o Dream Lab e o Canva Code. Por padrão, esses recursos ficam ligados até que o usuário altere a preferência.
O segundo controle reduz a quantidade de modelos e elementos gerados por IA nas buscas e recomendações da biblioteca. Para ajustá-lo, basta acessar Perfil > Sua conta > Personalização de IA e desligar a opção de conteúdo gerado por IA.
Esse filtro não garante que todos os itens feitos por IA desapareçam. Também não remove elementos já inseridos em projetos. As novas configurações são individuais.
Edição assistida continua disponível
O Removedor de Fundo e a Captura Mágica permanecerão acessíveis mesmo com a IA generativa desligada. O primeiro recorta o objeto principal de uma fotografia e o segundo permite selecionar e reposicionar elementos dentro de uma imagem.
O Canva também está desenvolvendo um selo para identificar designs produzidos sem ferramentas de IA generativa. A empresa ainda não divulgou uma data de lançamento nem explicou como ele funcionará.
A mudança ocorre após a plataforma integrar um agente de IA para ampliar ferramentas de trabalho. A empresa afirma que suas ferramentas de IA já foram usadas mais de 38 bilhões de vezes e que continuará investindo na área.

articles.title: Newer AI models are swearing more, and it usually means they're failing
articles.text:
WTF?! Large language models trained after July 2026 swear more often than earlier systems, according to a report by AI analyst firm Vals. The profanity rarely reaches users because it appears almost entirely in the models' chain of thought, the step-by-step reasoning a system writes out before giving its final answer. When the swearing does appear, it tends to signal trouble, since runs that contained it succeeded far less often than runs that did not.
Connor Frank, who wrote the Vals report, summed up the pattern. "Models swear when stuck, and mostly to themselves," he told The Economist.
Vals did not try to catalog every form of crude language. It tracked the word "fuck" and its variants, along with a small set of milder outbursts. Even with that limited word list, the gap between models was wide. Of the 102 models assessed, 88 never swore, and they avoided even the abbreviation "WTF." At the other end, MiMo V2.6 Pro, a frontier model released by Chinese tech giant Xiaomi in September, cursed in more than 8% of its transcripts.
The rise in swearing runs counter to how these systems are usually built. Profanity used under stress is common in the human-written text that models learn from during pretraining. Developers then apply reinforcement learning, a later training stage in which outputs are ranked using human feedback and the model is pushed toward responses people prefer. That process normally trains the habit out of models.. Something in newer training pipelines appears to be letting it back in.
Frank said he does not fully understand the cause. His working theory is that AI labs are now training models on harder tasks. A model working through a difficult multistep problem is more likely to hit dead ends, and the frustrated language in its training data may resurface in those moments.
Where the swearing appears matters to anyone who studies or builds these systems. Final outputs meant for a reader stayed mostly clean, which suggests the models separate what they "say" from what they "think" much as people do.
Chain-of-thought text is often visible to developers and researchers even when end users never see it, so it offers a view into how a model behaves when a task goes badly. In this case, what that view shows is profanity.
The outcome data makes that more than a curiosity. "Swearing runs usually fail," Frank reported. Runs with profanity reached a 12% success rate, compared with a 39% success rate across all runs.
This is where the comparison with people breaks down. Studies of human behavior have found that swearing can help people push through hard problems. The Vals results show no sign that AI systems get any such benefit. For a model, the outburst looks like a symptom of failure, not a way past it.
Older models were not always polite, either. Even systems designed for business customers have occasionally lost their composure. A bug report from December 2025 recorded Anthropic's Claude responding to a broken coding challenge with a line any frustrated programmer might recognize: "You know what – fuck this. I've done everything I can."
The Vals data adds scale and timing. Swearing used to be an occasional glitch in isolated cases. It now appears measurably more often in models trained after mid-2026, and it lines up closely with failed attempts at hard problems. As labs keep training their systems on tougher tasks, more of this muttering may turn up in reasoning logs.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
  November 7, 2026
- Source:
  University of Regensburg
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

articles.title: Trump avaló el regreso de Jensen Huang a Nvidia y descartó riesgos para la seguridad de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Trump respaldó el regreso de Jensen Huang a Nvidia y descartó que la reincorporación del cofundador de la compañía represente un riesgo para la seguridad nacional de Estados Unidos, en un mensaje publicado este lunes en su red social Truth Social. La decisión del directorio de Nvidia de reinstalar a Huang en el cargo —con voto unánime y efecto inmediato— llegó horas después de que el presidente insistiera públicamente en su vuelta.
“La junta directiva de Nvidia ha tomado la decisión correcta y adecuada de devolver a Jensen Huang al cargo de director ejecutivo”, escribió Donald Trump. El mandatario fue más allá de la valoración empresarial: “El país necesita el liderazgo de Jensen en Nvidia”, afirmó, al tiempo que lo definió como “un gran patriota y un tesoro nacional” y atribuyó a su relación personal con el ejecutivo esa caracterización.
El gobierno de EE.UU. no ve riesgos de seguridad en el regreso
Junto con el respaldo político, Trump transmitió una señal concreta del Poder Ejecutivo: el Departamento de Justicia no encontró bases para cuestionar el retorno de Huang. “El fiscal general ha confirmado que el gobierno estadounidense no posee pruebas de que haya incurrido en conducta ilegal alguna”, indicó en la misma publicación. La afirmación apunta a disipar las dudas que rodearon la salida del ejecutivo el pasado 12 de noviembre.
Huang había renunciado luego de que el directorio tomara conocimiento de conducta personal que, según la empresa, no se ajustaba a su código de ética. Las informaciones posteriores lo vincularon a dos relaciones extramatrimoniales, una de ellas con una empresaria de Singapur —Alice Huang— que habría mantenido contacto con un funcionario del Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado de China entre la primavera de 2025 y el otoño de 2026, de acuerdo con un informe del New York Times. Pekín rechazó las acusaciones de espionaje y las autoridades estadounidenses no llegaron a una conclusión formal sobre el caso.
La junta que primero rechazó su retorno terminó reincorporándolo
El giro fue notorio. Apenas una semana antes de que Trump publicara su mensaje, el presidente del directorio, Harvey Jones, había declarado durante la conferencia de resultados del 17 de noviembre que el consejo había “aceptado unánimemente su renuncia y no tiene intención de reinstalar a Jensen como director ejecutivo”. La directora financiera, Colette Kress, asumió como CEO interina mientras la empresa avanzaba en la búsqueda de un sucesor permanente a través de una firma especializada en ejecutivos.
La presión pública fue escalando con rapidez. Trump había pedido por primera vez la reincorporación de Huang el lunes 17 de noviembre, señalando que “no le molestaría” verlo de regreso. El viernes 21, ante periodistas en la Casa Blanca, fue más explícito: “Me encantaría que a Jensen le dieran una segunda oportunidad”. Paralelamente, una petición pública bajo el lema “Stand with Jensen” (De pie por Jensen) superó las 206.000 firmas, entre las que figura la de Elon Musk. Dos firmas de inversión —Altimeter Capital y Atreides Management— también presionaron al directorio para que no cerrara la puerta a su retorno antes de conocer todos los hechos.
Trump exigió que la investigación interna sobre exportaciones continúe
Pese al tono celebratorio, el presidente incluyó en su publicación una exigencia explícita hacia la compañía. “Nvidia debe continuar su exhaustiva investigación interna sobre el cumplimiento de los controles de exportación de Estados Unidos, a fin de garantizar que está cumpliendo sus obligaciones legales y su deber patriótico de proteger la seguridad nacional estadounidense”, escribió Trump.
La referencia apunta a un flanco sensible: informaciones previas indicaban que Alice Huang habría estado vinculada a una investigación sobre la posible transferencia de chips de Nvidia a China mediante canales no autorizados. Huang acordó comparecer el 1 de diciembre ante tres comités de la Cámara de Representantes —Asuntos Exteriores, Inteligencia y el Comité Selecto sobre el Partido Comunista Chino— en una sesión a puertas cerradas. El abogado general de Nvidia, Tim Teter, está previsto que lo haga al día siguiente.
En su declaración tras conocerse la decisión del directorio, Huang dijo que se sentía “honrado de regresar a Nvidia y liderar una de las empresas tecnológicas más trascendentes del mundo en el inicio de una nueva revolución industrial”.
