articles.title: Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control.
articles.text:
Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control.
They say that to understand where an industry is heading, you have to follow the money. And two acquisitions announced this past week suggest that established infrastructure vendors see a big opportunity in helping enterprises take greater control of the AI systems they deploy — and ensuring those systems are secure, reliable and trustworthy.
In early November, Applied Compute, a startup specializing in post-training and inference for open-weight AI models, announced it had raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation, less than 18 months after its founding. Then last Wednesday, cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks swooped in with a $4.5 billion bid to buy the startup outright.
The following day, search and observability giant Elastic announced plans to acquire HoneyHive, a four-year-old startup specializing in AI agent observability and evaluation.
While the deals target different parts of the enterprise AI stack, both point to a growing push by established vendors to bring more of the AI development and operations toolchain in-house.
An acquisition spree
A quick peek at the wider acquisitive landscape suggests a broader trend at play. Last month, observability giant Dynatrace completed its $915 million acquisition of Arize, an AI observability and evaluation platform. And back in July, SAP acquired Prior Labs, a specialist in AI models for structured data, while more recently, payments giant Stripe acquired AI model routing platform OpenRouter.
Palo Alto Networks and Elastic themselves have been on something of a buying spree, the former in particular.
Palo Alto Networks kicked off the year by completing its $3.35 billion acquisition of observability company Chronosphere in January, saying this was about “unifying observability and security for the AI era.” This was followed by its $21.1 billion purchase of identity security giant CyberArk. Since then, it has acquired endpoint security startup Koi, AI gateway provider Portkey, mobile observability specialist Embrace, and AI-native enterprise automation startup Console.
Elastic, meanwhile, acquired Deductive AI in August, bringing AI-powered incident investigation into its observability platform.
For Jason Andersen, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, such deals reflect several pressures facing established software vendors. Some need specialized AI technology better suited to their existing customers, while others see acquisitions as a way to accelerate their AI strategies and expand into new markets.
“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases.”
“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases,” Andersen tells The New Stack. “I also am seeing all sorts of companies using the acquisitions to jumpstart their own repositioning.”
Palo Alto Networks is a case in point. A veteran of the cybersecurity industry, it started out as a firewall specialist before expanding into cloud security, threat detection and security operations. And as with just about every major technology company today, AI is driving much of its strategy.
On the company’s earnings call last week, Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, suggested that Applied Compute could create an opportunity larger than the company’s core cybersecurity operations.
“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity,” Arora said. “This could be bigger than what we do today.”
“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do today.”
Applied Compute specializes in post-training and inference, helping enterprises customize open-weight models for their own needs and run them in production. Its slogan itself sums up its core raison d’être: “The best AI is built, not bought” — a somewhat ironic message, now that Palo Alto Networks is buying the company for $4.5 billion.
Applied Compute has worked with companies including Microsoft and Nvidia, while Palo Alto Networks itself said it had been a “prospective customer.” Arora sees securing an increasingly diverse mix of enterprise AI models as a big business opportunity.
“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured.”
“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Arora said in a press release announcing the deal.
In a separate LinkedIn post, Applied Compute CEO Yash Patil, who worked on post-training infrastructure and Codex at OpenAI before co-founding the company in May 2025, said that he and his two co-founders had built Applied Compute on the belief that “every company should own its intelligence,” arguing that businesses will increasingly need to develop and control their own AI models.
“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company.”
“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company,” he writes. “To do useful work, a model needs to access sensitive data and systems, comply with policies, and remain explainable, verifiable, and auditable. This is the reason we’ve always prioritized security, and why joining Palo Alto Networks will help us go further faster.”
Evaluating the AI opportunity
Elastic’s acquisition of HoneyHive, meanwhile, targets a different part of enterprise AI: understanding how agents behave, and whether they’re doing what they’re supposed to. HoneyHive, which claims big-name customers such as Nvidia and MongoDB, brings tracing, evaluation and testing capabilities that Elastic plans to integrate into its existing observability platform.
In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Elastic explicitly describes the HoneyHive acquisition as a move to help its customers “observe, evaluate, and trust the agents they run in production.”
In a separate blog post announcing the deal last Thursday, Santosh Krishnan, senior vice president of observability and security at Elastic, argues that the rise of autonomous agents creates a new challenge for developers: understanding whether their AI systems are making sound decisions, even when the underlying software is functioning as expected.
“Reliable agents need more than traditional application monitoring,” Krishnan writes. “AI observability provides visibility into agent behavior and the ability to evaluate the quality of its decisions and outcomes.”
By combining HoneyHive’s agent-specific capabilities with Elastic’s existing monitoring tools, the company hopes to give developers a clearer picture of how their agents interact with the applications and infrastructure supporting them.
“This combination could also enable teams to evaluate production telemetry more broadly, helping them understand not only how their AI applications are performing, but whether their agents are achieving the intended outcomes,” Krishnan adds.
But what does the acquisition mean for developers already using HoneyHive who don’t want to adopt the broader Elastic platform? Krishnan tells The New Stack that existing customers will continue to be supported during the integration, with HoneyHive’s capabilities eventually expected to become native Elastic offerings.
“Customers will retain the flexibility to adopt use-cases of interest, without committing to use all the capabilities of the platform,” Krishnan says, adding that more details on the combined product roadmap will be shared in the coming months.
One stack to rule them all?
While both deals reflect growing demand for greater control over enterprise AI, Andersen cautions against assuming that model training, evaluation and observability are all converging into a single stack.
“Training is very distinct and most organizations will likely never need to do training on a model at least until the skills become more commonplace and costs go down,” Andersen says.
Most agent platforms already include some observability capabilities, Andersen notes, but evaluation is a different story. Enterprises have several ways to assess model outputs, including using other AI models, and the right approach depends on what an agent is designed to do.
“I think that over time evaluations could become a major embedded component of agentic platforms, but right now they are distinct,” Andersen says.
Beyond questions around convergence, there are perhaps more immediate reasons for established vendors to acquire AI startups, including access to specialist talent and the potential to reduce costs.
“Aside from strengthening their customer position, a lot of these startups have really smart people to inject some new minds into a company,” Andersen says. “And / or it could be a way to save the incumbent money by bringing a technology in house, versus having to pay OpenAI or some other company.”
Palo Alto Networks’ deal, in particular, fits that mold: it brings Applied Compute’s research team in-house, giving the company additional expertise in developing and adapting AI models, with Patil set to become co-chief AI officer once the transaction closes.
And Andersen expects more deals to come, with buyers driven as much by necessity as by opportunity.
“The issue right now is that valuations are sky-high, as is the cost of money vis-à-vis interest rates,” he says. “So, while I can’t speculate on a specific name, I would say that these purchases are increasingly going to happen with buyers that are under some pressure to deliver better results.”

articles.title: ASUS va réduire la RAM de ses PC portables d'entrée de gamme de 16 à 8 Go
articles.text:
L’annonce était prévisible, mais elle permet au moins de clarifier la position d’ASUS sur le sort (probable) de ses PC portables d’entrée de gamme. Équipés pour la plupart de 16 Go de mémoire vive, devenus ces dernières années le nouveau standard pour les PC Windows 11, ces modèles risquent fort de voir leur quantité de RAM s’abaisser à 8 Go seulement dans un avenir proche.
Face à la hausse des prix de la mémoire vive, la flambée tarifaire observée en début d’année sur de nombreux PC portables de la marque taïwanaise ne suffit donc plus. Une déclaration décourageante, alors qu’ASUS a déjà relevé ses prix tout au long de l’année 2026 pour absorber la hausse du coût de la mémoire.
Sécurisez vos achats durant Black Friday avec la meilleure offre de l’année. Dénichez les bonnes affaires, Bitdefender s’occupe des arnaques.
8 Go suffisent désormais à offrir une « expérience acceptable »
Le co-CEO d’ASUS, S.Y. Hsu, a évoqué ce scénario le 12 novembre, lors de la présentation des résultats financiers du troisième trimestre 2026. Faute de pouvoir répercuter l’intégralité du surcoût de la mémoire vive sur les prix, ASUS fera payer un peu plus le consommateur (c’est même déjà le cas)… et lui en donnera aussi un peu moins.
« Auparavant, les ordinateurs de milieu ou d’entrée de gamme étaient généralement équipés de 16 Go de mémoire, mais ils pourraient désormais passer à 8 Go en raison de la hausse des coûts de la mémoire. Nous avons collaboré avec Microsoft sur ce point », a déclaré S.Y. Hsu devant les investisseurs.
« L’ancienne spécification de 16 Go visait avant tout à garantir une bonne expérience utilisateur. Sur le nouveau système d’exploitation, Microsoft a apporté des ajustements permettant d’offrir une expérience acceptable même avec 8 Go ».
En contrepartie de cette baisse de mémoire vive, qu’il envisage désormais ouvertement, ASUS met en avant une meilleure optimisation de Windows 11 (et vraisemblablement aussi de ses propres logiciels) sur les machines limitées à 8 Go de RAM. Optimisation que Microsoft prend effectivement très au sérieux depuis quelques mois et qui conduit déjà à des progrès de son système d’exploitation.
Sur ce terrain, Apple et son MacBook Neo (vendu 799 euros en France et limité lui aussi à 8 Go de RAM) ont mis en lumière la grande gourmandise de Windows 11 en termes de mémoire vive. La crise de la RAM a donc contraint Microsoft et ses partenaires à faire des efforts d’optimisation… un maigre lot de consolation, mais un lot de consolation tout de même.
Notons par contre qu’un PC à 8 Go ne peut prétendre aux fonctions d’IA locales de Windows 11, puisque Microsoft réserve son label Copilot+ aux machines dotées d’au moins 16 Go de RAM.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
  November 4, 2026
- Source:
  Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
  Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: Neuralink patient plays GTA VI using only his mind, shows how the controls work
articles.text:
In context: Another game has joined the list of titles that Neuralink patients have played using their minds. The company posted a video on X of an unnamed trial participant using the brain-computer interface to control the action in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto VI, which is a big step up from using a mouth stick and iPad – previously his only way to play games.
Neuralink shared the two-minute clip on November 20, just one day after GTA VI landed on consoles. It shows the player taking Jason under a bridge in a speedboat and steering into a narrow channel to collect a package. He also gets into a fistfight and a shootout, but the part where he flies a seaplane gives us a better idea of how the controls work.
Alongside the gameplay is a graphic of a PlayStation 5 controller that lights up as he plays. To pull the nose of the plane up, he imagines sliding his right hand forward. Thinking about tapping his ring finger registers a press of the square button. He mentions having a control mapped to his foot, too.
 – Neuralink (@neuralink) November 20, 2026
Before the surgery, the mouth stick limited him to a handful of games, and playing them left him with a sore jaw. "I was essentially like a bird just pecking at an iPad," he says. Being able to control a computer again meant that "you just immediately get your portal to the world back."
Back in March 2024, Neuralink's first implant recipient, Noland Arbaugh, showed how he could play chess just by thinking about where he wanted the cursor to go. He'd also managed to stay up until 6 am playing Civilization VI, something plenty of Civ fans can relate to.
A few months later, a second participant, Alex, paired his implant with a mouth-operated QuadStick to play Counter-Strike 2. Using the joystick alone had forced him to choose between moving and aiming. With the implant taking care of his aim, he could finally do both at once.
Neuralink is also working on Blindsight, an implant designed to give blind people a degree of vision by stimulating the brain's visual cortex. It received the FDA's breakthrough device designation in September 2024. At the time, Elon Musk compared the level of detail he expected from early versions to the graphics on an Atari.
Take-Two recently confirmed that day-one retail sales of Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI reached an estimated $3.79 billion, making it the most successful launch in any entertainment medium.

articles.title: British Gas launches new plug-in solar kit starting at £649 offering savings of up to £175 per year, predicting they'll be 'snapped up quickly'
articles.text:
British Gas launches new plug-in solar kit — two 465W panels cost £649 and could save up to £175 per year
Engineer setup is an option for an extra £100
- British Gas is launching a new plug-in solar kit for the UK
- You get two 465W solar panels with a ground-mounted bracket and an inverter for £649
- The kit comes with installation by a British Gas engineer for £749, and you can have an outdoor power socket added for an extra £250 on top of that
British Gas has got on board with plug-in solar with the announcement that it will sell kits starting from £649.
As an alternative to a traditional roof-based installation, plug-in solar has become popular in the UK since the initial batch of kits became legal at the end of the summer. Utility suppliers like Octopus are already on board, and British Gas is now joining the plug-in club.
The base kit with two Perlight PowerPlug 465W solar panels is the most affordable option priced at £649, coming with a ground-mounted bracket and an inverter. You can add a hundred quid on top to buy this kit with setup by a British Gas engineer included (so it's £749).
If you'd like an outdoor power socket to go with your kit, that's also a choice here, and it'll cost £999 to have an engineer visit, which provides the socket alongside installing the plug-in panels.
The Perlight PowerPlug panels measure 176 x 114cm and British Gas claims that a pair of panels represents a chance to save between £147 to £175 on a typical energy bill over the course of a full year.
Analysis: solar boom
It's good to see another energy supplier offering plug-in solar, as not everyone can afford a full rooftop installation, or even has permission for one (some folks are renting, of course). Some roofs don't suit solar panels, too, so it's good to have choices — and I like that British Gas is offering an engineer installation service too, for those who might be less confident on that side of the equation.
The potential savings that British Gas calculates means you could make back the money you paid for a basic kit in around 4.5 years, going by the leanest estimate of solar energy production. Naturally, how much you'll make from your two panels will vary considerably based on their location (ideally south-facing with no shading, which is what British Gas has assumed here), and how much sunlight the panels are getting.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
One caveat about buying plug-in solar panels right now is that it's not exactly the ideal time of year in the UK. We're just entering the three months of winter in which the sun is at its weakest, and the days are shortest, but still, British Gas expects demand to be high and "initial stock [is] predicted to be snapped up quickly". You can't help but think that the timing of the legalization of plug-in solar for the UK could have been better (as in at the start of summer rather than the end of the season).
It'd be no surprise if plug-in solar gained some serious momentum in the UK, mind, in 2027. After all, rooftop solar had a record 2026 with 270,000 installations in the UK, and on the other side of the Atlantic, as a recent Bloomberg report made clear, "plug-in solar is sweeping the US," with a lot of folks adopting these panels due to increasingly expensive electricity — more than 10 states now allow plug-in or 'guerrilla' solar legally. We're seeing electricity prices notching up in the UK as well, alongside all the more recent noises being made about possible power cuts as part of the government's 'Be Ready' campaign.
The attraction of plug-in solar is that it's an investment which is much more readily recouped when compared to a full rooftop installation, and you can also take the panels with you should you move house — making it less of a commitment in that respect, too.
Plug-in solar and battery systems are also waiting in the wings, and should be legal and ready to go on sale in the UK next year, too.

articles.title: SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway Flaws Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting SAP NetWeaver and Cisco Expressway vulnerabilities in the wild, the US cybersecurity agency CISA warned on Friday.
The NetWeaver flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score of 6.5), is a medium-severity issue that could allow unauthenticated attackers to leak or modify server information.
Successful exploitation could allow attackers to “inject JNDI environment properties or pass a URL used during JNDI lookup operations, enabling access to an unintended JNDI provider,” reads a NIST advisory.
SAP patched the bug with its November 2025 security updates. There appear to have been no reports of the security hole being exploited in the wild before CISA’s Friday alert.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the Expressway defect is a critical hardcoded credentials weakness that could allow attackers to execute system commands with root privileges.
The use of persistent cookies, combined with insufficient validation of client certificates in certain conditions, could allow attackers who possess the cookies to connect to the database service and invoke specific RPC commands.
It impacts Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices running vulnerable software versions and configured in a cluster, and was patched on October 21 in Expressway Series release X15.5.20.
On November 20, CISA added the Expressway security defect to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days.
CISA’s alert came two days after Russian cybercrime prevention firm F6 warned that threat actors started exploiting the vulnerability in attacks shortly after proof-of-concept (PoC) code was released publicly.
On Friday, CISA also expanded the KEV list with CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter bug exploited by China-linked espionage group Armory Castle (Warp Panda) as a zero-day, and CVE-2026-129448, a critical Apache Roller flaw patched on November 17 as a zero-day.

articles.title: London-based Acorda raises €2.15 million to help banks detect payment scams before money moves
articles.text:
Acorda, a London-based FinTech startup helping payment providers stop financial scams through shared risk data, has raised €2.15 million (£1.8 million) in a pre-Seed funding round.
The round was led by Concept Ventures, the first venture capital firm to back AI unicorn Eleven Labs, with participation from NFG Ventures, the firm founded by early Monzo investor and non-executive director Eileen Burbridge. A cohort of angel investors with experience across Monzo, Revolut, Coinbase and OakNorth Bank also participated in this round.
“Scam prevention is becoming an increasingly expensive problem for all banks and payment providers. Very few, if any, teams will have more experience addressing this challenge than the Acorda team,” said Burbidge, founder of NFG Ventures.
Founded in October 2026 by Jhamat Mahbubani, Sam Kelsey, and Robert Parrish, the three former leaders of Monzo’s scam prevention, Acorda was built around a problem the trio experienced first-hand. They spent three years at Monzo building machine-learning models that monitored payments from customer accounts to prevent scams, saving millions of pounds in the process.
They realised that banks know their own customers well, but know almost nothing about the recipients of funds being transferred out. The founders of Acorda call this the blind spot, which makes scams nearly impossible to detect. To banks, a victim handing money to a scammer looks almost identical to someone paying a friend back for dinner.
Acorda addresses this by acting as a single integration point for payment companies. Rather than requiring each firm to build bilateral data-sharing arrangements with each other, Acorda connects them all, enabling risk signals to be shared on both sides of a payment, often before money moves at all. The company says it is already running trials with three major global payment companies, and targets banks and cryptocurrency exchanges alike.
Mahbubani, co-founder and CEO of Acorda, said, “Banks have talented engineers and data scientists who are motivated to stop scams, but are missing the data they need. We want to provide better data in a way that they genuinely love to use.”
The fundraising comes as fraudulent payments globally reached an estimated €537 billion in 2025, a 9% year-on-year jump driven largely by AI-powered scam operations.
Acorda plans to use the new capital to demonstrate strong results with its initial cohort of payment company partners before broadening its reach. The company aims to prove that any payment provider, whether its a traditional bank or a cryptocurrency exchange, can meaningfully reduce scam activity by accessing better, shared data.
“The best founders are the ones who have lived the problem, and Jhamat, Sam and Rob have spent years on the front line of scam prevention at Monzo, building the models that protected customers and saved millions of pounds. They saw first-hand that the missing piece isn’t talent or intent, it’s data. They’ve spent years earning the trust of the industry and understand how banks actually work. That makes them uniquely placed to build the shared data layer payment providers have been missing,” said Oliver Kicks, GP at Concept Ventures.
As AI is increasingly used to create sophisticated scams and fraud, Acorda says the shared data layer, rather than siloed in-house data, will become the infrastructure the payments industry has long lacked.

articles.title: “Abuelo, estoy en problemas. Necesito dinero”: la estafa con IA que clona la voz y rostros de familiares
articles.text:
Una llamada breve, una voz conocida y un pedido urgente pueden ser suficiente para que una persona mayor entregue sus ahorros. Las estafas de emergencia familiar se apoyan en inteligencia artificial (IA) para clonar voces y rostros de familiares para pedir dinero bajo presión.
Según advierte la Comisión Federal de Comercio de Estados Unidos (FTC), el engaño se apoya en dos factores: la urgencia y la necesidad de ayudar.
Quien llama puede decir que sufrió un accidente, que necesita pagar una fianza o que tuvo un problema con su auto. El estafador exige reserva. El objetivo es impedir que la víctima consulte con otros familiares antes de enviar el dinero.
Cómo un delincuente suplanta a un familiar
Los delincuentes pueden hacerse pasar por hijos, nietos u otros allegados a través de llamadas, mensajes y videollamadas. Para reforzar la identidad falsa, utilizan herramientas de inteligencia artificial capaces de imitar una voz a partir de audios disponibles en redes sociales, videos públicos o mensajes de voz.
La FTC alerta sobre la manipulación de imágenes. Una videollamada no garantiza que la persona al otro lado de la pantalla sea quien dice ser: los estafadores pueden crear o modificar videos para simular el rostro y los gestos de un familiar. La voz y la imagen ya no son pruebas suficientes de identidad.
Qué datos usan para construir una historia convincente
Las redes sociales suelen aportar información que permite volver más persuasivo el relato. Publicaciones sobre viajes, estudios, lugares de residencia, cumpleaños o vínculos familiares pueden ayudar a los delincuentes a elegir a quién imitar y qué situación inventar.
Además, pueden utilizar direcciones, nombres de familiares o referencias a actividades cotidianas. Con esos datos, la llamada parece tener detalles que solo una persona cercana conocería.
La FTC sugiere revisar qué información personal queda expuesta en perfiles públicos y limitar la difusión de datos que puedan facilitar una suplantación.
Por qué piden mantener el secreto la llamada
El pedido de confidencialidad forma parte del mecanismo. El supuesto familiar puede decir que siente vergüenza, que no quiere preocupar a sus padres o que necesita resolver la situación sin que nadie más se entere. El secreto busca aislar a la víctima y evitar una verificación independiente.
La presión aparece en frases como “necesito el dinero ahora”, “no tengo tiempo” o “si no pagas hoy, tendré un problema mayor”. Esa urgencia busca provocar una reacción inmediata. Cuando la persona tiene miedo por un ser querido, puede dejar de lado señales que en otra circunstancia identificaría como sospechosas.
Qué formas de pago exigen los estafadores
Los pedidos suelen incluir mecanismos difíciles de revertir. Los delincuentes pueden exigir transferencias mediante empresas de envío de dinero, como Western Union o MoneyGram, pagos con criptomonedas, aplicaciones de pago o tarjetas de regalo cuyos códigos deben compartirse por teléfono o mensaje.
Expertos destacan que ninguna situación familiar urgente justifica pagar mediante tarjetas de regalo o criptomonedas a una persona cuya identidad no fue comprobada.
Estos métodos permiten que el dinero circule con rapidez y complican el rastreo o la recuperación posterior. La insistencia en una vía de pago específica constituye una señal de alerta.
Cómo actuar ante una llamada de emergencia
La primera pauta es detener la conversación. La FTC aconseja colgar o informar que se devolverá la llamada de inmediato. Después, conviene contactar al familiar por un número conocido, no por el que aparece en la llamada entrante, o comunicarse con otra persona cercana que pueda confirmar si existe una emergencia.
Asimismo, es útil acordar una palabra o frase familiar que sirva para validar pedidos urgentes. Si hubo un envío de dinero, la reacción debe ser rápida: es clave informar al banco, a la empresa de transferencias, a la plataforma de pagos o al emisor de la tarjeta de regalo.
Las autoridades advierten que actuar sin verificar puede derivar en una pérdida económica difícil de recuperar; consultar a otro familiar puede evitarla.

articles.title: Opinion: Jensen Huang didn’t believe in succession plans. Your startup shouldn’t make the same mistake
articles.text:
Erin Bury is the co-founder and CEO of online estate planning company Willful.
In a March 2026 podcast interview, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that he doesn’t believe in succession planning and that he could be CEO “until the last day of my life.” Seven months later, he resigned amid a scandal over his multiple alleged affairs, and his multi-billion-dollar company was left without a clear successor. 
Beyond the affair, this was Huang’s biggest mistake: believing that because he didn’t plan to exit the business, he didn’t need to plan for a successor or set the business up to run smoothly without him. Now, he’s been reinstated, perhaps further highlighting the company’s lack of a plan to move forward successfully without him at the helm.
“Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence.”
Every founder needs a succession plan, both for themselves and their key people, regardless of whether they plan to sell the business or not. Despite the importance, the CFIB reported in October that only six percent of Canadian small business owners have a formal written succession plan. We can’t predict the future; succession planning covers both planned absences, including parental leaves and sabbaticals, and unplanned absences due to illness, death, family caregiving requirements, or, like Huang, a public scandal.
If you’re a founder who falls into the 94 percent of business owners who don’t have a formal succession plan, here are the key steps to put in place.
Create a written succession plan for key leaders
Many business owners have playbooks for what to do if a crisis happens. Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence. At Willful, we work with the value creation firm Horizon; they had us go through the exercise of creating a formal succession plan for my husband and me, as well as our key leaders. It asked questions I hadn’t thought about, like:
- Who would take over this person’s responsibilities if they were unexpectedly out of the business?
- Would you need to engage a recruiter to replace the role externally, or is there a natural successor?
- What processes, relationships, and knowledge does this person own that aren’t documented anywhere?
- How and when would you communicate about this person’s absence?
- Who would need to be informed, and in what order?
- Do key stakeholders know about this plan, and have you discussed this with them to ensure alignment?
- What are your wishes in the event you pass away or leave the business? Would you want it to keep going, be sold, or wind down?
This written plan came in handy when a leader left the business months later. Instead of scrambling, I simply referred to the plan and ended up promoting a team member who was identified as a clear successor.
This also helped me imagine my own exit, whether because of an accident or leaving voluntarily. We need to ask ourselves hard questions as founders, one of which is “how would my business carry on without me, and what would my team need to succeed?”
Document key processes, people, and passwords
Knowing who would step in once you’re gone isn’t the same as ensuring everything in your head, and those of your leaders, is documented for that person. When I took parental leave, I created a Notion CEO playbook that outlined all key processes and functions that I owned and that no one else had insight into, including tutorial videos, contact information, written explanations, and links (there’s a full breakdown of prepping for parental leave in this article I wrote for BetaKit). It was a brain dump of everything I owned, and I felt so much peace of mind after I shared it with our COO, who acted as CEO while I was on leave.
You should document:
- Key logins and passwords (I use 1Password and have a shared vault for many key accounts).
- Key contacts for lawyers, board members, or other stakeholders that leaders don’t interface with as often.
- Key accountabilities and priorities, with deadlines and/or cadence if applicable (for example, “send investor update every quarter” with instructions on how to do that).
- Clear access to key documents and artifacts.
This can feel overwhelming to build, so you can work with an ops team, executive assistant, or virtual assistant to compile everything. And unlike when I created mine in 2021, AI tools can support it as well, if you’re comfortable using them. I asked Claude how it could help me with my succession plan, and it suggested drafting the plan outline, prompting the questions that should be considered, and helping to fill in gaps from scanning my ongoing communications and documents. It then recommended setting up a scheduled task that would audit my email, Slack, and Notion on a regular basis to both identify key stakeholder relationships and how they’ve changed over time, and keep information up to date.
Consider key person insurance
When we raised our first round of institutional funding, one of the stipulations was that we take out a key person life insurance policy and critical illness insurance on me. This means that if I have to step away from the business due to an illness, or if I pass away, the business will receive a payout in order to help with continuity (paying a recruiter, supporting bereavement resources for the team, hiring external resources to support during a transition, or any other costs).
While this is usually required by investors, it’s important to consider for any founder and for any of your key executives. It’s inexpensive and ensures that your business will have the buffer to figure out what’s next.
Ensure your plans are in order
As a founder, your business is one of your key assets, and if you are ill, injured, incapacitated, or pass away, you want to ensure you have proper estate plans in place that allow the people you choose to manage your business.
For example, power of attorney documents name someone to manage your finances if you’re incapacitated, and this person can do anything related to your business that you can do, except for acting as the director of a corporation. This is especially important if you’re a consultant or sole proprietor and you don’t have staff who can step in to support.
When you pass away, a carry-on business clause in your will means the executor can act on your behalf related to the business: keeping it active, winding it down, selling it, or taking other actions. Your will also instructs how your business assets should pass on (unless you have shareholder documents that outline this already), and a dual will can also separate your business assets from your personal assets to reduce probate fees owing.
And, as a business owner, term life insurance can be an inexpensive way to ensure your family would have the funds they need to carry on in your absence.
Keep it current
Your succession plan needs to be reviewed regularly, not just after a key person exits or is promoted. This can be an annual to-do you complete around tax time or in the New Year. Remember, this plan only works if it’s current.
For me, succession planning hits close to home. At Willful, I see daily the impact of people who don’t put plans in place. And as someone who has also been on parental leave twice, I’ve seen firsthand the need to create structures that allow us to step away. As a former business coach said to me, it’s about being needed but not necessary to run your business. Ensure that playbook is in place for your business, so it doesn’t end up in the lurch like Nvidia.
The opinions and analysis expressed in the above article are those of its author, and do not necessarily reflect the position of BetaKit or its editorial staff. It has been edited for clarity, length, and style.

articles.title: Brasil x Tanzânia: onde assistir, horário e escalações do jogo da Copa do Mundo Sub-17
articles.text:
O Brasil enfrenta a Tanzânia nesta terça-feira (24), às 12h (de Brasília), pela segunda rodada do Grupo I da Copa do Mundo Sub-17. A partida será disputada na Aspire Zone, em Doha, no Catar. Depois de vencer a Irlanda na estreia, a Seleção Brasileira busca mais um resultado positivo para encaminhar a classificação à próxima fase.
- Competição: Copa do Mundo Sub-17
- Rodada: segunda rodada do Grupo I
- Data: terça-feira, 24 de novembro de 2026
- Horário: 12h (de Brasília)
- Local: Aspire Zone, em Doha, no Catar
Confira aqui a tabela com todos os jogos de hoje!
Onde assistir a Brasil x Tanzânia?
A partida entre Brasil e Tanzânia pela Copa do Mundo Sub-17 terá transmissão ao vivo pelo Sportv, na TV fechada, e pela CazéTV, no YouTube.
Prováveis escalações
- Brasil: Gabriel Werneck; Marcos Pesseti, Daniel Silva, Breno Sales e Richard Wendel; Leonardo Cerci, Eduardo Pape e Lucca Caramico; Eduardo Conceição, Kauê Furquim e Rodrigo Junior.
  - Técnico: Carlos Eduardo Patetuci.
- Tanzânia: Haji Abdalah; Kassim Juma, Hussein Hussein, Emmanuel Yusuph e Idrisa Kilendemo; Innocent Chole e Razaki Mbegelendi; Hamis Mihambo, Sadam Hamis e Luqman Mbalasalu; Faraji Kayanda.
  - Técnico: Elieneza Nsanganzelu.
As escalações confirmadas são divulgadas cerca de uma hora antes da partida.
Como chegam Brasil e Tanzânia para o jogo?
O Brasil estreou com vitória por 2 a 1 sobre a Irlanda e lidera o Grupo I, com três pontos. A equipe comandada por Carlos Eduardo Patetuci tenta manter os 100% de aproveitamento para ficar mais perto da classificação à próxima fase. Costa Rica e Tanzânia aparecem na sequência, com um ponto cada, enquanto a Irlanda está na última posição.
A Seleção encerrou a preparação para o confronto nesta segunda-feira (23), com um treino no Al Thumama, em Doha. A atividade teve exercícios de troca de passes e coordenação, trabalhos táticos de saída de bola, construção de jogadas e organização defensiva, além de ensaios de jogadas de bola parada.
A Tanzânia, por sua vez, empatou por 2 a 2 com a Costa Rica na primeira rodada. A equipe chegou a ficar dois gols atrás no placar, mas conseguiu buscar o empate e soma um ponto no Grupo I. O time ocupa a terceira posição da chave.
O principal destaque da seleção africana é o atacante Faraji Kayanda, autor dos dois gols contra a Costa Rica. Na mesma partida, o jogador também desperdiçou uma cobrança de pênalti.

articles.title: Uber now lets you book rides that record the drive by default
articles.text:
Uber is piloting a new feature in the U.S. that offers rides in which drivers have enabled the company’s recording feature, Record My Ride.
The option, which uses the front camera of the Uber driver’s phone to record the entire drive, will show up as “Recorded Rides” in the app.
The ride-hailing company is starting the pilot in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis, and St. Louis and will expand to more locations later.
Uber said it is testing recorded rides specifically for rides booked at late night or those involving teens. Earlier this year, it introduced a live video streaming feature for rides booked for teenagers. In another test, the company had enabled audio recording for late-night trips in some cities.
The company is also testing a feature that will turn on recording when the app detects the ride going off-course, or when the vehicle might have had an accident.
The company said drivers can opt out of recording through the Settings panel. Similarly, riders can also decline permission to record their rides via an in-app notification.

articles.title: Vale, Chris Dickman: Australian science grieves the loss of a giant of ecology and conservation
articles.text:
Australia has lost one of its most distinguished ecologists and conservation champions, Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman.
Chris’s achievements and legacy are vast, much like his beloved Simpson Desert that he and his research team – known as “the ratcatchers” – have studied for well over 30 years. He and his team would camp out under the stars, carefully trapping and monitoring the desert’s animals and plants.
Without Chris, we wouldn’t know just how important even small but ferocious predators are in structuring ecological communities. One example is the brush-tailed mulgara, which preys on and regulates numbers of other predators, including the lesser hairy-footed dunnart.
Chris touched many in both his personal and professional roles. The authors of this article each knew Chris for many years.
Chris was honoured in a celebratory forum and festschrift, a collection of written tributes, in June that was attended by about 200 people and another 140 online. He died on November 17, 2026.
Science and service
Chris’s impressive career was marked by a dedication to the scientific field and service to the wider community.
He was an internationally renowned leader in wildlife conservation who studied everything from the small marsupial Antechinus to dunnarts, long-haired rats, mulgaras, quolls, sandy inland and spinifex hopping mice and the Tasmanian devil, to name but a few species.
His work shed light on the remarkable lives these animals lead as well as the challenges they face, including feral cats and foxes. Chris was among the first to draw attention to the contentious issue of dingo management by bringing experts together for a scientific forum.
With Lily van Eeden, Chris also led a team of researchers who first estimated three billion animals had been affected by Australia’s 2019-20 bushfire crisis, garnering global attention.
A living legacy
What follows are our personal reflections about Chris. We hope they help convey who he was, both as a person and a professional.
Glenda Wardle
Professor of Ecology and Evolution, University of Sydney
Chris was a true intellect, polymath and gentleman of science. He welcomed me to the University of Sydney in 1995 and led by example in all aspects of academic life. It would be hard to find a better role model.
Over several decades we shared a commitment to discovering the ecological secrets of the red sand country of the Simpson Desert. We faced adversity in the field through floods, fires and flies, but would always smile and keep working.
I will miss the hilarious stories we shared around campfires with the many wonderful students and volunteers that joined our research efforts. Together, we would dig and delight in the way the desert came to life, particularly after big flooding rains. I will miss Chris’s writing, which was both edifying and entertaining. I will remember him when listening to the Simon and Garfunkel song, The Sounds of Silence.
Aaron Greenville
Senior Lecturer of Spatial Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, University of Sydney
It was 1998 and I was a young second-year zoology student. We had just finished a lecture that sounded like an in-person BBC wildlife documentary. The lecturer was Chris Dickman.
Soon after, Chris encouraged us students to join the Royal Zoological Society of New South Wales and I promptly signed up. Little did I know that moment would change my life.
His enthusiastic, kind and generous nature has supported many a student, colleague and friend. His door was always open, regardless of how busy he was. Chris’ passion for the Simpson Desert was contagious and persuaded many people, including myself, to make a trip to the desert year after year. Chris led by example, creating a supportive and caring environment that has ultimately shaped how I lead my own research and teaching programs.
Chris was a true gentleman scientist, mentor and friend. I will miss him greatly.
Euan Ritchie
Professor of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, Deakin University
As a young PhD student, I attended the 2003 annual scientific meeting of the Australian Mammal Society in Sydney. At the time, Chris Dickman was president of the society. I was instantly struck by a few of his qualities, which in the years since have greatly shaped my own career.
Chris and his team were diligently uncovering the dynamics of the mighty Simpson Desert. Their work underscored the importance of long-term, systematic monitoring of wildlife to documenting the complex lives of mulgaras, dunnarts, native rodents and other sand-dwelling denizens. This is no mean feat, especially in an environment as unpredictable and ever-changing as the Simpson.
Chris was also a master communicator. He spoke with such clarity and with his distinctly dulcet tone, both qualities that gave his science such impact.
Most notably, Chris was incredibly generous with his time. He would ask me about my research and was always genuinely interested in what I had to say. He made young scientists like myself feel like we belonged, particularly in academia where imposter syndrome is rife. His mentorship and kind, thoughtful and supportive nature has helped me and many others pursue careers in ecology and conservation. For this, we are all forever grateful.
Thomas Newsome
Associate Professor of Global Ecology, University of Sydney
I was so lucky to have Chris as a lecturer during my undergraduate studies at The University of Sydney.
I fondly remember my first field trip with Chris, which involved sampling small mammals in the ancient forests of Barrington Tops in New South Wales, also known as Dungog. My peers and I slid around in the mud, attempting to reach the sampling sites, and learnt about the history of the area and its inhabitants. These early experiences shaped me as an ecologist.
I also had the privilege of working with Chris as a masters and then PhD student. I would approach him with so many ideas, some better than others. Chris always listened but, in his own style, would gently guide me in the right direction and towards fascinating topics. In our time together, we asked and answered questions about dingoes in the Tanami, foxes and cats in the Simpson, wolves in the United States and scavengers in Australia.
I owe Chris so much for his time and support. And I will forever treasure the memories of our adventures, alongside an appreciation for his knowledge and kindness.
Vale, Chris, our dear friend, mentor and colleague.
We farewell Chris here with an excerpt from his forthcoming festschrift, a collection of reflections written in his honour:
For science at its very best is not a solitary quest — It helps us see, to care and to learn what we all share
Know that in the shimmering moonlight on a distant dune crest or beside a dry creek’s trace,
The scientist with the stellar moustache was listening, and learning, with patience, skill and grace.

articles.title: AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
articles.text:
The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint.
Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”
To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.
Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice).
With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever.
To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.
Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency.
“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event.
In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found.
To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation.
Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall.
“Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
“In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports.
Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. Douglas notes that by using the term “low-emission energy,” the pledge still leaves the door open for natural gas (which produces less carbon pollution than coal when burned but is a significant source of methane pollution) to keep powering data centers.
“The Antalya A.I. pledge is a step in the right direction to address an important piece of the impacts, but needs teeth in order to translate into stronger protections for people and the planet,” the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council said in a statement when the pledge was first announced. “The speed, scale and scope of this challenge is bigger than perhaps anything before it, and the guardrails must be commensurate.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang reprend la tête de NVIDIA, onze jours après avoir démissionné
articles.text:
NVIDIA avait mandaté un cabinet de recrutement pour trouver un successeur à Jensen Huang. Onze jours après sa démission, le groupe a choisi Jensen Huang.
Le conseil d’administration a officialisé son retour ce lundi 23 novembre. Le cofondateur reprend immédiatement ses fonctions de président et de directeur général et retrouve son siège au conseil. La décision a été prise à l’unanimité, après plusieurs réunions avec lui. Parmi les administrateurs qui ont voté son retour figure donc le président du conseil, Harvey C. Jones, qui l’écartait publiquement six jours plus tôt.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
De la démission à la campagne pour son retour
Pour comprendre le revirement, il faut remonter au début du mois. NVIDIA ouvre une enquête indépendante après des informations selon lesquelles son patron aurait été la cible d’une opération de renseignement étrangère. Comme on le rapportait alors sur Clubic, les révélations portent notamment sur une liaison avec une ancienne dirigeante d’une entreprise cliente de NVIDIA, soupçonnée par le renseignement américain de travailler pour Pékin. Le 10 novembre, les administrateurs indépendants annoncent avoir mandaté Joon H. Kim, ancien procureur fédéral par intérim à New York, et son cabinet. Deux jours plus tard, Huang démissionne après 33 ans à la tête de NVIDIA.
Les appels à le réintégrer suivent presque aussitôt. Des salariés, des investisseurs et des patrons de la tech se mobilisent. Parmi eux, Elon Musk et Tim Sweeney, le patron d’Epic Games. Deux investisseurs, Brad Gerstner et Gavin Baker, demandent au conseil de garder l’option d’un retour sur la table. Le 17 novembre, Huang se dit publiquement prêt à reprendre le poste si les administrateurs le lui demandent. Il renouvelle aussi ses excuses et promet de coopérer avec l’enquête.
Six jours plus tôt, NVIDIA cherchait encore son remplaçant
Ce même 17 novembre, lors d’une conférence avec les investisseurs, Harvey C. Jones écarte publiquement l’idée de réembaucher Huang. NVIDIA a confié la recherche d’un nouveau PDG à Heidrick & Struggles et se dit prêt à examiner des candidatures internes et externes. Le Financial Times rapporte même que le conseil a approché Rene Haas, le patron d’Arm. On sait désormais qui a décroché le poste.
Colette Kress, qui a pris la direction générale par intérim tout en gardant les finances, revient à ses seules fonctions de directrice financière. Harvey C. Jones reste président du conseil, une fonction créée au moment du départ de Huang et qu’il continuera d’exercer à ses côtés.
Washington a été consulté, l’enquête se poursuit
Sur ce qui a fait changer le conseil d’avis, le communiqué livre deux éléments : les administrateurs disent avoir été convaincus par la franchise de Huang et sa capacité à diriger le groupe après plusieurs entretiens avec lui. Ils indiquent aussi avoir reçu l’avis de hauts responsables américains, sur lequel ils s’appuient pour estimer que sa réintégration ne présente aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale. NVIDIA ne dit ni qui s’est prononcé, ni ce qui a été dit au conseil.
L’enquête confiée à Joon H. Kim et à son cabinet ira à son terme, assure NVIDIA. Huang s’engage à y coopérer et le groupe continuera de répondre aux autorités. Le conseil s’est par ailleurs doté d’un comité consacré à la sécurité nationale et au contrôle des exportations, et NVIDIA cherche un responsable de la conformité. Le recrutement du PDG aura finalement été le plus rapide des deux.

articles.title: Uber s’attaque à SNCF Connect : les trains débarquent dans l’application (avec de belles remises)
articles.text:
La SNCF a un nouveau concurrent de taille : Uber. Près de quinze ans après son arrivée à Paris, où son application de VTC a bousculé le transport en ville, Uber annonce le 24 novembre que la France sera le troisième pays à accueillir Uber Trains, après le Royaume-Uni et l’Espagne.
Dès le 30 novembre, il sera possible de rechercher, comparer et réserver ses billets de train directement depuis l’application Uber, sans frais de réservation. Nous avons pu essayer le service en avant-première : SNCF Connect et Trainline ont du souci à se faire, la super-app américaine veut tout renverser.
Uber intègre les trains avec des remises alléchantes
Habitué des codes promo et des opérations commerciales sur les courses VTC et sur Uber Eats, Uber reprend cette recette avec Uber Trains. Au lancement, chaque réservation de train éligible rapporte 10 % de son montant en crédits Uber. Le tout est ajouté au porte-monnaie Uber et permet de réserver une course, de commander à manger ou de se faire livrer ses courses.
Lors de notre essai, un aller-retour Paris-Nice du 2 au 5 décembre facturé 149 € donnait droit à 14,90 € de crédits. L’application précise que la somme arrive sur le compte après le voyage : la remise n’est pas auto-appliquée.
Uber présente l’offre comme une opération liée au lancement, sans donner de date de fin. L’application, elle, ne mentionne aucune durée et promet simplement « 10 % de crédit sur tous les billets de trains ». On peut imaginer que différentes opérations promotionnelles se succèderont : Uber sera agressif pour concurrencer la SNCF. Pour l’instant, Uber ne facture aucuns frais de réservation.
Uber attaque directement SNCF Connect et Trainline
Uber ne vend pas les billets lui-même. Le service repose sur Omio, une plateforme allemande de réservation qui alimente déjà Uber au Royaume-Uni depuis 2022 et en Espagne depuis 2024.
Uber promet un large catalogue (TGV INOUI, TER, Intercités, OUIGO, Eurostar, Trenitalia, Renfe, Lyria) et permet d’utiliser les avantages des programmes de fidélité. Les cartes de réduction SNCF, comme la carte Avantage, la carte Liberté ou la carte Famille nombreuse, se renseignent avant la recherche.
Comme Trainline, Uber combine plusieurs opérateurs dans un même itinéraire. Pour notre Paris-Nice, l’application proposait un trajet OUIGO avec une correspondance à 61,50 € (6 h 35), ou un itinéraire passant par un Frecciarossa de Trenitalia, avec deux correspondances, à 92 € (7 h 40). On choisit sa place avant de payer : c’est le même parcours que dans les autres apps, avec l’interface Uber.
Le principal atout d’Uber tient à sa base d’utilisateurs : pas de nouveau compte ni de nouvelle application : tout est déjà enregistré. Uber mise sur cet aspect et sur la colère de certains envers SNCF Connect pour faire monter son service en puissance.
Uber, une super-app de services façon WeChat ?
Dans son communiqué, Uber explique que l’on peut réserver un billet et « prévoir une course » pour rejoindre la gare ou se déplacer à l’arrivée, le tout « depuis une même application ». Un avantage technique par rapport aux autres apps : Uber se mue peu à peu en super-app capable de tout faire, avec plein de services différences. Dans d’autres pays, Uber expérimente même la réservation d’hôtels.
Dans cette logique, le train sert de produit d’appel. Chaque billet vendu génère un crédit qui ramène l’utilisateur vers une course ou une commande. Uber ne gagnera pas forcément d’argent avec les trains, mais habitue les utilisateurs à un écosystème de plus en plus complet.
