articles.title: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
articles.text:
Probing DNS at Cloudflare
Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.
This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.
DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.
For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.
A little background
At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.
We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.
What is Flamingo?
Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.
Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.
Being delightful
When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.
One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.
For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.
TEST test-redirect
SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com
GET "http://$(hostname)/"
ASSERT STATUS IS 301
ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"
Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.
Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.
In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:
pub enum Action {
  Query {
    method: String,
    url: Expression,
    parameters: Vec<http::QueryParameters>,
  },
  DnsQuery {
    query_name: Expression,
    query_type: Expression,
    parameters: Vec<dns::DnsQueryParameters>,
  },
}
pub enum ActionOutput {
  Http(http::FetchResponse),
  Dns(dns::QueryResponse),
}
pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc<
  dyn Fn(
      Action,
      Arc<Ctx>,
      InterpreterConfig,
    )
      -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<ActionOutput>>
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;
pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc<
  dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;
What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.
pub async fn query(
  action: Action,
  ctx: Arc<Ctx>,
  cfg: InterpreterConfig,
) -> Result<ActionOutput> {
  let Action::Query {
    method,
    url,
    parameters,
  } = action
  else {
    bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}");
  };
  ...
}
pub async fn execute_module<F>(
  ctx: Arc<Ctx>,
  cfg: &InterpreterConfig,
  handler_lut: F,
) -> Result<ActionOutput>
where
  F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction),
{
  let func = handler_lut(action);
  let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?;
  ...
}
Using Flamingo to probe DNS
The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.
DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.
We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.
To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).
TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62
MOD dns
SET $hostname "some.probe.domain"
SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com
QUERY $hostname TXT
TARGET $authNs
ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR
ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA
ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")
Catching bugs (SLO and steady)
To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.
By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.
Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.
Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.
The road ahead
By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.
DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.
If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

articles.title: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension
articles.text:
As datasets grow, analytical queries can take longer to run, slowing down data exploration, pipelines, and applications. For developers using DuckDB, reducing query times helps keep analytics responsive and can lower compute costs.
NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release Sirius as a DuckDB core extension, bringing GPU acceleration to DuckDB’s analytical query engine. With two SQL commands, you can install and load Sirius to accelerate supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without rewriting your SQL or changing database schemas.
Sirius, developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine.
This post introduces the core extension, shows you how to run your first GPU query, and explains how Sirius integrates with DuckDB.
Accelerate DuckDB queries without rewriting SQL
Sirius accelerates supported queries as a whole. DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU. The core extension brings this capability into DuckDB’s standard workflow: install Sirius, load it, and run your queries.
With this release, you can:
- Install directly from DuckDB. Use INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius; to download and activate the extension.
- Retain familiar SQL. Execute supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without translating them into a separate GPU programming API.
- Use CPU fallback. Queries with unsupported features fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine.
Start with a small example, then apply the same workflow to your own analytical queries.
Run your first GPU query
You’ll need DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver.
Create a sample dataset
Open DuckDB with a file-backed database.
duckdb getting_started.duckdb
Use DuckDB’s TPC-H extension to generate a small analytical dataset for this example.
INSTALL tpch;
LOAD tpch;
CALL dbgen(sf=0.01);
CHECKPOINT;
The TPC-H extension creates the example tables, including lineitem, which contains order line items. It supplies sample data for this walkthrough and is separate from the Sirius extension.
The CHECKPOINT statement persists the generated data so Sirius can read the native DuckDB tables.
Install and load Sirius
In the same DuckDB session, install and load Sirius.
-- Sirius is approximately 700 MB; download time depends on your connection.
INSTALL sirius;
LOAD sirius;
The core extension automatically selects the CUDA backend for your driver. INSTALL downloads the extension, and LOAD activates it in the current connection.
Run an analytical query
With Sirius loaded, run the following SQL query.
SELECT
    l_returnflag,
    SUM(l_quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM lineitem
GROUP BY l_returnflag
ORDER BY l_returnflag;
This query groups line items by return flag and calculates the total quantity for each group. Supported queries execute on the GPU while retaining the same SQL syntax used with DuckDB.
The query returns:
l_returnflag  total_quantity
A                 380456.00
N                 774222.00
R                 381449.00
You now have a complete workflow: create data, load the extension, and execute an analytical query. The small dataset keeps setup quick and illustrates how to use Sirius; it is not intended to demonstrate a performance advantage.
Use the same approach with your own DuckDB tables or supported Parquet workflows. Queries with unsupported features automatically fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine.
Understand how Sirius executes queries
Sirius integrates GPU execution into DuckDB’s query-processing workflow. DuckDB remains the application’s SQL interface and handles query parsing and optimization. Sirius executes supported queries on the GPU and returns results through the same connection.
This integration lets developers continue expressing analytical operations in SQL while using GPU parallelism for supported workloads. The application receives query results through DuckDB, preserving the interface used by existing scripts and applications.
Compare Sirius GPU and DuckDB CPU benchmark results
We evaluated Sirius against CPU-based DuckDB using cold runs of queries derived from the TPC-H benchmark, with data stored in Amazon S3. Tests covered scale factors 100 (100 GB), 1,000 (1 TB), 3,000 (3 TB), and 10,000 (10 TB), measuring total query runtime and query-time compute cost under default and tuned settings. These tests used pinned development builds. Sirius timings exclude result fetch/export, while DuckDB timings include CSV output. Query-time compute costs cover measured instance runtime and exclude startup, validation, storage, S3, and idle time.
With tuned settings, Sirius running on AWS instances with two NVIDIA GPUs delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations. At SF1K, total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds. At SF3K, runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, delivering a 4.69x speedup. Query-time compute cost at SF3K also decreased by approximately 71%.
The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K. The tuned two-GPU configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds compared with 2,369.4 seconds for the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configuration. This represents a 3.25x speedup and approximately 79% lower query-time compute cost.
The results also show how workload size affects configuration choices. At SF100, one GPU offered the lowest cost, while two GPUs delivered the shortest runtime. At SF10K, the tuned two-GPU configuration outperformed the tuned single-GPU configuration in both runtime and cost. Tuning was particularly important at this scale: at SF10K, the default configuration with two GPUs was marked “did not finish,” while the tuned configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds.
The Sirius repository provides a benchmark runner, query definitions, configuration details, and setup instructions for reviewing the test setup and evaluating performance on your own hardware. Results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions.
Get started with Sirius
The Sirius core extension brings GPU-accelerated analytics into DuckDB’s familiar SQL workflow. Install the extension, run the example, and explore how GPU execution applies to your data.
As your data grows, use Sirius to accelerate supported queries while keeping your SQL, tools, and workflow in DuckDB. Share your results and feedback with the Sirius community.

articles.title: Merry Making: Play, Build and Create With NVIDIA Technologies This Holiday Season
articles.text:
The elves don’t have to be the only ones busy in the workshop this holiday season. With the lights twinkling and the gift wrap out, it’s the perfect time to give someone — or yourself — a spark to take a hobby to the next level.
For some, that means diving into a new game. For others, it’s video editing or even building a robot.
NVIDIA technologies offer something for everyone on Santa’s list. Read on to unwrap the details.
Make Time for One More Game
With the holiday break here, everyone can be online to score bragging rights or explore a world that’s only been seen in video game trailers.
For some players, an upgrade means a desktop that brings out the detail in every scene. For others, it’s a laptop they can take along when visiting family, or a way to play in the cloud on a device they already own.
The right setup depends on where and what to play:
- GeForce RTX 50 Series laptops and desktops power the action. Built on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, they feature fifth-generation Tensor Cores and fourth-generation RT Cores for AI-enhanced graphics, detailed ray-traced worlds and high frames-per-second gaming.
- NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs combine RTX graphics with NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform on a single superchip, bringing decades of NVIDIA innovation to slim, premium laptops and compact desktops on the familiar Windows platform. One PC can handle every workflow, from accelerated creation and immersive gaming to powerful local AI — with a variety of designs and all-day battery life.
- See games in a new light with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology, which boosts performance and enhances image quality. The newest feature, DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, infuses scenes with lifelike lighting and materials in supported games. Get a glimpse of NBA 2K27 with DLSS 5.
- NVIDIA Reflex and G-SYNC make gameplay more responsive and fluid. Reflex reduces system latency in supported games, while G-SYNC displays use variable refresh rates to deliver smooth, tear-free gaming.
- The GeForce NOW cloud gaming service enables playing top titles anywhere. Stream supported games on compatible laptops, TVs, handhelds and more. Connect to supported game stores to play owned PC games, with more than 4,500 titles available across the service.
Make Something Worth Sharing
For creators with a project that’s been on the backburner, the right gift this season can be the push to finally make it happen. Maybe it’s holiday clips becoming a short film, a snowy scene coming together in 3D or a livestream that brings friends across time zones to the same virtual table. Creators can use NVIDIA systems — such as GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX Spark devices — to keep up with the workflows, along with NVIDIA Studio tools and technologies for AI acceleration.
Studio Drivers support video editing, 3D design and livestreaming. In supported applications, faster processing gives more room to experiment and refine.
Build a Robot That Thinks
Every robot starts somewhere. This season, it could be under the tree.
Building a robot is an experiment in teaching a device to see or sense its surroundings. A first project might be as simple as using a camera to identify a candy cane or a gingerbread man, then moving on to an app that probes what the camera sees.
Testing brings new questions. Can the robot recognize the candy cane under twinkling lights? Can it tell a frosted gingerbread man from an unfrosted one? Each experiment leaves more to improve and explore.
The NVIDIA Jetson edge AI platform provides the hardware and software to build projects like these. It combines compact computers with the NVIDIA JetPack software development kit to help makers build robots, autonomous machines and intelligent devices.
A Jetson Developer Kit is a gift to explore computer vision, generative AI and multimodal robot control, with the option to add cameras and sensors suited to various projects. AI runs directly on the device, processing information from its surroundings. When ready to take a prototype further, production systems powered by Jetson modules provide a path to deployment.
See how Microduck comes to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super, bringing together robot movement, visual understanding and natural-language interaction. With Hermes Agent and NVIDIA Cosmos, developers can explore how AI connects everyday requests with actions in the physical world.
Bring an SO-101 arm to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin and explore agentic robotics. Give OpenClaw a simple request, and watch it plan the steps, call NVIDIA tools and check the results. OpenShell runs the agent securely in a sandbox, controlling its access to models and robot tools. Based on ASPIRE skills, the system reuses lessons from past attempts to guide future tasks.
Build a robot companion that chats, moves and understands what it sees, with NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Cosmos open models running locally on Jetson Orin Nano 8GB.
For more advanced projects, explore vision language action models and world action models to enable increasingly sophisticated robotic behaviors — beyond simple perception and predefined actions toward understanding natural language instructions, reasoning, planning multistep tasks and interacting with the physical world.
Dive into setup guides and project tutorials in Jetson AI Lab.
Whether it’s a gaming upgrade, a creative project or a first robot, the right tools can open up new possibilities well beyond the holidays.
Explore NVIDIA’s holiday lineup for gamers, creators and makers.
